# Technical Specification

# 1. Introduction

## 1.1 Executive Summary

This repository contains **`schedule`**, an open-source Python library that provides in-process periodic job scheduling with a deliberately human-readable, fluent configuration API. The version under documentation is **1.2.2**, declared in `setup.py` (`SCHEDULE_VERSION = "1.2.2"`) and mirrored in the Sphinx documentation configuration `docs/conf.py`. The distribution is published to PyPI as `schedule` and its documentation is hosted at `schedule.readthedocs.io`, both linked from `pyproject.toml` under `[project.urls]`.

The product is intentionally narrow in surface area. The entire runtime implementation is a single module, `schedule/__init__.py` (945 lines), accompanied by a PEP 561 marker file `schedule/py.typed`. Its self-description in the module docstring is precise: *an in-process scheduler for periodic jobs that uses the builder pattern for configuration*, letting callers run Python functions — or any other callable — at pre-determined intervals using a human-friendly syntax. `setup.py` classifies the package as `Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable`, `Operating System :: OS Independent`, and `Intended Audience :: Developers`.

### 1.1.2 Core Problem Addressed

The problem the library targets is stated directly in `docs/index.rst`: it is *"designed to be a simple solution for simple scheduling problems."* Developers who need a function to run every ten minutes, every hour, or every Wednesday at 13:15 have historically had two unattractive options — delegate to operating-system facilities such as cron (which requires external process management, separate deployment artifacts, and an opaque crontab syntax), or adopt a full distributed task framework (which requires brokers, workers, and additional operational surface). `schedule` removes both burdens for the simple case by keeping the schedule *inside the application process*: `README.rst` states the design goal as an "In-process scheduler for periodic jobs. No extra processes needed!"

The friction being eliminated is expressed concretely by the project's own lineage. Both `README.rst` and the module docstring credit Adam Wiggins' article *"Rethinking Cron"* and the `clockwork` Ruby module as the direct inspirations, and `setup.py` lists `cron` and `clockwork` among the package keywords — positioning the library as an in-language alternative to externalized cron-style scheduling rather than a replacement for distributed schedulers.

The resulting solution shape is a two-line integration: register jobs with a readable expression chain, then drive the scheduler from the host application's own loop. The canonical form documented in `README.rst` and `docs/index.rst` is:

```python
schedule.every().day.at("10:30").do(job)
while True:
    schedule.run_pending(); time.sleep(1)
```

### 1.1.4 Value Proposition

The value the repository actually delivers is verifiable from its own artifacts rather than asserted. Five properties dominate:

| Value driver | Substantiation in the repository |
|---|---|
| Zero required dependencies | `pyproject.toml` declares `dependencies = []`; `schedule/__init__.py` imports only standard-library modules (`datetime`, `functools`, `logging`, `random`, `re`, `time`, `typing`, `collections.abc`) |
| Zero additional infrastructure | Jobs execute inside the caller's own process and loop; `README.rst` — "No extra processes needed!" |
| Readability as a first-class goal | Fluent builder chain (`every(5).to(10).minutes`, `every().wednesday.at("13:15")`) implemented via chained properties in `schedule/__init__.py` lines 325–455 |
| Low adoption and exit cost | `docs/installation.rst` notes the library "consists of a single sourcefile MIT licenced" and can even be vendored manually; `LICENSE.txt` grants unrestricted MIT use |
| Type-safe, quality-gated delivery | `schedule/py.typed` ships type information (added in 1.2.0 per `HISTORY.rst`); `setup.cfg` configures mypy over the package; `.github/workflows/ci.yml` enforces tests, coverage, docs, formatting, and packaging checks on every push and pull request |

The business impact is therefore best characterized as **reduced operational and cognitive overhead for periodic in-process work**: no broker to provision, no external scheduler to synchronize with deployments, no dependency-tree expansion, and an API whose expressions read as English. The corollary — equally important and equally explicit in `docs/index.rst` — is that the library deliberately does not compete on persistence, sub-second precision, concurrency, or calendar localization; those trade-offs are documented in §1.3.2.


## 1.2 System Overview

### 1.2.1 Project Context

#### 1.2.1.1 Business Context and Market Positioning

`schedule` occupies a deliberately narrow position in the Python scheduling landscape, and the repository documents that position explicitly rather than leaving it to inference. `docs/index.rst` opens its non-goals section with the statement that Schedule is *not a 'one size fits all' scheduling library* and that it is *designed to be a simple solution for simple scheduling problems*.

The positioning is defined along three axes that are all traceable to repository artifacts:

| Positioning axis | Stated stance | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Execution locality | In-process scheduler — "No extra processes needed!" | `README.rst`, module docstring in `schedule/__init__.py` |
| Dependency posture | "Very lightweight and no external dependencies"; `dependencies = []` | `README.rst`, `pyproject.toml` |
| Ergonomics | "A simple to use API for scheduling jobs, made for humans" | `README.rst`, `docs/index.rst` |

Market lineage is equally explicit. The module docstring and `README.rst` both credit Adam Wiggins' article *"Rethinking Cron"* and the `clockwork` Ruby module as the design inspirations, and `setup.py` carries `cron` and `clockwork` in its keyword list. The library is therefore positioned as an *in-language alternative to cron-style externalized scheduling* for simple periodic work — not as a competitor to distributed task frameworks. Where distributed execution is genuinely needed, `docs/parallel-execution.rst` points users outward, noting that the queue-based pattern it demonstrates "also makes sense for a distributed application where the workers are separate processes that receive jobs from a distributed work queue."

Distribution reach reinforces the positioning: `pip install schedule` is the preferred channel per `docs/installation.rst`, but the same document records availability through Ubuntu/Debian (`python3-schedule`), Arch AUR (`python-schedule`), and conda-forge — while explicitly warning that these packages "are not maintained by the maintainers of this project" and that the Ubuntu/Debian packages are **OUTDATED** (0.3.2, from 2015, at the time of writing).

#### 1.2.1.2 Current System Limitations

This repository is not a replacement for or an upgrade of a predecessor system; it is a mature standalone library with a continuous 23-release history from 0.1.0 (2013-05-19) to 1.2.2 (2024-05-25) recorded in `HISTORY.rst`. Consequently, "current system limitations" are best read as the *documented behavioral limits of the library itself*, which the project publishes candidly in `docs/index.rst` and its companion pages:

| Limitation | Documented behavior | Source |
|---|---|---|
| No job persistence | The schedule is not remembered between restarts | `docs/index.rst` |
| No sub-second precision | Exact timing is out of scope | `docs/index.rst` |
| Serial execution only | "By default, schedule executes all jobs serially" | `docs/parallel-execution.rst` |
| No built-in background mode | "Out of the box it is not possible to run the schedule in the background" | `docs/background-execution.rst` |
| No calendar localization | Workdays and holidays are not modeled | `docs/index.rst` |
| Job duration is ignored | "Schedule does not account for the time it takes for the job function to execute" | `docs/index.rst` |
| Missed runs are not replayed | Intended behavior: a per-minute job driven hourly runs once, not 60 times | `schedule/__init__.py` `Scheduler.run_pending` docstring (lines 89–98) |
| Exceptions are not caught | Job exceptions "bubble up and interrupt schedule's `run_xyz` function" | `docs/exception-handling.rst` |
| Naive datetime storage | All internal datetimes are naive, so `next_run`/`last_run` are always in Python's local timezone | `docs/timezones.rst` |
| DST ignored without a timezone | Timezone-unaware jobs use naive local time; a 4-hour job may fire after 3 real hours when DST starts | `docs/timezones.rst` |

Two of these limits are architecturally load-bearing rather than incidental. First, the naive-datetime contract is preserved *on purpose*: `_schedule_next_run()` in `schedule/__init__.py` (lines 740–748) converts a timezone-aware computation back to local time and strips `tzinfo`, with an inline comment stating the goal is to keep the API consistent with older versions and remain backwards compatible. Second, serial execution is a considered choice — `docs/parallel-execution.rst` explains the reasoning as the difficulty of "find[ing] a model for parallel execution that makes everyone happy."

#### 1.2.1.3 Integration with the Existing Enterprise Landscape

The library integrates by *embedding*, not by deploying. There is no server, daemon, CLI entry point, or network listener anywhere in the package: `schedule/__init__.py` imports only `collections.abc`, `datetime`, `functools`, `logging`, `random`, `re`, `time`, and `typing`, and contains no socket, subprocess, filesystem, or serialization calls. Integration surfaces are therefore all inside the host application:

| Integration surface | Mechanism | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Host control loop | Caller invokes `run_pending()` on its own cadence; `idle_seconds()` allows sleeping exactly until the next due job | `docs/examples.rst`, `schedule/__init__.py` lines 89–101, 197–206 |
| Threaded / background operation | Caller supplies a `threading.Thread` + `threading.Event` wrapper around `run_pending()` | `docs/background-execution.rst` |
| Parallelism and worker pools | Caller registers `run_threaded(job_func)` or `jobqueue.put` as the job so a `queue.Queue` worker executes the real work | `docs/parallel-execution.rst` |
| Observability | Library emits `DEBUG` records to the standard logger named `schedule` | `docs/logging.rst`, `schedule/__init__.py` line 50 |
| Error handling policy | Caller wraps job functions (e.g. a `catch_exceptions` decorator that may return `schedule.CancelJob`) | `docs/exception-handling.rst` |
| Multi-tenant scheduling | Multiple independent `schedule.Scheduler()` instances are supported; each requires its own `run_pending()` call | `docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` |
| Timezone data | `pytz` imported lazily inside `Job.at()` only when a `tz` argument is passed | `schedule/__init__.py` lines 498–508; `docs/timezones.rst` |
| Type tooling | PEP 561 `py.typed` marker shipped via `package_data`; mypy configured over the package | `setup.py`, `schedule/py.typed`, `setup.cfg` |

#### 1.2.2.2 Major System Components

The runtime is a single module containing six top-level classes and eleven top-level functions (nine public, two private helpers).

| Component | Responsibility | Location |
|---|---|---|
| `Scheduler` | Job factory, registry (`self.jobs`), and synchronous executor; owns `run_pending`, `run_all`, `get_jobs`, `clear`, `cancel_job`, `next_run`, `idle_seconds` | lines 79–206 |
| `Job` | Mutable fluent builder holding interval, unit, `at_time`, `at_time_zone`, `start_day`, `latest`, `cancel_after`, `tags`, `last_run`, `next_run`; computes the next occurrence and executes the bound callable | lines 209–830 |
| `CancelJob` | Sentinel class a job may return to unschedule itself; recognized as either class or instance | lines 71–76, 172–175 |
| Exception hierarchy | `ScheduleError` → `ScheduleValueError` → `IntervalError` for configuration and validation faults | lines 53–68 |
| Module-level facade | `default_scheduler`, the `jobs` alias, and eight delegating shortcut functions plus the `repeat` decorator factory | lines 833–913 |
| Private helpers | `_move_to_next_weekday`, `_weekday_index`, `_move_to_at_time`, `_correct_utc_offset`, `_is_overdue`, `_decode_datetimestr` | lines 750–830, 916–945 |
| `logger` | Single `logging.getLogger("schedule")` instance used for all DEBUG diagnostics | line 50 |

#### 1.2.2.3 Core Technical Approach

The design rests on five decisions that are visible directly in `schedule/__init__.py`:

1. **Builder pattern for configuration.** The module docstring names the pattern explicitly. `Scheduler.every()` returns an *unconfigured* `Job`; each unit and weekday accessor is a property that mutates `self` and returns `self`, so `every(5).to(10).minutes` reads as prose while remaining a single mutable object. Registration is deferred to `do()`, which binds the callable, computes the first `next_run`, and only then appends the job to `scheduler.jobs` — meaning an incomplete chain never pollutes the registry.
2. **Fail-fast validation with a typed error hierarchy.** Singular accessors raise `IntervalError` when the interval is not 1 (`"Use seconds instead of second"`); weekday accessors reject intervals of 2 or more weeks; `at()` validates format with unit-specific regular expressions; `_schedule_next_run()` rejects unknown units; `until()` rejects past deadlines and unsupported types; `_weekday_index()` rejects unknown day names.
3. **Synchronous, ordered, best-effort execution.** `run_pending()` filters on `job.should_run` (`now >= next_run`) and executes the survivors in `sorted()` order — ordering made possible by `Job.__lt__` comparing `next_run`. Execution is single-threaded and in-line with the caller; missed occurrences are intentionally not replayed.
4. **Naive-local time as the public contract, with timezone math internal.** `_schedule_next_run()` performs its arithmetic in the requested timezone when one is present, applies `_move_to_at_time()` and `_correct_utc_offset()`, then converts back and strips `tzinfo` so `next_run` remains naive local — explicitly to preserve backwards compatibility. `_correct_utc_offset()` compares the UTC offset before and after normalization, shifts the moment to preserve the requested wall-clock time, and, when the requested time falls into a DST gap, schedules one offset later as a documented best effort.
5. **Optional dependency isolation.** `pytz` is imported *inside* `Job.at()` and only when a `tz` argument is supplied, which is what allows `pyproject.toml` to declare an empty `dependencies` list while still offering a `timezone` extra. `tox.ini` proves the contract by running every supported Python version both with and without `pytz` installed.

Cancellation is expressed through two complementary paths: a job may return `CancelJob` (or the class itself) and `Scheduler._run_job()` will unschedule it, or a deadline set with `until()` causes `Job.run()` to return `CancelJob` — before execution if already overdue, and after execution if the newly computed `next_run` exceeds the deadline, in which case cancellation takes priority over the job's own return value.

### 1.2.3 Success Criteria

The repository does not publish business SLAs, uptime targets, or adoption KPIs; no such artifact exists in the tree. The criteria below are therefore stated as the objectives the project *itself* verifies, every one of which is mechanically enforced by `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and `tox.ini` on every push and pull request against `master`, or is directly measurable from the source.

## 1.3 Scope

### 1.3.1 In-Scope

#### 1.3.1.1 Core Features and Functionalities

**Must-have capabilities.** The following are implemented in `schedule/__init__.py` and are the load-bearing obligations of the library. Each is exercised by `test_schedule.py` and documented under `docs/`.

| Must-have capability | Definition of the delivered behavior |
|---|---|
| Interval scheduling | `every(n)` combined with `seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`, `days`, `weeks` (and singular aliases valid only when `n == 1`) |
| Weekday scheduling | `monday` through `sunday`, restricted to a weekly interval; `_move_to_next_weekday` advances to the nearest matching day without moving if already on it |
| Clock-time anchoring | `at()` with unit-aware validated formats: `HH:MM(:SS)` daily, `(MM):SS` hourly, `:SS` minutely |
| Timezone-aware anchoring | `at(time, tz)` accepting an IANA string or a `pytz` timezone object, with DST-correct next-run computation |
| Randomized intervals | `to(latest)` producing an inclusive random interval between `interval` and `latest` |
| Deadline enforcement | `until()` accepting `datetime`, `timedelta`, `time`, or one of five string formats; the job never runs past its deadline |
| Callable binding | `do(func, *args, **kwargs)` binding any callable with positional and keyword arguments |
| Decorator registration | `@repeat(every(...).unit)` registering a function while returning it unmodified |
| Job lifecycle management | `tag`, `get_jobs`, `clear`, `cancel_job`, and the `CancelJob` self-unschedule sentinel |
| Execution entry points | `run_pending()` for due jobs in next-run order and `run_all(delay_seconds)` for forced execution |
| Introspection | `next_run` (globally or per tag), `idle_seconds`, and human-readable `__str__` / `__repr__` |
| Multiple schedulers | Independent `Scheduler()` instances alongside the module-level `default_scheduler` |
| Structured diagnostics | DEBUG-level records on the `schedule` logger for run, cancel, and clear operations |
| Distributed type information | PEP 561 `py.typed` marker plus inline annotations across the public surface |

**Primary user workflows.** `docs/examples.rst` catalogues fourteen supported workflows; these constitute the contractual usage surface of the library.

| Workflow | Entry point |
|---|---|
| Run a job on a recurring interval or weekday-at-time | `every(...).<unit>[.at(...)].do(job)` |
| Register a job declaratively via decorator | `@repeat(every(10).minutes)` |
| Pass positional/keyword arguments to a job | `do(job, name="Peter")` |
| Cancel one specific job | `schedule.cancel_job(job)` |
| Run a job exactly once | job returns `schedule.CancelJob` |
| Enumerate all scheduled jobs | `schedule.get_jobs()` |
| Cancel every scheduled job | `schedule.clear()` |
| Select or cancel a group of jobs by identifier | `get_jobs("friend")`, `clear("daily-tasks")` |
| Run at randomized intervals | `every(5).to(10).minutes` |
| Bound a job with a deadline | `until("18:30")`, `until(timedelta(hours=8))`, `until(datetime(...))` |
| Sleep precisely until the next due job | `idle_seconds()` (negative if overdue, `None` if idle) |
| Force-run everything, optionally spaced | `run_all()`, `run_all(delay_seconds=10)` |
| Schedule in a foreign timezone | `at("10:30", "America/New_York")` |
| Drive the scheduler continuously | `while True: run_pending(); sleep(1)` |

**Essential integrations.** In scope are exactly four integration contracts, all of which are consumer-side:

1. **The Python standard library** — `datetime`, `time`, `random`, `re`, `functools`, `logging`, `collections.abc`, and `typing` are the only imports in the runtime module.
2. **`pytz`, optionally and lazily** — imported inside `Job.at()` only when a timezone is supplied; declared as the `timezone` extra in `pyproject.toml` and validated by the `-pytz` tox environments.
3. **The `schedule` standard logger** — a single `logging.getLogger("schedule")` instance; consumers attach their own handlers and levels as shown in `docs/logging.rst`.
4. **Packaging and distribution toolchain** — setuptools ≥ 61 build backend (`pyproject.toml`), wheel build and twine upload to TestPyPI then PyPI (`docs/development.rst`), with `MANIFEST.in` controlling sdist contents (`README.rst`, `HISTORY.rst`, `LICENSE.txt`, `test_schedule.py`).

**Key technical requirements.**

| Requirement | Specification |
|---|---|
| Interpreter floor | `python_requires = ">=3.7"` in `setup.py`; `requires-python = ">= 3.7"` in `pyproject.toml` |
| Verified interpreters | 3.7, 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12 in the CI matrix |
| Platform neutrality | `Operating System :: OS Independent` classifier; CI executes on `ubuntu-latest` |
| Dependency budget | Zero required; one optional (`pytz`) |
| Type checking | `mypy -p schedule` must pass in every tox environment |
| Formatting | `black --check .` with black pinned to `20.8b1` |
| Documentation build | `sphinx-build -W` (warnings as errors), alabaster theme |
| Packaging metadata | `setup.py check --strict --metadata --restructuredtext` must pass |
| Versioning policy | Semantic versioning, per `docs/development.rst` |
| License | MIT (`LICENSE.txt`) |

#### 1.3.1.2 Implementation Boundaries

**System boundaries.** The library's boundary is the process boundary of the *host application*. Everything the package does happens between a call to `every()` and the return of `run_pending()`/`run_all()`; it owns no thread, no process, no port, and no file.

| Boundary dimension | Inside the boundary | Outside the boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Process model | Objects living in the caller's process; execution driven by the caller | Any daemon, service, or supervisor |
| Concurrency | Serial, in-line execution on the calling thread | Thread/process pools, event loops — supplied by the caller |
| State | In-memory `Scheduler.jobs` list | Any datastore, file, or cache |
| Time source | `datetime.datetime.now()` and, when requested, a `pytz` zone | NTP, external clock services |
| Failure handling | Configuration validation errors raised eagerly | Runtime job exceptions, which propagate to the caller |
| Interfaces | Python function/property calls only | HTTP, RPC, CLI, message brokers |

**User groups covered.** The audience is Python developers embedding the scheduler in their own code — `setup.py` declares `Intended Audience :: Developers` and there is no end-user interface of any kind in the repository. Within that audience, three distinct consumer profiles are served by explicit documentation: single-schedule application authors (`docs/examples.rst`), larger installations needing several independent schedulers (`docs/multiple-schedulers.rst`), and contributors to the library itself (`docs/development.rst`). Deliverables for all three — source, tests, docs, CI, and packaging metadata — are in scope for this repository.

**Geographic and market coverage.**

| Dimension | Coverage in scope |
|---|---|
| Platform reach | OS-independent Python package; validated on Linux runners in CI |
| Distribution reach | PyPI (primary), with documented third-party availability on Ubuntu/Debian, Arch AUR, and conda-forge — the latter explicitly not maintained by this project |
| Timezone reach | Any zone resolvable by `pytz`; 15 distinct IANA zones spanning the Americas, Europe, Asia, and Oceania are exercised in `test_schedule.py`, including quarter-hour offsets such as `Asia/Kathmandu` and the Chatham rule |
| Natural language | English only (`Natural Language :: English` classifier); documentation is English-only reStructuredText |
| Calendar/regional rules | Timezone offsets and DST transitions only |

**Data domains included.** The library handles exactly one data domain: *scheduling metadata held in memory for the lifetime of the process.* Per `Job.__init__`, this comprises `interval`, `latest`, `unit`, `at_time`, `at_time_zone`, `start_day`, `cancel_after`, `tags`, `last_run`, `next_run`, the owning `scheduler` reference, and `job_func` — a `functools.partial` that retains references to the callable and any arguments the caller bound. No business, personal, or persisted data is modeled, read, written, or transmitted anywhere in the package.

### 1.3.2 Out-of-Scope

#### 1.3.2.1 Explicitly Excluded Features and Capabilities

`docs/index.rst` devotes a dedicated section — "When **not** to use Schedule" — to naming the exclusions, making these authoritative rather than inferred. The table below pairs each published exclusion with the corroborating evidence found in the source.

| Excluded capability | Published position | Corroboration in source |
|---|---|---|
| Job persistence across restarts | Look elsewhere if you need the schedule remembered between restarts | No file, database, or serialization call exists in `schedule/__init__.py`; state is a plain in-memory list |
| Sub-second / exact timing | Look elsewhere if you need sub-second precision | `should_run` is a coarse `now >= next_run` comparison evaluated only when the caller polls |
| Concurrent execution | Look elsewhere if you need multiple threads | No threading, locking, or async construct appears anywhere in the module; `run_pending` is a serial loop |
| Localization of workdays/holidays | Look elsewhere if you need workday or holiday awareness | Only weekday names and timezone offsets are modeled |
| Accounting for job duration | "Schedule does not account for the time it takes for the job function to execute" | `run()` sets `last_run` then reschedules from the current moment |
| Built-in background operation | "Out of the box it is not possible to run the schedule in the background" | No thread is ever created by the library |
| Catching job exceptions | "Schedule doesn't catch exceptions that happen during job execution" | `Job.run()` invokes `job_func()` with no `try`/`except` |
| Replaying missed runs | Intended behavior that `run_pending()` does not run missed jobs | Docstring at `schedule/__init__.py` lines 89–98 |
| Timezone-aware public datetimes | All internal datetimes are naive; `next_run`/`last_run` are always local | `_schedule_next_run()` strips `tzinfo` for backwards compatibility (lines 740–748) |
| DST awareness without a timezone | Timezone-unaware jobs do not take clock changes into account | `at_time_zone is None` short-circuits `_correct_utc_offset` |
| Timezones outside `at()` | "Timezones are only available in the `.at` function" | `tz` is a parameter of `Job.at()` alone |
| `@repeat` on instance methods | "The `@repeat` decorator does not work on non-static class methods" | `docs/examples.rst` |
| Weekday selection on multi-week intervals | Using `.monday()` on a job scheduled every 2 or more weeks "is not supported" | `IntervalError` raised in each weekday property (lines 380–455) |
| Non-English localization | English-only classifier and documentation | `setup.py`, `docs/` |

Also outside the delivered artifact set: there is no CLI, no configuration file format, no admin or web interface, no authentication or authorization concept, no metrics/tracing exporter, no health endpoint, and no containerization or deployment manifest anywhere in the repository. `.github/` contains a single file, `workflows/ci.yml` — there are no issue templates, contributor guides, or code-of-conduct documents; contributor guidance lives instead in `docs/development.rst`.

#### 1.3.2.2 Future Phase Considerations

The repository contains **no roadmap, backlog, or planning document**; forward-looking intent must therefore be read from the two markers that do exist and from the trajectory recorded in `HISTORY.rst`.

| Forward-looking signal | Observation |
|---|---|
| Open design question in source | `schedule/__init__.py` line 840: the module-level `jobs` alias carries an inline `todo` asking whether it should be a copy (e.g. `jobs()`) instead of a live reference to `default_scheduler.jobs` |
| Documentation TODO rendering enabled | `docs/conf.py` sets `todo_include_todos = True` with `sphinx.ext.todo` loaded, so any future `todo` directives will surface in published docs |
| Interpreter support cadence | `HISTORY.rst` shows an established add-new/drop-old rhythm: 1.0.0 dropped Python 2.7 and 3.5 while adding 3.8/3.9; 1.2.0 dropped 3.6 while adding 3.10/3.11; 1.2.2 added 3.12 |
| Timezone hardening trend | The three most recent releases are dominated by timezone and DST corrections (#583 in 1.2.1; #601, #602, #604, #623 in 1.2.2), matching the head of the git history |
| Compatibility constraint on change | Semantic versioning is the declared policy, and the naive-local `next_run` contract is preserved deliberately — so any move to timezone-aware public datetimes would be a breaking change requiring a major release |

Items that a future phase would have to introduce from scratch — because no partial implementation exists — include persistence, concurrency primitives, missed-run catch-up, sub-second scheduling, holiday/workday calendars, and any form of remote or multi-process coordination.

#### 1.3.2.3 Integration Points Not Covered

| Integration not provided | Notes |
|---|---|
| Message brokers and distributed queues | `docs/parallel-execution.rst` shows how a *caller* can bridge to a queue (`jobqueue.put`) and mentions beanstalkd/beanstalkc, but no broker client ships with the package |
| Databases and durable stores | No database driver, ORM, or file persistence anywhere in the package |
| Thread pools, process pools, and async runtimes | Threading and queue patterns are documented as *user-implemented* examples only |
| OS schedulers (cron, systemd timers, Task Scheduler) | The library is positioned as an alternative to these, not an interface to them |
| Metrics, tracing, and alerting backends | Only standard-library `logging` at DEBUG level is emitted |
| Non-`pytz` timezone providers | `Job.at()` accepts a string or `pytz.BaseTzInfo` and raises `ScheduleValueError` otherwise; `zoneinfo` objects are not accepted |
| Distribution channels outside PyPI | Ubuntu, Debian, AUR, and conda-forge packages exist but `docs/installation.rst` states they are not maintained by this project |
| Configuration or secret management systems | Jobs are configured only through Python API calls; no config parsing exists |

#### 1.3.2.4 Unsupported Use Cases

| Use case | Why it is unsupported |
|---|---|
| Durable, restart-surviving schedules | Job state is in-memory only and is lost when the process exits |
| High-precision or real-time triggering | Resolution is bounded by how often the caller polls `run_pending()`; sub-second precision is an explicit non-goal |
| Long-running jobs on the scheduler thread | A long job blocks the serial loop and delays every other job; `docs/index.rst` directs such work off the main thread |
| Guaranteed at-least-once or catch-up semantics | Missed occurrences are intentionally skipped, never replayed |
| Multi-process or clustered scheduling with coordination | Each `Scheduler` is process-local with no leader election, locking, or shared state |
| Business-calendar scheduling (holidays, workdays, month-ends) | Only fixed intervals, weekdays, and clock times are modeled |
| Cron-expression compatibility | No cron-expression parser exists; scheduling is expressed exclusively through the fluent API |
| Unattended resilience to failing jobs | An uncaught job exception interrupts the `run_xyz` call; the caller must wrap jobs defensively |
| `@repeat` on non-static class methods | Explicitly documented as not working |
| Timezone-aware jobs without `pytz` | Raises `ModuleNotFoundError`; `docs/faq.rst` documents the resolution as installing `pytz` |
| Sub-minute `at()` anchoring on unsupported units | `at()` rejects any unit other than days, hours, or minutes (or a weekday-qualified week) with `ScheduleValueError` |
| Deadlines in the past | `until()` raises `ScheduleValueError` for a moment already elapsed |

# 2. Product Requirements

## 2.1 Feature Catalog

The repository contains **no requirements document, backlog, issue template, or acceptance-test specification**. `.github/` holds exactly one file (`workflows/ci.yml`), and there is no roadmap or planning artifact anywhere in the tree. The catalog below is therefore *reverse-derived* from three authoritative sources that do exist:

| Evidence source | Role in this catalog |
|---|---|
| `schedule/__init__.py` (945 lines) | Definitive statement of implemented behavior; every feature is anchored to a line range |
| `test_schedule.py` (1,599 lines, 81 test methods) | Executable specification; supplies the acceptance criteria in §2.2 |
| `docs/*.rst` (13 substantive pages) | Published contracts, worked examples, and explicit non-goals |
| `HISTORY.rst` | Release in which each capability first appeared — used for requirement version tracking in §2.5 |

**Status convention.** Every feature listed carries the status **Completed**: each is implemented in release 1.2.2 (`SCHEDULE_VERSION = "1.2.2"` in `setup.py`), covered by at least one passing test method (locally verified: `81 passed`), and the package is classified `Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable` in `setup.py`. No feature in this repository is in a proposed or partially built state — the only forward-looking marker in the source is an inline `todo` on the module-level `jobs` alias (`schedule/__init__.py` line 840) questioning whether it should return a copy.

**Priority convention.** Priority reflects observable emphasis inside the repository — centrality in the call graph, share of the test suite, and prominence in `README.rst` / `docs/index.rst` — not an external business mandate, because none is recorded in the tree.

**Documented non-goals are deliberately absent from this catalog.** `docs/index.rst` (lines 53–62) directs users elsewhere for job persistence, sub-second precision, concurrent execution, and workday/holiday localization; `docs/background-execution.rst` and `docs/parallel-execution.rst` present threading and queue patterns as *caller-implemented examples*. Accordingly, no persistence, concurrency, retry, catch-up, metrics, authentication, CLI, or configuration-file feature is claimed.

### 2.1.2 F-001 — Fluent Interval Scheduling

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-001 |
| Feature Name | Fluent Interval Scheduling |
| Feature Category | Scheduling Core |
| Priority Level | Critical |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — `Scheduler.every(interval=1)` (`schedule/__init__.py` 162–170) returns an *unconfigured* `Job`. Chained unit properties (325–378) set `Job.unit` to `seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`, `days`, or `weeks` and return `self`, so `every(10).minutes` is a single mutable object read as prose. Singular aliases (`second`, `minute`, `hour`, `day`, `week`) exist for the `interval == 1` case. `_schedule_next_run()` (700–748) turns the pair into `datetime.timedelta(**{unit: interval})` and advances the moment until it is strictly in the future.
- **Business Value** — This is the differentiator the project advertises: `README.rst` leads with "A simple to use API for scheduling jobs, made for humans", and the module docstring names the builder pattern explicitly. Readability is the product, not an aesthetic extra.
- **User Benefits** — No crontab string to author or review; schedules are self-documenting at the call site; both `every().hour` and `every(2).hours` are legal spellings, with the wrong spelling rejected with an actionable message.
- **Technical Context** — Properties mutate `self` rather than returning new objects, which is why an abandoned chain leaves no residue: registration happens only in `do()` (F-007). Interval arithmetic is pure `datetime`; there is no clock other than `datetime.datetime.now()`.

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | None — this is the root of every scheduling expression |
| System dependencies | `datetime` (timedelta arithmetic, `now()`); `typing` for annotations |
| External dependencies | None |
| Integration requirements | Requires F-007 to bind a callable and register, and F-009 for the job to execute |

### 2.1.3 F-002 — Weekday Scheduling

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-002 |
| Feature Name | Weekday Scheduling |
| Feature Category | Scheduling Core |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — Seven properties, `monday` through `sunday` (`schedule/__init__.py` 380–455), set `Job.start_day` and return `self.weeks`, making `every().wednesday.at("13:15")` a weekly job anchored to a weekday. `_move_to_next_weekday()` (916–928) advances a moment to the nearest matching weekday and deliberately does **not** move it when it is already that day; `_weekday_index()` (931–945) validates the day name.
- **Business Value** — Covers the "every Wednesday at 13:15" class of work that would otherwise require a cron expression, using the same fluent grammar as interval scheduling.
- **User Benefits** — Weekday names read naturally, same-day scheduling works as users expect (a Wednesday 22:38:10 job created at 22:38:05 on a Wednesday fires the same day — `test_weekday_at_todady`), and multi-week weekday combinations are rejected loudly rather than silently misbehaving.
- **Technical Context** — Weekday scheduling is intentionally restricted to a weekly interval: each accessor raises `IntervalError` when `interval != 1` with the message "Scheduling .<day>() jobs is only allowed for weekly jobs…". `_schedule_next_run()` additionally enforces `unit == "weeks"` whenever `start_day` is set (721–724).

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | F-001 (weekday accessors delegate to the `weeks` unit) |
| System dependencies | `datetime` (`weekday()`, `timedelta`) |
| External dependencies | None |
| Integration requirements | Composes with F-003 (`at()` is permitted because `start_day` is set) and F-016 for the interval guard |

### 2.1.4 F-003 — Clock-Time Anchoring (`at()`)

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-003 |
| Feature Name | Clock-Time Anchoring |
| Feature Category | Scheduling Core |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — `Job.at(time_str, tz=None)` (`schedule/__init__.py` 471–559) pins a job to a wall-clock time. The accepted format is inferred from the unit: `HH:MM(:SS)` for daily and weekday jobs, `(MM):SS` for hourly jobs, `:SS` for minutely jobs. `_move_to_at_time()` (750–771) then overwrites the relevant components of the computed moment — always second and microsecond, minute for `days`/`hours`/weekday jobs, hour for `days`/weekday jobs.
- **Business Value** — Enables the canonical example that appears in `README.rst` and `docs/index.rst` (`every().day.at("10:30")`), which is the most common real-world scheduling request the library serves.
- **User Benefits** — One method covers three granularities; each unit has its own validation message so a mis-typed format is diagnosed precisely (for example `every().hour.at("2:30:00")` is rejected with "Invalid time format for an hourly job (valid format is (MM)?:SS)").
- **Technical Context** — Validation is three anchored regular expressions (lines 513, 518, 524) plus an explicit 0–23 hour bound (544–549). `at()` is rejected outright unless the unit is `days`, `hours`, or `minutes`, or a weekday has been selected (493–496), and a non-string argument raises `TypeError` (510–511).

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | F-001 (unit must already be `days`/`hours`/`minutes`) or F-002 (weekday selected) |
| System dependencies | `re` for format validation; `datetime.time` for the stored value |
| External dependencies | None (unless the optional `tz` argument is used — see F-004) |
| Integration requirements | Feeds `_schedule_next_run()` (F-001) and is the only entry point for F-004 |

### 2.1.5 F-004 — Timezone-Aware Scheduling with DST Correction

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-004 |
| Feature Name | Timezone-Aware Scheduling with DST Correction |
| Feature Category | Time Correctness |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — Passing `tz` to `at()` (`schedule/__init__.py` 498–508) stores a `pytz` zone on `Job.at_time_zone`. `_schedule_next_run()` then performs its arithmetic in that zone (`datetime.datetime.now(self.at_time_zone)`, line 717) and `_correct_utc_offset()` (773–817) keeps the requested wall-clock time stable across UTC-offset changes; when the requested time falls inside a DST gap it schedules one offset later as a documented best effort. The result is converted back to local time and stripped of `tzinfo` (740–747) so the public `next_run` contract stays naive-local.
- **Business Value** — Lets a single process schedule work in the timezone of a remote market or team, which `docs/timezones.rst` demonstrates end-to-end (a Berlin host scheduling `at("10:30", "America/New_York")` yields `next_run` 15:30 local). This is the area the project has invested the most in: releases 1.2.1 and 1.2.2 are dominated by timezone fixes.
- **User Benefits** — Correct behavior across the two hard cases users cannot easily test themselves — the spring-forward gap and the autumn fold — with the documented outcomes published in `docs/timezones.rst`.
- **Technical Context** — `pytz` is imported *inside* `at()` (line 499) and only when `tz` is supplied, which is what allows `pyproject.toml` to declare `dependencies = []`. Zones may be given as a string or a `pytz.BaseTzInfo` object; anything else raises `ScheduleValueError`. Timezone support exists nowhere else in the API — `docs/timezones.rst` states that timezones are only available in the `.at` function.

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | F-003 — `tz` is a parameter of `at()` alone |
| System dependencies | `datetime` (`astimezone`, `utcoffset`, `replace`) |
| External dependencies | `pytz`, declared as the optional `timezone` extra in `pyproject.toml`; absent `pytz`, using `tz` raises `ModuleNotFoundError` (`docs/faq.rst`) |
| Integration requirements | Must not break the zero-dependency contract of F-017; validated by the six `-pytz` tox environments alongside six without |

### 2.1.6 F-005 — Randomized Interval Scheduling (`to()`)

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-005 |
| Feature Name | Randomized Interval Scheduling |
| Feature Category | Scheduling Core |
| Priority Level | Medium |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — `Job.to(latest)` (`schedule/__init__.py` 561–574) records an upper bound; `_schedule_next_run()` then draws `random.randint(self.interval, self.latest)` (line 712) on every reschedule, so `every(5).to(10).minutes` runs every N minutes with 5 ≤ N ≤ 10, inclusive on both ends.
- **Business Value** — Spreads load and avoids thundering-herd alignment between multiple processes running the same schedule, without the caller writing jitter logic.
- **User Benefits** — A single chained call converts any fixed schedule into a jittered one; the randomized range is visible in the job's `repr` ("Every 5 to 30 minutes do job()").
- **Technical Context** — The draw happens per scheduling cycle rather than once at definition time, so successive intervals differ. An inverted range is rejected with `ScheduleError("`latest` is greater than `interval`")` at scheduling time (709–711).

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | F-001 (the unit and base interval it randomizes) |
| System dependencies | `random.randint` |
| External dependencies | None |
| Integration requirements | Surfaces through F-013 (`__repr__` renders the `to` clause) |

### 2.1.7 F-006 — Deadline-Bounded Jobs (`until()`)

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-006 |
| Feature Name | Deadline-Bounded Jobs |
| Feature Category | Job Lifecycle |
| Priority Level | Medium |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — `Job.until(until_time)` (`schedule/__init__.py` 576–642) sets `Job.cancel_after` from a `datetime.datetime`, a `datetime.timedelta` (relative to now), a `datetime.time` (today's date), or a string in one of five `strptime` formats. `_is_overdue()` (819–820) is consulted twice inside `run()`: before execution (the job is skipped and unscheduled) and after execution (if the newly computed `next_run` is past the deadline, `CancelJob` is returned and takes priority over the job's own return value).
- **Business Value** — Expresses time-boxed work — "poll every hour until 18:30" — without the caller tracking end-times or cleaning up afterwards. `docs/examples.rst` documents the contract plainly: the job will not run after the deadline.
- **User Benefits** — Five accepted input shapes cover absolute, relative, and time-only deadlines; expired jobs disappear from the registry automatically, so no stale entries accumulate.
- **Technical Context** — A deadline already in the past is rejected at configuration time with `ScheduleValueError("Cannot schedule a job to run until a time in the past")` (638–641); an unsupported type raises `TypeError`; an unparseable string raises `ScheduleValueError("Invalid string format for until()")`. Parsing is delegated to `_decode_datetimestr()` (822–830), which tries each format in order.

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | F-001 (a job under construction); F-010 for the unscheduling mechanism |
| System dependencies | `datetime` (`strptime`, `combine`, `timedelta`) |
| External dependencies | None |
| Integration requirements | Deadline enforcement occurs inside `Job.run()`, so it only takes effect when the caller drives F-009 |

### 2.1.8 F-007 — Callable Binding and Job Registration (`do()`)

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-007 |
| Feature Name | Callable Binding and Job Registration |
| Feature Category | Job Definition |
| Priority Level | Critical |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — `Job.do(job_func, *args, **kwargs)` (`schedule/__init__.py` 644–664) is the terminal call of every chain. It wraps the callable and its arguments in `functools.partial`, copies metadata with `functools.update_wrapper`, computes the first `next_run`, verifies a scheduler is associated, and only then appends the job to `scheduler.jobs`.
- **Business Value** — Defines the boundary between configuration and commitment: nothing is scheduled until a callable is attached, which is what makes an interrupted definition chain harmless.
- **User Benefits** — Any callable is accepted — named functions, lambdas, and `functools.partial` objects are all exercised in the test suite — and arguments supplied at definition time are forwarded verbatim at execution time.
- **Technical Context** — Ordering matters: `_schedule_next_run()` runs *before* `scheduler.jobs.append(self)` (657–663), so a job with an invalid unit raises `ScheduleValueError` and never enters the registry. A `Job` constructed directly without a scheduler raises `ScheduleError` on `do()`.

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | F-001 (a valid unit must be set); optionally F-002…F-006 for refinement |
| System dependencies | `functools.partial`, `functools.update_wrapper` |
| External dependencies | None |
| Integration requirements | Registry mutation targets the owning `Scheduler` (F-015); registered jobs become visible to F-009, F-011, and F-012 |

### 2.1.9 F-008 — Decorator-Based Registration (`@repeat`)

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-008 |
| Feature Name | Decorator-Based Registration |
| Feature Category | Developer Ergonomics |
| Priority Level | Medium |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — `repeat(job, *args, **kwargs)` (`schedule/__init__.py` 899–913) is a decorator factory. Its inner `_schedule_decorator` calls `job.do(decorated_function, *args, **kwargs)` and returns the **original** function unchanged, so `@repeat(every(10).minutes)` registers a job as a side effect of definition while leaving the function directly callable.
- **Business Value** — Moves schedule declaration next to the function it governs, which keeps job inventories readable in application code.
- **User Benefits** — Declarative registration with argument support (`@repeat(every().minute, 1, 2, "three", foo=23)`), and the decorated symbol remains the plain function for direct calls and unit testing.
- **Technical Context** — The decorator is a thin adapter over F-007; it adds no scheduling semantics of its own. `docs/examples.rst` records one limitation explicitly: the decorator does not work on non-static class methods.

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | F-007 (delegates to `Job.do`); a job expression from F-001 (typically via the F-015 facade) |
| System dependencies | None beyond the Python decorator protocol |
| External dependencies | None |
| Integration requirements | The decorated job lands in whichever scheduler produced the job expression |

### 2.1.10 F-009 — Serial Execution Engine (`run_pending` / `run_all`)

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-009 |
| Feature Name | Serial Execution Engine |
| Feature Category | Execution |
| Priority Level | Critical |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — `Scheduler.run_pending()` (`schedule/__init__.py` 89–101) selects jobs whose `should_run` is true (`now >= next_run`, 666–672) and executes them in `sorted()` order — ordering supplied by `Job.__lt__` comparing `next_run` (257–262). `Scheduler.run_all(delay_seconds=0)` (103–120) forces every job to run regardless of schedule, sleeping `delay_seconds` between jobs to spread load. `Job.run()` (674–698) invokes the bound callable, stamps `last_run`, and immediately reschedules.
- **Business Value** — Keeps execution inside the caller's own process and loop — the "No extra processes needed!" claim in `README.rst` — so no broker, daemon, or deployment artifact is required.
- **User Benefits** — The host application retains complete control over cadence and threading; `run_all()` provides a deterministic way to flush every job, which is also how the test suite triggers execution.
- **Technical Context** — Execution is strictly serial and in-line on the calling thread; `docs/parallel-execution.rst` states this is a deliberate design choice. Missed occurrences are never replayed — the `run_pending()` docstring (93–97) calls this intended behavior. Job exceptions are not caught (line 691 has no `try`/`except`), which `docs/exception-handling.rst` documents as bubbling up and interrupting the `run_xyz` call.

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | F-007 (only registered jobs are considered); F-001 for the `next_run` values compared |
| System dependencies | `datetime.datetime.now()`; `time.sleep` for `run_all` spacing |
| External dependencies | None |
| Integration requirements | The caller must drive the loop (`docs/examples.rst`); F-010 cancellation is applied through `_run_job`; F-014 emits DEBUG records per run |

### 2.1.11 F-010 — Job Cancellation (`CancelJob` / `cancel_job`)

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-010 |
| Feature Name | Job Cancellation |
| Feature Category | Job Lifecycle |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — Two complementary paths exist. A job may return the `CancelJob` sentinel (`schedule/__init__.py` 71–76) and `Scheduler._run_job()` (172–175) will unschedule it — accepting either the class itself or an instance. Alternatively the caller invokes `Scheduler.cancel_job(job)` (150–160), which removes the job from the registry and treats an unknown job as a silent no-op logged at DEBUG.
- **Business Value** — Supports run-once and self-terminating jobs without the caller maintaining external bookkeeping; `docs/examples.rst` presents "return `schedule.CancelJob`" as the canonical way to run a job exactly once.
- **User Benefits** — Cancellation can be driven from inside the job (return the sentinel) or outside it (call `cancel_job`), and passing something that is not a scheduled job never raises.
- **Technical Context** — `cancel_job` swallows `ValueError` from `list.remove`, so cancelling twice is safe. F-006 reuses this path by returning `CancelJob` from `Job.run()` when a deadline is reached.

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | F-009 (the sentinel is inspected in `_run_job`); F-007 for registry membership |
| System dependencies | `list.remove` semantics on `Scheduler.jobs` |
| External dependencies | None |
| Integration requirements | Reused by F-006 for deadline expiry; exposed at module level by F-015; logged by F-014 |

### 2.1.12 F-011 — Job Tagging, Retrieval and Bulk Clearing

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-011 |
| Feature Name | Job Tagging, Retrieval and Bulk Clearing |
| Feature Category | Job Management |
| Priority Level | Medium |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — `Job.tag(*tags)` (`schedule/__init__.py` 457–469) attaches any number of hashable identifiers to a job, storing them in a `set` so duplicates are discarded. `Scheduler.get_jobs(tag)` (122–133) returns a copy of the whole registry or only jobs carrying the tag; `Scheduler.clear(tag)` (135–148) deletes all jobs or only the tagged subset.
- **Business Value** — Gives applications a grouping primitive for managing families of jobs — `docs/examples.rst` shows `clear('daily-tasks')` preventing every job in that group from running again.
- **User Benefits** — Group selection and group cancellation use the same identifier vocabulary; tags are arbitrary hashables (strings, integers, booleans) rather than a fixed enumeration.
- **Technical Context** — `tag()` enforces hashability eagerly with `TypeError("Tags must be hashable")`. `get_jobs()` returns a *copy* (`self.jobs[:]`), so callers cannot mutate the registry accidentally; `clear()` uses in-place slice deletion/assignment so the `jobs` alias exposed by F-015 continues to reference the same list object.

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | F-007 (jobs must be registered to be retrievable or clearable) |
| System dependencies | `collections.abc.Hashable`; `set` semantics |
| External dependencies | None |
| Integration requirements | Tag filtering is also consumed by F-012 (`get_next_run(tag)`); clearing and cancelling emit F-014 DEBUG records |

### 2.1.13 F-012 — Schedule Introspection (`next_run` / `idle_seconds`)

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-012 |
| Feature Name | Schedule Introspection |
| Feature Category | Observability |
| Priority Level | Medium |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — `Scheduler.get_next_run(tag=None)` (`schedule/__init__.py` 177–193), exposed also as the `next_run` property (line 195), returns the earliest `next_run` among all jobs or among jobs carrying a tag, and `None` when there are no jobs or no match. `Scheduler.idle_seconds` (197–206) converts that instant into seconds from now, returning `None` when nothing is scheduled.
- **Business Value** — Lets the host loop sleep exactly as long as necessary instead of polling every second, which is the pattern `docs/examples.rst` recommends for efficiency.
- **User Benefits** — A two-line idle loop replaces fixed-interval polling; a tag argument narrows the question to one group of jobs; the `None` return is a clean "nothing scheduled" signal rather than an exception.
- **Technical Context** — Selection uses `min(jobs_filtered)`, relying on the same `Job.__lt__` ordering as F-009. `docs/examples.rst` documents that the value is negative when the next job is already overdue.

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | F-001 (computed `next_run` values); F-007 (registration); F-011 for the tag filter |
| System dependencies | `datetime` subtraction and `total_seconds()` |
| External dependencies | None |
| Integration requirements | Consumed by caller-owned loops together with F-009; mirrored at module level by F-015 |

### 2.1.14 F-013 — Human-Readable Job Representation

| Feature Name | Human-Readable Job Representation |
| Feature Category | Developer Ergonomics |
| Priority Level | Medium |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — `Job.__str__` (`schedule/__init__.py` 264–276) produces the structured form `Job(interval=…, unit=…, do=…, args=…, kwargs=…)`; `Job.__repr__` (278–323) produces an English sentence such as `Every 1 day at 10:30:00 do job() (last run: [never], next run: 2022-03-20 15:30:00)`, singularizing the unit when the interval is 1 and rendering the `to` clause for randomized jobs.

- **Technical Context** — Both methods fall back to `repr(self.job_func)` when the callable has no `__name__` (covering lambdas and `functools.partial`), and substitute `"()"`, `"{}"`, and `"[None]"` placeholders when `job_func` is still `None`. `HISTORY.rst` records these as deliberate fixes (1.1.0 issue #430; 1.2.0 issue #569, "Fix crash repr on partially constructed job").

### 2.1.16 F-015 — Scheduler Instancing and Module-Level Facade

| Metadata | Value |

| Unique ID | F-015 |
| Feature Name | Scheduler Instancing and Module-Level Facade |
| Feature Category | API Surface |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — The module instantiates `default_scheduler = Scheduler()` (`schedule/__init__.py` line 837), exposes its registry as the `jobs` alias (line 840), and provides eight delegating shortcuts — `every`, `run_pending`, `run_all`, `get_jobs`, `clear`, `cancel_job`, `next_run`, `idle_seconds` (843–896). Independently, applications may instantiate any number of `Scheduler()` objects, each owning its own `self.jobs` list (86–87).

- **Technical Context** — Every shortcut is a one-line delegation, so module-level and instance-level behavior cannot diverge. Each scheduler is fully independent — `docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` notes that `run_pending()` must be called on every scheduler. ### 2.1.17 F-016 — Typed Error Hierarchy and Fail-Fast Validation

| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-016 |
| Feature Name | Typed Error Hierarchy and Fail-Fast Validation |
| Feature Category | Reliability |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview** — Three exception classes form a hierarchy: `ScheduleError` → `ScheduleValueError` → `IntervalError` (`schedule/__init__.py` 53–68). Configuration faults are raised at definition time rather than at execution time: wrong singular/plural spelling, weekday accessors on multi-week intervals, invalid `at()` units and formats, out-of-range hours, invalid timezone types, inverted `to()` ranges, past or unparseable `until()` values, unknown weekday names, and missing or invalid units.
- **Business Value** — Misconfiguration surfaces at startup where it is cheap to fix, instead of silently producing a schedule that never fires. `HISTORY.rst` records the hierarchy as a deliberate 0.6.0 investment (issue #271) and improved error messages in 1.1.0 (issues #280, #439).
- **User Benefits** — Callers can catch broadly (`ScheduleError`) or narrowly (`IntervalError`); messages name the fix, for example "Use seconds instead of second" and "Invalid unit (valid units are `days`, `hours`, and `minutes`)".
- **Technical Context** — Because registration happens last inside `do()` (F-007), a chain that raises never enters the registry. `test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler` proves that abandoned chains leave a fresh `Scheduler` fully usable — the behavior `HISTORY.rst` attributes to 0.5.0 issue #125.

**Dependencies**

| Dependency type | Detail |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite features | Cross-cutting; enforced by F-001…F-007 |
| System dependencies | Python exception machinery; `re` for format checks |
| External dependencies | `pytz.exceptions.UnknownTimeZoneError` propagates unchanged for unknown zone names (F-004) |
| Integration requirements | Callers wishing to guard *runtime* job failures must wrap their own functions — `docs/exception-handling.rst` — because the library does not catch job exceptions |

The runtime module imports only standard-library names (`schedule/__init__.py` 41–48).

| Integration requirements | F-004 must keep `pytz` imported lazily; CI must stay green on Python 3.7 through 3.12 |

## 2.2 Functional Requirements Table

Every requirement below is stated so that it can be verified against the repository. Acceptance criteria cite the implementing line range in `schedule/__init__.py` and, wherever one exists, the test method in `test_schedule.py` that already asserts the behavior. Where **no** automated test covers a requirement, that is stated explicitly rather than implied.

### 2.2.1 Requirement Conventions and Global Baseline

| Convention | Meaning as applied in this section |
|---|---|
| Priority `Must-Have` | The feature does not function, or a published contract in `docs/` is broken, without it |
| Priority `Should-Have` | Documented convenience or diagnostic behavior; absence degrades usability, not correctness |
| Priority `Could-Have` | Ergonomic refinement with no functional consequence |
| Complexity `High` | Multi-branch time arithmetic or offset correction (concentrated in `_schedule_next_run`, `_move_to_at_time`, `_correct_utc_offset`) |
| Complexity `Medium` | Input parsing/validation or registry mutation with several branches |
| Complexity `Low` | Single-branch property, delegation, or accessor |

The following baselines apply to **every** requirement in this section and are not repeated per feature; only feature-specific deltas are listed in the tables below.

| Baseline dimension | Repository-wide position |
|---|---|
| Performance | All operations are in-process and in-memory. The costliest paths are linear in the number of registered jobs: `run_pending()` filters and sorts due jobs (`schedule/__init__.py` 99–101), `get_next_run()` takes `min()` over the registry (188–193), `clear()`/`get_jobs()` rebuild or copy the list (122–148). There is no I/O of any kind. **No latency, throughput, or availability target is published anywhere in the repository**; scheduling resolution is bounded by how often the caller invokes `run_pending()`, and sub-second precision is an explicit non-goal (`docs/index.rst`). Reference point: the full 81-method suite executes in 0.12 s on Python 3.12. |
| Data requirements | Exactly one data domain — in-memory scheduling metadata for the life of the process. The fields are those assigned in `Job.__init__` (227–255): `interval`, `latest`, `job_func`, `unit`, `at_time`, `at_time_zone`, `last_run`, `next_run`, `start_day`, `cancel_after`, `tags`, `scheduler`. Nothing is serialized, persisted, or transmitted. |
| Security requirements | The module contains no authentication, authorization, cryptography, network, subprocess, filesystem, deserialization, or `eval`/`exec` code — imports are limited to `collections.abc`, `datetime`, `functools`, `logging`, `random`, `re`, `time`, `typing` (41–48). Jobs execute synchronously with the full privileges of the host process, so the caller-supplied callable is the trust boundary; exceptions from it are not caught (`docs/exception-handling.rst`). `random` is used for interval jitter only and is not a security primitive. |
| Compliance requirements | MIT license (`LICENSE.txt`); PEP 561 type distribution via `schedule/py.typed`; PEP 517/518 build metadata (`pyproject.toml`); semantic versioning declared in `docs/development.rst`; formatting enforced by `black==20.8b1`; static typing enforced by `mypy -p schedule`. No personal, financial, or regulated data is processed, so no data-protection regime is in scope. |

### 2.2.2 F-001 — Fluent Interval Scheduling

| ID | Description | Acceptance criteria | Priority / Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| F-001-RQ-001 | `every(interval=1)` returns an unconfigured `Job` bound to the scheduler without registering it | `Scheduler.every` (162–170) returns a `Job` whose `unit` is `None`; the registry is unchanged until `do()`. `test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler` (test_schedule.py:1591) abandons two chains and `run_pending()` still succeeds | Must-Have / Low |
| F-001-RQ-002 | Plural unit properties set `Job.unit` to `seconds`/`minutes`/`hours`/`days`/`weeks` and return the same job for chaining | `test_time_units` (108) asserts `every().<unit>.unit == "<unit>"` for all five units (325–378) | Must-Have / Low |
| F-001-RQ-003 | Singular aliases are legal only when `interval == 1`; otherwise `IntervalError` naming the plural form | `test_time_units` (108) and `test_at_time` (268) assert `IntervalError` for `every(interval=2).second/.minute/.hour/.day/.week`; `test_singular_time_units_match_plural_units` (236) asserts alias equivalence | Must-Have / Low |
| F-001-RQ-004 | `next_run` equals now plus `interval × unit`, advanced by whole periods until strictly in the future | Lines 729–734 (`period = timedelta(**{unit: interval})`, `while next_run <= now`). `test_next_run_time` (463), `_day_end` (486), `_hour_end` (510), `_minute_end` (557) assert exact datetimes under `mock_datetime` | Must-Have / Medium |

| Technical specification | Detail |
|---|---|
| Input parameters | `interval: int` (default 1) to `every()`; unit selected by attribute access, no arguments |
| Output / response | The same mutated `Job` (fluent chaining); after `do()`, `Job.next_run` is a naive local `datetime` |
| Performance criteria | Constant-time arithmetic per reschedule; the `while` loop advances by whole periods, so cost is proportional to elapsed periods only when a job is far overdue |
| Data requirements | `Job.interval`, `Job.unit`, `Job.next_run` (in memory) |

| Validation rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Business rules | Exactly five units are legal; singular spellings represent the `interval == 1` case only |
| Data validation | `_schedule_next_run()` rejects a missing or unknown unit with `ScheduleValueError` (704–708) — see F-016-RQ-002 |
| Security requirements | Baseline only; `interval` is used solely as a `timedelta` component |
| Compliance requirements | Annotated (`interval: int`) and covered by the `mypy -p schedule` gate |

| ID | Description | Acceptance criteria | Priority / Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| F-009-RQ-001 | `run_pending()` executes only jobs whose `next_run` has been reached, in ascending `next_run` order | Lines 99–101 with `should_run` (666–672) and `Job.__lt__` (257–262). `test_run_pending` (1387) asserts zero executions before the first due moment and the exact cumulative counts afterwards | Must-Have / Medium |
| F-009-RQ-002 | Missed occurrences are never replayed — a job runs at most once per `run_pending()` call regardless of how many periods elapsed | Docstring 93–97 states this is intended behavior. `test_run_pending` advances the clock by a minute, an hour, a day and four days and asserts counts of 1, 2, 3 and 4 rather than one per elapsed period | Must-Have / Medium |
| F-009-RQ-003 | `run_all(delay_seconds=0)` executes every registered job regardless of schedule, sleeping `delay_seconds` between jobs | Lines 103–120 iterate a copy of the registry and `time.sleep(delay_seconds)` after each job. `test_run_all` (1273) asserts all three jobs ran; `docs/examples.rst` documents `run_all(delay_seconds=10)` | Must-Have / Low |
| F-009-RQ-004 | Exceptions raised by a job propagate to the caller and interrupt the `run_xyz` call | `Job.run` calls `self.job_func()` with no `try`/`except` (line 691); documented in `docs/exception-handling.rst`. **No test asserts propagation**; it is verified by inspection and by the published contract | Must-Have / Low |

| Technical specification | Detail |
|---|---|
| Input parameters | `run_pending()` takes none; `run_all(delay_seconds: int = 0)` |
| Output / response | `None`; side effects are job invocations, `last_run`/`next_run` updates, and possible unscheduling |
| Performance criteria | One `now()` call per `should_run` evaluation; a sort over due jobs per call; `run_all` blocks for `delay_seconds × job count`. Execution is serial on the calling thread, so total time includes every job's own duration — `docs/index.rst` states job duration is not accounted for |
| Data requirements | Reads and mutates `Scheduler.jobs`, `Job.last_run`, `Job.next_run` |

| Validation rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Business rules | Serial execution is deliberate (`docs/parallel-execution.rst`); the caller owns the loop and cadence; no background thread is ever created (`docs/background-execution.rst`) |
| Data validation | `should_run` asserts `next_run` is set, which holds for every registered job because `do()` computes it first |
| Security requirements | Jobs run in the caller's thread with its privileges; an uncaught exception aborts the remaining due jobs for that call |
| Compliance requirements | `run_all`'s zero-second default has been the contract since 0.1.8 per `HISTORY.rst` |

| F-012-RQ-001 | `next_run` / `get_next_run(tag)` returns the earliest `next_run` across all jobs or across jobs with the given tag, and `None` when there are no jobs or no match | Lines 177–195 (`min(jobs_filtered).next_run`). `test_next_run_property` (1480) asserts the hourly job wins over the daily job; `test_next_run_with_tag` (222) asserts per-tag results and `None` for an unmatched tag | Should-Have / Low |
| F-012-RQ-002 | `idle_seconds` returns the seconds until the next run, a negative value when the next run is already past, and `None` when nothing is scheduled | Lines 197–206. `test_idle_seconds` (1491) asserts `None` before any job, `3600` for an hourly job, and `None` again after cancellation; the negative case is documented in `docs/examples.rst` | Should-Have / Low |

| Data requirements | `Job.next_run` values and `Job.tags` |

Every relationship documented below is a call, attribute, or state dependency that exists in `schedule/__init__.py`, or an integration pattern published in `docs/`. No inferred or aspirational relationships are included.

| Relationship | Evidence |

| F-001 → F-002, F-003, F-005, F-006, F-007 | All refinement methods are `Job` methods reached by chaining from the object `Scheduler.every()` returns (`schedule/__init__.py` 162–170) |
| F-002 → F-003 | `at()` accepts a weekday-qualified job because its unit guard also passes when `start_day` is set (493–496) |
