# 4. Process Flowchart

## 4.1 System Workflows

`schedule` is an in-process library, not a deployed service. It exposes no HTTP endpoint, no CLI, no message consumer, and no database connection — the runtime module `schedule/__init__.py` imports only eight standard-library modules (lines 41–48). Consequently the "business processes" documented here are **API-level workflows executed inside the host application's own process and on the host application's own thread**, and the "systems" that participate in integration workflows are the host control loop, the optional `pytz` package, the Python `logging` subsystem, and the caller-supplied callable.

Four actors recur throughout every workflow in this section:

| Actor | Boundary | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Developer / host code | Outside the library | Builds job definitions, owns the control loop and its cadence, handles exceptions |
| Module facade / `Scheduler` | Library | Creates jobs, holds the in-memory registry, selects and dispatches due jobs |
| `Job` | Library | Validates configuration, computes `next_run`, invokes the callable, signals cancellation |
| Caller-supplied callable | Outside the library | Performs the actual work; runs synchronously inside the dispatch cycle |

Section 2.3.2 contains a coarse, feature-level view of the job lifecycle. The workflows below are the detailed engineering view of that same lifecycle: they add swimlanes per actor, the exact order of every validation gate, the internals of next-run computation, and every error and recovery edge.

### 4.1.1 Core Business Processes

#### 4.1.1.1 High-Level System Workflow

The following diagram is the end-to-end user journey: a developer defines jobs, hands control to a polling loop, and the library repeatedly selects, dispatches, and reschedules work against a purely in-memory registry until the process exits.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph HostApp["Host Application Process (caller-owned)"]
        HStart([Application start]) --> HImport["import schedule"]
        HImport --> HDefine["Define jobs:<br/>every n .unit .at .to .until .tag .do fn<br/>F-001..F-008"]
        HDefine --> HLoop["Control loop:<br/>while True: run_pending; sleep 1<br/>docs/index.rst 46-48"]
        HLoop --> HExit([Process exit — all state lost])
    end
    subgraph Library["schedule Library (in-process, single module)"]
        LFactory["Scheduler.every returns<br/>unconfigured Job — 162-170"]
        LValidate{"Configuration<br/>valid?<br/>F-016"}
        LCompute["_schedule_next_run<br/>700-748"]
        LRegister["scheduler.jobs.append job<br/>line 663 — only commit point"]
        LSelect["run_pending: filter should_run,<br/>sort by next_run — 99-101"]
        LDispatch["_run_job: job.run — 172-175"]
        LReschedule["last_run = now;<br/>recompute next_run — 692-693"]
        LCancelCheck{"CancelJob returned<br/>or deadline passed?"}
        LRemove["Scheduler.cancel_job<br/>jobs.remove — 150-160"]
        LFactory --> LValidate
        LValidate -->|"invalid"| LRaise["Raise IntervalError /<br/>ScheduleValueError /<br/>TypeError / ScheduleError<br/>job never registered"]
        LValidate -->|"valid"| LCompute
        LCompute --> LRegister
        LSelect --> LDispatch
        LDispatch --> LReschedule
        LReschedule --> LCancelCheck
        LCancelCheck -->|"yes"| LRemove
        LCancelCheck -->|"no"| LSelect
    end
    subgraph Registry["In-Memory State (Scheduler.jobs list, 86-87)"]
        RJobs[("jobs: List[Job]<br/>no persistence,<br/>no cache, no file")]
    end
    subgraph External["Optional External Collaborators"]
        EPytz["pytz — lazily imported<br/>inside at() line 499"]
        ELogger["logging logger 'schedule'<br/>DEBUG only — line 50"]
        ECallable["Caller-supplied callable<br/>invoked unguarded — line 691"]
    end
    HDefine --> LFactory
    HLoop --> LSelect
    LRegister --> RJobs
    LSelect -.->|"reads"| RJobs
    LRemove -.->|"mutates"| RJobs
    LCompute -.->|"tz math when at tz used"| EPytz
    LDispatch -.->|"DEBUG records"| ELogger
    LDispatch --> ECallable
    ECallable -.->|"exception propagates<br/>out of run_pending"| HLoop
    LRaise --> HDefine
```

Three properties of this high-level flow drive everything that follows. First, the library never owns a thread — the arrow from `HLoop` into `LSelect` is a plain function call, so all execution latency is the caller's cadence. Second, the only writable state is the `jobs` list created at `schedule/__init__.py` lines 86–87; the process-exit terminal is therefore a total loss of schedule state. Third, the failure edge from the callable returns to the host loop rather than to the library, because `Job.run()` invokes `self.job_func()` at line 691 with no exception guard.

#### 4.1.1.2 Job Definition Journey (F-001 – F-008)

Definition is a fluent builder chain. Every intermediate call mutates and returns the same `Job` instance, and the chain has exactly one commit point: `scheduler.jobs.append(self)` at line 663. Any validation failure before that line leaves the registry untouched, which is the mechanism behind `test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler` (`test_schedule.py` 1591–1599).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    DevStart([Developer defines a job]) --> Every["every interval — default 1<br/>Scheduler.every 162-170<br/>F-001-RQ-001"]
    Every --> UnitChoice{"Select time unit"}
    UnitChoice -->|"plural: seconds/minutes/<br/>hours/days/weeks"| SetUnit["unit assigned, return self<br/>325-378 — F-001-RQ-002"]
    UnitChoice -->|"singular: second/minute/<br/>hour/day/week"| SingularGate{"interval == 1?"}
    SingularGate -->|"no"| ErrInterval["IntervalError<br/>'Use seconds instead of second'<br/>328/339/350/361/372"]
    SingularGate -->|"yes"| SetUnit
    UnitChoice -->|"weekday: monday..sunday"| WeekdayGate{"interval == 1?"}
    WeekdayGate -->|"no"| ErrWeekday["IntervalError<br/>weekly-only rule<br/>383-449 — F-002-RQ-002"]
    WeekdayGate -->|"yes"| SetStartDay["start_day set,<br/>unit forced to weeks<br/>F-002-RQ-001"]
    SetStartDay --> SetUnit
    SetUnit --> Refine{"Optional refinements"}
    Refine -->|".to latest"| ToStep["latest assigned — 561-574<br/>F-005-RQ-001"]
    Refine -->|".at time_str, tz"| AtStep["Validation chain — see 4.2.5.1<br/>471-559 — F-003, F-004"]
    Refine -->|".until moment"| UntilStep["Deadline parsed — see 4.2.5.2<br/>576-642 — F-006"]
    Refine -->|".tag labels"| TagStep{"all tags Hashable?"}
    TagStep -->|"no"| ErrTag["TypeError 'Tags must be hashable'<br/>467 — F-011-RQ-001"]
    TagStep -->|"yes"| TagSet["tags updated as a set<br/>duplicates discarded"]
    ToStep --> Refine
    AtStep --> Refine
    UntilStep --> Refine
    TagSet --> Refine
    Refine -->|"terminate chain"| DoCall["do job_func, args, kwargs<br/>644-664 — F-007"]
    DoCall --> Bind["functools.partial binding +<br/>update_wrapper — 655-656<br/>F-007-RQ-001/002"]
    Bind --> FirstCompute["_schedule_next_run — 657<br/>first next_run computed"]
    FirstCompute --> UnitValid{"unit in seconds/minutes/<br/>hours/days/weeks?"}
    UnitValid -->|"no"| ErrUnit["ScheduleValueError<br/>705-708 — F-016-RQ-002"]
    UnitValid -->|"yes"| LatestValid{"latest >= interval<br/>when to used?"}
    LatestValid -->|"no"| ErrLatest["ScheduleError<br/>'latest is greater than interval'<br/>711 — F-005-RQ-002"]
    LatestValid -->|"yes"| SchedulerBound{"job.scheduler is None?"}
    SchedulerBound -->|"yes"| ErrNoSched["ScheduleError — job not<br/>associated with a scheduler<br/>659-662 — F-007-RQ-003"]
    SchedulerBound -->|"no"| Append["scheduler.jobs.append job — 663"]
    Append --> Registered([Job registered and due-tracked])
    ErrInterval --> Abandoned([Chain aborted — job NEVER appended<br/>F-016-RQ-003])
    ErrWeekday --> Abandoned
    ErrTag --> Abandoned
    ErrUnit --> Abandoned
    ErrLatest --> Abandoned
    ErrNoSched --> Abandoned
```

The ordering in the diagram is load-bearing. `do()` performs binding (line 655), then computation (line 657), then the scheduler-presence check (lines 658–662), and only then registration (line 663) — so a job whose unit was never set raises `ScheduleValueError` from `_schedule_next_run` before it can ever enter the registry.

#### 4.1.1.3 Poll and Dispatch Cycle (F-009)

`Scheduler.run_pending()` is the workhorse. It is a single synchronous pass with three phases — filter, sort, dispatch — and it deliberately performs no catch-up: the docstring at lines 93–97 states that a per-minute job polled hourly runs once, not sixty times. `test_run_pending` (`test_schedule.py` 1387–1425) asserts exactly that with a call-count progression of 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 across widening time jumps, and direct execution in the checkout confirms that a one-second job left 300 seconds overdue is invoked exactly once.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph HostLoop["Host Application — owns the thread and the cadence"]
        TickStart([Loop iteration begins]) --> CallRun["schedule.run_pending<br/>facade 850-854"]
        SleepStep["time.sleep 1 — caller convention<br/>docs/index.rst 46-48"] --> TickStart
        Propagate["Unhandled exception reaches caller<br/>loop aborts unless caller guards"]
    end
    subgraph SchedulerLane["Scheduler.run_pending — 89-101"]
        Filter["runnable_jobs = generator over jobs<br/>where job.should_run — 99"]
        DueCheck{"now >= job.next_run?<br/>should_run 666-672<br/>F-009-RQ-001"}
        SortStep["sorted runnable_jobs<br/>ordering by Job.__lt__ next_run — 100"]
        NextJob{"More due jobs<br/>in this cycle?"}
        RunJobCall["_run_job job — 172-175"]
        Inspect{"return value is CancelJob<br/>instance or class?"}
        Remove["cancel_job: jobs.remove +<br/>DEBUG record — 150-160<br/>F-010-RQ-001"]
        Filter --> DueCheck
        DueCheck -->|"no — skipped this cycle"| NextJob
        DueCheck -->|"yes"| SortStep
        SortStep --> NextJob
        NextJob -->|"yes — earliest next_run first"| RunJobCall
        RunJobCall --> Inspect
        Inspect -->|"yes"| Remove
        Inspect -->|"no"| NextJob
        Remove --> NextJob
    end
    subgraph JobLane["Job.run — 674-698"]
        PreDeadline{"_is_overdue now?<br/>cancel_after passed — 686"}
        SkipRun["DEBUG 'Cancelling job'<br/>return CancelJob without executing<br/>687-688 — F-006-RQ-003"]
        LogRun["DEBUG 'Running job' — 690"]
        Invoke["ret = self.job_func<br/>691 — NO try/except"]
        Stamp["last_run = now — 692"]
        Recompute["_schedule_next_run — 693<br/>recomputed from now, not from slot"]
        PostDeadline{"new next_run past<br/>cancel_after? — 695"}
        ReturnCancel["return CancelJob<br/>priority over job return value"]
        ReturnValue["return ret — 698"]
        PreDeadline -->|"yes"| SkipRun
        PreDeadline -->|"no"| LogRun
        LogRun --> Invoke
        Invoke --> Stamp
        Stamp --> Recompute
        Recompute --> PostDeadline
        PostDeadline -->|"yes"| ReturnCancel
        PostDeadline -->|"no"| ReturnValue
    end
    subgraph CallableLane["Caller-supplied callable"]
        Body["Business logic executes<br/>synchronously, blocking the loop"]
        Raised{"raises exception?"}
        Body --> Raised
    end
    CallRun --> Filter
    NextJob -->|"no — cycle complete"| SleepStep
    RunJobCall --> PreDeadline
    Invoke --> Body
    Raised -->|"no"| Stamp
    Raised -->|"yes — F-009-RQ-004"| Propagate
    ReturnCancel --> Inspect
    ReturnValue --> Inspect
    SkipRun --> Inspect
```

Two dispatch behaviours were verified directly against the checkout. Ordering is by `next_run` ascending — with job A overdue by 5 seconds and job B overdue by 50 seconds, B executed first, which follows from `sorted(runnable_jobs)` at line 100 combined with `Job.__lt__` at lines 257–262. And because the callable runs inline at line 691, a job that blocks for *n* seconds delays every other job in the same cycle by *n* seconds; `docs/index.rst` line 65 states this plainly in bold: schedule does not account for the time a job takes to execute.

`Scheduler.run_all(delay_seconds=0)` (lines 103–120) is the forced-execution variant of the same cycle. It skips the `should_run` filter entirely, iterates a copy (`self.jobs[:]`, line 118) so that self-cancelling jobs cannot corrupt the iteration, and sleeps `delay_seconds` after **every** job including the last — measured at 0.40 s for two jobs with `delay_seconds=0.2`.

#### 4.1.1.4 Next-Run Computation (F-001 – F-005)

`_schedule_next_run()` runs twice per job generation: once at definition time from `do()` (line 657) and once immediately after each successful execution (line 693). It is the single point where interval arithmetic, weekday alignment, clock anchoring, jitter, and timezone correction meet.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    CStart([_schedule_next_run invoked<br/>from do or after each run]) --> UnitGate{"unit whitelisted?<br/>704"}
    UnitGate -->|"no"| CErrUnit["ScheduleValueError<br/>705-708"]
    UnitGate -->|"yes"| JitterGate{"latest set by to?<br/>709"}
    JitterGate -->|"yes"| RangeGate{"latest >= interval?"}
    RangeGate -->|"no"| CErrLatest["ScheduleError — 711"]
    RangeGate -->|"yes"| Draw["interval = random.randint<br/>interval, latest — 712<br/>redrawn every cycle — F-005-RQ-001"]
    JitterGate -->|"no"| UseFixed["interval unchanged — 714"]
    Draw --> NowStep
    UseFixed --> NowStep["now = datetime.now at_time_zone — 717<br/>zone-aware only when tz supplied<br/>F-004-RQ-003"]
    NowStep --> SeedStep["next_run = now — 719"]
    SeedStep --> WeekGate{"start_day set?<br/>721"}
    WeekGate -->|"yes"| WeekUnitGate{"unit == weeks?"}
    WeekUnitGate -->|"no"| CErrWeeks["ScheduleValueError<br/>'unit should be weeks' — 723"]
    WeekUnitGate -->|"yes"| MoveWeekday["_move_to_next_weekday — 724<br/>same weekday NOT advanced;<br/>otherwise nearest future match<br/>F-002-RQ-003"]
    WeekGate -->|"no"| AtGate
    MoveWeekday --> AtGate{"at_time set?<br/>726"}
    AtGate -->|"yes"| MoveAt["_move_to_at_time — 750-771<br/>replace second + microsecond always;<br/>minute for days/hours; hour for days"]
    MoveAt --> FixateOffset["_correct_utc_offset fixate_time=True — 769"]
    AtGate -->|"no"| PeriodStep
    FixateOffset --> PeriodStep["period = timedelta unit: interval — 729"]
    PeriodStep --> MultiGate{"interval != 1?<br/>730"}
    MultiGate -->|"yes"| AddOnce["next_run += period — 731"]
    MultiGate -->|"no"| AdvanceLoop
    AddOnce --> AdvanceLoop{"next_run <= now?<br/>733"}
    AdvanceLoop -->|"yes"| Advance["next_run += period — 734"]
    Advance --> AdvanceLoop
    AdvanceLoop -->|"no"| CorrectStep["_correct_utc_offset<br/>fixate_time = at_time is not None<br/>736-738 — F-004-RQ-004"]
    CorrectStep --> TzGate{"at_time_zone set?<br/>742"}
    TzGate -->|"yes"| ToLocal["astimezone then replace tzinfo=None<br/>744-746 — backward compatibility"]
    TzGate -->|"no"| Assign
    ToLocal --> Assign["self.next_run = next_run<br/>748 — always naive local"]
    Assign --> CEnd([next_run published for should_run,<br/>min, idle_seconds, repr])
```

Because the seed is `now` (line 717) rather than the previous scheduled slot, rescheduling is relative to completion time: a ten-second job that ran seven seconds late is next scheduled more than ten seconds after its previous target. This is the drift acknowledged in `docs/index.rst`. The randomized branch re-draws on every cycle — twenty consecutive draws of `every(5).to(10).seconds` produced all six possible values.

#### 4.1.1.5 UTC Offset and DST Correction (F-004)

`_correct_utc_offset()` (lines 773–817) is the deepest decision point in the library. It behaves as a no-op for naive jobs, as a `pytz` normalisation for interval jobs, and as a wall-clock-preserving correction for `at()`-anchored jobs — with an explicit best-effort branch for times that do not exist during a spring-forward gap.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    OStart([_correct_utc_offset moment, fixate_time<br/>773-817]) --> ZoneGate{"at_time_zone is None?<br/>781"}
    ZoneGate -->|"yes"| Passthrough["return moment unchanged<br/>782 — naive path"]
    ZoneGate -->|"no"| Before["offset_before = moment.utcoffset — 788"]
    Before --> Normalize["moment = at_time_zone.normalize moment — 789"]
    Normalize --> After["offset_after = moment.utcoffset — 790"]
    After --> SameGate{"offset unchanged?<br/>792"}
    SameGate -->|"yes"| ReturnNormal["return normalized moment<br/>794 — no DST boundary crossed"]
    SameGate -->|"no"| FixGate{"fixate_time requested?<br/>798"}
    FixGate -->|"no — interval job"| ReturnShifted["return normalized moment<br/>800 — wall clock allowed to shift"]
    FixGate -->|"yes — at anchored job"| Diff["offset_diff = after - before — 802"]
    Diff --> Restore["moment -= offset_diff — 805<br/>preserve requested HH:MM:SS"]
    Restore --> ReNorm["re_normalized_offset =<br/>normalize moment .utcoffset — 809"]
    ReNorm --> GapGate{"re_normalized_offset<br/>!= offset_after?<br/>810"}
    GapGate -->|"yes — DST gap,<br/>requested time does not exist"| BestEffort["moment += offset_diff — 816<br/>best effort: schedule one offset later<br/>example 02:23 becomes 03:23"]
    GapGate -->|"no"| ReturnFixed["return moment with<br/>wall clock preserved — 817"]
    BestEffort --> ReturnFixed
    Passthrough --> OEnd([corrected moment returned to caller])
    ReturnNormal --> OEnd
    ReturnShifted --> OEnd
    ReturnFixed --> OEnd
```

`docs/timezones.rst` documents the observable outcomes of these branches: a job at `02:30` in `Europe/Berlin` runs once at `03:30` during the spring-forward gap and then returns to `02:30`; during the autumn fold it runs only at the first `02:30`; and jobs **without** a timezone do not account for clock changes at all, so a four-hour interval can elapse in three real hours. Thirty `test_tz_*` methods plus seven `test_align_utc_offset_*` methods in `test_schedule.py` pin these behaviours, including six regression tests named after upstream issues 592, 605, and 608.

#### 4.1.1.6 Cancellation and Deadline Lifecycle (F-006, F-010)

Six distinct triggers remove a job from dispatch. Five are explicit code paths; the sixth is process exit, which is unschedulable state loss rather than an operation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    LStart([Registered job in scheduler.jobs]) --> Trigger{"Which unschedule<br/>trigger fires first?"}
    Trigger -->|"caller calls cancel_job job"| ExplicitPath["cancel_job — 150-160"]
    Trigger -->|"job body returns CancelJob"| SelfPath["_run_job inspects return — 174<br/>isinstance or class identity"]
    Trigger -->|"deadline reached before run"| PreDeadlinePath["run detects _is_overdue now<br/>686-688 — job body skipped"]
    Trigger -->|"deadline reached after run"| PostDeadlinePath["run detects _is_overdue next_run<br/>695-697 — body already executed once more"]
    Trigger -->|"caller calls clear or clear tag"| BulkPath["clear — 135-148"]
    Trigger -->|"process exits"| ProcessEnd["Registry is in-memory only —<br/>all jobs vanish, no persistence"]
    ExplicitPath --> Present{"job present in<br/>jobs list?"}
    Present -->|"yes"| RemoveOk["DEBUG 'Cancelling job'<br/>jobs.remove — 157-158"]
    Present -->|"no"| NoOp["ValueError caught;<br/>DEBUG 'Cancelling not-scheduled job'<br/>159-160 — silent no-op<br/>F-010-RQ-002"]
    SelfPath --> RemoveOk
    PreDeadlinePath --> SelfPath
    PostDeadlinePath --> SelfPath
    BulkPath --> BulkMode{"tag supplied?"}
    BulkMode -->|"no"| ClearAll["DEBUG 'Deleting all jobs'<br/>del jobs[:] — 144-145"]
    BulkMode -->|"yes"| ClearTag["DEBUG 'Deleting all jobs tagged'<br/>slice-assign filter — 147-148"]
    RemoveOk --> Gone([Job no longer dispatched;<br/>Python object may still be held by caller])
    NoOp --> Gone
    ClearAll --> Gone
    ClearTag --> Gone
    ProcessEnd --> Gone
    Gone --> Requeue{"Caller wants it back?"}
    Requeue -->|"yes"| Redefine["Full redefinition required:<br/>every ... .do fn — no reactivate API"]
    Requeue -->|"no"| LEnd([Terminal state])
```

`test_until_time` (`test_schedule.py` 312–390) exercises both deadline paths on the same job definition: a five-second job with a deadline of `11:35:20` created at `11:35:10` runs once at `11:35:15` and remains registered, runs a second time at `11:35:20` and is then removed because the new `next_run` exceeds the deadline, whereas jumping straight to `11:35:50` produces zero invocations and immediate removal.

#### 4.1.1.7 Tag-Based Job Management (F-011, F-012)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Label["Labelling (definition time)"]
        TagCall["job.tag 'daily-tasks', 'reports'<br/>457-469"] --> HashGate{"every tag Hashable?"}
        HashGate -->|"no"| TagErr["TypeError<br/>'Tags must be hashable' — 467"]
        HashGate -->|"yes"| TagStore["tags set updated —<br/>duplicates silently discarded"]
    end
    subgraph Query["Query (any time)"]
        GetAll["get_jobs — 130-131"] --> CopyAll["returns jobs[:] — a shallow COPY,<br/>so caller mutation of the list is safe"]
        GetTag["get_jobs 'daily-tasks' — 133"] --> FilterList["list comprehension where<br/>tag in job.tags"]
        NextTag["next_run 'daily-tasks' — 885-889"] --> FilterMin{"any job carries<br/>the tag?"}
        FilterMin -->|"no"| NoneOut["returns None — 191-192"]
        FilterMin -->|"yes"| MinOut["min jobs_filtered .next_run — 193"]
    end
    subgraph Bulk["Bulk removal"]
        ClearAllCall["clear — 143-145"] --> DelAll["DEBUG 'Deleting all jobs'<br/>then del jobs[:]"]
        ClearTagCall["clear 'daily-tasks' — 146-148"] --> DelTag["DEBUG 'Deleting all jobs tagged'<br/>then slice-assign the survivors"]
    end
    TagStore --> GetTag
    TagStore --> NextTag
    TagStore --> ClearTagCall
    CopyAll --> Outcome([Caller holds Job references for<br/>inspection, repr, or cancel_job])
    FilterList --> Outcome
    MinOut --> Outcome
    NoneOut --> Outcome
    DelAll --> Removed([Jobs no longer dispatched])
    DelTag --> Removed
    TagErr --> Aborted([Chain aborted])
```

Tags are the library's only grouping construct, and the same filter is reused by `get_next_run(tag)` at line 190 — which is why `next_run("unknown-tag")` returns `None` rather than raising.

#### 4.1.1.8 Decorator-Based Registration (F-008)

`repeat()` is a decorator factory whose `job` argument is an already-constructed `Job`. Because the argument is evaluated eagerly at decoration time, registration — and any validation failure — happens while the decorated module is being imported.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Decorator["@repeat registration path — 899-913"]
        RStart(["from schedule import every, repeat"]) --> RFactory["repeat every().minute, args, kwargs<br/>evaluates every() eagerly at<br/>decoration time"]
        RFactory --> RInner["_schedule_decorator receives<br/>the decorated function"]
        RInner --> RDo["job.do decorated_function,<br/>args, kwargs — 910"]
        RDo --> RGates{"same validation gates<br/>as the explicit do path"}
        RGates -->|"fail"| RRaise["Exception raised at IMPORT time<br/>of the module being decorated"]
        RGates -->|"pass"| RAppend["job appended to<br/>default_scheduler.jobs"]
        RAppend --> RReturn["decorator returns the ORIGINAL<br/>function unchanged — 911"]
    end
    RReturn --> RUsable(["Function remains directly callable;<br/>it is also dispatched by run_pending"])
    RRaise --> RFail(["Module import fails —<br/>no job registered"])
    RLimit["Constraint: @repeat does not work on<br/>non-static class methods<br/>docs/examples.rst"]
    RReturn -.-> RLimit
```

### 4.1.2 Integration Workflows

Section 2.3.3 enumerates the integration points as a table. This subsection renders each of them as a flow, and states which integration categories from the section prompt have no counterpart in this repository.

#### 4.1.2.1 Primary Integration Sequence — Host, Library, `pytz`, Logger, Callable

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Dev as Developer / Host code
    participant Facade as schedule module facade
    participant Sched as Scheduler
    participant Job as Job
    participant Pytz as pytz (optional)
    participant Log as logger 'schedule'
    participant Fn as Job callable

    Note over Dev,Fn: Definition phase — synchronous, in-process
    Dev->>Facade: every(1)
    Facade->>Sched: Scheduler.every(1)
    Sched->>Job: Job(interval=1, scheduler=self)
    Job-->>Dev: unconfigured Job (not registered)
    Dev->>Job: .day
    Dev->>Job: .at("12:42", "Europe/Amsterdam")
    Job->>Pytz: import pytz then pytz.timezone(tz)
    Pytz-->>Job: tzinfo object
    Job-->>Dev: self (at_time + at_time_zone set)
    Dev->>Job: .do(task, name="Peter")
    Job->>Job: functools.partial + update_wrapper
    Job->>Job: _schedule_next_run()
    Job->>Pytz: normalize / utcoffset for DST correction
    Pytz-->>Job: corrected zone-aware moment
    Job->>Sched: scheduler.jobs.append(self)
    Job-->>Dev: registered Job

    Note over Dev,Fn: Execution phase — repeated on the caller's cadence
    loop every poll iteration (caller sleeps ~1s)
        Dev->>Facade: run_pending()
        Facade->>Sched: run_pending()
        Sched->>Job: should_run (now >= next_run)
        alt job is due
            Sched->>Job: run()
            Job->>Log: DEBUG "Running job Job(...)"
            Job->>Fn: job_func()
            alt callable succeeds
                Fn-->>Job: return value or CancelJob
                Job->>Job: last_run = now and _schedule_next_run()
                Job-->>Sched: value (or CancelJob on deadline)
            else callable raises
                Fn-->>Dev: exception propagates through run_pending
            end
            opt CancelJob observed
                Sched->>Log: DEBUG "Cancelling job"
                Sched->>Sched: jobs.remove(job)
            end
        else not due
            Sched-->>Facade: job skipped this cycle
        end
    end
```

The `pytz` interaction is the only third-party call in the runtime path, and it is confined to `Job.at()` and the correction helpers. The import itself is executed inside `at()` at line 499, so applications that never pass a timezone never import `pytz` — which is how `pyproject.toml` can declare `dependencies = []` while offering a `timezone = ["pytz"]` extra. When the extra is missing but a timezone is requested, the failure is a plain `ModuleNotFoundError`; `docs/faq.rst` documents `pip install pytz` as the resolution.

#### 4.1.2.2 Background Execution — Caller-Owned Thread

`docs/background-execution.rst` line 4 states that running the schedule in the background is not possible out of the box, then publishes the pattern the caller should implement. The library contributes nothing to this flow beyond `run_pending()`; the thread, the stop signal, and the cadence all belong to the host.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Main as Main thread (host)
    participant Ev as threading.Event
    participant Th as ScheduleThread (host-owned)
    participant Sched as schedule default_scheduler
    participant Fn as background_job

    Main->>Sched: every().second.do(background_job)
    Main->>Ev: cease_continuous_run = Event()
    Main->>Th: ScheduleThread().start()
    Main->>Main: continues with other work
    loop until the Event is set
        Th->>Ev: is_set()?
        Ev-->>Th: False
        Th->>Sched: run_pending()
        Sched->>Fn: job_func() executed on the background thread
        Fn-->>Sched: return value
        Th->>Th: time.sleep(interval)
    end
    Main->>Ev: stop_run_continuously.set()
    Th->>Ev: is_set()?
    Ev-->>Th: True
    Th-->>Main: thread run loop returns and thread ends
    Note over Main,Fn: Pattern is published in docs/background-execution.rst<br/>lines 16-38 and is implemented by the caller, not the library
```

Because the library contains no locking primitives — a grep of `schedule/__init__.py` finds no `threading`, `asyncio`, or lock construct — concurrent mutation of one `Scheduler` from several threads is unsynchronised, and the documentation offers no such pattern.

#### 4.1.2.3 Event and Queue Processing — Producer/Consumer Hand-Off

The closest thing to event processing in this repository is the queue pattern in `docs/parallel-execution.rst` lines 43–62, where the scheduled job body is `jobqueue.put` and the real work happens on a worker thread. The scheduler becomes a pure producer and its cycle time becomes independent of job duration.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant HLoop as Host poll loop
    participant Sched as Scheduler
    participant JobA as Job (jobqueue.put)
    participant Q as queue.Queue (host-owned)
    participant W as Worker thread (host-owned)
    participant Fn as Real job callable

    HLoop->>Sched: run_pending()
    Sched->>JobA: run()
    JobA->>Q: jobqueue.put(job)
    Q-->>JobA: enqueued immediately
    JobA->>JobA: last_run = now, next_run recomputed
    JobA-->>Sched: returns without doing the work
    Sched-->>HLoop: cycle complete in near-zero time
    par worker consumes independently
        W->>Q: jobqueue.get() (blocking)
        Q-->>W: job_func
        W->>Fn: job_func()
        Fn-->>W: completes after arbitrary duration
        W->>Q: task_done()
    end
    Note over HLoop,Fn: docs/parallel-execution.rst lines 43-62.<br/>The scheduler thread never blocks on job duration,<br/>so schedule drift caused by long jobs is avoided.
```

The same document also shows the lighter-weight variant `schedule.every(10).seconds.do(run_threaded, job)`, where the job body starts a fresh `threading.Thread` per occurrence, and notes that the queue model extends naturally to separate worker processes drawing from a distributed work queue.

#### 4.1.2.4 Multiple Independent Schedulers

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph HostProc["Single host process — one thread, one loop"]
        LoopStart([while True]) --> S1Call["scheduler1.run_pending"]
        S1Call --> S2Call["scheduler2.run_pending"]
        S2Call --> Sleep["time.sleep 1"]
        Sleep --> LoopStart
    end
    subgraph Sched1["Scheduler instance 1 — hourly tier"]
        R1[("jobs list<br/>fooJob, barJob<br/>every().hour")]
        D1{"any job due?"}
        R1 --> D1
    end
    subgraph Sched2["Scheduler instance 2 — per-second tier"]
        R2[("jobs list<br/>fooJob, barJob<br/>every().second")]
        D2{"any job due?"}
        R2 --> D2
    end
    S1Call --> R1
    S2Call --> R2
    D1 -->|"yes"| E1["dispatch serially<br/>within instance 1"]
    D1 -->|"no"| Skip1["nothing to do"]
    D2 -->|"yes"| E2["dispatch serially<br/>within instance 2"]
    D2 -->|"no"| Skip2["nothing to do"]
    E1 --> S2Call
    Skip1 --> S2Call
    E2 --> Sleep
    Skip2 --> Sleep
    Note1["Registries are fully isolated:<br/>module-level clear/get_jobs/next_run<br/>affect only default_scheduler<br/>docs/multiple-schedulers.rst 20-34"]
    Sched1 -.-> Note1
    Sched2 -.-> Note1
```

`docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` line 32 carries the operational caveat as an inline comment in its own example: `run_pending` must be called on every scheduler. A missed call silently starves that instance's jobs, since nothing else drives them.

#### 4.1.2.5 Logging and Notification Integration (F-014)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Ops as Operator / host app
    participant Root as logging root config
    participant SL as Logger 'schedule'
    participant Sched as Scheduler
    participant Job as Job
    participant Sink as Handler / log sink

    Ops->>Root: logging.basicConfig()
    Ops->>SL: getLogger('schedule').setLevel(DEBUG)
    Note over SL,Sink: The library creates the logger at import (line 50)<br/>but never attaches a handler or sets a level
    Ops->>Sched: run_all()
    Sched->>SL: debug("Running *all* %i jobs with %is delay in between", n, delay)
    SL->>Sink: DEBUG record emitted
    Sched->>Job: _run_job(job)
    Job->>SL: debug("Running job %s", self)
    SL->>Sink: DEBUG record with Job __str__ rendering
    Job-->>Sched: return value
    Ops->>Sched: clear()
    Sched->>SL: debug("Deleting *all* jobs")
    SL->>Sink: DEBUG record emitted
    Note over Ops,Sink: Only DEBUG records exist — 8 emission sites total.<br/>There is no WARNING/ERROR path, no metric, and no alert hook,<br/>so failures are observed through the propagated exception instead.
```

The eight emission sites are lines 113–117 (`run_all` header), 144 and 147 (`clear`), 157 and 160 (`cancel_job` success and no-op), 687 and 696 (deadline cancellations), and 690 (job start). `docs/logging.rst` also publishes a `print_elapsed_time` decorator as the recommended way to obtain per-job duration telemetry, since the library measures nothing itself.

#### 4.1.2.6 Batch Processing Sequence — The Repository's Only Automated Pipeline

There is no runtime batch processor in this codebase. The only scheduled/automated batch sequence in the repository is the continuous-integration pipeline in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, which fans out five jobs on every push and pull request against `master` and fans back in through the single `needs: test` dependency.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Trigger([push or pull_request<br/>targeting master]) --> Fanout{"GitHub Actions<br/>dispatches 5 jobs"}
    Fanout -->|"job: test<br/>matrix 3.7-3.12, max-parallel 6"| TestJob["checkout@v3 then setup-python@v4<br/>then pip install tox tox-gh-actions<br/>then tox"]
    TestJob --> ToxEnvs["tox-gh-actions expands each version to<br/>pyXX and pyXX-pytz — 12 environments"]
    ToxEnvs --> Pytest["py.test test_schedule.py schedule -v<br/>--cov schedule --cov-report term-missing"]
    Pytest --> PytestGate{"81 tests pass?"}
    PytestGate -->|"no"| Fail(["Workflow fails —<br/>merge blocked"])
    PytestGate -->|"yes"| Mypy["python -m mypy -p schedule<br/>--install-types --non-interactive"]
    Mypy --> MypyGate{"types clean?"}
    MypyGate -->|"no"| Fail
    MypyGate -->|"yes"| Cov["pip3 install coveralls then<br/>coveralls --service=github<br/>COVERALLS_PARALLEL=true"]
    Cov --> Finish["job: coveralls — needs: test<br/>coveralls --finish --service=github"]
    Fanout -->|"job: docs"| DocsJob["tox -e docs =<br/>sphinx-build -W -b html<br/>warnings are errors"]
    Fanout -->|"job: formatting"| FmtJob["tox -e format =<br/>black --check . (black==20.8b1)"]
    Fanout -->|"job: setuppy"| SetupJob["tox -e setuppy =<br/>setup.py check --strict<br/>--metadata --restructuredtext"]
    DocsJob --> DocsGate{"docs build clean?"}
    DocsGate -->|"no"| Fail
    DocsGate -->|"yes"| Pass
    FmtJob --> FmtGate{"formatting matches?"}
    FmtGate -->|"no"| Fail
    FmtGate -->|"yes"| Pass
    SetupJob --> SetupGate{"metadata and README valid?"}
    SetupGate -->|"no"| Fail
    SetupGate -->|"yes"| Pass
    Finish --> Pass(["All gates green —<br/>coverage summary posted"])
```

#### 4.1.2.7 Data Flow Summary and Absent Integration Categories

| Data flow | Direction | Carrier | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Job configuration | Host → library | Method arguments on the fluent chain | `schedule/__init__.py` 162–664 |
| Job registration | Library → in-memory registry | `list.append` | line 663 |
| Due-job selection | Registry → dispatcher | Generator + `sorted()` | lines 99–101 |
| Work invocation | Library → host callable | `functools.partial` call | line 691 |
| Cancellation signal | Host callable → library | `CancelJob` return value | lines 174–175 |
| Zone/DST data | `pytz` → library | `timezone()`, `normalize()`, `utcoffset()` | lines 499–508, 789–809 |
| Diagnostics | Library → `logging` | 8 `logger.debug` records | line 50 and emission sites |
| Introspection | Registry → host | `get_jobs`, `next_run`, `idle_seconds`, `repr` | lines 122–206, 264–323 |

The section prompt anticipates several integration categories that do not exist here, and their absence is verifiable rather than assumed. There is no API interaction of the network kind — no HTTP client or server, no socket, and no RPC construct appears anywhere in the module. There is no event bus, broker, or subscription mechanism; the only queue in the repository is the caller-owned `queue.Queue` in a documentation example. There is no data-flow-between-systems in the persistence sense, because no file, database, or serialization call exists in the runtime module. Section 2.3.3 records the same conclusion for the feature layer.

This subsection provides the structured metadata the section prompt requires for each workflow drawn in §4.1: explicit start and end points, the system boundary each step sits inside, every decision diamond, the user touchpoints, the error and recovery edges, and the timing characteristics. Workflows are referenced by the short identifiers below.

| ID | Workflow | Diagram location |
|---|---|---|
| WF-1 | High-level system workflow | §4.1.1.1 |
| WF-2 | Job definition journey | §4.1.1.2 |
| WF-3 | Poll and dispatch cycle | §4.1.1.3 |
| WF-4 | Next-run computation | §4.1.1.4 |
| WF-5 | UTC offset and DST correction | §4.1.1.5 |
| WF-6 | Cancellation and deadline lifecycle | §4.1.1.6 |
| WF-7 | Tag-based job management | §4.1.1.7 |
| WF-8 | Decorator-based registration | §4.1.1.8 |

| IN-2 | Background execution | §4.1.2.2 |
| IN-3 | Queue producer/consumer hand-off | §4.1.2.3 |

| IN-5 | Logging and notification | §4.1.2.5 |
| IN-6 | CI batch pipeline | §4.1.2.6 |

### 4.2.1 Start Points, End Points and System Boundaries

| Workflow | Start point | Terminal end points | Boundary crossed |
|---|---|---|---|
| WF-1 | Application start and `import schedule` | Process exit (all state lost) | Host process only — no external boundary |
| WF-2 | `Scheduler.every(interval)` (line 162) | `Registered` (append at 663) or `Abandoned` (any raise before 663) | Host code → library |
| WF-3 | Caller invokes `run_pending()` (line 850) | Cycle complete → caller sleeps; or exception escapes to caller | Library → caller callable → back to library |
| WF-4 | `_schedule_next_run()` entry (line 700) | `next_run` assigned (line 748) or a validation raise | Internal; crosses into `pytz` only when `at_time_zone` is set |
| WF-5 | `_correct_utc_offset()` entry (line 773) | Corrected moment returned (782, 794, 800, 817) | Library → `pytz` |
| WF-6 | Registered job in `scheduler.jobs` | `Gone` — dispatch stops; re-entry requires full redefinition | Host code and/or job return value → library |
| WF-7 | `tag()` at definition time | Caller holds `Job` references, or jobs removed | Host code → library |
| WF-8 | Module import evaluates `@repeat(every()...)` | Function registered and returned unchanged, or import fails | Import machinery → library |
| IN-1 | `every(1)` on the facade | Loop continues indefinitely on the caller's cadence | Host ↔ library ↔ `pytz` ↔ logging ↔ callable |
| IN-2 | `ScheduleThread().start()` in host code | `Event.set()` ends the thread's run loop | Host thread → library (unsynchronised) |
| IN-3 | `run_pending()` dispatches `jobqueue.put` | Worker completes the real work and calls `task_done()` | Library → host queue → host worker thread |
| IN-4 | `while True` over several `Scheduler` instances | Loop continues; each instance is independent | Host loop → N isolated registries |
| IN-5 | Host sets the `schedule` logger to DEBUG | Records delivered to the host's handlers | Library → `logging` → host sink |
| IN-6 | `push` or `pull_request` to `master` | All gates green, or workflow failure blocking merge | GitHub Actions → tox → pytest/mypy/Sphinx/black/setuptools → Coveralls |

The system boundary of the product itself is narrow and worth stating precisely: everything inside `schedule/__init__.py` is in scope, and the thread of control, the exception policy, the log sinks, the concurrency model, and any durability are all outside it. Section 1.3 records the same boundary at the scope level.

### 4.2.2 Decision Point Register

Every decision diamond drawn in §4.1 maps to a concrete branch in the source. The table below is the consolidated register.

| Workflow | Decision | Source and outcome |
|---|---|---|
| WF-2 | Singular unit used with `interval != 1`? | 326–372 → `IntervalError`, chain aborted |
| WF-2 | Weekday accessor with `interval != 1`? | 380–455 → `IntervalError`, chain aborted |
| WF-2 | All `tag()` arguments hashable? | 466–467 → `TypeError`, chain aborted |
| WF-2 | `job.scheduler is None` at `do()`? | 658–662 → `ScheduleError`, never registered |
| WF-3 | `now >= next_run` (`should_run`)? | 672 → job enters this cycle or is skipped entirely |
| WF-3 | More due jobs remaining in the cycle? | 100 → iterate in `next_run` order, else cycle ends |
| WF-3 | Return value is `CancelJob` (instance or class)? | 174 → `cancel_job()` or leave registered |
| WF-3 | Deadline already passed before running? | 686 → skip the body and return `CancelJob` |
| WF-3 | New `next_run` past the deadline after running? | 695 → return `CancelJob`, overriding the job's value |
| WF-4 | `unit` in the five-unit whitelist? | 704 → proceed or `ScheduleValueError` |
| WF-4 | `latest` set, and is `latest >= interval`? | 709–712 → draw `random.randint` or `ScheduleError` |
| WF-4 | `start_day` set, and is `unit == "weeks"`? | 721–723 → weekday alignment or `ScheduleValueError` |
| WF-4 | `at_time` set? | 726 → apply `_move_to_at_time` |
| WF-4 | `interval != 1`? | 730 → add one extra period before the advance loop |
| WF-4 | `next_run <= now`? | 733 → keep adding the period until strictly future |
| WF-4 | `at_time_zone` set? | 742 → convert to naive local before publishing |
| WF-5 | `at_time_zone is None`? | 781 → return unchanged |
| WF-5 | Offset changed by `normalize()`? | 792 → return, or continue to the fixate branch |
| WF-5 | `fixate_time` requested? | 798 → preserve wall clock, or accept the shift |
| WF-5 | Re-normalised offset differs (DST gap)? | 810 → shift one offset later as a best effort |
| WF-6 | Job present in the list when cancelled? | 156–160 → removal or silent no-op |
| WF-6 | `clear()` called with a tag? | 143–148 → delete all, or filter by tag |
| WF-7 | Any job carries the requested tag? | 191–193 → earliest `next_run`, or `None` |
| IN-2 | `Event.is_set()`? | Host-side loop guard in `docs/background-execution.rst` line 32 |
| IN-6 | Each gate: tests, mypy, docs, formatting, metadata | Any failure fails the workflow |

### 4.2.3 User Touchpoints, Error States and Recovery Paths

The only user interface is the Python API; there is no CLI, configuration file, admin console, or web interface anywhere in the repository. Touchpoints are therefore API calls, and the "user" is the developer or operator of the host application.

| Touchpoint | Surface | Workflow | Failure mode surfaced to the user |
|---|---|---|---|
| Define a schedule | `every` → unit → `at`/`to`/`until`/`tag` → `do` | WF-2 | `IntervalError`, `ScheduleValueError`, `TypeError`, `ScheduleError` at the call site |
| Register by decorator | `@repeat(every()...)` | WF-8 | Same exceptions, raised during module import |
| Drive the schedule | `run_pending()`, `run_all(delay_seconds)` | WF-3 | Any exception raised by the job body propagates here |
| Inspect the schedule | `get_jobs(tag)`, `next_run(tag)`, `idle_seconds()`, `repr(job)` | WF-7 | Returns `None`/empty rather than raising |
| Stop work | `cancel_job(job)`, `clear(tag)`, returning `CancelJob` | WF-6 | Cancelling an unknown job is a deliberate no-op |
| Observe behaviour | `logging.getLogger('schedule')` at DEBUG | IN-5 | Silence if the level is not lowered — the library adds no handler |

| Error state | Where it appears | Recovery path |
|---|---|---|
| Invalid configuration | WF-2, WF-4, WF-8 | Fix the chain and re-run it; the registry was never mutated, proven by `test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler` |
| Missing `pytz` | WF-5 via line 499 | `pip install pytz` per `docs/faq.rst`; only affects `at()` calls that pass a timezone |
| Unknown timezone name | `pytz.timezone()` at line 502 | Correct the IANA name; `pytz.exceptions.UnknownTimeZoneError` propagates unchanged |
| Non-existent wall-clock time (DST gap) | WF-5 line 810 | Automatic — the job is scheduled one offset later; no user action, no exception |
| Job body raises | WF-3 line 691 | Caller-side only: guard the loop, or wrap the callable with the `catch_exceptions` decorator from `docs/exception-handling.rst` |
| Deadline reached | WF-6 lines 686 and 695 | Automatic unschedule; re-arm by defining a new job with a new `until()` |
| Process restart | WF-1 terminal | Re-run the definition code — there is no persistence to restore from |

### 4.2.4 Timing and SLA Considerations

**No service-level agreement, timeout, watchdog, retry budget, or deadline for job bodies exists in this repository.** A search across all 32 tracked files for `timeout`, `sla`, `retry`, `backoff`, `watchdog`, and `circuit` returns no matches, and the only sleep in the runtime module is `time.sleep(delay_seconds)` at line 120, used solely to space out `run_all()`. What the code and documentation do establish is a set of timing *characteristics*, which the following table records exactly.

| Timing property | Value / behaviour | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduling resolution | Whole seconds; `at()` accepts second precision, sub-second is a documented non-goal | `at()` regexes 513–527; `docs/index.rst` non-goals |
| Dispatch latency | Bounded by the caller's poll period, not by the library; the documented convention is `time.sleep(1)` | `docs/index.rst` 46–48; `README.rst` |
| Due-window semantics | `now >= next_run` — a job stays due indefinitely until it is polled | line 672 |
| Missed occurrences | Never replayed, regardless of how long the gap is | docstring 93–97; verified once-only execution after a 300 s gap |
| Serialisation cost | A job blocking for *n* seconds delays every later job in the same cycle by *n* seconds | inline call at line 691; `docs/index.rst` line 65 |
| Reschedule anchor | `now` at completion, not the intended slot — so execution time accumulates as drift | line 717; verified in the checkout |
| `run_all` spacing | `delay_seconds` is slept after every job including the last; total ≈ *n* × delay | line 120; measured 0.40 s for 2 jobs at 0.2 s |
| Exact-wait option | `idle_seconds()` returns the precise wait, negative when overdue, `None` when the registry is empty | 197–206; `test_idle_seconds` 1491 |
| Randomised spacing | `to()` re-draws uniformly in `[interval, latest]` on every reschedule | line 712; 20 draws covered all values 5–10 |
| DST gap handling | Best-effort shift of one UTC offset (for example 02:23 becomes 03:23) | 810–816; `docs/timezones.rst` |
| CI pipeline timing | No `timeout-minutes` is configured on any job; up to 6 matrix entries run in parallel | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` line 15 |
| Test suite duration | The 81-test suite completes in well under a second locally | measured `81 passed` on Python 3.12.3 |

The interaction of poll cadence, serial execution, and duration-induced drift is what a reader most often needs to reason about. The gantt below shows a two-second job and a three-second blocking job sharing one loop.

```mermaid
gantt
    title Poll cadence, dispatch latency and duration-induced drift
    dateFormat HH:mm:ss
    axisFormat %H:%M:%S
    section Host loop
    Tick 1 run_pending      :t1, 12:00:00, 1s
    Sleep 1s after tick 1   :t2, after t1, 1s
    Tick 2 run_pending      :t3, after t2, 1s
    Sleep 1s after tick 2   :t4, after t3, 1s
    Tick 3 run_pending      :t5, after t4, 1s
    section Job A every 2s
    Waits until due 12:00:02   :a0, 12:00:00, 2s
    Executes on tick 2         :a1, after a0, 1s
    Next run recomputed from now :a2, after a1, 2s
    section Job B blocking 3s
    Queued behind Job A        :b1, 12:00:03, 1s
    Blocks the loop 3s         :b2, after b1, 3s
    Next run drifts by run time :b3, after b2, 2s
```

Callers who need the tightest achievable latency without busy-waiting use the `idle_seconds()` loop published in `docs/examples.rst`, which also gives the loop a clean exit when the registry drains.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    IStart([Host chooses the precise-wait loop<br/>docs/examples.rst]) --> Query["n = schedule.idle_seconds<br/>197-206"]
    Query --> NoneGate{"n is None?"}
    NoneGate -->|"yes — registry empty"| Break(["break — no jobs remain,<br/>loop exits cleanly"])
    NoneGate -->|"no"| SignGate{"n > 0?"}
    SignGate -->|"yes"| SleepExact["time.sleep n —<br/>wakes exactly at next_run"]
    SignGate -->|"no — n is negative,<br/>work is already overdue"| NoSleep["skip sleeping"]
    SleepExact --> Dispatch["schedule.run_pending"]
    NoSleep --> Dispatch
    Dispatch --> Requery{"jobs still registered?"}
    Requery -->|"yes"| Query
    Requery -->|"no"| Break
```

### 4.2.5 Validation Rules

All validation in this library is **fail-fast and definition-time**. There is no runtime validation of job results, no schema, and no sanitisation of the values a job returns — the only value the library interprets from a job body is the `CancelJob` sentinel.

#### 4.2.5.1 Data Validation — the `at()` Clock and Timezone Chain

`Job.at()` applies six gates in a fixed order. The order matters because an earlier gate can mask a later one: the unit gate fires before the timezone is resolved, and the timezone is resolved before the time string is even type-checked.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    VStart([".at time_str, tz called<br/>471-559"]) --> G1{"unit in days/hours/minutes<br/>OR start_day set?<br/>493"}
    G1 -->|"no"| E1["ScheduleValueError<br/>'Invalid unit valid units are<br/>days, hours, and minutes'<br/>494-496 — F-003-RQ-001"]
```

| Unit | Pattern (line) | Accepted in tests | Rejected in tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| `days` / weekday | `^[0-2]\d:[0-5]\d(:[0-5]\d)?$` (513) | `"10:30"`, `"20:59"`, `"10:30:50"` | `"2:30:000001"`, `"::2"`, `".2"`, `"2"`, `":2"`, `" 2:30:00"`, `"59:59"` |

The accepted and rejected sets above are taken verbatim from `test_at_time` (`test_schedule.py` 268–310), `test_at_time_hour` (411–443) and `test_at_time_minute` (445–461). Note the leading-space rejections: the patterns are anchored, so whitespace is never tolerated. Beyond the regex, the day/weekday path additionally range-checks the hour against 0–23 at lines 544–549, which is what rejects `"25:00:00"` even though the pattern's `[0-2]\d` would admit it.

#### 4.2.5.3 Business Rules by Workflow Step

These are the domain rules the library enforces, expressed as rules rather than as code.

| Rule | Enforced at | Consequence if violated |
|---|---|---|
| A job must declare exactly one time unit before it can be registered | `_schedule_next_run` whitelist, line 704 | `ScheduleValueError`; `every().do(fn)` cannot register |
| Singular unit aliases are reserved for `interval == 1` | 326–372 | `IntervalError` naming the plural form to use |
| Weekday scheduling is weekly-only — "every 2 or more weeks" is unsupported | 380–455 | `IntervalError` with the explicit weekly-only message |
| A `start_day` is only meaningful with the `weeks` unit | 721–723 | `ScheduleValueError` (`unit` should be `weeks`) |
| Only day, hour and minute jobs (or weekday jobs) may be clock-anchored | 493–496 | `ScheduleValueError` listing the valid units |
| Timezones are configurable only through `at()` | `at()` signature, line 471 | No other API accepts a zone; `docs/timezones.rst` states the restriction |
| A randomised range must be non-inverted (`latest >= interval`) | 709–711 | `ScheduleError` |
| A deadline must lie in the future at definition time | 638–641 | `ScheduleValueError` |
| A deadline suppresses execution rather than truncating it — the body is skipped once the moment has passed | 686–688 | Job returns `CancelJob` without running |
| Tags must be hashable | 466–467 | `TypeError`; duplicates are collapsed by the set |
| A job must be bound to a scheduler to be registered | 658–662 | `ScheduleError` |
| Registration is the last step, so invalid jobs never reach the registry | 657–663 | Scheduler integrity preserved (`test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler`) |
| Same weekday today is not skipped when computing the next weekly run | 924–927 | A Wednesday job defined on Wednesday can still run today |
| Public datetimes are naive local values | 742–746 | Zone-aware inputs are converted back before publication |
| Missed occurrences are never replayed | 99–101 and docstring 93–97 | At most one execution per job per poll cycle |
| Cancelling an unknown job is a no-op, not an error | 156–160 | Idempotent teardown |

#### 4.2.5.4 Authorization Checkpoints

There are **no authorization checkpoints in any workflow**, and this is a structural property rather than an oversight. `schedule/__init__.py` contains no authentication, authorization, credential, token, encryption, or permission logic — a case-insensitive search of the module for `auth`, `token`, `password`, `secret`, `credential`, and `encrypt` returns nothing. The library also has no notion of a user, a principal, a role, or a tenant: the `Job` field set defined at lines 227–255 carries only scheduling data, and the closest thing to a grouping key is the free-form `tags` set.

The practical consequence for architects is that **the trust boundary is the host process**. Any code able to import the module can register a job, cancel any job, or clear the entire registry, because `default_scheduler` is a module-level singleton (line 837) and `jobs` is a direct alias to its mutable list (line 840). Where isolation between logical tenants is required, the only mechanism the repository supports is separate `Scheduler()` instances (§4.1.2.4) — and even that is an organisational convention, not an enforced permission boundary. Section 1.3 records the absence of an authentication or authorization concept at the scope level.

#### 4.2.5.5 Regulatory Compliance Checks

No workflow performs a regulatory compliance check, and no such requirement is expressed anywhere in the repository: searches for `gdpr`, `hipaa`, `pci`, and `compliance` return no matches in the runtime module. The only compliance-relevant artifact in the tree is licensing — `LICENSE.txt` is the MIT License (Copyright © 2013 Daniel Bader), declared as `license = {text = "MIT License"}` in `pyproject.toml`, `license="MIT"` in `setup.py`, and via the `License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License` classifier. `docs/installation.rst` leans on that permissiveness when it notes that the library is a single MIT-licensed source file that may be vendored manually, while discouraging the practice.

Two data-handling facts matter for downstream compliance reviews, and both are properties of the flows already documented. First, the DEBUG records emitted at lines 113–117 and 690 render the job through `Job.__str__`, which includes the bound `args` and `kwargs`; any sensitive value passed to `do()` will therefore appear in logs whenever the host lowers the `schedule` logger to DEBUG. Second, nothing is ever written outside the process — there is no file, database, network, or serialization call in the module — so the library itself creates no data-at-rest obligation. Retention, residency, and redaction are entirely properties of the host application's logging configuration and of the job bodies it schedules.


## 4.3 Technical Implementation

### 4.3.1 State Management

#### 4.3.1.1 The Complete State Model

All state in this system lives in two places: the twelve instance attributes a `Job` assigns in `__init__` (lines 227–255) and the single list a `Scheduler` creates in `__init__` (lines 86–87). There is no other store, no module-level mutable state besides `default_scheduler` and its `jobs` alias, and no derived index or secondary structure.

| `Job` attribute | Type / default | Written by | Read by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `interval` | `int`, constructor argument | `every(interval)` | period arithmetic, `repr` |
| `latest` | `Optional[int]`, `None` | `to(latest)` (line 573) | jitter draw at 712 |
| `job_func` | `Optional[functools.partial]`, `None` | `do()` (655–656) | `run()` at 691, `__str__`/`__repr__` |
| `unit` | `Optional[str]`, `None` | unit and weekday properties (325–455) | whitelist at 704, `timedelta` key at 729 |
| `at_time` | `Optional[datetime.time]`, `None` | `at()` (558) | `_move_to_at_time`, `fixate_time` flag |
| `at_time_zone` | untyped, `None` | `at(tz=...)` (502–504) | `now` construction 717, `_correct_utc_offset` |
| `last_run` | `Optional[datetime]`, `None` | `run()` after a successful call (692) | `__repr__` timestats |
| `next_run` | `Optional[datetime]`, `None` | `_schedule_next_run()` (748) | `should_run`, `__lt__`, `min()`, `idle_seconds` |
| `start_day` | `Optional[str]`, `None` | weekday properties (380–455) | weekday alignment 721–724, `at()` unit gate |
| `cancel_after` | `Optional[datetime]`, `None` | `until()` (606–632) | `_is_overdue` (819–820) |
| `tags` | `Set[Hashable]`, empty set | `tag()` (469) | `get_jobs`, `clear`, `get_next_run` |
| `scheduler` | `Optional[Scheduler]`, constructor argument | `Scheduler.every()` (169) | registration guard 658–663 |

Two observations follow directly from this model. The `Job` is **mutable throughout its life** — `next_run` and `last_run` are rewritten in place on every execution — so a caller holding a `Job` reference always observes current values, which is what makes `repr(job)` a useful diagnostic. And `next_run` is the only piece of *derived* state: everything else is either configuration supplied by the caller or a timestamp of fact.

#### 4.3.1.2 Job State Transitions

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    direction TB
    [*] --> Unconfigured : Scheduler.every(interval) — 162-170
    Unconfigured --> UnitBound : plural unit property sets unit — 325-378
    Unconfigured --> WeekdayBound : monday..sunday sets start_day + weeks — 380-455
    Unconfigured --> DefinitionFailed : IntervalError on singular unit or weekday with interval != 1
    UnitBound --> UnitBound : .to(latest) / .at(...) / .until(...) / .tag(...)
    WeekdayBound --> UnitBound : returns self.weeks
    UnitBound --> DefinitionFailed : ScheduleValueError / TypeError from at() or until()
    UnitBound --> Registered : .do(func) computes next_run then appends — 655-663
    UnitBound --> DefinitionFailed : ScheduleValueError on invalid unit, ScheduleError on latest or missing scheduler
    DefinitionFailed --> [*] : object garbage-collected, never in scheduler.jobs
    Registered --> Idle : next_run in the future
    Idle --> Due : wall clock reaches next_run (should_run True — 672)
    Due --> Idle : caller has not polled yet — no catch-up queue
    Due --> DeadlineExpired : _is_overdue(now) before execution — 686
    Due --> Running : Job.run invokes job_func — 691
    Running --> Rescheduled : last_run stamped, next_run recomputed — 692-693
    Running --> Faulted : callable raised — last_run and next_run unchanged
    Faulted --> Due : still overdue, retried on the next poll with no backoff
    Rescheduled --> Idle : new next_run inside deadline
    Rescheduled --> DeadlineExpired : new next_run past cancel_after — 695
    Rescheduled --> SelfCancelled : callable returned CancelJob — 174
    DeadlineExpired --> Unscheduled : _run_job calls cancel_job
    SelfCancelled --> Unscheduled : _run_job calls cancel_job
    Idle --> Unscheduled : caller invokes cancel_job / clear / clear(tag)
    Due --> Unscheduled : caller invokes cancel_job / clear / clear(tag)
    Unscheduled --> [*] : removed from scheduler.jobs, requires full redefinition
```

The `Due → Idle` self-loop is not an idle transition, it is the missed-run contract: the wall clock can pass many scheduled instants while the job sits in `Due`, and the job still executes only once when the caller finally polls. The `Faulted → Due` edge is equally important — a job whose callable raised is left exactly as it was, with stale `last_run` and `next_run`, so it re-qualifies as due immediately and is attempted again on the next cycle without any backoff, ceiling, or dead-letter state.

#### 4.3.1.3 Scheduler Registry State Transitions

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> Empty : Scheduler() — jobs = [] (86-87)
    Empty --> Populated : job.do(...) appends (663)
    Populated --> Populated : further do() appends / tag() mutations
    Populated --> Populated : run_pending or run_all mutate next_run and last_run in place
    Populated --> Populated : cancel_job removes one entry (158)
    Populated --> Empty : clear() executes del jobs[:] (145)
    Populated --> Populated : clear(tag) slice-assigns the surviving jobs (148)
    Populated --> Empty : last remaining job cancelled or self-cancelled
    Empty --> Empty : cancel_job on an unknown job — ValueError swallowed (159-160)
    Empty --> [*] : process exits — registry is memory-only, nothing is written or restored
    Populated --> [*] : process exits — every pending schedule is lost
```

#### 4.3.1.4 Data Persistence Points

**There are no persistence points.** The runtime module performs no file, database, or serialization operation of any kind: it imports only `collections.abc`, `datetime`, `functools`, `logging`, `random`, `re`, `time`, and `typing` (lines 41–48), and searches of the module for `open(`, `pickle`, `json`, `sqlite`, `shelve`, `dbm`, and `os.` return nothing. `docs/index.rst` lists job persistence first among the reasons to choose a different library.

| Candidate persistence concern | Actual behaviour |
|---|---|
| Schedule durability across restarts | None — the registry is rebuilt only by re-executing the definition code |
| Job execution history | Only `last_run` on the live object; overwritten on each run, never appended to a log of runs |
| Crash recovery / journaling | None — an interrupted process leaves no artifact to replay |
| Configuration storage | None — configuration is Python code; there is no config file format |
| External state hand-off | Only what a job body chooses to do; the queue pattern in `docs/parallel-execution.rst` is the documented way to move work to durable infrastructure |

Applications that require durability must therefore treat the definition code itself as the schedule's source of truth and re-establish it at start-up — which is precisely why `@repeat` (§4.1.1.8) registering at import time is a coherent design for this library.

#### 4.3.1.5 Caching Requirements

There is no cache. No `functools.lru_cache`, memoization decorator, TTL structure, or invalidation hook appears anywhere in the module. The only value that behaves cache-like is `next_run`: it is computed once per generation and then read many times by `should_run`, `__lt__`, `min()`, `idle_seconds`, and `__repr__`. Its invalidation rule is a single line — `_schedule_next_run()` recomputes and overwrites it at line 748 — and it is invoked in exactly two places, `do()` (line 657) and `run()` (line 693). Two consequences are worth recording:

- Mutating a job's configuration after registration does **not** refresh `next_run`; the new configuration only takes effect after the next execution recomputes it, because nothing observes attribute writes.
- `Scheduler.get_next_run()` and `idle_seconds` are computed on demand from the live list (lines 177–206) rather than maintained incrementally, so they are always consistent with the registry and never stale.

#### 4.3.1.6 Transaction Boundaries

The library provides no transactions and makes no atomicity claim; the boundaries below are the *effective* units of work implied by the code, and they matter because several of them are deliberately non-atomic.

| Unit of work | Boundary and guarantee | Failure behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Job definition (`do()`) | Effectively atomic with respect to the registry: computation at 657 precedes the append at 663 | Any raise leaves the registry unchanged — the central integrity property of §4.1.1.2 |
| Single job execution (`Job.run()`) | **Not atomic.** Invocation (691), timestamping (692) and rescheduling (693) are three separate steps | A raise after side effects have occurred leaves the work done but the schedule un-advanced, so the same occurrence is attempted again |
| Poll cycle (`run_pending()`) | Not atomic. The due set is computed first (99) and then dispatched (100–101) | An exception mid-cycle abandons the remaining due jobs for that cycle; nothing is rolled back |
| Forced run (`run_all()`) | Not atomic; iterates a snapshot copy `self.jobs[:]` (118) | Earlier jobs stay executed; later jobs are never attempted |
| Cancellation (`cancel_job()`) | Single `list.remove` inside a `try` (156–160) | `ValueError` is swallowed, making the operation idempotent |
| Bulk clear | `del self.jobs[:]` (145) or one slice assignment (148) | No partial-clear path exists in the code |
| Cross-scheduler operations | No boundary at all — each `Scheduler` is independent | A failure while polling `scheduler1` prevents `scheduler2.run_pending()` from being reached in that iteration |

Because the module contains no locking primitive of any kind, none of these boundaries is protected against concurrent mutation. The library documents no thread-safety guarantee: `docs/parallel-execution.rst` and `docs/background-execution.rst` both hand thread ownership to the caller, and `docs/index.rst` lists concurrent execution as a non-goal. Applications that mutate one `Scheduler` from several threads must serialise that access themselves.

The most operationally significant line in the table is the second one. Since the timestamp and the reschedule happen *after* the callable returns, job bodies are effectively **at-least-once within a cycle** when they fail part-way through: any externally visible side effect that completed before the exception will be repeated on the retry. Idempotent job bodies, or the `cancel_on_failure` wrapper described below, are the two mitigations the repository documents.

### 4.3.2 Error Handling

#### 4.3.2.1 Error Taxonomy and Propagation

The library defines a three-level exception hierarchy at lines 53–68 — `ScheduleError` → `ScheduleValueError` → `IntervalError` — and raises from 28 sites: twelve `IntervalError`, eleven `ScheduleValueError`, three built-in `TypeError`, and two `ScheduleError`. Every one of them fires during **definition**. At **execution** time the library raises nothing of its own; it simply does not interfere with whatever the job body raises.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    EStart([Error surfaces somewhere<br/>in the schedule flow]) --> Phase{"Which phase?"}
    Phase -->|"Definition time<br/>builder chain"| DefClass{"Which guard fired?"}
    DefClass -->|"interval rule<br/>328-449"| IntervalErr["IntervalError<br/>subclass of ScheduleValueError"]
    DefClass -->|"format, unit, timezone type,<br/>hour range, deadline<br/>494-547, 625-641, 705-723, 942"| ValueErr["ScheduleValueError<br/>subclass of ScheduleError"]
    DefClass -->|"wrong Python type<br/>467, 511, 634"| TypeErr["TypeError<br/>built-in, not in the hierarchy"]
    DefClass -->|"latest < interval 711,<br/>no scheduler bound 659"| SchedErr["ScheduleError<br/>hierarchy root"]
    IntervalErr --> DefOutcome["Exception raised to the definition<br/>call site; job never appended;<br/>scheduler untouched — F-016-RQ-003"]
    ValueErr --> DefOutcome
    TypeErr --> DefOutcome
    SchedErr --> DefOutcome
    DefOutcome --> DefRecover["Recovery: caller fixes the chain and<br/>re-runs it. Verified by<br/>test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler"]
    Phase -->|"Execution time<br/>inside job_func"| RunFault["Exception raised by the<br/>caller-supplied callable — line 691"]
    RunFault --> NoGuard["No try/except exists around<br/>line 691 — F-009-RQ-004"]
    NoGuard --> Consequence["last_run NOT stamped;<br/>next_run NOT recomputed;<br/>job stays registered and overdue"]
    Consequence --> Bubble["Exception propagates through<br/>_run_job then run_pending/run_all<br/>to the caller's loop"]
    Bubble --> LoopFate{"Does the caller<br/>guard the loop?"}
    LoopFate -->|"no"| LoopDies["Loop terminates; remaining due jobs<br/>in this cycle are never dispatched;<br/>whole schedule stops"]
    LoopFate -->|"yes — try/except<br/>around run_pending"| LoopSurvives["Loop continues; the failed job is<br/>retried on the next poll because it<br/>is still overdue — no backoff, no cap"]
    RunFault --> Wrapped{"Is the callable wrapped in the<br/>documented catch_exceptions<br/>decorator?"}
    Wrapped -->|"yes, cancel_on_failure=False"| Swallow["Traceback printed by the wrapper;<br/>run continues normally and the job<br/>is rescheduled"]
    Wrapped -->|"yes, cancel_on_failure=True"| SelfKill["Wrapper returns schedule.CancelJob;<br/>_run_job unschedules the job<br/>docs/exception-handling.rst 13-31"]
    Wrapped -->|"no"| NoGuard
    Phase -->|"Timezone resolution"| TzFault{"pytz importable?"}
    TzFault -->|"no"| ModErr["ModuleNotFoundError from line 499;<br/>resolution documented in docs/faq.rst<br/>as pip install pytz"]
    TzFault -->|"yes, unknown zone"| ZoneErr["pytz UnknownTimeZoneError<br/>from line 502"]
    ModErr --> DefOutcome
    ZoneErr --> DefOutcome
    Phase -->|"DST boundary"| DstFault["Requested wall-clock time does not<br/>exist in the target zone"]
    DstFault --> DstFallback["Best-effort fallback: schedule one<br/>offset later — 810-816<br/>no exception raised"]
    LoopSurvives --> EEnd([Steady state resumed])
    LoopDies --> EEnd
    Swallow --> EEnd
    SelfKill --> EEnd
    DefRecover --> EEnd
    DstFallback --> EEnd
```

`docs/exception-handling.rst` line 4 states the contract that the flowchart encodes: exceptions thrown during job execution bubble up and interrupt schedule's `run_xyz` function. Direct execution in the checkout confirms the full consequence chain — a `ZeroDivisionError` raised by a job body emerged from `run_pending()`, the job remained in the registry, and its timestamps were untouched.

Only two `try` blocks exist in the entire module, and neither guards user code: line 156 wraps `list.remove` to make cancellation idempotent, and line 826 wraps `strptime` so `_decode_datetimestr` can try five formats in turn.

#### 4.3.2.2 Retry Mechanisms

**No retry mechanism exists.** There is no attempt counter, no maximum-attempts setting, no exponential or jittered backoff, no dead-letter list, and no circuit breaker; a search across all tracked files for `retry`, `retries`, `backoff`, and `circuit` returns nothing.

What does exist is an emergent re-attempt behaviour that architects must not mistake for a retry policy:

| Property | Actual behaviour |
|---|---|
| Trigger | The job stays overdue because `next_run` was never advanced past the failure |
| Delay | None — it re-qualifies as due on the very next poll, so the effective interval becomes the caller's poll period |
| Attempt limit | None — it repeats for as long as the callable keeps failing |
| Jitter | Only if `to()` was configured, and only once a run *succeeds* and reaches line 693 |
| Prerequisite | The caller must have guarded its own loop; otherwise the first failure ends the loop and there is no re-attempt at all |
| Distinguishability | The library records nothing about the failure, so a failing job is indistinguishable from a healthy one in the registry |

The `to()` helper is worth calling out explicitly: `random.randint` at line 712 exists to spread load across occurrences, as `docs/examples.rst` describes, not to back off after errors.

#### 4.3.2.3 Fallback Processes

Three fallback behaviours are implemented, all narrow and all deterministic.

| Fallback | Trigger | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| DST-gap displacement | Requested wall-clock time does not exist in the target zone | Schedules one UTC offset later — the docstring's example is 02:23 becoming 03:23 (lines 810–816) |
| Multi-format deadline decoding | A `until()` string does not match the first format tried | Tries all five `strptime` formats in order, returning `None` only if every one fails (822–830) |
| Idempotent cancellation | `cancel_job()` on a job that is not registered | Swallows `ValueError` and logs a DEBUG record instead of raising (159–160) |

Everything else that might be expected to have a fallback does not have one: there is no alternative timezone provider if `pytz` is absent (the `ModuleNotFoundError` simply propagates — `zoneinfo` appears nowhere in the repository), no degraded mode if a job body fails, and no secondary scheduler to take over work.

#### 4.3.2.4 Error Notification Flows

Notification is limited to Python logging at a single level, and the library never notifies anyone about a job failure — the exception itself *is* the notification, delivered by propagation to the caller.

| Event | Notification | Level and site |
|---|---|---|
| `run_all` starting | Job count and delay | DEBUG, 113–117 |
| Job about to run | `Job.__str__` rendering | DEBUG, 690 |
| Job cancelled by deadline (pre- or post-run) | `Job.__str__` rendering | DEBUG, 687 and 696 |
| Job explicitly cancelled | `Job.__str__` rendering | DEBUG, 157 |
| Cancellation of an unknown job | Distinct "not-scheduled" message | DEBUG, 160 |
| All jobs cleared / tag cleared | Two distinct messages | DEBUG, 144 and 147 |
| **Job raised an exception** | **No log record at all** | — |
| **DST fallback applied** | **No log record at all** | — |

The library creates the logger at line 50 and never attaches a handler or sets a level, so these records are invisible until the host lowers the `schedule` logger to DEBUG as shown in `docs/logging.rst`. There is no WARNING or ERROR path, no metrics counter, no tracing span, and no alerting hook anywhere in the module; §4.1.2.5 shows the wiring the host must supply, and `docs/logging.rst` publishes a `print_elapsed_time` decorator as the recommended way to add per-job timing telemetry.

#### 4.3.2.5 Recovery Procedures

| Scenario | Procedure | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Job fails transiently and should keep trying | Guard the host loop with `try/except` around `run_pending()` | The job stays overdue and is attempted next cycle — no library support required |
| Job fails and should stop permanently | Wrap the callable with `catch_exceptions(cancel_on_failure=True)` so it returns `CancelJob` | `docs/exception-handling.rst` 13–31; `_run_job` unschedules at 174–175 |
| Job fails and should be logged but continue | Same decorator with `cancel_on_failure=False` — prints the traceback and returns `None` | `docs/exception-handling.rst`; the job reschedules normally |
| A whole class of jobs must be stopped | `clear(tag)` after tagging the group | 146–148; `docs/examples.rst` uses a `daily-tasks` tag |
| One known job must be stopped | `cancel_job(job)` using the reference returned by `do()` | 150–160 |
| Everything must be stopped | `clear()` | 143–145 |
| Run-once semantics | Return `schedule.CancelJob` from the job body | 174–175; `docs/examples.rst` |
| Bounded lifetime | `until(...)` at definition time | 576–642; both expiry paths in §4.1.1.6 |
| Catch up after downtime | `run_all()` — forces every job once, ignoring due state | 103–120; note this runs each job **once**, it does not replay missed occurrences |
| Recover after a process restart | Re-execute the definition code | No persistence exists to recover from |
| Deeper customisation | Subclass the scheduler | Suggested by `docs/exception-handling.rst` line 33, which links an external example |

The recurring theme across every row is that **recovery is a host-application responsibility**, expressed through the library's small vocabulary of `CancelJob`, `cancel_job`, `clear`, `until`, and `run_all`. The library's own contribution to reliability is narrower but strong: it guarantees that a job which fails validation never enters the registry, and that cancellation is always idempotent.

### 4.4.2 Deadline and Cancellation Signal Sequence (SEQ-2)

The cancellation signal deserves its own sequence because it is the only value the library interprets from a job body, and because the same `until()` configuration produces three materially different outcomes depending on when the caller polls. The timings below are the exact scenario asserted by `test_until_time` (`test_schedule.py` 366–390).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Host as Host loop
    participant Sched as Scheduler
    participant Job as Job (until 11:35:20)
    participant Fn as Job callable
    participant Log as logger 'schedule'

    Note over Host,Log: t = 11:35:15 — inside the deadline
    Host->>Sched: run_pending()
    Sched->>Job: should_run — now >= next_run
    Job-->>Sched: True
    Sched->>Job: run()
    Job->>Job: _is_overdue(now) is False
    Job->>Log: DEBUG "Running job"
    Job->>Fn: job_func()
    Fn-->>Job: return None
    Job->>Job: last_run = 11:35:15, next_run = 11:35:20
    Job-->>Sched: None — job stays registered
    Note over Host,Log: t = 11:35:20 — new next_run lands exactly on the deadline
    Host->>Sched: run_all()
    Sched->>Job: run()
    Job->>Fn: job_func() — second and final execution
    Fn-->>Job: return None
    Job->>Job: next_run recomputed to 11:35:25, beyond cancel_after
    Job->>Log: DEBUG "Cancelling job"
    Job-->>Sched: CancelJob (overrides the callable return value)
    Sched->>Log: DEBUG "Cancelling job"
    Sched->>Sched: jobs.remove(job) — registry now empty
    Note over Host,Log: Alternative branch — the clock jumps past the deadline first
    Host->>Sched: run_pending() at 11:35:50
    Sched->>Job: run()
    Job->>Job: _is_overdue(now) is True
    Job->>Log: DEBUG "Cancelling job"
    Job-->>Sched: CancelJob — callable never invoked (zero executions)
    Sched->>Sched: jobs.remove(job)
```

Two details in this sequence are easy to miss when reading the source. The post-run check at line 695 returns `CancelJob` **instead of** the value the callable returned, so a job that both produced a result and expired reports only the cancellation — the docstring at lines 679–680 states this priority explicitly. And `Scheduler._run_job` accepts either the `CancelJob` class or an instance of it (line 174), which is why the documented idiom `return schedule.CancelJob` works without instantiation.

### 4.4.4 Diagram Conventions

| Convention | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Rounded terminal node | A start or end point of the workflow |
| Rectangle | A process step that mutates state or performs computation |
| Diamond | A decision point with a corresponding branch in the source |
| Cylinder | The in-memory `Scheduler.jobs` registry |
| Subgraph | A swim lane: one actor, thread, or system boundary |
| Solid arrow | Direct control flow (a call or a return) |
| Dotted arrow | A read, an emission, or an advisory relationship |
| Trailing number in a label | The line number in `schedule/__init__.py` that implements the step |
| `F-xxx` / `F-xxx-RQ-yyy` in a label | The feature or requirement identifier from §2.1, §2.2 and §2.5 |

Because every process step and decision point carries its implementing line number, each diagram doubles as a navigation index into the 945-line source file — which is the practical reason the annotations are present rather than a stylistic one.
