#### 5.3.7.1 ADR-001 — In-Process Embedded Library

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Context | Periodic work must run inside an existing Python application without provisioning cron entries or a scheduler service |
| Decision | Ship a passive library with no process, thread, listener, or configuration surface of its own |
| Evidence | Module docstring lines 5–6; `README.rst` "No extra processes needed!"; stdlib-only imports at lines 41–48 |
| Consequences | Trivial embedding and zero operational footprint; the host owns the loop, the threads, and every restart concern |

#### 5.3.7.2 ADR-002 — Fluent Builder for Configuration

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Context | Schedules are read far more often than written, and the target audience is human readers of the calling code |
| Decision | Use a mutable builder whose unit and weekday accessors are properties returning `self` |
| Evidence | Module docstring names the builder pattern; accessors at lines 325–455 |
| Consequences | Declarations read as prose and the returned object doubles as the cancellation handle; twelve `IntervalError` guards are required to keep singular and plural forms unambiguous |

#### 5.3.7.3 ADR-003 — Validate, Compute, Then Register

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Context | A mutable builder can be abandoned half-configured, and a scheduler must not be corrupted by that |
| Decision | Make the registry append the final statement of `do()`, after binding, computation, and the scheduler check |
| Evidence | Lines 655–663; `test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler`; `HISTORY.rst` 0.5.0 |
| Consequences | Registry integrity is guaranteed; the cost is that `every()` returns an object which is not yet scheduled, which callers must understand |

#### 5.3.7.4 ADR-004 — Serial, Caller-Driven Dispatch

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Context | Any built-in concurrency model imposes a policy on every host |
| Decision | Execute due jobs one at a time, in `next_run` order, on the caller's thread; never replay missed occurrences |
| Evidence | `run_pending` 89–101 and its docstring; `Job.__lt__` 257–262; `docs/parallel-execution.rst` line 6 |
| Consequences | No locking, no reentrancy, deterministic order; a slow job delays the rest of the cycle, and the host must move long work off the dispatch thread |

#### 5.3.7.5 ADR-005 — In-Memory Registry, No Persistence

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Context | Durability would require a storage format, a configuration surface, and a migration story |
| Decision | Keep all state in `Scheduler.jobs` and persist nothing |
| Evidence | Line 87; `docs/index.rst` non-goals; no serialization or file API in the module |
| Consequences | No configuration, no credentials, no schema; every restart requires re-declaration, and cross-process schedule sharing is impossible |

#### 5.3.7.6 ADR-006 — Naive Local `next_run` as the Public Contract

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Context | Timezone support was added in 1.2.0, long after `next_run` semantics were established |
| Decision | Compute in the requested zone, then convert to local time and strip `tzinfo` so `next_run` and `last_run` remain naive |
| Evidence | Verbatim comment and conversion at lines 740–746; `docs/timezones.rst` |
| Consequences | Existing consumers are unaffected by the feature; callers cannot read the originating zone back off a job, and zone-unaware jobs remain DST-agnostic |

#### 5.3.7.7 ADR-007 — Optional `pytz` Through a Lazy Import

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Context | Correct DST handling needs a zone database, but the product promises no external dependencies, and the 3.7 floor predates `zoneinfo` |
| Decision | Import `pytz` inside `Job.at()` only when a `tz` argument is supplied, and expose it as the `timezone` extra |
| Evidence | Line 499; `pyproject.toml` lines 13 and 19–20; `tox.ini` factor-conditional `pytz: pytz` |
| Consequences | The declared dependency set stays empty and both paths are CI-verified; the failure mode moves to call time as a `ModuleNotFoundError`, which `docs/faq.rst` documents |

#### 5.3.7.8 ADR-008 — Typed Error Hierarchy plus a Return-Value Sentinel

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Context | Configuration mistakes and lifecycle decisions are different kinds of event and should not share a mechanism |
| Decision | Raise a three-level hierarchy for configuration faults; express self-cancellation as a `CancelJob` return value honoured as class or instance |
| Evidence | Lines 53–76; line 174; `HISTORY.rst` 0.6.0 introduced the hierarchy, 0.2.0 introduced `CancelJob` |
| Consequences | Hosts can catch a whole family of configuration errors and express run-once semantics with one return; `TypeError` sits outside the hierarchy and must be caught separately |

#### 5.3.7.9 ADR-009 — DEBUG-Only Logging with No Handler Configuration

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Context | A library that configures logging interferes with its host |
| Decision | Create one logger named `schedule`, emit only DEBUG records with lazy `%` formatting, and attach nothing |
| Evidence | Line 50 and the eight emission sites; `docs/logging.rst` |
| Consequences | Silent by default and fully host-controlled; there is no WARNING/ERROR path, and job failures and DST fallbacks are not logged at all |

#### 5.3.7.10 ADR-010 — Single-Module Package with Exported Type Information

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Context | The library must be auditable, vendorable, and safely consumable by typed codebases |
| Decision | Keep the whole runtime in `schedule/__init__.py` and ship a `py.typed` marker validated by `mypy -p schedule` in every environment |
| Evidence | 945-line module; `setup.py` line 20; `setup.cfg`; `tox.ini`; `docs/installation.rst` |
| Consequences | The implementation can be read or even copied in one file and consumers get checked annotations; there are no plugin seams, so extension means subclassing |

### 5.3.8 Assumptions Underlying These Decisions

Each assumption below is stated somewhere in the repository, and each one is load-bearing — if it is false for a given adopter, a different scheduler is the correct choice.

- The host application is long-running and will call `run_pending()` regularly; nothing happens otherwise.
- Losing the schedule on restart is acceptable, because the definition code can always re-create it.
- Job bodies are short relative to their interval, or the host has moved them off the dispatch thread.
- Approximate timing is sufficient: `docs/index.rst` states that job execution time is not accounted for and lists exact timing as a non-goal.
- Job bodies are idempotent or failure-tolerant, since a fault leaves `next_run` un-advanced and the occurrence is re-attempted with no backoff.
- The host owns error policy, thread management, and log routing.
- Only a single interpreter observes any given registry; there is no locking, leader election, or cross-process coordination.
- If timezone anchoring is used, `pytz` is installed and the zone identifier is valid at the moment `at()` is called.

## 5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns

Every cross-cutting concern in this system resolves the same way: the library contributes a minimal, dependency-free primitive and the host application supplies the policy. This subsection records what the library provides, what it deliberately does not, and where the responsibility therefore lies. Section 4.3.2 covers the behavioural detail of error handling; the treatment here is architectural, organised by ownership.

### 5.4.1 Monitoring and Observability Approach

The library's entire observability contribution is one named logger. There is no metrics registry, no counter, no gauge, no health endpoint, and no exporter of any kind — a case-insensitive search of all 32 tracked files finds no reference to metrics, Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, StatsD, Sentry, or any health-check concept.

| Observability capability | Provided by the library | Host responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Activity logging | Eight DEBUG records covering run, run-all, cancel, and clear | Attach handlers and lower the `schedule` logger to DEBUG |
| Job duration measurement | None — job execution time is not measured or recorded | Wrap the callable; `docs/logging.rst` publishes a `print_elapsed_time` decorator for exactly this |
| Failure counting or alerting | None — a failing job produces no record and is indistinguishable from a healthy one in the registry | Wrap the callable or guard the loop, then emit whatever the host's stack requires |
| Schedule state inspection | `get_jobs(tag)`, `next_run(tag)`, `idle_seconds()`, `__str__`, `__repr__` | Poll or render these values into the host's telemetry |
| Liveness signal | None | Derive one from the host's own loop |

The three introspection primitives are worth treating as the observability API. `idle_seconds()` is the most informative: it returns the seconds until the next occurrence, a **negative** value when a job is overdue, and `None` when the registry is empty. A negative value is therefore the only signal the system offers that dispatch is falling behind, and `__repr__` renders each job as a human sentence including its last and next run — with `[never]` for a job that has not yet executed.

### 5.4.2 Logging and Tracing Strategy

| Property | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Logger | A single module-level `logging.getLogger("schedule")` | Line 50 |
| Levels used | DEBUG only; no INFO, WARNING, ERROR, or CRITICAL path exists | Eight `logger.debug` sites at 113, 144, 147, 157, 160, 687, 690, 696 |
| Handlers and levels | None configured by the library, so records are invisible until the host opts in | `docs/logging.rst` shows the `basicConfig` plus `setLevel(DEBUG)` wiring |
| Formatting | Lazy `%`-style arguments, so message rendering costs nothing when DEBUG is disabled | All eight call sites |
| Message content | Job count and delay for `run_all`; the job's `__str__` rendering for run, cancel, and clear operations | 113–117, 690, 687, 696, 157, 160 |
| Events *not* logged | Job exceptions, DST-gap displacement, job registration, reschedule outcomes | Verified by enumerating all eight sites |
| Distributed tracing | Not present — no span, context propagation, or correlation identifier anywhere | No tracing library reference in any tracked file |
| Correlation handle | The job object itself; tags provide the only grouping dimension | `tag()` 457–469 |

Two architectural consequences follow. First, because the library never configures handlers, it cannot interfere with a host's logging setup — which is what allows it to be embedded in applications with strict logging policies. Second, because job failures are not logged, the exception *is* the notification: an adopter that swallows exceptions in its loop without logging them will have no record of the failure from any source.

### 5.4.3 Error Handling Patterns

The architecture uses two distinct error-handling patterns, separated by lifecycle phase.

**Fail-fast at the configuration boundary.** All 28 `raise` sites fire during definition, before or during `do()`, and none of them can leave a partially configured job in the registry. The pattern's guarantee is total: a validation fault costs the caller an exception and costs the system nothing.

**Transparent pass-through at the execution boundary.** The invocation at line 691 has no `try`/`except` around it. `docs/exception-handling.rst` states the contract directly: exceptions thrown during job execution bubble up and interrupt the `run_xyz` function. The library adds no retry, no backoff, no attempt cap, no dead-letter path, and no circuit breaker — verified by the absence of `retry`, `retries`, `backoff`, and `circuit` from every tracked file. Only two `try` blocks exist in the module, and neither guards user code: one makes `cancel_job()` idempotent, the other lets deadline parsing try five formats in turn.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Origin([A fault occurs somewhere in the system]) --> Owner{"Which side of the boundary<br/>owns the fault?"}
    Owner -->|"Library — configuration<br/>is malformed"| LibGuard["A guard raises before the job is<br/>appended: IntervalError, ScheduleValueError,<br/>TypeError or ScheduleError"]
    LibGuard --> LibEffect["Registry untouched, no partial state,<br/>nothing logged"]
    LibEffect --> LibHand["Exception surfaces at the caller's<br/>definition call site"]
    LibHand --> HostFix["Host responsibility: correct the chain<br/>and re-declare the job"]
    Owner -->|"Optional dependency —<br/>timezone requested"| TzGuard{"Is pytz importable and<br/>is the zone known?"}
    TzGuard -->|"not importable"| TzMissing["ModuleNotFoundError from the lazy import"]
    TzGuard -->|"unknown zone"| TzUnknown["pytz UnknownTimeZoneError"]
    TzGuard -->|"wrong argument type"| TzType["ScheduleValueError for a value that is<br/>neither a string nor a pytz zone"]
    TzMissing --> LibHand
    TzUnknown --> LibHand
    TzType --> LibHand
    Owner -->|"Environment — requested wall<br/>clock does not exist"| DstGap["Daylight-saving gap detected during<br/>offset correction"]
    DstGap --> DstFix["Best-effort displacement of one offset<br/>later, no exception and no log record"]
    DstFix --> Steady([Steady state resumed])
    Owner -->|"Host callable —<br/>the job body fails"| JobFault["Exception raised inside the bound partial"]
    JobFault --> NoGuard["The library holds no try or except around<br/>the invocation, so nothing is caught,<br/>counted, logged or retried"]
    NoGuard --> Frozen["last_run and next_run are not advanced<br/>and the job stays registered and overdue"]
    Frozen --> Escape["Exception propagates out of run_pending<br/>or run_all to the caller"]
    Escape --> Policy{"Which host-side policy<br/>is in place?"}
    Policy -->|"none"| LoopDies["Dispatch loop terminates and the rest of<br/>the due set for that cycle is skipped"]
    Policy -->|"guarded loop"| LoopLives["Loop continues, the job re-qualifies on the<br/>next poll with no backoff and no attempt cap"]
    Policy -->|"catch_exceptions wrapper,<br/>continue on failure"| Wrapped["Traceback printed by the wrapper and the<br/>job reschedules normally"]
    Policy -->|"catch_exceptions wrapper,<br/>cancel on failure"| SelfKill["Wrapper returns CancelJob and the<br/>dispatcher unschedules the job"]
    Policy -->|"deadline or tag governance"| Bounded["until() expiry or clear(tag) removes the<br/>job without host code inspecting the fault"]
    LoopDies --> HostFix2["Host responsibility: restart the process and<br/>re-declare every job, nothing is recovered"]
    LoopLives --> Steady
    Wrapped --> Steady
    SelfKill --> Steady
    Bounded --> Steady
    HostFix --> Steady
    HostFix2 --> Steady
```

| Fault class | Library behaviour | Recommended host pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Invalid configuration | Raise before registration; registry unchanged | Fix the declaration — there is nothing to clean up |
| Missing `pytz` or unknown zone | Propagate `ModuleNotFoundError` or `UnknownTimeZoneError` from `at()` | Install the extra and validate zone identifiers at start-up, as `docs/faq.rst` advises |
| Nonexistent local time at a DST gap | Displace by one offset, silently | Accept the documented displacement, or anchor in UTC |
| Job body raises | Nothing is caught; the schedule is not advanced; the exception escapes the loop | Guard the loop, or wrap the callable with the `catch_exceptions` decorator from `docs/exception-handling.rst` |
| A job must stop after failing | Not automatic | Return `CancelJob` from the wrapper, or use `until()` / `clear(tag)` |
| Cancelling an unregistered job | Swallowed and logged at DEBUG — idempotent by design | No handling needed |

The critical architectural nuance is that the invocation, the timestamp, and the reschedule are three separate statements (691, 692, 693). A fault after a side effect has occurred leaves the work done but the schedule un-advanced, so the same occurrence is attempted again on the next poll. Section 4.3.1.6 records this as at-least-once-within-a-cycle behaviour; idempotent job bodies are the mitigation.

### 5.4.4 Authentication and Authorization Framework

**No authentication or authorization framework exists, and none is architecturally required.** The library crosses no trust boundary: it exposes no network interface, no CLI, no multi-tenant surface, and no privileged operation. Any caller able to invoke `schedule.every()` already holds the right to execute arbitrary code in that interpreter, so an access-control layer inside the library would guard nothing.

| Aspect | Finding |
|---|---|
| Identity model | None — jobs have no owner, principal, or subject; `tags` are arbitrary hashables used for grouping only |
| Access control | None — every module function operates on the process-global `default_scheduler` without any check |
| Privilege boundary | The Python process boundary, owned entirely by the host |
| Verification | No `authentication`, `authorization`, `credential`, `password`, `rbac`, `token`, `tls`, or `encrypt` logic exists in any tracked file; the sole `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` reference is CI-only |
| Host responsibility | Any authorization over *who may define or cancel jobs* must be enforced by the host before it calls the API; any credentials a job body needs are the host's to supply and protect |

One derived caution belongs here rather than under security: DEBUG records embed the job's rendering, which includes bound argument values. A host that enables DEBUG on the `schedule` logger and passes sensitive arguments to `do()` will emit those values into its log stream.

### 5.4.5 Performance Characteristics and Service Levels

**No service-level agreement, latency budget, throughput target, or uptime commitment exists anywhere in the repository.** This is verified rather than assumed: a case-insensitive search across all tracked files finds no SLA, uptime, availability, timeout, or watchdog statement, and `docs/index.rst` publishes the opposite — exact timing is a non-goal and "Schedule does not account for the time it takes for the job function to execute."

The characteristics below are the observable ones, each traceable to code or to a documented statement.

| Characteristic | Behaviour | Determined by |
|---|---|---|
| Dispatch latency | A job runs no earlier than `next_run` and no later than `next_run` plus one poll period plus the time taken by earlier jobs in the same cycle | Host poll cadence; the documented convention is `sleep(1)` |
| Timing precision | Whole-second granularity at best; sub-second precision is a published non-goal | `at()` accepts seconds; `docs/index.rst` |
| Missed occurrences | Never replayed — a per-minute job polled hourly runs once, not sixty times | `run_pending` docstring 93–97 |
| Schedule drift | Rescheduling is relative to *now*, so job duration and poll delay accumulate | `_schedule_next_run` reads the clock at line 717 |
| Per-poll cost | O(n) due filter over the registry plus O(k log k) ordering of the k due jobs | Lines 99–100 |
| Introspection cost | O(n) for `get_next_run` via `min()`; O(n) for `cancel_job` via `list.remove` | Lines 193, 158 |
| Memory profile | Linear in job count; each job retains its callable and all bound arguments | `functools.partial` at line 655 |
| Concurrency | None inside the library; one job at a time on the caller's thread | No threading primitive exists in the module |
| Forced-run cost | `run_all(delay_seconds=n)` sleeps after **every** job, including the last, so total added time is job count × delay | Line 120 |
| Clock source | `datetime.datetime.now()` read directly at nine sites; there is no injected clock or monotonic source | Lines 206, 608, 611, 628, 638, 672, 686, 692, 717 |

Three levers exist for improving the timing profile, all host-side: drive the loop from `idle_seconds()` instead of a fixed sleep to remove polling slack; move long-running bodies onto host threads or a `queue.Queue` worker as `docs/parallel-execution.rst` demonstrates, which `docs/index.rst` states is required "to guarantee a stable execution schedule"; and apply `to()` jitter to spread simultaneous occurrences across a window.

The only performance-adjacent quality gates in the repository are correctness gates rather than budgets: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs five jobs on every push and pull request to `master`, and `tox.ini` expands to twelve environments covering six interpreters with and without `pytz`. The 81-method suite completes in well under a second on a current interpreter, which is why it functions as a routine local gate.

### 5.4.6 Disaster Recovery and Continuity

There is no disaster-recovery mechanism, and there is nothing to recover: no backup, restore, replication, failover, snapshot, or journal exists — verified by the absence of `backup`, `restore`, `disaster`, `failover`, and `replica` from every tracked file. The registry is memory-only, so process termination is total schedule loss by design. `docs/index.rst` places job persistence first among the reasons to select a different library, which makes this a stated boundary rather than a gap.

| Scenario | System behaviour | Continuity procedure |
|---|---|---|
| Process restart, planned or unplanned | The registry is gone; nothing is replayed, and no occurrence missed during downtime is made up | Re-execute the definition code at start-up — the code is the schedule's source of truth |
| Host loop terminated by an unhandled job exception | Jobs remain registered in memory but nothing dispatches; the failing job's `next_run` is stale | Guard the loop, or wrap callables so failures cannot escape |
| A job must be forced after downtime | `run_all()` executes every job exactly once regardless of due state, then reschedules them normally | Use `run_all()` as a catch-up trigger, understanding that it does not replay individual missed occurrences |
| A whole class of jobs must be quarantined | `clear(tag)` removes them; `cancel_job(job)` removes one | Tag groups at definition time so they can be governed later |
| Runaway or obsolete job | `until()` bounds its lifetime at definition time; returning `CancelJob` ends it from inside | Prefer bounded jobs for anything time-limited |
| Corrupted or mis-specified schedule | Configuration faults cannot enter the registry, so no corrupt state is reachable | Correct the declaration and re-run it |
| Multiple processes for redundancy | Not supported — each process holds an independent registry with no coordination, locking, or leader election | The host must arrange external coordination if duplicate execution is unacceptable |

The continuity model that follows is a **stateless-redeclaration model**: durability is achieved by making the definition code deterministic and idempotent, not by persisting state. This is also why `@repeat`, which registers at import time, is architecturally coherent here — importing the module re-establishes the schedule as a side effect of loading the application.

### 5.4.7 Responsibility Matrix

| Concern | Library provides | Host must provide |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduling arithmetic and DST correctness | Complete implementation, exercised by 37 timezone-focused tests across 15 zones | Valid zone identifiers and the `pytz` extra when timezones are used |
| Execution | Serial dispatch of the due set in `next_run` order | The loop, its cadence, and its thread |
| Concurrency | Nothing | Threads, queues, or worker processes |
| Durability | Nothing | Re-declaration on start-up |
| Error policy | Fail-fast configuration validation and idempotent cancellation | Catching, logging, retrying, and cancelling on failure |
| Observability | Eight DEBUG records on one logger | Handlers, levels, duration measurement, metrics, alerting |
| Security | No trust boundary to defend | Authorization over API access and protection of anything a job body touches |
| Capacity management | `to()` jitter and `run_all(delay_seconds)` spacing | Sizing, back-pressure, and moving long work off the dispatch thread |

- `docs/examples.rst` - Established the `idle_seconds()`-driven loop, the `until()` call forms, tag-based governance, and `run_all(delay_seconds)` usage.
- `docs/faq.rst` - Established the documented resolution for a missing `pytz` at `at()` call time.
- `docs/installation.rst` - Established the Python version support statement, the single optional dependency, and the single-source-file vendoring note cited in the tradeoff table.
- `docs/development.rst` - Established the release procedure (wheel build, TestPyPI then PyPI) referenced in the distribution integration table.
- `docs/reference.rst` - Established the published API surface enumerated in the interface tables.

# 6. SYSTEM COMPONENTS DESIGN

## 6.1 Core Services Architecture

### 6.1.1 Applicability Assessment

**Core Services Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

The subject of this specification is the Python `schedule` library at release 1.2.2 (`setup.py` line 5). It is not a service, a system of services, or a distributed application. It is a single importable Python package whose entire runtime is `schedule/__init__.py` — 945 lines — accompanied by the zero-byte PEP 561 marker `schedule/py.typed`. The distributable artifact contains no daemon, no executable, no network listener, and no process of its own; it becomes active only when a host application the library does not own imports it and calls into it. Section 5.1.1.1 records the architecture style as an *in-process embedded library*, and Section 5.3.7.1 records that style as ADR-001.

Because there is exactly one runtime component and no process or network boundary anywhere in the repository, the concerns this section exists to document — service boundaries between independently deployable units, inter-service communication, service discovery, load balancing across replicas, circuit breaking between callers and providers, auto-scaling, failover, and cross-node data redundancy — have **no implementation locus in this codebase**. Documenting them as though they existed would misrepresent the system.

This sub-section establishes that determination with verifiable evidence. Sub-sections 6.1.2 through 6.1.4 then do the constructive work that remains genuinely informative: they document the **in-process component model** that plays the structural role services would play, and they record, for each distributed-systems concern named in the section scope, (a) what mechanism — if any — exists inside the library, (b) the artifact that proves the absence of the rest, and (c) the host-side composition that this repository's own documentation prescribes in its place. Where a concern is fully covered by an earlier section, this section cross-references rather than restates it.

#### 6.1.1.1 Determination Criteria and Findings

Each criterion below is a structural precondition for a core-services architecture. Every one of them fails, and each failure is verified against a named artifact rather than inferred.

| Precondition for service architecture | Verification performed | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| Two or more independently deployable units | `git ls-files` enumerates 32 tracked files; one package directory, `schedule/`, with a single module | **Fails** — one deployable unit, importable only |
| An executable or service entry point | `setup.py` declares `packages`, `package_data`, `classifiers`, `python_requires`; it declares no `entry_points`, `console_scripts`, or `scripts` | **Fails** — the wheel installs an import target, never a runnable process |
| A network or IPC surface | Symbol search of `schedule/__init__.py` for `socket`, `http`, `urllib`, `requests`, `grpc`, `asyncio`, `async def`, `subprocess`, `multiprocessing` | **Fails** — zero code matches; the only textual hits are three reference URLs in the module docstring (lines 36–38) |
| Out-of-process state shared between units | The sole store is `self.jobs: List[Job] = []` (line 87); no `open(`, `pickle`, `json`, database or cache client appears in the module | **Fails** — state is process-local memory, documented in Section 5.1.3.4 |
| Deployment or orchestration descriptors | Filesystem search for `Dockerfile*`, `docker-compose*`, `*.yaml`, `*.yml`, `*.tf`, `Procfile`, `*.service`, `Chart.yaml`, nginx/Envoy/Consul configuration | **Fails** — the only YAML in the repository is `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, a CI definition |
| Resilience or discovery infrastructure in the dependency set | `pyproject.toml` declares `dependencies = []`; case-insensitive search for `tenacity`, `backoff`, `circuitbreaker`, `pybreaker`, `retrying`, `consul`, `etcd`, `eureka`, `zookeeper`, `haproxy`, `kubernetes`, `prometheus`, `opentelemetry` | **Fails** — no match in any tracked file; the single optional package is `pytz` |

The zero-dependency position is not merely declared, it is structurally enforced: the only third-party import in the module is `import pytz` **inside** `Job.at()` at line 499, reached only when a caller supplies a timezone, and `pyproject.toml` exposes it as the optional extra `timezone = ["pytz"]`. `tox.ini` expands to twelve environments — every supported interpreter both with and without `pytz` — so the without-extra import graph is proven to contain no third-party code at all.

#### 6.1.1.2 Unit of Deployment and Runtime Topology

The unit of deployment is a wheel installed with `pip install schedule` (`docs/index.rst`, `docs/installation.rst`). Its runtime topology has exactly one node, and that node belongs to the adopter.

| Topology attribute | Value in this system | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Processes contributed by the library | Zero — `README.rst` advertises "No extra processes needed!" | `README.rst`; module docstring lines 5–6 |
| Threads contributed by the library | Zero — no threading primitive exists in the module | Import block, lines 41–48 |
| Control flow ownership | The host: nothing executes unless the host calls `run_pending()` or `run_all()` | `Scheduler.run_pending` lines 89–101 |
| Interpreter range | CPython 3.7 through 3.12 | `python_requires=">=3.7"`; CI matrix in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` line 17 |
| Concurrency inside the boundary | None — one job at a time on the caller's thread | Section 5.3.7.4 (ADR-004) |
| Coordination between processes | None — each process holds an independent registry with no locking or leader election | Section 5.4.6; Section 5.3.8 |

**Diagram 6.1.1-A — Reference service topology contrasted with the verified single-process topology.** Every element in the left-hand group is absent from the repository; the right-hand group is the complete runtime picture, and its outermost two layers are supplied by the adopter, not by this codebase.

#### 6.1.1.3 Why the Design Excludes Distributed Concerns

The exclusions are deliberate, published product boundaries rather than gaps awaiting implementation. Four statements in the repository's own documentation establish this.

| Published position | Statement in the repository | Consequence for this section |
|---|---|---|
| Scope is intentionally narrow | `docs/index.rst` frames the library as "a simple solution for simple scheduling problems" and lists four capabilities for which readers should look elsewhere: job persistence, sub-second precision, concurrent execution, and localization | Persistence, concurrency and precision — the substrate of scaling and failover — are out of scope by design |
| Concurrency is a rejected feature, not a missing one | `docs/parallel-execution.rst` line 6: "By default, schedule executes all jobs serially. The reasoning behind this is that it would be difficult to find a model for parallel execution that makes everyone happy." | There is no executor to scale, pool, or balance inside the library |
| Background operation is host-owned | `docs/background-execution.rst` line 4: "Out of the box it is not possible to run the schedule in the background." | The library owns no lifecycle that could be supervised, restarted, or failed over |
| Distribution is explicitly external | `docs/parallel-execution.rst` line 68 notes that the queue-based model "also makes sense for a distributed application where the workers are separate processes that receive jobs from a distributed work queue," naming beanstalkd as an example | Horizontal work distribution is delegated to infrastructure outside the library; beanstalkd is a suggestion, not a dependency — it appears in no manifest |

The corollary matters for adopters: this library is a component **within** a service, not a service itself. Any core-services architecture in a system that uses `schedule` is the surrounding application's architecture. The library contributes a timing primitive to one process of that architecture and deliberately declines to participate in the rest.

#### 6.1.1.4 What Plays the Role of Services

To keep this section useful rather than merely negative, the remainder documents the in-process structures that occupy the architectural positions services would occupy. The mapping below is the organising principle for sub-sections 6.1.2 through 6.1.4; it is an analogy for orientation, not a claim that these are services.

| Position in a service architecture | In-process counterpart in this system | Documented in |
|---|---|---|
| Independently deployable service | Not present; the closest unit of isolation is a `Scheduler` **instance**, each owning a private registry | 6.1.2.1 |
| Inter-service RPC or messaging | Direct synchronous Python calls in both directions, plus a `CancelJob` return-value sentinel | 6.1.2.2 |
| Service registry and discovery | The in-memory `jobs` list with tag-based filtering — a linear scan, not an index | 6.1.2.3 |
| Load balancer | Deterministic next-run ordering, `to()` jitter, and `run_all(delay_seconds)` spacing; no replica distribution exists | 6.1.2.4 |
| Circuit breaker | Absent from the library; approximated host-side by returning `CancelJob` from a guard wrapper — a permanent trip with no reset | 6.1.2.5 |
| Retry, backoff, fallback | No explicit mechanism; an implicit re-attempt on the next poll arises from where `Job.run()` fails | 6.1.2.6 |
| Horizontal replica scaling | Not supported by the library; host-side threads, worker queues, or multiple `Scheduler` instances | 6.1.3 |
| Failover, redundancy, disaster recovery | None; continuity is achieved by re-declaring the schedule at start-up | 6.1.4 |


### 6.1.2 In-Process Component Architecture

Because no services exist (6.1.1), the structural analysis that a "service components" analysis would perform is performed here against the in-process components of `schedule/__init__.py`. Section 5.1.2 provides the authoritative component inventory and Section 5.1.3 the authoritative data-flow description; this sub-section examines the same components specifically through the lens of the six concerns named in the section scope — boundaries, communication, discovery, load balancing, circuit breaking, and retry/fallback — and records for each what exists, what is verifiably absent, and what the host must supply.

#### 6.1.2.1 Component Boundaries and Responsibilities

The only boundary in the system is an **import boundary** (Section 5.1.1.3). Inside it, responsibilities are separated along a registry/specification split rather than along deployment lines.

| Component | Responsibility owned | Boundary characteristics |
|---|---|---|
| `Scheduler` (lines 79–206) | Owns the job registry; creates jobs; selects the due set; dispatches serially in next-run order; removes cancelled jobs | Instantiable — each instance is a private, uncoordinated registry; the strongest isolation unit in the system |
| `Job` (lines 209–830) | Accumulates its own configuration fluently; computes its next occurrence; invokes the bound callable; registers itself once complete | Holds a back-reference to its owning `Scheduler` (line 255) and appends itself exactly once (line 663); mutable for its whole life |
| Module facade (lines 833–913) | Provides `default_scheduler`, the live `jobs` alias, eight one-line delegating functions, and the `repeat` decorator factory | Process-global mutable state; unrelated components sharing an interpreter share this one registry |
| Contract types (lines 53–76) | Define the `ScheduleError` → `ScheduleValueError` → `IntervalError` hierarchy and the `CancelJob` sentinel | Pure vocabulary crossing the boundary in both directions; no behaviour |

Two boundary properties are architecturally load-bearing and are the closest analogues of service-level isolation guarantees:

- **Deferred admission.** `Scheduler.every()` returns a `Job` that is *not* in the registry; only `do()` appends it, and only as its final statement after binding, first-occurrence computation, and the scheduler back-reference check (lines 655–663). A fault anywhere in the chain therefore leaves the registry byte-for-byte unchanged. `test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler` (`test_schedule.py` lines 1591–1599) encodes this as a requirement: a scheduler with two abandoned definition chains still polls cleanly.
- **Instance-level partitioning.** `docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` states that "for larger installations it might be desirable to have multiple schedulers" and that this is supported. Independent `Scheduler()` objects give fully separate registries — but the host must call `run_pending()` on **every** one of them (`docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` lines 31–35), and there is no coordination, shared clock, or cross-instance visibility. Partitioning buys isolation of *state*, never of *execution*.

The absence of finer isolation is equally definite: there is no worker abstraction, no executor interface, no plugin seam, and no sandbox around the invoked callable. The callable runs synchronously with the full privileges of the host process, which Section 2.4.4 records as the system's real trust boundary.

#### 6.1.2.2 Communication Patterns

All communication is synchronous, in-process, and expressed in plain Python objects. There is no wire protocol, serialization format, schema, broker, or callback registry anywhere in the module — Section 5.3.3 records the same finding, and notes that the only "message" the library ever produces is a `logging.LogRecord`.

| Channel | Direction and mechanism | Contract |
|---|---|---|
| Configuration and control | Host → library; direct method calls on a fluent, mutable `Job` plus the eight facade functions | Fail-fast: 28 raise sites, all at definition time, all before registration |
| Execution trigger | Host → library; explicit polling via `run_pending()` or `run_all(delay_seconds)` | Nothing runs otherwise; missed occurrences are never replayed (docstring, lines 93–97) |
| Work invocation | Library → host; a zero-argument `functools.partial` called at line 691 | No exception guard, no timeout, no isolation, no return-value inspection except the sentinel |
| Lifecycle signal | Host callable → library; `return CancelJob` | Honoured as either the class or an instance (line 174), then unscheduled via `cancel_job` |
| Diagnostics | Library → host; eight `logger.debug` records on the logger named `schedule` | Fire-and-forget, lazily `%`-formatted, no handler attached by the library |
| Fault reporting | Bidirectional; Python exceptions | Configuration faults raised by the library; execution faults passed through untouched |

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Host as Host loop (adopter-owned)
    participant Facade as Module facade
    participant Sched as Scheduler
    participant JobObj as Job
    participant Work as Host callable
    Note over Host,Work: Definition phase — registration is deferred to do()
    Host->>Facade: every(10).minutes
    Facade->>Sched: every(interval)
    Sched-->>JobObj: construct unregistered Job
    Host->>JobObj: .tag("group").until(deadline).do(fn, args)
    JobObj->>JobObj: bind functools.partial, compute first next_run
    JobObj->>Sched: append self to jobs (line 663)
    Note over Host,Work: Dispatch phase — one poll of the host loop
    Host->>Facade: run_pending()
    Facade->>Sched: run_pending()
    Sched->>JobObj: read should_run for every job (O of n)
    Sched->>Sched: sort the due subset by next_run
    loop for each due job, serially
        Sched->>JobObj: run()
        alt deadline from until() already passed
            JobObj-->>Sched: CancelJob without executing
        else job is runnable
            JobObj->>Work: invoke bound partial
            alt callable returns normally
                Work-->>JobObj: return value
                JobObj->>JobObj: stamp last_run, recompute next_run
                JobObj-->>Sched: value, or CancelJob if next_run is past the deadline
            else callable raises
                Work--)Sched: exception propagates, last_run and next_run unchanged
                Sched--)Host: exception escapes run_pending, remaining due jobs skipped
            end
        end
        opt CancelJob was signalled
            Sched->>Sched: cancel_job removes the job from the registry
        end
    end
    Host->>Host: sleep for a fixed period, or for idle_seconds()
```

**Diagram 6.1.2-A — Component interaction sequence for one definition and one dispatch cycle.** The two dashed-arrow steps show the fail-fast execution path verified empirically: an exception from a job body escapes `run_pending()` and the remaining due jobs in that cycle are skipped.

#### 6.1.2.3 Discovery Mechanisms

No service discovery exists, and none is needed: there is nothing to locate across a network. The functional analogue is **registry lookup within one process**, and it is deliberately primitive.

| Discovery concern | Mechanism in this system | Cost and limits |
|---|---|---|
| Registration | `Job.do()` appends to `Scheduler.jobs` as its last statement (line 663) | O(1); a job is invisible until fully configured |
| Enumeration | `Scheduler.get_jobs()` returns a copy of the list whose elements are the live `Job` objects (lines 122–133) | O(n); callers can mutate scheduled jobs through the returned handles |
| Selection by identity | `tag(*tags)` unions hashable tags into `Job.tags`; `get_jobs(tag)` filters by set membership | Linear scan, not an index (Section 2.4.3, F-011); unhashable tags raise `TypeError` (lines 466–467) |
| Temporal lookup | `get_next_run(tag)` returns `min(...).next_run`; `idle_seconds` subtracts the wall clock from it | O(n) per call; both return `None` when the registry is empty or no tag matches |
| Deregistration | `cancel_job(job)` removes one job; `clear(tag)` removes a group; `CancelJob` self-removes | `list.remove` is O(n); `clear()` mutates in place so the module-level `jobs` alias stays valid |

There is no health checking, heartbeat, TTL, lease, or liveness concept attached to a registry entry: a registered job is assumed present and correct until something removes it. A failing job is, as Section 5.4.1 records, indistinguishable in the registry from a healthy one.

#### 6.1.2.4 Load Distribution Strategy

There is no load balancer and nothing to balance across — one thread executes one job at a time. What the library does provide are three deterministic controls over *when* work lands, which together form the whole of its load-distribution capability.

| Control | Mechanism | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Deterministic ordering | `sorted(runnable_jobs)` in `run_pending` (line 100), ordered by `Job.__lt__` on `next_run` (lines 257–262) | Within a cycle the most overdue job runs first; ordering is total and reproducible |
| Forced-run spacing | `run_all(delay_seconds)` sleeps `delay_seconds` after each job, including the last (lines 118–120) | The docstring's stated purpose is to "distribute system load generated by the jobs more evenly over time"; total added time is job count × delay |
| Interval jitter | `to(latest)` sets an inclusive upper bound; `random.randint(interval, latest)` is drawn inside `_schedule_next_run` (line 712) | Re-drawn on **every** reschedule, so identical schedules in separate processes de-synchronise over time (Section 2.4.3, F-005) |

Everything beyond this is host-side and comes from the repository's own recipes rather than from library code. `docs/parallel-execution.rst` supplies two, and the second is the only pattern in the repository that resembles bounded resource allocation:

- **Unbounded fan-out** — register `run_threaded(job_func)`, which starts a new `threading.Thread` per firing (lines 19–27). Simple, with no ceiling on concurrent threads.
- **Bounded worker pool** — "If you want tighter control on the number of threads use a shared jobqueue and one or more worker threads": register `jobqueue.put` as the job body so firing *enqueues* rather than executes, and let a fixed set of worker threads drain the `queue.Queue` (lines 34–66). Concurrency is then capped by worker count, and the queue absorbs bursts.

Note that `random.randint` is not a cryptographic generator and `to()` must not be relied on for unpredictability (Section 5.3.6).

#### 6.1.2.5 Circuit Breaker Patterns

**No circuit breaker exists in the library.** This is verified rather than assumed: no breaker library appears in any manifest (6.1.1.1), the module contains no failure counter, threshold, state machine, half-open probe, or reset timer, and Section 5.4.3 records that the library adds "no retry, no backoff, no attempt cap, no dead-letter path, and no circuit breaker." Only two `try` blocks exist in the entire module and neither guards user code: one makes `cancel_job()` idempotent (lines 156–160), the other tries five deadline formats in turn (lines 825–830).

What the repository does provide is a host-composable **trip-and-remove** pattern, published in `docs/exception-handling.rst` (lines 13–31). A decorator wraps the job body, catches everything, prints the traceback, and — when constructed with `cancel_on_failure=True` — returns `schedule.CancelJob`, which the dispatcher honours by removing the job from the registry. Verified behaviour: with such a guard in place, the registry drops to zero entries after the first failure.

| Breaker property | Behaviour of the documented pattern | Gap versus a conventional breaker |
|---|---|---|
| Trip condition | The first uncaught exception in the wrapped body | No failure threshold, error-rate window, or slow-call detector |
| Open state | The job is deleted from the registry, so it can never fire again | Not a state — it is destruction; nothing tracks that a breaker is "open" |
| Half-open / reset | None; recovery requires re-declaring the job | No probe, no cool-down, no automatic close |
| Fallback on trip | Only whatever the wrapper itself does, typically printing a traceback | No alternate provider, cached value, or degraded response |

Two library features give coarser, time- and group-scoped equivalents of the same idea: `until()` (lines 576–642) installs a definition-time fuse that removes the job once its deadline passes, and `clear(tag)` (lines 135–148) sheds an entire tagged group in one call. Both are governance controls rather than failure-reactive ones — they fire on time or on operator action, never on an error signal.

#### 6.1.2.6 Retry and Fallback Mechanisms

The library implements no retry policy, no backoff, no attempt cap, and no fallback provider. It nevertheless exhibits a specific, consequential **implicit re-attempt** behaviour that adopters must understand, and which arises purely from statement ordering inside `Job.run()`.

The invocation, the timestamp, and the reschedule are three separate statements — lines 691, 692 and 693. When the callable raises, the exception propagates out of line 691, so `last_run` is never stamped and `next_run` is never advanced. The job therefore remains registered, remains overdue, and re-qualifies on the very next poll. Direct verification against this checkout: a job whose body raises unconditionally is attempted once per poll — three attempts across three polls — with `last_run` still `None` and `next_run` never advanced, while the failing job stays in the registry.

| Retry dimension | Actual behaviour | Implication for adopters |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | Implicit; the un-advanced `next_run` leaves the job due | Not configurable and not opt-out; it is a side effect of failure |
| Cadence | Once per host poll — every second under the documented `sleep(1)` loop | A persistently failing job becomes a hot loop at the poll frequency |
| Backoff and cap | None; no exponential delay, jitter, or maximum attempts | Unbounded until the host intervenes |
| Idempotency requirement | A fault after a side effect leaves the work done but the schedule un-advanced | The same occurrence is retried, so job bodies must be idempotent (Sections 4.3.1.6 and 5.4.3) |

Only one genuine fallback chain exists anywhere in the module, and it is a parsing convenience rather than a runtime resilience feature: `_decode_datetimestr` (lines 822–830) attempts five `strptime` formats in order and returns `None` if all fail, after which `until()` raises `ScheduleValueError`. There is no fallback for a failed job — no alternate callable, no cached result, no dead-letter destination, and no compensating action.

The retry, backoff and fallback policy is therefore entirely the host's to write, using the three composition points the library exposes: wrapping the callable (`docs/exception-handling.rst`), guarding the dispatch loop, or returning `CancelJob` to stop re-attempts altogether. Section 5.4.3 diagrams the full set of host-side policy outcomes.


### 6.1.3 Scalability Design

The library has no scaling machinery of its own: no executor, no pool, no queue, no partition manager, and no elasticity controller. Its scalability design is therefore best stated as a division of labour — the library scales *registry size* trivially and *throughput* not at all, and every throughput lever lives in the host. Section 2.4.3 records the per-feature performance characteristics and Section 5.4.5 the observable service-level behaviour; this sub-section covers the scaling and capacity dimensions named in the section scope.

#### 6.1.3.1 Vertical and Horizontal Scaling Approach

| Scaling dimension | What the library supports | Where the ceiling sits |
|---|---|---|
| Registry size (vertical, data) | Unbounded in principle; cost per poll is linear in job count | Host memory; each job retains its callable and all bound arguments (line 655) |
| Throughput per registry (vertical, compute) | None — one job at a time on the caller's thread | Aggregate job duration; a slow job delays every later job in the same cycle (Section 2.4.3, F-009) |
| Concurrency (vertical, compute) | None inside the library; no threading primitive exists in the module | Host-supplied threads or worker queues (`docs/parallel-execution.rst`) |
| Registry partitioning (horizontal, logical) | Multiple `Scheduler()` instances, each with a private registry | The host must poll every instance; partitioning "add[s] no parallelism" (Section 2.4.3, F-015) |
| Multi-process replication (horizontal, physical) | Not supported — no locking, leader election, or shared state | Each process would execute the full schedule independently (Section 5.4.6) |

The horizontal row deserves emphasis because it is the row most likely to be misread. Running two host processes that both declare the same jobs does not distribute the work — it **duplicates** it. Each process holds an independent in-memory registry with no coordination of any kind (Section 5.3.8), so every occurrence fires once per process. Where duplicate execution is unacceptable, the host must arrange external coordination; where genuine work distribution is required, `docs/parallel-execution.rst` line 68 directs the reader to a distributed work queue consumed by separate worker processes — infrastructure that is deliberately outside this repository.


**Diagram 6.1.3-A — Scalability architecture: the baseline dispatch model and the four escalation tiers.** Only Tier 0 is library code. Tiers 1–3 are recipes published in `docs/parallel-execution.rst` and `docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` that the host implements; Tier 4 is explicitly outside the repository.

#### 6.1.3.2 Auto-Scaling Triggers and Rules

**No auto-scaling exists, and no trigger, rule, threshold, metric, or controller is defined anywhere in the repository.** This is verified: there is no metrics registry, counter, gauge, or exporter (Section 5.4.1), no orchestration descriptor of any kind (6.1.1.1), and no configuration surface through which a scaling rule could be expressed (Section 5.1.1.3). Elasticity, if required, is the host's to implement outside the library.

Two library values are nevertheless the only signals a host-side controller could act on, and both are pull-only:

| Signal | Meaning | Suitability as a scaling trigger |
|---|---|---|
| `idle_seconds()` returning a negative value | The next occurrence is already in the past — dispatch is falling behind | The only backlog indicator the system offers (Section 5.4.1); coarse, since it reports lateness, not queue depth |
| `len(get_jobs(tag))` | Current registry population, optionally per group | Reflects declared work, not load — a large registry of hourly jobs implies almost no load |

Because job duration is never measured or recorded (Section 5.4.1), a host that needs utilisation data must produce it itself; `docs/logging.rst` publishes a `print_elapsed_time` decorator that measures and logs per-job duration, which is the repository's own suggested starting point.

#### 6.1.3.3 Resource Allocation Strategy

Resource allocation is implicit and, apart from one pattern, uncapped.

| Resource | Allocation model | Bound |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | One thread — the host's calling thread — for both polling and execution | Nothing throttles a job body; there is no timeout anywhere in the module |
| Memory | One `Job` object per registered job, retaining the callable and every bound argument through `functools.partial` | Linear in job count; measured at roughly 1.1 KB per job for a no-argument body on CPython 3.12 |
| Threads | Zero allocated by the library | Whatever the host's chosen recipe allocates — unbounded for thread-per-firing, capped by worker count for the queue pattern |
| Timezone data | One `pytz` zone object referenced per job that requested one (lines 500–504) | No shared cache and no eviction; no zone database loads unless a timezone is requested |
| File handles, sockets, connections | None — the module performs no I/O | Not applicable |

The single deliberate capping mechanism in the repository is the shared `queue.Queue` plus fixed worker set from `docs/parallel-execution.rst` (lines 34–66), introduced there precisely for "tighter control on the number of threads". Adopters requiring back-pressure should note that the queue is unbounded in that recipe as written; a bounded queue is a host-side substitution.

#### 6.1.3.4 Performance Optimisation Techniques

Every optimisation actually present in the codebase is a cost-avoidance measure rather than a throughput multiplier.

| Technique | Implementation | Benefit |
|---|---|---|
| Filter before sorting | `run_pending` sorts only the due subset, not the registry (lines 99–100) | O(n) scan plus O(k log k) ordering, where k is usually far smaller than n |
| Lazy log formatting | All eight `logger.debug` calls pass `%`-style arguments rather than pre-formatted strings | Message rendering costs nothing when no handler accepts DEBUG |
| Lazy optional import | `import pytz` inside `Job.at()` (line 499) | Hosts that never use timezones load no third-party code and no zone database |
| Compute-once derived state | `next_run` is recomputed from exactly two call sites, lines 657 and 693 | Poll-time work is a comparison, not a recomputation (Section 5.3.5) |
| Precise sleeping | `idle_seconds()` lets the host sleep exactly until the next occurrence and exit when it returns `None` (`docs/examples.rst` lines 247–271) | Removes polling slack and wasted wake-ups; the first of the three levers named in Section 5.4.5 |
| Occurrence jitter | `to()` re-draws the interval on each reschedule (line 712) | Spreads simultaneous occurrences and de-synchronises identical schedules across processes |
| Forced-run spacing | `run_all(delay_seconds)` (lines 118–120) | Prevents a thundering herd when every job is forced at once |

The dominant optimisation, however, is architectural and host-side: moving long-running bodies off the dispatch thread. `docs/index.rst` lines 65–67 state that the library "does not account for the time it takes for the job function to execute" and that offloading long jobs is required "to guarantee a stable execution schedule."

#### 6.1.3.5 Capacity Planning Guidelines

No capacity model, benchmark, throughput target, or SLA is published anywhere in this repository — Section 5.4.5 and Section 2.4.3 both record that finding, and the only timing reference point either offers is the 81-method test suite completing in 0.12 s on Python 3.12. The guidance below is therefore derived from the algorithms plus measurements taken directly against this checkout; the figures are indicative of one interpreter on one machine, not a commitment.

Measured on CPython 3.12.3, median of 200 polls, with no job due (so the cost is purely the registry scan):

| Registered jobs | `run_pending()` scan, median | `idle_seconds` evaluation, median |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 4.2 µs | 3.0 µs |
| 100 | 36.2 µs | 18.3 µs |
| 1,000 | 362.5 µs | 171.9 µs |
| 10,000 | 3,664.2 µs | 1,782.2 µs |

Both curves are strictly linear at roughly 0.36 µs and 0.18 µs per registered job respectively, exactly as the O(n) filter at lines 99–100 and the `min()` scan at line 193 predict. The practical conclusion is that **registry size is almost never the constraint**: a 1,000-job registry polled every second consumes on the order of 0.4 ms of CPU per second for scanning. Capacity planning should therefore be driven by job bodies.

| Planning question | Basis for the answer | Rule of thumb from the evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Will the registry fit? | Linear memory, ~1.1 KB per trivial job plus the size of bound arguments | Thousands of jobs are inexpensive; large bound payloads dominate long before job count does |
| Will polling keep up? | Linear scan at sub-microsecond per job | Negligible below roughly 10,000 jobs at a one-second cadence |
| Will the schedule stay on time? | Serial execution; job duration is not accounted for | The sum of all job durations in any cycle must be comfortably shorter than the shortest interval, or long bodies must be offloaded |
| How late can a job be? | `next_run` plus one poll period plus the duration of earlier jobs in the same cycle (Section 5.4.5) | Reduce the poll period, or drive the loop from `idle_seconds()`, to shrink the first term |
| What happens under sustained overload? | Missed occurrences are never replayed (docstring, lines 93–97) | Occurrences are silently dropped rather than queued; a negative `idle_seconds()` is the only warning |
| What is the cost of forcing everything? | `run_all(delay_seconds)` sleeps after every job, including the last | Total added time is job count × delay; size the delay against the maintenance window |
| Does the timezone path cost more? | Up to two `normalize()` calls and two offset comparisons per reschedule (lines 773–817) | The most expensive scheduling path (Section 2.4.3, F-004); still negligible against real job bodies |


### 6.1.4 Resilience Patterns

The library's resilience posture can be stated in one sentence: **it guarantees that bad configuration can never corrupt the registry, and it guarantees nothing about the execution of job bodies.** Everything protective sits on the definition side of the boundary; on the execution side the library is deliberately transparent, passing faults through to the host untouched. Section 5.4.3 documents the resulting error-handling architecture and Section 5.4.6 the continuity model; this sub-section catalogues the resilience patterns themselves — which are implemented, which are absent, and which the host must compose — and maps the blast radius of each failure mode.

#### 6.1.4.1 Fault Tolerance Mechanisms

The mechanisms below are the complete set of fault-tolerance features implemented in `schedule/__init__.py`. Each is verifiable at the cited lines.

| Mechanism | Fault it tolerates | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| Validate-then-register | An abandoned or malformed definition chain corrupting the registry | The registry append is the final statement of `do()` (lines 655–663); asserted by `test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler` |
| Fail-fast validation | Invalid units, singular/plural misuse, weekday misuse, bad clock strings, past deadlines, unhashable tags | 28 raise sites, all at definition time, across lines 328–449, 467–639, 705–723 and 942 |
| Idempotent cancellation | Cancelling a job that is not registered | `list.remove` wrapped in `try`/`except ValueError` with a DEBUG record (lines 156–160); asserted by `test_cancel_job` |
| Dual sentinel recognition | A job returning the `CancelJob` class instead of an instance, or vice versa | `isinstance(ret, CancelJob) or ret is CancelJob` (line 174) |
| Deadline fuse | A job outliving its intended window, in either direction | `until()` is checked *before* execution and again *after* rescheduling, with cancellation taking priority over the return value (lines 686–698) |
| Tolerant introspection | Querying an empty registry or an unmatched tag | `get_next_run` and `idle_seconds` return `None` rather than raising (lines 188–192, 204–205) |
| Defensive rendering | A job with no `job_func`, or a callable without `__name__` | Fallbacks in `__str__` and `__repr__` (lines 265–268, 290–300) |
| Clock-change correction | A wall-clock anchor that shifts or does not exist under DST | `_correct_utc_offset` normalises the offset and, on a DST gap, displaces by one offset — silently and by design (lines 773–817) |
| Parse fallback chain | An acceptable but unanticipated deadline string format | Five `strptime` formats attempted in order (lines 822–830) |

Classifying the conventional resilience patterns against this implementation gives the following picture. "Host-composed" means the repository publishes a recipe but ships no code.

| Resilience pattern | Status in this system | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Fail-fast validation | **Implemented** | 28 definition-time raise sites; no partial state reachable |
| Idempotent operations | **Implemented** for cancellation; **required** of job bodies | Lines 156–160; the re-attempt semantics of 6.1.2.6 make idempotency an adopter obligation |
| Timeout | **Absent** | No timeout, alarm, or watchdog exists; the callable at line 691 may run indefinitely |
| Bulkhead / isolation | **Absent** | One thread, one registry, no partition of execution; a slow job delays all later jobs in the cycle |
| Circuit breaker | **Host-composed** | `catch_exceptions(cancel_on_failure=True)` returns `CancelJob`; a permanent trip with no reset (6.1.2.5) |
| Retry with backoff | **Absent**; an unconfigurable next-poll re-attempt occurs instead | Statement ordering at lines 691–693 (6.1.2.6) |
| Fallback / graceful substitute | **Absent** for job execution | No alternate callable, cached result, or dead-letter path |
| Health check / liveness | **Absent** | No endpoint, heartbeat, or probe; Section 5.4.1 records that a failing job is indistinguishable from a healthy one |
| Supervision / auto-restart | **Absent** | The library owns no lifecycle to supervise (`docs/background-execution.rst` line 4) |
| Load shedding | **Implicit** | Missed occurrences are dropped rather than queued (docstring, lines 93–97) |

#### 6.1.4.2 Failure Modes and Blast Radius

| Failure mode | Immediate effect | Blast radius |
|---|---|---|
| Job body raises | Exception escapes `run_pending()`; `last_run` and `next_run` are not advanced | The remaining due jobs in that cycle are skipped; the job stays registered and re-qualifies on the next poll |
| Host loop terminates on that exception | No further dispatch occurs, though jobs remain in memory | Every job in that registry stops silently — the widest in-process radius |
| Job body blocks or runs long | The dispatch thread is occupied | Every later job in the cycle is delayed; drift accumulates because rescheduling is relative to *now* |
| `pytz` absent when `at(tz=…)` is called | `ModuleNotFoundError` from the lazy import at line 499 | Definition-time only; the registry is unaffected (`docs/faq.rst` prescribes `pip install pytz`) |
| Requested wall-clock time falls in a DST gap | Best-effort displacement of one offset later | That job's next occurrence only; nothing is raised and nothing is logged |
| Process exits, planned or not | The registry ceases to exist | Total schedule loss; nothing is replayed on restart (Section 5.4.6) |
| Two host processes declare the same schedule | Both dispatch independently | Every occurrence executes once per process — duplication, not distribution |
| A registered `Job` is mutated by host code | `next_run` is not refreshed; there is no observer | That job's timing until its next recomputation (Section 5.3.5) |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Fault([Fault originates]) --> Class{"Which class<br/>of fault?"}
    Class -->|"malformed definition"| ToLib["Configuration fault"]
    Class -->|"job body fails"| ToExec["Execution fault"]
    Class -->|"clock or zone anomaly"| ToEnv["Environment fault"]
    Class -->|"process ends"| ToProc["Lifecycle fault"]
    subgraph LibLayer["Layer 1 — contained by the library"]
        direction TB
        C1["Guard raises before the registry append<br/>lines 655 to 663"]
        C2["until() fuse cancels the job before or<br/>after execution, lines 686 to 698"]
        C3["cancel_job tolerates unknown jobs<br/>lines 156 to 160"]
        C4["Offset correction absorbs DST shifts and<br/>displaces gap times, lines 773 to 817"]
        C1 --> Held["Registry integrity preserved,<br/>steady state resumed"]
        C2 --> Held
        C3 --> Held
        C4 --> Held
    end
    subgraph HostLayer["Layer 2 — contained only if the host composes it"]
        direction TB
        H1["Wrap the callable: catch_exceptions,<br/>docs/exception-handling.rst"]
        H2["Return CancelJob to trip permanently"]
        H3["Guard the dispatch loop so it survives"]
        H4["Offload the body to a thread or worker queue,<br/>docs/parallel-execution.rst"]
        H1 --> Contained["Fault absorbed, loop survives"]
        H2 --> Contained
        H3 --> Contained
        H4 --> Contained
    end
    subgraph Uncontained["Layer 3 — uncontained by design"]
        direction TB
        U1["Exception escapes run_pending and the<br/>rest of the due set is skipped"]
        U2["No timeout, so a blocking body stalls dispatch<br/>indefinitely"]
        U3["Registry is memory only, so process exit is<br/>total schedule loss"]
        U1 --> Recover["Recovery requires host action:<br/>re-declare the schedule at start-up"]
        U2 --> Recover
        U3 --> Recover
    end
    ToLib --> C1
    ToEnv --> C4
    ToExec --> H1
    ToExec -.->|"no host guard in place"| U1
    ToProc --> U3
```

**Diagram 6.1.4-A — Resilience pattern implementation: the three containment layers and which fault class each one stops.** Layer 1 is library code; Layer 2 exists only if the adopter implements the published recipes; Layer 3 is uncontained by design and recovers only through host action.

#### 6.1.4.3 Disaster Recovery Procedures

There is no disaster-recovery mechanism in this repository, and no runbook, backup script, snapshot format, journal, or restore path exists — Section 5.4.6 records the verified absence of `backup`, `restore`, `disaster`, `failover` and `replica` across every tracked file, and `docs/index.rst` lists job persistence first among the reasons to choose a different library. The continuity model is **stateless re-declaration**: the definition code, held in version control, is the schedule's only durable representation, and re-executing it at start-up is the entire recovery procedure.

Expressed in conventional recovery terms, and derived strictly from observed behaviour rather than any stated commitment:

| Recovery dimension | Value implied by the implementation |
|---|---|
| Recovery point | No state is persisted, so nothing in-flight survives; occurrences missed during downtime are never replayed |
| Recovery time | Host process start-up plus the time to re-execute the definition code — registration is O(1) per job |
| Recovery mechanism | Import the module and re-run the definitions; `@repeat` (lines 899–913) makes this a side effect of import |
| Catch-up option | `run_all()` forces every job exactly once regardless of due state and reschedules them normally, which triggers work but does **not** replay individual missed occurrences |
| Verification of recovery | `get_jobs()`, `next_run()` and `idle_seconds()` confirm the registry was rebuilt as intended |

Two properties make this model safer than it first appears. Registration is deterministic, so a restart produces exactly the schedule the code describes; and because configuration faults cannot enter the registry, no corrupt state is reachable to recover *from* (Section 5.4.6).

#### 6.1.4.4 Data Redundancy Approach

There is no redundancy, because there is exactly one copy of the runtime state and no facility for a second.

| Aspect | Finding |
|---|---|
| Store count | One — `Scheduler.jobs`, an in-memory list created at line 87; `default_scheduler` (line 837) is the process-global instance |
| Replication | None; no second reader, writer, follower, or shadow registry exists anywhere in the module |
| Copy semantics | `get_jobs()` returns a copy of the *list*, but its elements are the live `Job` objects — a shallow copy, not a snapshot |
| Live alias hazard | Module-level `jobs` (line 840) aliases the scheduler's list; deletions therefore mutate in place (lines 145, 148) to keep the alias valid, and the source carries an inline `todo` questioning the choice |
| Durable copy of intent | The definition code in version control — the only representation that survives a restart |

The practical guidance that follows is to treat the declaration code as the artifact requiring redundancy and review, since no runtime copy of the schedule exists to protect.

#### 6.1.4.5 Failover Configuration

**No failover configuration exists, and the architecture cannot support one without external help.** There is no leader election, no lock, no lease, no shared registry, and no cross-process coordination of any kind (Sections 5.3.8 and 5.4.6). The consequences are specific:

| Failover approach | Outcome in this system |
|---|---|
| Active/active — two processes running the same declarations | Both dispatch every occurrence; work is duplicated, not shared or failed over |
| Active/passive — a standby process holding the same declarations | Achievable only if the host arranges external coordination; the library offers no lock, heartbeat, or liveness signal to arbitrate with |
| In-process supervision — a watchdog restarting dispatch | The host must implement it; `docs/background-execution.rst` supplies only a thread wrapper and a `threading.Event` stop signal, not supervision |
| Instance-level redundancy inside one process | Not meaningful — multiple `Scheduler` instances partition state but share the one thread and die with the process |

Where duplicate execution is unacceptable and redundancy is required, the coordination must live outside the library — which is precisely the situation `docs/parallel-execution.rst` line 68 addresses by pointing at a distributed work queue consumed by separate worker processes.

#### 6.1.4.6 Service Degradation Policies

The library has no automatic degradation policy — no threshold, no priority class, and no shed-load rule. It does, however, expose a coherent set of primitives from which a host can express degradation, plus one implicit behaviour that already is a form of load shedding.

| Degradation control | Scope and trigger | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Silent occurrence dropping | Automatic and unconditional whenever polling falls behind | Missed occurrences are never replayed; a job polled hourly runs once, not sixty times (docstring, lines 93–97) |
| Group shedding | Operator- or host-initiated, per tag | `clear(tag)` removes a tagged group in one call; `docs/examples.rst` describes this as preventing every job in the group "from running again" |
| Single-job shedding | Host-initiated, per job handle | `cancel_job(job)`, tolerant of an already-removed job |
| Self-termination | Decided inside the job body | `return CancelJob`, honoured as class or instance |
| Time-boxed operation | Fixed at definition time | `until()` cancels the job once its deadline passes, checked on both sides of execution |
| Load spreading under forced runs | Host-initiated during maintenance or catch-up | `run_all(delay_seconds)` spaces every execution |
| De-synchronisation | Configured per job | `to()` jitter re-drawn on each reschedule, spreading coincident occurrences |
| Cooperative shutdown | Host-initiated | The `threading.Event` returned by the `run_continuously()` recipe stops the dispatch thread between polls (`docs/background-execution.rst` lines 27–38, 54) |

Two properties of this set should be recorded explicitly for adopters. First, degradation is always **subtractive** — every control removes or delays work, and none reduces fidelity while continuing to serve, because there is no partial-service concept in the library. Second, silent dropping means degradation is unobservable by default: the only signal that dispatch is falling behind is a negative return from `idle_seconds()` (Section 5.4.1), and nothing logs a missed occurrence.
