- Section 5.3 Technical Decisions — ADR-001 (embedded library), ADR-004 (serial caller-driven dispatch), ADR-005 (in-memory registry), ADR-007 (lazy `pytz`), ADR-008 (typed errors plus `CancelJob`), ADR-009 (DEBUG-only logging), the communication-pattern table, and the single-interpreter assumption
- Section 5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns — the error-handling architecture, the explicit absence of retry/backoff/breaker/dead-letter, the observable performance characteristics, the disaster-recovery position, and the library-versus-host responsibility matrix

#### 6.1.5.4 Verification Performed Directly Against the Checkout

- `git ls-files` — enumerated the complete 32-file tracked inventory that bounds every absence claim in 6.1.1
- Recursive `find` for `.blitzyignore` — confirmed no path exclusions apply to this repository
- Filesystem search for `Dockerfile*`, `docker-compose*`, `*.yaml`, `*.yml`, `*.tf`, `Procfile`, `*.service`, `Chart.yaml`, nginx/Envoy/Consul configuration — returned only `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
- Symbol search of `schedule/__init__.py` for network, IPC, concurrency and serialization constructs — returned no code matches, only three docstring URLs
- Case-insensitive repository search for `tenacity`, `backoff`, `circuitbreaker`, `pybreaker`, `retrying`, `consul`, `etcd`, `eureka`, `zookeeper`, `haproxy`, `kubernetes`, `prometheus`, `opentelemetry` — no matches
- Execution of the library on CPython 3.12.3 — confirmed that a raising job body propagates out of `run_pending()`, that the remaining due jobs in that cycle are skipped, that the failing job stays registered with `last_run` unset and `next_run` un-advanced and is re-attempted once per poll, that a `CancelJob`-returning guard empties the registry, and that the module exposes neither `__version__` nor `__all__`
- Timing and memory measurement on CPython 3.12.3 — produced the linear registry-scan figures and the ~1.1 KB-per-job memory figure quoted in 6.1.3.5, explicitly labelled indicative rather than a published benchmark

No external or web sources were required for this section; every claim is grounded in the repository or in an earlier section of this specification.


## 6.2 Database Design

### 6.2.1 Applicability Assessment

**Database Design is not applicable to this system.**

The subject of this specification is the Python `schedule` library at release 1.2.2 (`setup.py`). Its entire runtime is one module — `schedule/__init__.py`, 945 lines — shipped alongside the zero-byte PEP 561 marker `schedule/py.typed`. The library declares no database, embeds no engine, links no driver, defines no schema, and performs no filesystem or serialization operation of any kind. All state it manages lives in a single Python list for the lifetime of the host process, and that list is discarded when the process exits.

This determination is not an inference from the small size of the codebase. It was established by exhaustive scans across all 32 tracked files, enumerated with `git ls-files`, and each scan is recorded below with the pattern it applied and the result it returned. Section 3.5 reaches the same conclusion from the technology-stack perspective; this sub-section supplies the structural verification, and sub-sections 6.2.2 through 6.2.7 then do the constructive work that remains genuinely useful — documenting the in-memory job registry that occupies the position a database would occupy, and recording for every concern named in this section's scope (entity relationships, indexing, partitioning, replication, backup, migration, retention, privacy, audit, access control, query optimization, connection pooling, read/write splitting, batch processing) either the mechanism that plays that role in-process or the artifact that proves its absence.

#### 6.2.1.1 Determination Criteria and Findings

Each row below is a structural precondition for a database design. Every one of them fails, and every failure is verified against an executed scan rather than assumed.

| Precondition for a database design | Verification performed | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| A database engine, embedded or remote | Keyword scan of all 32 tracked files for `sqlite3`, `psycopg`, `pymongo`, `sqlalchemy`, `mysql`, `mariadb`, `asyncpg`, `peewee`, `tortoise`, `motor`, `cassandra`, `dynamodb`, `elasticsearch`, `neo4j`, `influx`, `clickhouse`, `duckdb`, `create_engine`, `declarative_base` | **Fails** — zero matches repository-wide |
| A cache, key-value, or object store | Same scan extended with `redis`, `memcache`, `boto3` | **Fails** — zero matches; no cache tier and no blob service |
| A schema, DDL, or data file | File-extension census of tracked files, plus a grep for `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, `INSERT INTO`, `PRIMARY KEY`, `FOREIGN KEY` | **Fails** — no `.sql`, `.db`, `.sqlite`, `.json`, or `.csv` file exists; the word "schema" appears nowhere in the repository |
| Migration or schema-versioning tooling | Grep for `alembic`, `flyway`, `liquibase`, `knex`, `prisma`, `typeorm`, `migrate`, `migration` | **Fails** — zero matches; no migration directory exists |
| File-based persistence or serialization | Grep of `schedule/__init__.py` for `open(`, `pickle`, `json`, `shelve`, `dbm`, `marshal`, `csv`, `tempfile`, `pathlib`, `os.`, `write(`, `read(` | **Fails** — zero matches; the module's complete import set is eight standard-library modules (lines 41–48) plus a function-local `import pytz` (line 499) |
| Connection configuration or credentials | Grep of the runtime module for `environ`, `getenv`, `dsn`, `connect`, `url`, `uri`, `password`, `secret`, `token`, `credential` | **Fails** — no environment variable is read and no connection string exists; the only two hits are false positives where the word "hourly" substring-matches "url" (lines 478, 520) |
| A data-tier deployment descriptor | Filesystem search for `docker-compose*`, `Dockerfile*`, `*.tf`, `Chart.yaml`, `.env*`, `*.yaml` | **Fails** — the only YAML in the repository is `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, a CI definition |
| Any indexed data-layer file or folder | Semantic searches for persistent data models and object-relational mappings, for migration/schema/storage-layer folders, and for cache or state-store implementations | **Fails** — all three searches returned empty result sets |

For completeness, the repository contains exactly three filesystem interactions in total, none of them in the runtime module and none of them persistence: `setup.py` line 13 opens `README.rst` to populate packaging metadata, `docs/conf.py` line 24 manipulates `sys.path` for Sphinx autodoc, and `test_schedule.py` sets the `TZ` environment variable (lines 29, 80–92) to make local-time assertions deterministic.

#### 6.2.1.2 The Absence Is a Published Product Boundary

The lack of a data tier is a deliberate, documented product decision rather than an unimplemented feature. A scan of every tracked file for the terms `persist`, `database`, `storage`, and `durab` returns exactly **one** match in the entire repository — `docs/index.rst` line 59 — and it appears under the heading "When **not** to use Schedule", where the documentation states plainly that the library is not a one-size-fits-all solution and is designed for simple scheduling problems. Job persistence, described there as remembering the schedule between restarts, is listed **first** among the four capabilities for which readers are told to look elsewhere; the other three are sub-second precision, concurrent execution, and localization.

Two consequences follow, and both are architecturally load-bearing:

- The library needs **no configuration surface at all** — no connection string, no credentials, no pool sizing, no retention setting — which is why `pyproject.toml` declares `dependencies = []` and the module reads no environment variable.
- Durability is contractually the **host application's** responsibility. The canonical usage pattern in `README.rst` and `docs/index.rst` re-declares every job in code before entering the polling loop, so the declaration source itself is the schedule's only durable representation. Sub-section 6.2.6 develops this boundary.

#### 6.2.1.3 What Plays the Role of a Database

To keep this section constructive rather than merely negative, the remainder analyses the in-memory job registry through a database-design lens. The mapping below is the organising principle for sub-sections 6.2.2 through 6.2.6; it is an analogy for orientation, not a claim that any of these structures is a database.

| Database concern | Counterpart in this system | Documented in |
|---|---|---|
| Persistent store | `Scheduler.jobs`, a `List[Job]` created in memory at lines 86–87 | 6.2.2.1 |
| Table and record | One `Job` instance per scheduled job, with twelve attributes assigned in `__init__` (lines 227–255) | 6.2.2.2 |
| Entity relationships | Object references: registry-to-job containment, job-to-scheduler back-reference, job-to-partial binding, job-to-tag set, job-to-timezone | 6.2.2.3 |
| Constraints | 28 validation raise sites plus one assertion, all enforced at definition time | 6.2.2.4 |
| Indexes | None; an ordering key (`Job.__lt__`) and per-record tag sets are the only access aids | 6.2.2.5 |
| Partitioning | Multiple independent `Scheduler()` instances, partitioned and polled by the host | 6.2.2.6 |
| Replication | None; exactly one copy of the state exists, with no follower, journal, or shadow registry | 6.2.2.7 |
| Backup and restore | None; the declaration code in version control is the only recoverable artifact | 6.2.2.8 |
| Schema migration and versioning | None; the record shape evolves through semantically versioned API releases recorded in `HISTORY.rst` | 6.2.3.1, 6.2.3.2 |
| Archival and retention | Process lifetime only, with automatic eviction of expired and self-cancelling jobs | 6.2.3.3, 6.2.4.1 |
| Read and write mechanisms | Six methods on `Scheduler` plus one on `Job`; all are direct list operations | 6.2.3.4 |
| Caching | None; `next_run` is a compute-once derived value with a single invalidation site | 6.2.3.5, 6.2.5.2 |
| Query optimization | Filter-before-sort in `run_pending`; linear scans elsewhere | 6.2.5.1 |
| Connection pooling, read/write splitting | Not applicable — there are no connections, no replicas, and no protocol boundary | 6.2.5.3, 6.2.5.4 |
| Batch processing | `run_all(delay_seconds)` forced sweeps and bulk `clear(tag)` deletion | 6.2.5.5 |
| Audit trail | Eight `logger.debug` records; `last_run` is overwritten rather than appended | 6.2.4.4 |
| Access control | Python module and attribute scope only; no authentication or authorization concept exists | 6.2.4.5 |


### 6.2.2 Schema Design of the In-Memory State Model

No schema exists in the database sense — there is no DDL, no catalog, and no declarative model. What exists is an implicit record structure fixed by the twelve attribute assignments in `Job.__init__` (lines 227–255) and a single container declared in `Scheduler.__init__` (lines 86–87). This sub-section documents that structure as the system's *de facto* schema, and records for each conventional schema concern either the mechanism that plays its role or the verified absence of one. Section 4.3.1.1 documents the same attributes from a state-management perspective, including which code writes and reads each one; the treatment here is storage-oriented and does not repeat it.

#### 6.2.2.1 The Single Store

| Store property | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Declaration | `self.jobs: List[Job] = []` | `Scheduler.__init__`, lines 86–87 |
| Stated purpose | Scheduler objects are factories that "keep record of scheduled jobs and handle their execution" | Class docstring, lines 80–84 |
| Number of stores | One per `Scheduler` instance; no secondary structure, index, or derived collection exists anywhere in the module | Verified across all 945 lines |
| Process-global instance | `default_scheduler = Scheduler()` | Line 837 |
| Public alias | `jobs = default_scheduler.jobs` — a live reference to the same list object, carrying an inline `todo` questioning whether it should be a copy | Line 840 |
| Medium and lifetime | Interpreter heap; created on instantiation, destroyed with the process | No serialization exists (6.2.1.1) |

The live alias at line 840 has a direct structural consequence that shapes several methods: because external code may hold the same list object, every deletion path mutates the list **in place** — `del self.jobs[:]` (line 145) and slice assignment (line 148) — rather than rebinding it. Verified empirically on CPython 3.12.3: `schedule.jobs is schedule.default_scheduler.jobs` returns `True`, and after `schedule.clear()` the alias is still the same list object with length zero.

#### 6.2.2.2 Record Structure and Data Types

Each row of the store is one mutable `Job` object. There is no fixed-width layout, no null bitmap, and no type enforcement beyond the annotations, which exist for `mypy` (configured over the package in `setup.cfg`) and are erased at runtime.

| Attribute | Stored type | Nullable / default | Role in the record |
|---|---|---|---|
| `interval` | `int` | Non-null; constructor argument | Quantity of time units between occurrences |
| `latest` | `Optional[int]` | `None` | Inclusive upper bound for a randomized interval |
| `job_func` | `Optional[functools.partial]` | `None` until `do()` | The bound callable together with its retained arguments |
| `unit` | `Optional[str]` | `None` | Time unit: `seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`, `days`, or `weeks` |
| `at_time` | `Optional[datetime.time]` | `None` | Wall-clock anchor within the unit |
| `at_time_zone` | Unannotated — the only field without a type | `None` | Retained `pytz` zone object; relevant only when `at_time` is set |
| `last_run` | `Optional[datetime.datetime]` | `None` | Timestamp of the most recent execution, naive local |
| `next_run` | `Optional[datetime.datetime]` | `None` until computed | The only derived field; sole ordering and due-ness key |
| `start_day` | `Optional[str]` | `None` | Lowercase weekday name; relevant only when `unit == "weeks"` |
| `cancel_after` | `Optional[datetime.datetime]` | `None` | Deadline after which the record is evicted |
| `tags` | `Set[Hashable]` | Empty set | Denormalized group labels stored inside the record |
| `scheduler` | `Optional[Scheduler]` | Constructor argument | Back-reference to the owning registry |

Three properties of this record shape are worth recording explicitly:

- **All timestamps are naive local values.** `_schedule_next_run` computes with a timezone-aware `now` when `at_time_zone` is set (line 717) but converts the result back to naive local time before storing it (lines 740–747), a conversion the source comments attribute to backward compatibility. `docs/timezones.rst` states the same contract from the user's perspective.
- **The record is mutable for its whole life.** `next_run` and `last_run` are rewritten in place on every execution, so any holder of a `Job` reference always observes current values.
- **Record size is dominated by bound arguments.** `do()` retains the callable and every positional and keyword argument in a `functools.partial` (line 655) for the record's entire lifetime. Measured on CPython 3.12.3, a job whose body is a no-argument lambda occupies roughly 1.1 KB; anything captured through `do()` adds to that figure and is never released until the record is evicted.

#### 6.2.2.3 Entity Relationships

Relationships are ordinary Python object references, resolved by pointer rather than by key lookup. There are no join keys, no association tables, and no cascade rules.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    SCHEDULER ||--o{ JOB : "registry holds zero or more"
    JOB ||--|| BOUND_CALLABLE : "binds exactly one at do()"
    JOB }o--o{ TAG : "labelled by, stored in-record"
    JOB }o--o| TIMEZONE : "retains one zone when at(tz) used"
    SCHEDULER {
        list jobs "the only store, line 87"
    }
    JOB {
        int interval "non-null"
        int latest "randomized upper bound"
        str unit "seconds to weeks"
        str start_day "weekday name, weeks only"
        time at_time "wall-clock anchor"
        datetime next_run "derived, ordering key"
        datetime last_run "overwritten each run"
        datetime cancel_after "eviction deadline"
        set tags "denormalized labels"
        partial job_func "bound callable"
        tzinfo at_time_zone "unannotated field"
        Scheduler scheduler "back-reference, line 255"
    }
    BOUND_CALLABLE {
        callable func "host-supplied"
        tuple args "retained for record lifetime"
        dict keywords "retained for record lifetime"
    }
    TAG {
        Hashable value "must be hashable, line 467"
    }
    TIMEZONE {
        str zone_name "resolved by pytz.timezone"
    }
```

**Diagram 6.2.2-A — Entity-relationship model of the in-memory registry.** Only `SCHEDULER` and `JOB` are stored entities. `BOUND_CALLABLE` is the `functools.partial` created at line 655; `TAG` and `TIMEZONE` are values held inside the job record, not rows in any collection.

| Relationship | Cardinality and direction | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| Registry containment | One `Scheduler` to zero-or-more `Job` | `list.append` in `do()` (line 663); ordinary list membership thereafter |
| Owner back-reference | Each `Job` to at most one `Scheduler` | Assigned in the constructor (line 255) from `Scheduler.every()` (line 169); mandatory before registration |
| Callable binding | One `Job` to exactly one `functools.partial` | Created and wrapped at lines 655–656; invoked at line 691 |
| Tag labelling | Many `Job` to many tag values, denormalized per record | `self.tags.update(tags)` (line 468); set semantics collapse duplicates, verified empirically |
| Timezone retention | Each `Job` to at most one `pytz` object | Written only at lines 502 and 504; re-read on every reschedule |

Two absences matter for anyone modelling this system. There is **no tag entity and no inverted index** — a tag exists only inside the records that carry it, so group lookup is a scan of the registry (6.2.2.5). And the containment relationship is **not integrity-checked in both directions**: the back-reference is validated before insertion (line 658), but nothing prevents host code from appending to `scheduler.jobs` directly or from mutating a registered job, and no observer refreshes `next_run` when it does (Section 5.3.5).

#### 6.2.2.4 Constraint Catalog

Constraints are expressed as imperative guards rather than declarations, and they are concentrated almost entirely at **definition time** — 28 `raise` sites plus one assertion, all in `schedule/__init__.py`. The effect is equivalent to validating a row before insertion: `do()` computes the first occurrence and checks the owner reference *before* appending (lines 655–663), so a rejected definition never reaches the store.

| Constraint class | Rule enforced | Enforcement site and error |
|---|---|---|
| Unit domain (write) | Singular selectors (`second`, `minute`, `hour`, `day`, `week`) require `interval == 1` | `IntervalError` at lines 328, 339, 350, 361, 372 |
| Unit domain (weekday) | `monday`…`sunday` require `interval == 1` | `IntervalError` at lines 383, 394, 405, 416, 427, 438, 449 |
| Unit domain (schedule) | `unit` must be one of `seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`, `days`, `weeks` | `ScheduleValueError` at line 705 |
| Unit dependency | `start_day` requires `unit == "weeks"` | `ScheduleValueError` at line 723 |
| Weekday name domain | Day name must be a lowercase `monday`…`sunday` | `ScheduleValueError` at line 942 (`_weekday_index`) |
| Range invariant | `latest >= interval` before drawing `random.randint(interval, latest)` | `ScheduleError` at line 711 |
| Anchor precondition | `at()` requires `unit` in `days`/`hours`/`minutes`, or a `start_day` | `ScheduleValueError` at line 494 |
| Format pattern (daily) | `^[0-2]\d:[0-5]\d(:[0-5]\d)?$` | Checked at line 513; `ScheduleValueError` at 514 |
| Format pattern (hourly) | `^([0-5]\d)?:[0-5]\d$` | Checked at line 518; `ScheduleValueError` at 519 |
| Format pattern (minutely) | `^:[0-5]\d$` | Checked at line 524; `ScheduleValueError` at 525 |
| Value range | Hour component must be 0–23 | `ScheduleValueError` at line 547 |
| Type constraint | `at()` accepts only `str`; timezone accepts only `str` or `pytz.BaseTzInfo` | `TypeError` at line 511; `ScheduleValueError` at line 506 |
| Type constraint | `until()` accepts `datetime`, `timedelta`, `time`, or one of five string formats | `ScheduleValueError` at 625, `TypeError` at 634 |
| Temporal constraint | `cancel_after` must not be in the past at write time | `ScheduleValueError` at lines 638–639 |
| Type constraint | Every tag must be hashable | `TypeError` at line 467 |
| Referential integrity | A record cannot be inserted without an owning `Scheduler` | `ScheduleError` at lines 658–662 |
| Not-null invariant | Every registered record must have a computed `next_run` | `assert` at line 671, relied upon by `should_run` |

The three regular expressions at lines 513, 518 and 524 are the only pattern constraints in the entire codebase. The `until()` deadline check is the only temporal constraint. Enforcement at **read** time is limited to the deadline test in `_is_overdue` (line 820), which drives eviction rather than rejection.

Equally important is what the store does *not* constrain:

| Conventional constraint | Status in this system |
|---|---|
| Primary key / uniqueness | **Absent.** `Job` defines neither `__eq__` nor `__hash__`, so records are distinguished only by object identity. Calling `do()` twice on the same job object inserts it twice — verified: registry length 2, both entries the identical object |
| Foreign-key cascade | **Absent.** Deleting a record does not touch anything it references; a snapshot taken by `get_jobs()` still holds an evicted job — verified |
| Check constraint on the payload | **Absent.** `job_func` is accepted as any callable; nothing validates its signature, duration, or return type beyond the `CancelJob` sentinel test at line 174 |
| Not-null on `tags` / `last_run` | **Not applicable.** Both are legitimately empty until used |
| Unique index on tags | **Absent.** Set semantics enforce uniqueness only *within* one record |

#### 6.2.2.5 Indexing Strategy

**There is no index.** No secondary structure, hash map, sorted container, or inverted index exists anywhere in the module; every lookup walks the list. Two mechanisms serve the purpose an index would serve, and both are computed on demand.

| Access aid | Mechanism | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Ordering key on `next_run` | `Job.__lt__` compares `self.next_run < other.next_run` (lines 257–262) | Enables `sorted()` in `run_pending` (line 100) and `min()` in `get_next_run` (line 193); O(n) for `min`, O(k log k) for the due subset |
| Tag membership | `tag in job.tags` against a per-record `set` (line 133) | O(1) per record, but the registry itself is scanned — O(n) overall |
| Due-ness predicate | `should_run` compares the wall clock to `next_run` (line 672) | O(1) per record; O(n) per poll across the registry |

Measured against this checkout on CPython 3.12.3 with 1,000 registered jobs (median of five batches of 200 calls): `get_jobs()` — a slice copy with no predicate — costs 2.3 µs; `get_jobs("bulk")` matching every record costs 26.4 µs; `get_jobs("nope")` matching none costs 21.5 µs. The near-identical hit and miss figures confirm that cost is driven by the scan, not by selectivity: there is nothing an index could short-circuit. Section 6.1.3.5 reports the corresponding poll-scan and `idle_seconds` curves, both strictly linear.

The ordering key carries one operational constraint worth noting: because `__lt__` dereferences `next_run` on both operands, a registry containing a record with `next_run = None` cannot be sorted — verified to raise `TypeError`. This is precisely why insertion is deferred until after `_schedule_next_run()` has run (line 657), making the not-null invariant of 6.2.2.4 a prerequisite for the index rather than an incidental check.

#### 6.2.2.6 Partitioning Approach

There is no data partitioning in the storage sense — no sharding key, no range or hash distribution, no partition catalog. The only partitioning primitive is **instance-level separation**: each `Scheduler()` owns a private list, so a host can distribute records across several registries. `docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` documents this explicitly, stating that multiple schedulers may be desirable for larger installations and that it is supported.

| Partitioning aspect | Behaviour | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Partition unit | One `Scheduler` instance = one independent registry | Lines 86–87; verified that two instances hold distinct list objects |
| Partition key | None — the host decides which registry receives a job when it calls `every()` on that instance | `Scheduler.every()`, lines 162–170 |
| Cross-partition query | None; `get_jobs`, `get_next_run` and `idle_seconds` each read one registry only | Lines 122–206 |
| Coordination between partitions | None — no shared clock, lock, or visibility | `docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` requires the host to call `run_pending()` on every scheduler |
| Rebalancing or migration | None; a record cannot be moved between registries — its `scheduler` back-reference is set at construction | Line 255 |
| Benefit obtained | Isolation of state and lifecycle only; no parallelism is gained | Section 6.1.3.1 |

The `default_scheduler` at line 837 is the implicit single partition used by the module-level facade. Because `jobs` (line 840) aliases its list, every component sharing an interpreter and using the facade functions shares one partition — a property adopters should weigh when a library and its host both schedule work.

#### 6.2.2.7 Replication Configuration

**No replication exists and none can be configured.** The module contains no follower, journal, change stream, write-ahead log, snapshot mechanism, or second reader of the registry; there is no primary/replica concept because there is no second copy of the data. Section 6.1.4.4 records the same finding as a redundancy assessment, and Section 6.1.4.5 records why failover cannot be arranged inside the library.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Conventional["Conventional replication architecture — no element here is implemented, configured, or depended upon by this repository"]
        direction LR
        Primary[("Primary store<br/>accepts writes")]
        Journal["Write-ahead log<br/>or change stream"]
        Replica1[("Read replica 1")]
        ReplicaN[("Read replica N")]
        Vault["Snapshot / backup vault"]
        Primary --> Journal
        Journal --> Replica1
        Journal --> ReplicaN
        Primary --> Vault
    end
    subgraph Verified["Verified topology — one registry per interpreter, zero replication"]
        direction TB
        Source["Declaration code in version control<br/>the only durable representation"]
        ProcA["Host process A<br/>independent interpreter"]
        ProcB["Host process B<br/>independent interpreter"]
        RegA1["Scheduler registry<br/>jobs list in memory"]
        RegA2["Second Scheduler instance<br/>separate partition, same process"]
        RegB1["Scheduler registry<br/>independent copy, no link to A"]
        Outcome{{"Every occurrence fires once per process:<br/>duplication, not replication"}}
        Source -->|"re-executed at each start-up"| ProcA
        Source -->|"re-executed at each start-up"| ProcB
        ProcA --> RegA1
        ProcA --> RegA2
        ProcB --> RegB1
        RegA1 --> Outcome
        RegB1 --> Outcome
    end
    Primary -.->|"no driver, journal, follower, lock,<br/>lease, or leader election exists"| ProcA
```

**Diagram 6.2.2-B — Replication architecture: the conventional model contrasted with the verified single-copy topology.** The left group is documented only to record what is absent. In the right group, the two processes are wholly independent: running the same declarations in both duplicates execution rather than replicating state.

| Replication concern | Finding |
|---|---|
| Replica count | Zero. One list object per `Scheduler`, created at line 87 |
| Replication mode | None — no synchronous, asynchronous, or logical replication path exists |
| Copy semantics inside the process | `get_jobs()` returns a copy of the *list* whose elements are the live records (line 131) — a shallow copy, not a snapshot; verified |
| Conflict resolution | Not applicable; no second writer exists. There is also no lock, so concurrent host threads mutating one registry are unprotected (Section 4.3.1.6) |
| Cross-process consistency | Not applicable and not achievable in-library; each process holds an uncoordinated registry |
| Failover / promotion | None; see Section 6.1.4.5 |

#### 6.2.2.8 Backup Architecture

**No backup architecture exists.** There is no dump, export, snapshot, archive, or restore path in the codebase; the repository-wide scans in 6.2.1.1 found no serialization primitive of any kind in the runtime module, and Section 6.1.4.3 records the verified absence of `backup`, `restore`, `disaster`, `failover` and `replica` across every tracked file.

| Backup dimension | Actual position |
|---|---|
| What is backed up | Nothing at runtime. The **declaration code** — the `every(...).do(...)` chains and `@repeat` decorations in the host application — is the only durable representation of the schedule, and version control is its backing store |
| Backup mechanism | Not applicable; no state can be exported because no serializer exists |
| Restore procedure | Re-execute the declaration code at start-up. `README.rst` and `docs/index.rst` show exactly this pattern before entering the polling loop; `@repeat` (lines 899–913) makes registration a side effect of import |
| Recovery point | Nothing in flight survives; occurrences missed while the process was down are never replayed, because `run_pending()` does not run missed jobs (docstring, lines 93–97) |
| Recovery time | Process start-up plus re-registration, which is O(1) per record |
| Verification of a restore | `get_jobs()`, `next_run()` and `idle_seconds()` confirm the registry was rebuilt as intended |

The one property that makes this model tolerable is determinism: because every constraint in 6.2.2.4 is enforced *before* insertion, re-running the declaration code produces exactly the registry the code describes, and no partially valid record can ever have existed to recover from.


### 6.2.3 Data Management

Data management for this system means managing objects in a list for the duration of a process. There is no migration engine, no archival tier, and no cache. What follows documents the mechanisms that do exist — the record-shape evolution history, the complete inventory of storage and retrieval operations, and the one compute-once derived value that is sometimes mistaken for a cache.

#### 6.2.3.1 Migration Procedures

**No data migration procedure exists, and none is possible.** There is no schema catalog to alter, no migration directory, no versioned change script, and no stored data to transform — the repository-wide scan for `alembic`, `flyway`, `liquibase`, `knex`, `prisma`, `typeorm`, `migrate` and `migration` returns zero matches (6.2.1.1). Because the registry is rebuilt from declaration code on every start-up (6.2.2.8), a change to the record shape takes effect the moment the new library version is imported; there is never an old copy of the data left behind to convert.

What does require managed evolution is the **record shape itself**, and the repository's history shows that it has been managed additively. Every release that extended the record added an optional attribute defaulting to `None` or to an empty set, so declaration code written against an earlier version continues to produce valid records.

| Release | Change to the record shape | Attribute affected |
|---|---|---|
| 0.2.0 (2013-11-09) | Cancellation introduced via `cancel_job()` and the `CancelJob` return value | Added the eviction paths, no new field |
| 0.4.0 (2016-11-28) | Ability to tag jobs and cancel by tag; fixed `run_all()` when more than one job deletes itself in one iteration | Added `tags`; motivated the snapshot copy at line 118 |
| 0.5.0 (2017-11-16) | Random intervals added; partially scheduled jobs kept from breaking the scheduler (#125) | Added `latest`; established validate-then-register |
| 0.6.0 (2019-01-20) | `at()` accepts one-second precision (#267); proper exception hierarchy (#271) | Extended `at_time` to seconds |
| 1.1.0 (2021-04-09) | `.until()` deadlines (#195), `@repeat` (#148), tag-filtered retrieval (#419), type annotations (#427) | Added `cancel_after`; annotated the whole record |
| 1.2.0 (2023-04-10) | Timezone support for `.at()` (#517), next run by tag (#463), `py.typed` (#521) | Added `at_time_zone` |
| 1.2.1 / 1.2.2 (2023-11-01, 2024-05-25) | Cross-timezone and DST correctness fixes (#583, #601, #602, #604, #623) | No shape change — altered how `next_run` is computed |

The practical migration procedure for an adopter is therefore an ordinary dependency upgrade followed by a process restart, since re-declaration is the only way records are ever created. The one migration-like hazard is behavioural rather than structural: releases 1.2.1 and 1.2.2 changed the *computed value* of `next_run` for timezone-anchored jobs, so an upgrade can shift firing times without any change to the declaration code.

#### 6.2.3.2 Versioning Strategy

| Versioning aspect | Mechanism | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Scheme | Semantic versioning | `docs/development.rst` line 68 states the project follows semantic versioning |
| Authoritative version literal | `SCHEDULE_VERSION = "1.2.2"`, consumed by `version=` and the download URL | `setup.py` lines 5, 6, 21 |
| Second version literal | `version` and `release` both `"1.2.2"` for Sphinx | `docs/conf.py` lines 69, 71 |
| Release procedure | Update `HISTORY.rst` and `AUTHORS.rst`, bump the version in both files, tag `X.Y.Z`, build a wheel, upload to TestPyPI then PyPI | `docs/development.rst` lines 49–68 |
| Runtime introspection | None — the module exposes no `__version__` attribute and no `__all__` | Verified against the checkout |
| Record-level versioning | None — no schema-version column, revision counter, or `updated_at` field exists on a `Job` | `Job.__init__`, lines 227–255 |
| Dynamic metadata | `pyproject.toml` declares `version` dynamic, so `setup.py` is the single build-time source | `pyproject.toml` |

Two consequences follow. Because the version literal is duplicated in `setup.py` and `docs/conf.py`, keeping them synchronised is a manual release step that the documentation calls out explicitly. And because no version is embedded in a record and nothing is persisted, there is no possibility of a version mismatch between stored data and running code — the class of problem that schema versioning exists to solve cannot arise here.

#### 6.2.3.3 Archival Policies

**There is no archive.** No cold store, no history table, no retention tier, and no export path exist. Records leave the registry by deletion only, and nothing is written anywhere when they do.

| Archival concern | Actual behaviour | Site |
|---|---|---|
| Historical record of executions | None. `last_run` is **overwritten** on each run rather than appended to any log of runs | Line 692 |
| Retention of evicted records | None. Once removed from the list, a record is unreachable and garbage-collected unless the caller still holds a reference | Lines 145, 148, 158 |
| Automatic eviction on expiry | A job whose deadline has passed is removed instead of archived — `CancelJob` is returned before execution, or after rescheduling if the new occurrence exceeds the deadline | Lines 686–688, 695–697, 174–175 |
| Automatic eviction on self-cancellation | A job body returning `CancelJob` (class or instance) is removed by the dispatcher | Line 174 |
| Bulk purge | `clear()` empties the registry; `clear(tag)` purges a group | Lines 143–148 |
| Growth bound | The registry does not grow without bound: expired and self-cancelling records are removed automatically | Verified paths above |

The absence of an execution history has one architectural implication worth stating plainly: **the system retains no evidence that a job ever ran** beyond the single mutable `last_run` timestamp on the live record. Any requirement for run history must be satisfied outside the library, which is why `docs/logging.rst` publishes a `print_elapsed_time` decorator as the suggested starting point for per-job telemetry.

#### 6.2.3.4 Storage and Retrieval Mechanisms

The complete data-access surface is six methods on `Scheduler` plus one on `Job`. Every one is a direct operation on the underlying list; there is no query language, no cursor, no transaction, and no prepared statement.

| Operation | Mechanism and site | Complexity |
|---|---|---|
| Insert | `Job.do()` appends as its final statement, after binding the callable and computing the first occurrence (lines 655–663) | O(1) amortized |
| Read all | `get_jobs()` returns `self.jobs[:]` — a new list holding the live records (line 131) | O(n) copy |
| Read by group | `get_jobs(tag)` filters on set membership (line 133) | O(n) scan |
| Read minimum | `get_next_run(tag)` returns `min(...).next_run`, or `None` for an empty registry or unmatched tag (lines 188–193) | O(n) |
| Read derived | `idle_seconds` subtracts the wall clock from `next_run`, or returns `None` (lines 204–206) | O(n) via `next_run` |
| Read due subset | `run_pending()` filters on `should_run`, then sorts only the due records (lines 99–100) | O(n) filter + O(k log k) sort |
| Update | Mutation in place during execution: `last_run` stamped, `next_run` recomputed (lines 692–693); `tag()` unions labels (line 468) | O(1) per record |
| Delete one | `cancel_job(job)` calls `list.remove` inside a `try`, swallowing `ValueError` (lines 156–160) | O(n), idempotent |
| Delete all / group | `del self.jobs[:]` or one slice assignment (lines 145, 148) | O(1) / O(n), in place |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Definition["Definition — host declares the schedule"]
        direction TB
        DStart["Host calls every(interval)<br/>lines 162-170"]
        DBuild["Fluent configuration mutates the record:<br/>unit, start_day, at_time, at_time_zone,<br/>latest, cancel_after, tags"]
        DGuard{{"All definition-time constraints satisfied?<br/>28 raise sites, 6.2.2.4"}}
        DReject["Exception raised to the caller;<br/>record never reaches the store"]
        DBind["do() binds functools.partial<br/>and computes first next_run — 655-657"]
        DStart --> DBuild --> DGuard
        DGuard -->|"no"| DReject
        DGuard -->|"yes"| DBind
    end
    subgraph Store["The store — one in-memory list per Scheduler"]
        direction TB

        Registry[("jobs: List of Job<br/>line 87, heap only")]

        Insert --> Registry
        Registry --- Alias
    end
    subgraph Retrieval["Retrieval — all reads are list scans"]
        direction TB
        RAll["get_jobs() — slice copy, live elements"]
        RTag["get_jobs(tag) — O(n) membership scan"]
        RMin["get_next_run(tag) — min() over next_run"]

        RDue["run_pending() — filter should_run, sort the due subset"]
    end

        direction TB

        MRemove["cancel_job removes the record — 158"]
        MStay["Record stays registered with new next_run"]

        MEvict -->|"no"| MStay
    end

    Registry --> RAll
    Registry --> RTag

    MStay --> Registry

```

**Diagram 6.2.3-A — Data flow through the in-memory store: declaration, insertion, retrieval, mutation, eviction, and loss at process exit.** The dashed path at the bottom is the entire durability story — there is no write to any medium, so recovery means re-running the definition code.

Two retrieval semantics deserve emphasis because they are easy to misread as isolation guarantees. `get_jobs()` copies the **list**, not the records: callers receive live handles and can mutate scheduled jobs through them, and a snapshot taken before a `clear()` still references the evicted records — both verified empirically. And `get_next_run()` / `idle_seconds` are computed on demand from the live list rather than maintained incrementally, so they can never be stale (Section 4.3.1.5).

#### 6.2.3.5 Caching Policies

**There is no cache and no caching policy.** No `functools.lru_cache`, memoization decorator, TTL structure, eviction rule, or invalidation hook appears anywhere in the module, and no cache server appears in any manifest (6.2.1.1). Section 4.3.1.5 documents the one value that behaves cache-like — `next_run`, computed once per generation at line 748 and then read many times by `should_run`, `__lt__`, `min()`, `idle_seconds` and `__repr__`, with exactly two invalidation sites (`do()` at line 657 and `run()` at line 693).

Two retention behaviours are commonly mistaken for caching and should be classified precisely:

| Behaviour | What it actually is | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `job_func = functools.partial(job_func, *args, **kwargs)` (line 655) | **Argument binding**, not caching. Strong references to the callable and every bound argument are held for the record's whole life | Registry memory grows linearly with job count and with the size of captured payloads (6.2.2.2); nothing evicts these references before the record is deleted |
| `at_time_zone` retention (lines 502–504) | **Per-record reference retention**, not a shared cache. Each job holds its own zone object and re-reads it on every reschedule | Avoids repeated zone resolution for that job; there is no shared pool, no eviction, and no zone data is loaded at all unless a timezone is requested |

The only genuine caching decision in the codebase is therefore a decision *not* to cache the two derived reads: `get_next_run()` and `idle_seconds` recompute from the live list on every call rather than maintaining a cached minimum. The trade is explicit — O(n) per call in exchange for a value that is always consistent with the registry and an implementation with no invalidation surface to get wrong.


### 6.2.4 Compliance Considerations

A case-insensitive scan of every tracked file for `gdpr`, `hipaa`, `pci`, `privacy`, `encrypt`, `redact`, `mask`, `pii`, `consent` and `audit` returns **zero matches**. The repository contains no data-protection policy, no encryption or masking helper, no consent concept, and no audit facility; the only compliance-relevant artifact is `LICENSE.txt`, the MIT License, copyright 2013 Daniel Bader, mirrored in `setup.py`, `pyproject.toml` and the PyPI classifiers.

This does not mean compliance is irrelevant to adopters — it means every control is inherited from the host process. The sub-sections below state, for each control area named in this section's scope, exactly what the library does and where the responsibility transfers.

#### 6.2.4.1 Data Retention Rules

| Retention question | Rule enforced by the implementation |
|---|---|
| How long is a record kept? | For the lifetime of the host process, or until it is deleted — whichever comes first. Nothing survives process exit because nothing is written (6.2.1.1) |
| Is retention configurable? | No. There is no TTL setting, no maximum age, no size cap, and no configuration surface of any kind — the module reads no environment variable and parses no configuration file |
| Is there an automatic expiry mechanism? | Yes, but only per record and only when the declaration requested it: `until()` writes `cancel_after` (lines 606–632), and `_is_overdue` (line 820) drives removal before execution (lines 686–688) or after rescheduling (lines 695–697) |
| Can a record delete itself? | Yes — returning `CancelJob` from the job body causes the dispatcher to remove it (line 174) |
| Is execution history retained? | No. `last_run` is overwritten on each run (line 692); there is no run log, no version history, and no soft-delete or tombstone |
| Is deletion recoverable? | No. Removal from the list is immediate and unlogged beyond one DEBUG record; the object is garbage-collected once no reference remains |
| Who can shorten retention? | Any code in the same interpreter, via `cancel_job(job)`, `clear(tag)` or `clear()` (lines 135–160) |

The net position is a retention model with exactly two settings — *until the process ends* and *until the declared deadline* — and no third option. Adopters with a mandated retention period for scheduling metadata must therefore implement it outside the library, because the library holds nothing after exit and offers no hook to hold anything longer.

#### 6.2.4.2 Backup and Fault Tolerance Policies

There is no backup policy, no restore procedure, and no fault-tolerance policy for the store. Section 6.2.2.8 documents the absence of a backup architecture; Section 6.1.4.3 records the verified absence of `backup`, `restore`, `disaster`, `failover` and `replica` across every tracked file; Section 5.4.6 documents the stateless-redeclaration continuity model. The relevant compliance statement is therefore a statement of guarantees, and it is deliberately narrow.

| Guarantee | Status | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| A rejected definition cannot corrupt the store | **Guaranteed** | The append is the final statement of `do()` (lines 655–663); asserted by `test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler` (`test_schedule.py` lines 1591–1599) |
| Deleting an unknown record cannot fail | **Guaranteed** | `ValueError` swallowed in `cancel_job` (lines 156–160); asserted by `test_cancel_job` |
| A sweep is safe against concurrent eviction | **Guaranteed for `run_all`** | It iterates the snapshot `self.jobs[:]` (line 118) — the fix recorded for release 0.4.0, where more than one self-deleting job in one iteration was a defect |
| The store survives a job failure | **Guaranteed** | A raising callable leaves the record in place with `last_run` and `next_run` untouched (Section 4.3.2.1) |
| The store survives process restart | **Not guaranteed — impossible** | No serialization exists; total loss by design |
| Writes are atomic under concurrency | **Not guaranteed** | No lock exists anywhere in the module; concurrent host threads mutating one registry are unprotected (Section 4.3.1.6) |
| Occurrences missed during an outage are replayed | **Not guaranteed — explicitly refused** | `run_pending()` does not run missed jobs (docstring, lines 93–97) |

#### 6.2.4.3 Privacy Controls

The library stores no personal data of its own: the twelve attributes of a record are intervals, units, weekday names, clock times, timezone references and timestamps (6.2.2.2). Personal or otherwise sensitive data can nevertheless enter the store through exactly one door — the arguments a caller binds through `do(job_func, *args, **kwargs)`, which the `functools.partial` at line 655 retains for the record's entire lifetime.

That matters because of a single, easily overlooked interaction: **bound arguments are rendered into log output.** `Job.__str__` (lines 264–276) interpolates `job_func.args` (line 274) and `job_func.keywords` (line 275) into its message, and `Job.__repr__` (lines 278–323) renders each argument through `repr()` (lines 296–298). Five of the module's eight `logger.debug` calls pass a job through `%s` or `str(...)` — lines 157, 160, 687, 690 and 696 — so every bound argument appears in the log record. `docs/logging.rst` shows this in its own sample output, where the rendered message includes the `args` and `kwargs` of the job.

| Privacy control | Status in this system |
|---|---|
| Data minimisation | Effectively enforced for library-owned fields — the record holds only scheduling metadata; whatever the caller binds is the caller's choice |
| Encryption at rest | Not applicable — nothing is at rest; no data ever leaves memory |
| Encryption in transit | Not applicable — the module performs no network or IPC operation |
| Masking / redaction | **Absent.** No masking helper exists, and `__str__`/`__repr__` cannot be configured to suppress arguments |
| Log exposure of bound arguments | **Present and unmitigated in-library.** Mitigation is host-side: keep the `schedule` logger above DEBUG, or bind identifiers rather than sensitive values |
| Right-to-erasure equivalent | Deletion is immediate and complete (`cancel_job`, `clear`), but only for the live record — anything the job body wrote elsewhere is outside the library's reach |
| Data residency / cross-border transfer | Not applicable — no data leaves the process except through log records the host routes |

The controls that do exist are therefore structural rather than feature-based: because the library never persists, never transmits, and never spawns a process, the residual privacy surface is exactly two items — what the adopter binds into a job, and where the adopter routes the `schedule` logger.

#### 6.2.4.4 Audit Mechanisms

**There is no audit mechanism in the compliance sense.** No audit table, append-only journal, tamper-evident record, or change-data-capture stream exists. The closest available signal is the DEBUG log, and its properties disqualify it as an audit trail while still making it useful for diagnostics.

| Event affecting the store | Record emitted | Site |
|---|---|---|
| Forced sweep begins | Job count and delay | Line 113 |
| Entire registry cleared | Fixed message | Line 144 |
| Tagged group cleared | Message including the tag value | Line 147 |
| Record deleted | Message including the full rendered record | Line 157 |
| Deletion of an unregistered record attempted | Distinct "not-scheduled" message | Line 160 |
| Record about to execute | Full rendered record | Line 690 |
| Record evicted on deadline (pre- or post-run) | Full rendered record | Lines 687, 696 |
| **Record inserted** | **None** — `do()` emits no log record | Lines 644–664 |
| **Record mutated** (`last_run`, `next_run` rewritten) | **None** | Lines 692–693 |
| **Job body raised an exception** | **None** | Line 691 |

| Audit property | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Completeness | Incomplete — insertion, mutation and failure are silent, so the log cannot reconstruct the registry's history |
| Availability by default | Off. The library creates the logger at line 50 and never attaches a handler or sets a level; records are invisible until the host lowers the `schedule` logger to DEBUG (`docs/logging.rst`) |
| Integrity | None — ordinary log records with no signing, sequencing, or tamper evidence |
| Durability | None from the library; whatever the host's handler configuration provides |
| Attribution | None — no actor, principal, or call-site identity is recorded, because there is no identity concept |
| Timestamping | Not added by the library; supplied by the host's log formatter |

#### 6.2.4.5 Access Controls

**No access control exists at the data layer, and none can be configured.** There is no authentication, authorization, role, permission, or credential concept anywhere in the repository — consistent with the absence of any connection or credential handling (6.2.1.1). Access is governed entirely by Python scope, which in practice means anything running in the interpreter has full read and write access to every registry.

| Access-control dimension | Actual position | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Authentication / authorization | None; no caller identity exists | No auth code in any of the 32 tracked files |
| Reachability of the default store | Any imported code can reach it through `schedule.default_scheduler` or the `schedule.jobs` alias | Lines 837, 840 |
| Read/write separation | None. `get_jobs()` returns **live** record handles (line 131), so read access confers mutation access to those records | Verified: returned elements are the same objects as in the registry |
| Field-level encapsulation | None; all twelve record attributes are public, with no private naming or property guard | `Job.__init__`, lines 227–255 |
| Isolation between consumers | Only by convention — a component may create its own `Scheduler()` instead of using the shared default (6.2.2.6) | `docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` |
| Privilege of the executed payload | The bound callable runs synchronously with the full privileges of the host process; there is no sandbox, timeout, or capability restriction | Line 691; Section 6.1.2.1 |
| Effective trust boundary | The host process itself — anything able to import the module is fully trusted | Section 2.4.4 |

The practical guidance for adopters is therefore an isolation strategy rather than a permission strategy: components that must not interfere with one another should own separate `Scheduler` instances and avoid the module-level facade, since the facade's registry is shared process-global mutable state whose live alias at line 840 carries an inline `todo` acknowledging the exposure.


### 6.2.5 Performance Optimization

Every optimization present in the data path is a cost-avoidance measure applied to list operations. There is no query planner to influence, no statistics to maintain, no buffer pool to size, and no connection to reuse. The figures quoted below were measured directly against this checkout on CPython 3.12.3 and are indicative of one interpreter on one machine; no benchmark, throughput target, or SLA is published anywhere in the repository (Sections 5.4.5 and 2.4.3).

#### 6.2.5.1 Query Optimization Patterns

Three optimization patterns exist in the read path, and all three are structural rather than configurable.

| Pattern | Implementation | Benefit |
|---|---|---|
| Filter before sorting | `run_pending()` builds a generator of due records, then sorts only that subset (lines 99–100) | O(n) predicate scan plus O(k log k) ordering, where k — the due count — is normally far smaller than n |
| Compute once, read many | `next_run` is written from exactly two call sites, `do()` (line 657) and `run()` (line 693), and read by `should_run`, `__lt__`, `min()`, `idle_seconds` and `__repr__` | Poll-time work is a datetime comparison, not a recomputation of the schedule |
| Short-circuit on emptiness | `get_next_run` returns `None` immediately when the registry is empty and again when a tag matches nothing (lines 188–192) | Avoids `min()` over an empty sequence and makes the empty case O(1) |

Measured read costs, and the write costs they must be weighed against:

| Operation at 1,000 records | Measured cost | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `get_jobs()` — full read | 2.3 µs | Slice copy only; no predicate evaluated |
| `get_jobs(tag)` — matching all | 26.4 µs | Linear scan with O(1) set membership per record |
| `get_jobs(tag)` — matching none | 21.5 µs | Near-identical to the hit case: cost is the scan, not selectivity |
| `run_pending()` with nothing due | 362.5 µs | The pure predicate scan; see Section 6.1.3.5 for the full curve |
| Insertion via `do()` | 3.78 µs per record | Bind, wrap, compute the first occurrence, append |
| Insertion with a timezone anchor | 23.84 µs per record | Roughly 6× the plain path — zone resolution plus UTC-offset correction (lines 773–817) make this the most expensive write |

The optimization ceiling is therefore set by the absence of an index (6.2.2.5): every group lookup and every minimum lookup is a full pass, and no amount of tuning changes that because there is nothing to tune. The practical consequence is benign at realistic scales — a 1,000-record registry polled once per second spends on the order of 0.4 ms per second scanning — and Section 6.1.3.5 records the conclusion that registry size is almost never the constraint. Where a host needs frequent tag-scoped lookups over a large registry, the effective optimization is architectural: partition into separate `Scheduler` instances (6.2.2.6) so each scan covers fewer records.

#### 6.2.5.2 Caching Strategy

The caching strategy is a deliberate decision **not** to cache. Section 6.2.3.5 documents the absence of any cache structure and classifies the two retention behaviours that resemble one; Section 4.3.1.5 documents the `next_run` compute-once semantics and its single invalidation point. The trade-off, stated in optimization terms:

| Candidate cache | Decision and rationale |
|---|---|
| Cached minimum `next_run` on the `Scheduler` | Not implemented. `get_next_run()` rescans on every call (line 193), which costs O(n) but can never be stale and requires no invalidation on insert, delete, or reschedule |
| Cached due set between polls | Not implemented. Each `run_pending()` re-evaluates `should_run` for every record, so a mutation between polls is always observed |
| Memoized occurrence arithmetic | Not implemented. `_schedule_next_run` recomputes from `datetime.now()` each time; no `functools.lru_cache` appears anywhere in the module |
| Shared timezone-object pool | Not implemented. Each record holds its own zone reference (lines 502–504); no zone data loads at all unless a timezone is requested |

The one caching-adjacent behaviour with a real cost profile is argument retention: the `functools.partial` created at line 655 pins the callable and every bound argument for the record's lifetime, which is why measured memory is roughly 1.1 KB for a trivial job and grows with the payload an adopter captures (6.2.2.2).

#### 6.2.5.3 Connection Pooling

**Connection pooling is not applicable.** There are no connections to pool: the module opens no socket, no file handle, and no database session, and it imports no client library — its complete import set is eight standard-library modules plus a function-local `pytz` (6.2.1.1). Consequently there is no pool size, no acquisition timeout, no idle eviction, no health probe, and no leak to detect.

For completeness, the closest analogue anywhere in the repository is a *thread* pool rather than a connection pool, and it is a host-side recipe rather than library code: `docs/parallel-execution.rst` describes registering `jobqueue.put` as the job body so that firing enqueues work onto a shared `queue.Queue` drained by a fixed set of worker threads, which the documentation introduces as the way to get tighter control over the number of threads. Section 6.1.3.3 records this as the only deliberate resource-capping pattern the repository publishes.

#### 6.2.5.4 Read/Write Splitting

**Read/write splitting is not applicable.** There is exactly one copy of the data and no replica to route reads to (6.2.2.7), so there is no primary/secondary distinction, no replication lag to reason about, and no routing policy to configure.

Two implementation details nevertheless separate readers from writers in a way that is worth recording, because they are the reason concurrent iteration and mutation do not corrupt the list:

| Mechanism | Effect | Site |
|---|---|---|
| Snapshot copy before a forced sweep | `run_all` iterates `self.jobs[:]`, so records evicted during the sweep cannot disturb the iteration — the defect fixed in release 0.4.0, where more than one self-deleting job in a single iteration misbehaved | Line 118 |
| Copy-on-read for enumeration | `get_jobs()` returns a new list, so a caller iterating results is unaffected by concurrent insertion or deletion of *list entries* — though the record objects themselves remain live and mutable | Line 131 |

Neither is a concurrency guarantee. The module contains no lock of any kind, so two host threads mutating one registry are unprotected (Section 4.3.1.6), and the copies above protect the *list structure* during a sweep rather than the *record contents*.

#### 6.2.5.5 Batch Processing Approach

Three batch operations exist, and one of them has a cost profile that materially favours the batch form over the per-record equivalent.

| Batch operation | Mechanism | Measured or structural cost |
|---|---|---|
| Forced sweep of every record | `run_all(delay_seconds=0)` runs every record regardless of due state, iterating a snapshot copy | O(n) dispatch plus the aggregate duration of every job body |
| Load-spread sweep | `run_all(delay_seconds=d)` sleeps `d` after each job to "distribute system load generated by the jobs more evenly over time" (docstring, lines 107–109) | Verified: with three records and `d = 0.05 s` the sweep took 0.150 s — the sleep executes after **every** job **including the last**, so total added time is job count × d |
| Bulk deletion | `clear()` performs one `del self.jobs[:]`; `clear(tag)` performs one slice assignment | Measured over 2,000 records: `clear()` = 473 µs versus 3.48 ms for a `cancel_job()` loop — roughly 7× cheaper, because each `cancel_job` does an O(n) `list.remove` (line 158), making the loop quadratic |
| Bulk registration | Repeated `do()` calls; there is no batch-insert API | Measured at 3.78 µs per record (23.84 µs with a timezone anchor), linear in count |

Two behaviours must not be mistaken for batch semantics. `run_all()` executes each record **once** and reschedules it normally — it is a forced sweep, not a replay of missed occurrences, which `run_pending()` explicitly never performs (docstring, lines 93–97). And no batch operation is transactional: a sweep that raises part-way leaves earlier records executed and later ones untouched (Section 4.3.1.6), and there is no rollback because nothing is journalled.

The optimization guidance that follows from the measurements is narrow but concrete: prefer `clear(tag)` over a cancellation loop when shedding a group, size `delay_seconds` against the maintenance window rather than the job count alone, and remember that timezone-anchored records cost roughly six times as much to create and to reschedule as plain interval records.


### 6.2.6 Host-Side Persistence Responsibilities

Because the library owns no data tier, every persistence concern crosses the import boundary to the adopter. This sub-section records where that transfer happens and what the repository itself prescribes on the other side. Nothing here describes unimplemented library features — each row is either an observable library behaviour or a pattern published in this repository's own documentation.

#### 6.2.6.1 Responsibility Boundary

| Persistence concern | Provided by the library | Owned by the host application |
|---|---|---|
| Holding the active schedule | The in-memory registry for the life of the process (lines 86–87) | Nothing — this is the one thing the library does own |
| Making the schedule durable | Nothing; no serializer exists | Keeping the declaration code in version control and re-executing it at start-up |
| Restoring after restart | Nothing to restore from | Re-running the declarations, or relying on `@repeat` (lines 899–913) to register at import time |
| Recording that a job ran | A single overwritten `last_run` field (line 692) and one DEBUG record (line 690) | Any run history, metrics, or audit trail — `docs/logging.rst` publishes a `print_elapsed_time` decorator as a starting point |
| Storing the job's own output | Nothing; the return value is inspected only for the `CancelJob` sentinel (line 174) | Whatever the job body writes to the host's own stores |
| Preventing duplicate execution across processes | Nothing; no lock, lease, or leader election exists | External coordination, since two processes running the same declarations each fire every occurrence (6.2.2.7) |
| Retention beyond process exit | Nothing | Any mandated retention of scheduling metadata (6.2.4.1) |
| Protecting sensitive values | Nothing; bound arguments are rendered into DEBUG records (6.2.4.3) | Logger level and handler routing, or binding identifiers instead of sensitive payloads |

#### 6.2.6.2 The Re-Declaration Pattern

The documented recovery model is re-declaration, and the repository demonstrates it in its own canonical example: `README.rst` and `docs/index.rst` both register every job in code and only then enter the polling loop of `run_pending()` followed by `time.sleep(1)`. Two properties make this dependable rather than fragile, and both are consequences of decisions documented earlier in this section:

- **Determinism.** Every constraint is enforced before insertion (6.2.2.4), so re-running the declarations reproduces exactly the registry the code describes, and no partially valid record can ever have existed.
- **Idempotence at start-up.** A fresh process begins with an empty registry (line 87), so re-declaration cannot duplicate records within that process — the duplication hazard is *across* processes, not across restarts.

The `@repeat` decorator makes the pattern structural rather than procedural: because it calls `job.do(...)` at decoration time and returns the original function unchanged (lines 899–913), importing the module that declares the jobs *is* the registration step. Adopters should note the corollary — import order becomes schedule-definition order, and a module imported twice under different names would register twice.

#### 6.2.6.3 Documented Hand-Off to Durable Infrastructure

Where work must survive the process, the repository's own guidance is to move the *work* out rather than to persist the *schedule*. `docs/parallel-execution.rst` shows the mechanism: register `jobqueue.put` as the job body (lines 55–59) so that a firing enqueues a work item onto a shared `queue.Queue` drained by worker threads, and line 68 extends the same model to a distributed application whose workers are separate processes consuming from a distributed work queue — naming beanstalkd with the beanstalkc library as the author's own preference.

Two boundaries must be stated precisely here. First, that queue is **in-memory** as written (`queue.Queue`), so the recipe as published moves work off the dispatch thread without making it durable; a durable broker is an adopter substitution. Second, beanstalkd and beanstalkc are **suggestions in prose only** — neither appears in `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, or `requirements-dev.txt`, and the zero-dependency position of the distribution is unaffected.

#### 6.2.6.4 What an Adopter Must Supply for Durable Schedules

The following is the complete set of gaps an adopter must close if restart-surviving schedules are required. It is derived from the verified absences catalogued in 6.2.1 through 6.2.5, and each item names the library behaviour that creates the gap.

| Required capability | Gap in the library | Library behaviour that creates it |
|---|---|---|
| Persisted schedule definitions | No serializer, no store, no format | No file, database, or serialization call exists in the module |
| Replay of occurrences missed while down | Missed occurrences are never replayed | `run_pending()` intentionally does not run missed jobs (lines 93–97); `run_all()` forces each job once but replays nothing |
| Single-firing guarantee across replicas | No coordination primitive | No lock, lease, or leader election; each registry is process-local |
| Durable execution history | `last_run` is overwritten in place | Line 692; no run log is appended anywhere |
| Change auditing of the schedule itself | Insertion and mutation emit no records | `do()` logs nothing; `last_run`/`next_run` rewrites log nothing (6.2.4.4) |
| Access restriction on the registry | Any code in the interpreter has full access | Process-global `default_scheduler` and the live `jobs` alias (lines 837, 840) |

The library's own documentation reaches the same conclusion from the opposite direction: `docs/index.rst` lists job persistence first among the reasons to choose a different library. Adopters whose requirements include any row above are, by the project's own guidance, either composing these capabilities themselves around a deliberately minimal timing primitive or selecting a different scheduler.

## 6.3 Integration Architecture

### 6.3.1 Applicability Assessment

**Integration Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

The subject of this specification is the Python `schedule` library at release 1.2.2 (`setup.py` line 5). It is a single importable module — `schedule/__init__.py`, 945 lines — shipped with the zero-byte PEP 561 marker `schedule/py.typed`. It exposes no network endpoint, consumes no remote API, speaks no wire protocol, connects to no message broker, sits behind no gateway, and holds no contract with any external service at runtime. Its entire integration surface is a **Python import boundary**: a host application the library does not own imports it, calls its functions, and receives synchronous calls back into its own callables in the same thread of the same process.

The determination is not inferred from the small size of the codebase. It was established by exhaustive scans across all 32 tracked files, and each scan is recorded below with the patterns applied and the result returned. Section 3.4 reaches the same conclusion from the technology-stack perspective — recording that the shipped library integrates with no external service whatsoever — and Section 6.1 records the structural reason: there is one runtime component and no process or network boundary anywhere in the repository.

This sub-section establishes that determination with verifiable evidence. Sub-sections 6.3.2 through 6.3.5 then perform the work that remains genuinely informative for an adopter, because a library that is *embedded into* other systems still has an integration story — it simply is not a network one. They document (a) the in-process API that is the actual integration contract and what each conventional API-design concern maps to within it, (b) the message-passing semantics of the dispatch loop and the one sentinel value that crosses the boundary in-band, (c) the single optional third-party package and the build-time service contracts that do exist, and (d) sequence diagrams for the key flows across the boundary. Where a concern is already covered by an earlier section, this section cross-references rather than restates it.

#### 6.3.1.1 Determination Criteria and Findings

Each row below is a structural precondition for an integration architecture. Every one of them fails, and each failure is verified against an executed scan rather than assumed.

| Precondition for integration architecture | Verification performed | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| A network or IPC protocol implementation | Word-boundary scan of all tracked files for `socket`, `urllib`, `requests`, `aiohttp`, `httpx`, `ssl`, `grpc`, `xmlrpc`, `smtplib`, `ftplib`, `paramiko`, `websocket` | **Fails** — zero matches. The eight `http` hits are documentation hyperlinks and a copyright URL (`LICENSE.txt` line 3; `docs/_templates/sidebarintro.html` lines 3–5, 10; `docs/index.rst` line 96; `docs/development.rst` line 39; `docs/faq.rst` line 78) |
| A served API surface | Scan for `fastapi`, `django`, `flask`, `wsgi`, `asgi`, `starlette`, `openapi`, `swagger`, `endpoint`, `graphql`, word-boundary `REST` | **Fails** — zero code matches. The single `flask` hit is a commented-out Pygments style at `docs/conf.py` line 114 |
| A message broker, queue, or stream client | Scan for `kafka`, `pika`, `rabbit`, `amqp`, `celery`, `redis`, `sqs`, `sns`, `boto3`, `nats`, `mqtt`, `zmq`, `pubsub`, `kinesis` | **Fails** — zero matches repository-wide |
| Authentication, authorization, or rate limiting | Scan for `oauth`, `jwt`, `api_key`, `apikey`, word-boundary `token`, `authenticate`, `authorization`, `rbac`, `ratelimit`, `throttle`, `cors`, `tls`, `certificate` | **Fails** — zero matches. `auth` and `permission` hits are author metadata and MIT licence text |
| A gateway, proxy, or ingress configuration | Scan for `gateway`, `nginx`, `kong`, `ingress`, `webhook`; filesystem search for deployment descriptors | **Fails** — zero matches; the only YAML in the repository is `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, a CI definition |
| Asynchronous or concurrent transport machinery | Scan for `asyncio`, `async`, `await`, `subprocess`, `multiprocessing` | **Fails** — zero matches. `threading` and `queue` appear **only** in documentation recipes (`docs/background-execution.rst` lines 10, 27, 29; `docs/parallel-execution.rst` lines 12, 20, 41, 53, 61) |
| A third-party client dependency | `pyproject.toml` declares `dependencies = []`; `setup.py` declares no `install_requires` | **Fails** — one optional package, `pytz`, exposed as the extra `timezone` and imported lazily at `schedule/__init__.py` line 499 |
| Any external I/O at all | Scan of the runtime module for `open(`, file writes, serialization, and environment reads | **Fails** — the only `open(` in the repository is `setup.py` line 13, reading `README.rst` for packaging metadata at build time |

The complete import set of the runtime module is the decisive artifact: eight standard-library imports at lines 41–48 (`collections.abc.Hashable`, `datetime`, `functools`, `logging`, `random`, `re`, `time`, `typing`) and a single function-local `import pytz` at line 499. There is nothing in that graph capable of reaching another system.

#### 6.3.1.2 The Boundary That Exists Instead

What the library has in place of an integration architecture is one import boundary and two planes that never meet: a runtime plane containing only the adopter's process, and an engineering plane containing the build-time services enumerated in Section 3.4.2.

