**Diagram 6.3.1-A — Integration boundary: the runtime plane, the verified-absent surfaces, and the build-time engineering plane.** Only the runtime plane exists while the library is executing. The engineering plane participates once, at install time, by delivering a wheel; the dashed link is the sole connection between the two planes, and it is not a runtime integration.

| Boundary property | Value in this system | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Boundary type | Python import plus direct method calls; no serialization, marshalling, or transport | Import set at lines 41–48; call at line 691 |
| Inbound entry points | Nine module-level functions (lines 843–892), the `repeat` decorator factory (line 899), and the `Scheduler`/`Job` classes | Module facade; `docs/reference.rst` |
| Outbound calls made by the library | Exactly one — the bound `functools.partial` created in `do()` (line 655) and invoked in `run()` (line 691) | `Job.run`, lines 674–698 |
| Data representation crossing the boundary | Live Python objects; no schema, envelope, or wire format anywhere in the module | Section 5.3.3 records the same finding |
| Processes or ports contributed | Zero — `README.rst` advertises "No extra processes needed!" | `README.rst`; module docstring lines 5–6 |
| Trust boundary | The host process itself; the invoked callable runs unsandboxed with full host privileges | Section 2.4.4; Section 6.1.2.1 |

#### 6.3.1.3 The Absence Is a Published Product Boundary

The lack of external integration is a deliberate, documented product position rather than an unimplemented roadmap item. Four statements in the repository establish this, and each has a direct consequence for the scope of this section.

| Published position | Statement in the repository | Consequence for integration architecture |
|---|---|---|
| The library is in-process by definition | `docs/index.rst` line 17 and `README.rst` line 17: "In-process scheduler for periodic jobs. No extra processes needed!" | There is no process boundary to integrate across, so no protocol is required |
| Zero dependencies is a feature | `README.rst` line 18 and the module docstring line 16: "Very lightweight and no external dependencies" | Integrating a client library would contradict the stated product property |
| Background operation is host-owned | `docs/background-execution.rst` line 4: "Out of the box it is not possible to run the schedule in the background." | The library owns no lifecycle, so it cannot originate or receive traffic on its own |
| Distribution of work is explicitly external | `docs/parallel-execution.rst` line 68 recommends a distributed work queue consumed by separate worker processes, naming beanstalkd with the beanstalkc library | The only broker-shaped integration the project endorses is one the **adopter** builds; neither package appears in any manifest |

The `docs/index.rst` section headed "When **not** to use Schedule" reinforces the same boundary from the capability side, directing readers elsewhere for job persistence, sub-second precision, concurrent execution, and localization. A library that declines persistence and concurrency has, by construction, nothing to synchronise with an external system.

#### 6.3.1.4 What Plays the Role of an Integration

To keep this section constructive rather than merely negative, the remainder analyses the in-process boundary through an integration lens. The mapping below is the organising principle for sub-sections 6.3.2 through 6.3.5; it is an analogy for orientation, not a claim that any of these mechanisms is a remote integration.

| Conventional integration concern | Counterpart in this system | Documented in |
|---|---|---|
| Protocol specification | The fluent builder grammar plus a nine-function delegation facade, invoked as direct Python calls | 6.3.2.1 |
| Interface definition artifact | Type annotations shipped under PEP 561 (`schedule/py.typed`) and reST docstrings rendered by autodoc | 6.3.2.2 |
| Authentication | None; there is no caller identity concept anywhere in the repository | 6.3.2.3 |
| Authorization | Python module and attribute scope only; the process-global registry is reachable by any imported code | 6.3.2.3 |
| Rate limiting and throttling | No request-rate control exists; interval configuration, `to()` jitter, and `run_all(delay_seconds)` spacing are the only pacing levers | 6.3.2.4 |
| API versioning | Semantic versioning of the released package, plus one in-code legacy-output contract at line 741 | 6.3.2.5 |
| Documentation standards | Sphinx with autodoc over the module, gated in CI by `sphinx-build -W` | 6.3.2.6 |
| Event processing | Time-triggered polling driven by the host; no event bus, subscription, or callback registry | 6.3.3.1 |
| Message queue architecture | None in the library; a host-side `queue.Queue` producer/consumer recipe is published | 6.3.3.2 |
| Stream processing | None; no continuous data flow of any kind exists | 6.3.3.3 |
| Batch processing flow | `run_all(delay_seconds)` forced sweeps and bulk `clear(tag)` shedding | 6.3.3.4 |
| Integration error handling | Exceptions propagate untouched to the host; `CancelJob` is the only in-band control signal | 6.3.3.5 |
| Third-party integration pattern | One optional package, `pytz`, consumed through a deferred in-function import | 6.3.4.1 |
| Legacy system interface | No legacy system; the library instead preserves a legacy *output format* and a Python 3.7 floor | 6.3.4.2 |
| API gateway configuration | Not applicable; no descriptor, proxy, or ingress artifact exists | 6.3.4.3 |
| External service contract | Build-time only: GitHub, GitHub Actions, Coveralls, PyPI, TestPyPI, Read the Docs | 6.3.4.4 |


### 6.3.2 API Design

There is no network API in this system: no route table, no request handler, no serializer, no status codes, and no transport. The "API" of `schedule` is a **library API** — a set of Python callables invoked in-process — and it is the only contract the project publishes to the outside world. This sub-section documents that contract as the integration interface it actually is, and records for each conventional API-design concern either the mechanism that plays its role or the verified absence of one.

#### 6.3.2.1 Protocol Specification

The protocol is direct synchronous Python method invocation. It has four phases, and the phase order is enforced by the code rather than by documentation: an unconfigured `Job` cannot be registered, and an unregistered `Job` cannot be dispatched.

| Phase | Operation and site | Protocol semantics |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Factory | `Scheduler.every(interval=1)` returns a new `Job` (lines 162–170); the facade `every()` delegates to `default_scheduler` (line 843) | The returned object is **not** in the registry; nothing is committed |
| 2. Configuration | Fluent unit and weekday properties (lines 325–455), `tag()` (line 457), `at()` (line 471), `to()` (line 560), `until()` (line 575) — each returns `self` or a unit property | Chainable in any order the grammar permits; every guard raises before mutation is observable |
| 3. Commit | `Job.do(job_func, *args, **kwargs)` binds the callable, computes the first occurrence, verifies the owner reference, then appends to `scheduler.jobs` (lines 644–664) | The append at line 663 is the commit point; a fault anywhere earlier leaves the registry unchanged |
| 4. Dispatch | `Scheduler.run_pending()` (lines 89–101) or `run_all(delay_seconds)` (lines 103–120), invoked by the host | Synchronous, serial, ordered by `next_run`; the library never self-triggers |

The grammar of phase 2 is the distinctive part of the interface — the project describes it as "the builder pattern for configuration" in the module docstring (lines 6–7) and markets it as "Job scheduling for humans."

```python
schedule.every(10).minutes.do(job)                      # interval form
schedule.every().day.at("10:30", "Europe/Amsterdam").do(job)   # anchored form
```

The following table specifies the complete public entry-point surface. All nine facade functions are one-line delegations to the process-global `default_scheduler` created at line 837.

| Entry point | Signature | Contract |
|---|---|---|
| `every` | `every(interval: int = 1) -> Job` | Returns an unregistered `Job`; facade at line 843, method at line 162 |
| `run_pending` | `run_pending() -> None` | Runs the due subset in `next_run` order; **never** replays missed occurrences (docstring lines 93–97); facade line 850 |
| `run_all` | `run_all(delay_seconds: int = 0) -> None` | Runs every job regardless of due state over a snapshot copy, sleeping `delay_seconds` after each; facade line 857 |
| `get_jobs` | `get_jobs(tag: Optional[Hashable] = None) -> List[Job]` | Copy of the list, elements are live records; O(n) tag scan; facade line 864 |
| `clear` | `clear(tag: Optional[Hashable] = None) -> None` | Bulk deregistration, in place to preserve the `jobs` alias; facade line 871 |
| `cancel_job` | `cancel_job(job: Job) -> None` | Idempotent removal; swallows `ValueError` for unknown jobs; facade line 878 |
| `next_run` | `next_run(tag=None) -> Optional[datetime]` | Earliest occurrence or `None`; facade line 885 over `get_next_run` (line 177) |
| `idle_seconds` | `idle_seconds() -> Optional[float]` | Seconds until the next occurrence, negative when overdue, `None` when empty; facade line 892 |
| `repeat` | `repeat(job, *args, **kwargs)` | Decorator factory; registers the decorated function and returns it unchanged (lines 899–913) |
| `Scheduler`, `Job` | Classes | Direct instantiation for multi-registry hosts (`docs/multiple-schedulers.rst`) |
| `ScheduleError`, `ScheduleValueError`, `IntervalError` | Exception classes | The fault vocabulary crossing the boundary (lines 53–68) |
| `CancelJob` | Marker class | The only in-band control message a host callable can send back (lines 71–76) |
| `default_scheduler`, `jobs` | Module data | The shared registry instance and a **live alias** to its list (lines 837, 840) |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph HostLayer["Host application - owns the thread, the cadence and the callables"]
        direction TB
        Decl["Declaration code:<br/>every(...).do(fn) or the repeat decorator"]
        Loop["Driver loop: run_pending() then sleep,<br/>or sleep for idle_seconds()"]
```

**Diagram 6.3.2-A — API architecture: the four in-process layers of the published interface and the contract vocabulary that crosses between them.** Every arrow is an ordinary Python call or return; nothing on this diagram is serialized, queued, or transported.

Protocol properties that an integrator must plan around, all verified in the implementation:

| Protocol property | Behaviour | Site |
|---|---|---|
| Synchronicity | Fully synchronous; `run_pending()` returns only after every due job has finished | Lines 99–101 |
| Concurrency model | One job at a time on the caller's thread; no locking anywhere in the module | Section 6.1.2.1 |
| Timeouts | None — the invoked callable may run indefinitely | Line 691 |
| Idempotency and correlation | No request identity, correlation ID, or deduplication concept; `Job` defines neither `__eq__` nor `__hash__` | Section 6.2.2.4 |
| Back-pressure | None; missed occurrences are silently dropped rather than queued | Docstring lines 93–97 |
| Content negotiation | Not applicable; arguments are live Python objects retained in a `functools.partial` | Line 655 |

#### 6.3.2.2 Interface Definition and Contract Artifacts

There is no OpenAPI document, IDL, protobuf schema, or JSON Schema in the repository — none is possible without a wire format. The equivalent machine-readable contract is Python typing, published under PEP 561.

| Contract artifact | What it specifies | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|
| `schedule/py.typed` | A zero-byte marker declaring that the package ships inline type information for downstream type checkers | Shipped via `package_data={"schedule": ["py.typed"]}` in `setup.py`; added in release 1.2.0 per `HISTORY.rst` |
| Inline annotations | Parameter and return types on the facade functions, `Scheduler` methods, and the twelve `Job` attributes (lines 227–255) | `setup.cfg` sets `[mypy] files=schedule`; `tox.ini` runs `python -m mypy -p schedule` in every environment |
| reST docstrings | Per-method `:param:` and `:return:` field lists — for example `Scheduler.every` (lines 163–168) and `Job.until` (lines 578–603) | Rendered into the published reference by autodoc (6.3.2.6) |
| `HISTORY.rst` | The versioned ledger of contract changes, per release, with issue numbers | Included verbatim into the documentation by `docs/changelog.rst` |

Two absences are worth recording because integrators frequently probe for them: the module defines **no `__all__`**, so the public surface is established by documentation and convention rather than declaration, and it exposes **no `__version__` attribute**, so a host cannot interrogate the installed contract version at runtime (Section 6.2.3.2). The `at_time_zone` attribute is also the one record field carrying no annotation (line 239).

#### 6.3.2.3 Authentication and Authorization

**No authentication method and no authorization framework exist, and neither can be configured.** This is not a gap to be closed: with no protocol boundary there is no caller to authenticate and no request to authorize. The repository-wide scans in 6.3.1.1 returned zero matches for every credential, identity, and permission construct, and Section 3.4.3 records that the only credentials anywhere in the project are CI and publishing credentials held outside the tree.

| Access-control dimension | Actual position | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Caller identity | None; no principal, session, or context object is passed to or produced by any entry point | Signatures at lines 843–913 |
| Access to the shared registry | Any code in the interpreter can reach `schedule.default_scheduler` or mutate the live `schedule.jobs` alias | Lines 837, 840 |
| Read/write separation | None; `get_jobs()` returns live `Job` handles, so read access confers mutation access | Line 131; Section 6.2.4.5 |
| Privilege of the executed payload | The bound callable runs synchronously with the full privileges of the host process; no sandbox, capability restriction, or timeout | Line 691; Section 6.1.2.1 |
| Isolation between consumers | By convention only — a component may own a private `Scheduler()` instead of using the facade | `docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` |
| Effective trust boundary | The host process; anything able to import the module is fully trusted | Section 2.4.4 |

The practical guidance for integrators is therefore an isolation strategy rather than a permission strategy: a library that schedules its own work inside someone else's application should instantiate its own `Scheduler` rather than share the process-global default, because the default registry is shared mutable state whose alias at line 840 carries an inline `todo` acknowledging the exposure.

#### 6.3.2.4 Rate Limiting Strategy

**No rate limiting exists.** There is no quota, token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window, concurrency cap, or `429`-equivalent rejection anywhere in the module — the scans in 6.3.1.1 found no `ratelimit` or `throttle` reference in any tracked file. Nothing calls into the library at a rate the library must defend against: the host controls the call rate by construction, since `run_pending()` executes only when the host invokes it.

What the library provides instead is **pacing** — three deterministic controls over when work lands, which are the closest analogues to a throttling policy and are the whole of the capability.

| Pacing control | Mechanism | Effect on load |
|---|---|---|
| Interval declaration | `every(interval)` plus a unit, converted to `datetime.timedelta(**{unit: interval})` during rescheduling (line 730) | Sets the nominal firing rate per job; the only rate the library "enforces" |
| Randomized interval | `to(latest)` bounds an inclusive range; `random.randint(interval, latest)` is re-drawn on **every** reschedule (line 712) | De-synchronises coincident jobs and identical schedules in separate processes; `random` is not cryptographic (Section 5.3.6) |
| Forced-sweep spacing | `run_all(delay_seconds)` sleeps after each job, including the last (lines 118–120) | Docstring purpose is to "distribute system load generated by the jobs more evenly over time"; total added time is job count × delay |

Two adjacent behaviours complete the picture and must not be mistaken for throttling. Serial execution imposes an implicit ceiling — one job at a time, so aggregate throughput is bounded by aggregate job duration rather than by any policy (Section 6.1.3.1). And overload handling is **load shedding, not queuing**: when polling falls behind, missed occurrences are dropped silently and never replayed, with a negative return from `idle_seconds()` the only available signal (Section 6.1.4.6).

#### 6.3.2.5 Versioning Approach

Versioning is applied to the released package, not to any endpoint or payload — there is no URI version segment, no `Accept` header negotiation, and no per-message schema version, because there is no message.

| Versioning aspect | Mechanism | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Scheme | Semantic versioning | `docs/development.rst` line 68 states the project follows semantic versioning |
| Current release | 1.2.2 | `SCHEDULE_VERSION = "1.2.2"` in `setup.py` line 5, mirrored in `docs/conf.py` |
| Change ledger | `HISTORY.rst`, per release, with issue references; surfaced in the docs via `docs/changelog.rst` | 1.2.0 added timezone support in `.at()` and `py.typed`; 1.1.0 added `@repeat`, `.until()` and tag-filtered retrieval |
| Compatibility posture | Extensions have been additive: each release that grew the interface added optional parameters or new methods rather than changing existing signatures — `HISTORY.rst` line 131 records release 0.2.0 introducing features "in a backwards compatible way" | `Job.__init__` defaults every added field to `None` or an empty set (lines 227–255) |
| Deprecation machinery | **None** — the module never imports `warnings` and emits no `DeprecationWarning`; removals are announced in `HISTORY.rst` only | Verified: no `warnings` reference in any tracked file |
| Interpreter compatibility floor | `python_requires=">=3.7"`, with 3.7–3.12 classifiers and a matching CI matrix | `setup.py`; `.github/workflows/ci.yml` line 17 |
| Runtime introspection | Not available; no `__version__` attribute exists | Section 6.2.3.2 |

One in-code compatibility contract deserves specific mention because it is the only place the library trades correctness of representation for interface stability. `_schedule_next_run` performs its arithmetic in the requested timezone but converts the result back to a **naive local** datetime before storing it, with the source comment at lines 740–741 stating that this keeps the API "consistent with older versions" and "backwards compatible". `docs/timezones.rst` publishes the same contract to users: all datetimes inside the library are stored naive, so `next_run` and `last_run` are always local-time values. Integrators reading those attributes are consuming a deliberately legacy-shaped output.

The corresponding risk is behavioural rather than structural: releases 1.2.1 and 1.2.2 changed the *computed value* of `next_run` for timezone-anchored jobs while leaving every signature intact, so a patch-level upgrade can shift firing times without any change to the calling code.

#### 6.3.2.6 Documentation Standards

The interface documentation is generated from the code, published as a Sphinx site, and gated in continuous integration, which makes it the closest equivalent this project has to a maintained API specification.

| Standard | Implementation | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|
| Source format | reStructuredText; `source_suffix = ".rst"` with `master_doc = "index"` | `docs/conf.py` lines 50, 57 |
| Generator and theme | Sphinx with `sphinx.ext.autodoc`, `sphinx.ext.todo`, `sphinx.ext.coverage`, `sphinx.ext.viewcode`; alabaster theme; `autodoc_member_order` set to source order | `docs/conf.py` lines 35–36; `docs/development.rst` |
| Reference generation | `docs/reference.rst` declares `.. module:: schedule`, `autodata` for `default_scheduler` and `jobs`, `autofunction` for all eight delegating functions, `autoclass` with `:members:` and `:undoc-members:` for `Scheduler` and `Job`, and `autoexception` for `CancelJob` | Docstrings are therefore the single source of truth for the published reference |
| Docstring convention | reST field lists — `:param:` and `:return:` — on public methods | Rendered directly into the reference page |
| Build gate | `tox -e docs` runs `sphinx-build -W -b html`, promoting **warnings to errors**; a dedicated `docs` job runs it on every push and pull request | `tox.ini`; `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |
| Packaging-metadata gate | `tox -e setuppy` runs `python setup.py check --strict --metadata --restructuredtext`, validating the reST that becomes the PyPI long description | `tox.ini`; `setuppy` job in CI |
| Narrative coverage | Eleven task-oriented guides plus a changelog in the `index.rst` toctree: installation, examples, background execution, parallel execution, timezones, exception handling, logging, multiple schedulers, FAQ, reference, development | `docs/index.rst` |
| Published location | `schedule.readthedocs.io`, declared as the `Documentation` project URL | `pyproject.toml`; `README.rst` |

Two properties make this standard notable for integrators. Because the reference is entirely autodoc-driven, a signature change that is not reflected in its docstring produces documentation that silently disagrees with the code — the `-W` flag catches malformed markup, not stale prose. And because `docs/reference.rst` enables `:undoc-members:`, every public member of `Scheduler` and `Job` appears in the published reference whether or not it carries a docstring, which makes the rendered page an accurate enumeration of the interface surface even where prose is missing.


### 6.3.3 Message Processing

No message-processing infrastructure exists in this system. There is no broker, no queue client, no topic, no subscription, no envelope format, and no acknowledgement protocol — the scans in 6.3.1.1 returned zero matches for every broker and stream client, and Section 5.3.3 records that the only "message" the library ever produces is a `logging.LogRecord`. What this sub-section documents instead is the **dispatch semantics** of the polling loop, because those semantics occupy the position message processing would occupy: they determine when work is triggered, what value may flow back, what happens to work that cannot be delivered on time, and how faults travel across the import boundary.

#### 6.3.3.1 Event Processing Patterns

The library is **time-triggered, not event-driven**. Nothing is published, nothing is subscribed, and no callback registry exists other than the job registry itself. The only "event" is a comparison between the wall clock and a precomputed timestamp, performed by `should_run` (line 672) once per job per poll, and that comparison happens only because the host chose to call into the library at that moment.

| Event-processing concern | Mechanism in this system | Verified position |
|---|---|---|
| Event source | The host's own loop; `run_pending()` and `run_all()` are the only triggers | The library never self-triggers; `docs/background-execution.rst` line 4 states background operation is unavailable out of the box |
| Event detection | `datetime.datetime.now() >= self.next_run` evaluated per job (line 672) | Polling, not notification; there is no timer, signal handler, or `select` loop |
| Event ordering | The due subset is sorted by `next_run` via `Job.__lt__` (lines 257–262) before dispatch | Deterministic and total within a cycle; the most overdue job runs first |
| Subscription model | None; a job is registered once by `do()` (line 663) and has no topic, filter, or predicate other than its own schedule | Tag sets support grouped *lookup*, not routing |
| Fan-out | None in the library — one registration produces one invocation per occurrence | Host-side fan-out recipes are documented in `docs/parallel-execution.rst` |
| Delivery guarantee | At most once per poll cycle, and only if the host polls; occurrences missed while not polling are dropped, never replayed | Docstring lines 93–97; reiterated in the `run_continuously()` docstring in `docs/background-execution.rst` |
| Registration timing | Optionally at **import** time — `@repeat(every().hour)` calls `job.do(...)` at decoration and returns the original function unchanged (lines 899–913) | Makes import order the schedule-definition order |

Exactly three message-shaped values cross the boundary in this system, and enumerating them completely is more useful than any taxonomy:

| Message | Direction and payload | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| Invocation | Library → host; a zero-argument call of the `functools.partial` bound in `do()` (line 655), carrying the arguments captured at declaration time | Invoked at line 691; no timeout, guard, or isolation |
| `CancelJob` sentinel | Host callable → library; the class **or** an instance, returned from the job body | `isinstance(ret, CancelJob) or ret is CancelJob` (line 174) then `cancel_job` removes the record |
| Diagnostic record | Library → host logging subsystem; eight `logger.debug` calls on the logger named `schedule` (lines 113, 144, 147, 157, 160, 687, 690, 696) | Fire-and-forget, lazily `%`-formatted, no handler attached by the library (`docs/logging.rst`) |

Every other return value from a job body is passed through untouched: `Job.run()` returns it to `Scheduler._run_job`, which inspects it only for the sentinel and then discards it (lines 172–175). There is no result channel, no reply queue, and no place a job's output is stored.

#### 6.3.3.2 Message Queue Architecture

**No message queue exists in the library.** The job registry is superficially queue-like and is occasionally described that way — `HISTORY.rst` line 139 refers to "the job queue" when recording a 0.1.11 bug fix — but it lacks every property that defines a queue, and the differences are operationally significant.

| Queue property | Registry behaviour | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Ordering discipline | Not FIFO by arrival; ordering is recomputed per cycle from `next_run` (line 100) | Insertion order is irrelevant; a newly added overdue job runs before an older one |
| Consumption semantics | Records are **not** consumed by execution — a job is rescheduled in place (line 693) and remains registered | The registry is a set of standing declarations, not a backlog of work items |
| Acknowledgement, visibility, redelivery | None; no ack, nack, lease, visibility timeout, or in-flight state exists | Failure leaves the record due, which produces an implicit next-poll re-attempt (Section 6.1.2.6) |
| Durability | None; the list lives on the interpreter heap and dies with the process (Section 6.2.2.1) | Nothing survives a restart; recovery is re-declaration |
| Dead-letter destination | None | A permanently failing job either repeats or must be removed by the host |
| Back-pressure | None; overload results in silently dropped occurrences rather than queue growth | A negative `idle_seconds()` is the only backlog indicator |

The repository does publish a genuine in-process queue architecture, but as a **host-side composition recipe** rather than library code. `docs/parallel-execution.rst` lines 34–66 register `jobqueue.put` as the job body so that a firing *enqueues* a work item instead of executing it, and a fixed set of worker threads drains a `queue.Queue`; the documentation introduces it as the way to get tighter control over the number of threads. Line 68 extends the same model to separate worker processes consuming a distributed work queue, naming beanstalkd with the beanstalkc Python library as the author's own preference. Two boundaries must be stated precisely: the published queue is `queue.Queue`, which is in-memory and unbounded as written, so the recipe moves work off the dispatch thread without making it durable; and beanstalkd and beanstalkc appear in prose only — neither is present in `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, or `requirements-dev.txt`, so the zero-dependency position of the distribution is unaffected.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph TriggerSrc["Trigger source - no event bus, only the host clock"]
        direction TB
        HostTick["Host loop calls run_pending()<br/>or run_all(delay_seconds)"]
        ClockCmp["should_run compares now with next_run<br/>line 672"]
        HostTick --> ClockCmp
    end
    subgraph InLinePath["Default path - in-line serial dispatch, no queue involved"]
        direction TB
        DueSet["Due subset filtered then sorted, lines 99 to 100"]
        RunOne["Job.run invokes the bound partial, line 691"]
        RetCheck{{"Return value inspected only for the<br/>CancelJob sentinel, line 174"}}
        Remove["cancel_job removes the record, line 158"]
        Keep["Record kept with a recomputed next_run, line 693"]
        DueSet --> RunOne
        RunOne --> RetCheck
        RetCheck -->|"CancelJob class or instance"| Remove
        RetCheck -->|"any other value, discarded"| Keep
    end
    subgraph HostQueuePath["Host-composed path - docs/parallel-execution.rst lines 34 to 66"]
        direction TB
        Producer["Registered body is jobqueue.put,<br/>so firing enqueues a work item"]
        QNode[["queue.Queue - in memory, unbounded as published"]]
        WorkerNode["Worker threads: get, call, task_done"]
        Producer --> QNode
        QNode --> WorkerNode
    end
    subgraph DiagPath["Diagnostic channel - the only messages the library emits"]
        direction TB
        LogRecs["8 logger.debug records on logger schedule<br/>lines 113, 144, 147, 157, 160, 687, 690, 696"]
        HostHandler["Host-owned handler; nothing is emitted until<br/>the host lowers the level to DEBUG"]
        LogRecs --> HostHandler
    end
    ClockCmp --> DueSet
    RunOne -.->|"when the declared body is jobqueue.put"| Producer
    RunOne -.-> LogRecs
    Remove -.-> LogRecs
```

**Diagram 6.3.3-A — Message flow: clock-triggered in-line dispatch, the optional host-composed queue hand-off, and the diagnostic channel.** Only the two left-hand groups and the diagnostic channel are library behaviour; the queue group is a documented recipe the adopter implements with the standard library.

#### 6.3.3.3 Stream Processing Design

**Stream processing is not applicable.** There is no continuous data flow in this system: no stream, topic, partition, offset, watermark, window, or checkpoint concept exists, and no stream-processing dependency appears in any manifest. The library moves no data at all — it moves *control*, by calling a function the host supplied, and the only value returned is inspected for a single sentinel and discarded (line 174).

For completeness, two properties preclude a streaming interpretation even at the conceptual level. Occurrences are not a replayable log: there is no offset to rewind to and missed occurrences are never regenerated (docstring lines 93–97). And there is no state store for windowed computation — the only state is the registry itself, which holds declarations rather than data (Section 6.2.2.1).

#### 6.3.3.4 Batch Processing Flows

Three batch-shaped flows exist. All are synchronous, all operate on the in-memory registry, and none is transactional.

| Batch flow | Mechanism | Semantics and cost |
|---|---|---|
| Forced sweep of every job | `run_all(delay_seconds=0)` iterates the snapshot `self.jobs[:]` and runs each record regardless of due state (lines 118–120) | Each job executes **once** and is rescheduled normally; this is a forced sweep, not a replay of missed occurrences |
| Load-spread sweep | `run_all(delay_seconds=d)` sleeps `d` after every job, including the last | Docstring purpose is to distribute generated load more evenly; total added time is job count × delay (Section 6.2.5.5) |
| Bulk deregistration | `clear()` performs one `del self.jobs[:]`; `clear(tag)` performs one slice assignment (lines 143–148) | Roughly seven times cheaper than a `cancel_job()` loop, which is quadratic because each removal is an O(n) `list.remove` (Section 6.2.5.5) |
| Bulk registration | Repeated `do()` calls; there is no batch-insert entry point | Linear in count; timezone-anchored records cost roughly six times as much to create (Section 6.2.5.1) |

`docs/logging.rst` demonstrates the sweep flow end to end: `schedule.run_all()` followed by `schedule.clear()`, producing the DEBUG records "Running *all* 1 jobs with 0s delay in between", "Running job Job(...)", and "Deleting *all* jobs". Two properties bound the batch model. A sweep is not atomic — if a job body raises part-way through, earlier records have executed and later ones have not, and there is no rollback because nothing is journalled (Section 6.2.5.5). And `run_all` is the only catch-up-adjacent facility in the system: it triggers work, but it cannot reconstruct individual occurrences that were missed while the process was down (Section 6.2.6.4).

#### 6.3.3.5 Error Handling Strategy

The error-handling strategy across the boundary is deliberately asymmetric: **the library validates aggressively on the way in and does not intervene at all on the way out.** `docs/exception-handling.rst` line 4 states the contract without qualification — Schedule does not catch exceptions raised during job execution, so any such exception bubbles up and interrupts the `run_xyz` function. Section 5.4.3 documents the resulting error-handling architecture and Section 6.1.4.1 catalogues the fault-tolerance mechanisms; what follows is the boundary-crossing view.

| Fault class | Where it is raised | Boundary behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Configuration fault | Definition time, in the fluent grammar — 28 raise sites producing `ScheduleValueError`, `IntervalError`, `ScheduleError`, or `TypeError` | Contained: the record never reaches the registry, because the append is the final statement of `do()` (lines 655–663) |
| Missing optional dependency | Definition time, at the lazy `import pytz` (line 499) when `at(tz=…)` is used without pytz installed | `ModuleNotFoundError` reaches the caller; the registry is unaffected; `docs/faq.rst` prescribes `pip install pytz` |
| Execution fault | Inside the host's own callable, invoked at line 691 | **Uncontained by design**: propagates out of `run_pending()`, so `last_run` and `next_run` are not advanced and the remaining due jobs in that cycle are skipped |
| Deadline expiry | `_is_overdue` checks before execution and again after rescheduling (lines 686–688, 695–697) | Converted into the `CancelJob` sentinel, which takes priority over the job's own return value |
| Environment anomaly | DST gap or fold handling inside `_correct_utc_offset` (lines 773–817) | Absorbed silently — the occurrence is displaced by one offset with nothing raised and nothing logged |

There are only two `try` blocks in the entire module and neither guards host code: one makes `cancel_job()` idempotent by swallowing `ValueError` (lines 156–160), and the other tries five `strptime` formats in turn when parsing an `until()` deadline (lines 822–830). No retry, backoff, attempt cap, dead-letter path, or circuit breaker exists anywhere in the library (Sections 6.1.2.5 and 6.1.2.6).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    FaultSrc([Fault occurs during a poll cycle]) --> Where{"Which side of the<br/>import boundary?"}
    Where -->|"library validation"| LibSide["Configuration or dependency fault"]
    Where -->|"host callable"| HostSide["Execution fault inside the job body"]
    subgraph LibContained["Contained by the library - registry integrity preserved"]
        direction TB
        Raise["Typed exception raised to the caller<br/>before the registry append"]
        Intact["Registry unchanged; other jobs unaffected"]
        Raise --> Intact
    end
    subgraph HostIntercept["Interception points the host may compose - all outside the library"]
        direction TB
        Wrap["Wrap the callable: catch_exceptions decorator,<br/>docs/exception-handling.rst lines 13 to 31"]
        Signal["Return schedule.CancelJob to unschedule permanently"]
        GuardLoop["Guard the driver loop so it survives the exception"]
        Offload["Offload the body to a thread or worker queue,<br/>docs/parallel-execution.rst"]
        Wrap --> Signal
    end
    subgraph Uncaught["Uncontained by design when no guard is present"]
        direction TB
        Escape["Exception escapes run_pending()"]
        Skip["Remaining due jobs in this cycle are skipped"]
        Stale["last_run and next_run unchanged, so the job<br/>stays due and is re-attempted next poll"]
        Escape --> Skip
        Skip --> Stale
    end
    LibSide --> Raise
    HostSide --> Wrap
    HostSide --> GuardLoop
    HostSide --> Offload
    HostSide -.->|"no host guard in place"| Escape
    Signal -.->|"dispatcher removes the record, line 174"| Intact
```

**Diagram 6.3.3-B — Error handling across the integration boundary: what the library contains, what the host may intercept, and what is uncontained by design.**

The documented mitigation is a host-side decorator, and it is the one place where error handling and the message protocol meet: `docs/exception-handling.rst` lines 13–31 publish `catch_exceptions(cancel_on_failure=False)`, which wraps the job body with `functools.wraps`, catches everything, prints `traceback.format_exc()`, and — when constructed with `cancel_on_failure=True` — returns `schedule.CancelJob`, converting a fault into the library's own unschedule signal. The same page offers subclassing the scheduler as an alternative, linking an external community gist. Because the only in-band signal available is "remove me", host-composed error policy is necessarily binary: absorb the fault and let the schedule continue, or terminate the job permanently. There is no severity, no backoff, and no partial-degradation option in the protocol.


### 6.3.4 External Systems

At runtime the library integrates with exactly one external artifact — the optional `pytz` package — and with no external *system* at all. Every other external party in this project sits on the engineering side of the boundary: source hosting, continuous integration, coverage reporting, package distribution, and documentation publishing, all enumerated authoritatively in Section 3.4.2. This sub-section documents those relationships as integration contracts: what is consumed, in which direction, on what trigger, and what happens when the counterparty is absent.

#### 6.3.4.1 Third-Party Integration Pattern: The `pytz` Optional Extra

The single third-party integration in the runtime is an in-process library call, and the pattern used is a **deferred, gated import** — the strictest form of optional dependency available in Python packaging.

| Contract element | Specification | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Declaration | Optional extra `timezone = ["pytz"]`; the required dependency list is empty | `pyproject.toml` `[project.optional-dependencies]`; `dependencies = []` |
| Version constraint | **None** — the requirement is unpinned and unbounded | `pyproject.toml`; no constraint appears in `setup.py` either |
| Import site | `import pytz` inside `Job.at()`, executed only when the `tz` parameter is not `None` | `schedule/__init__.py` line 499 |
| Accepted input types | A `str` resolved through `pytz.timezone(tz)`, or an existing `pytz.BaseTzInfo` instance; anything else raises `ScheduleValueError` | Lines 500–507 |
| Consumed surface | `pytz.timezone()`, the `pytz.BaseTzInfo` type for the isinstance check, and `<zone>.normalize()` used twice inside `_correct_utc_offset` | Lines 501, 503, 789, 809 |
| Retention | The resolved zone object is stored on the record as `at_time_zone` and re-read on every reschedule | Lines 502, 504; Section 6.2.3.5 |
| Failure mode when absent | `ModuleNotFoundError` raised at definition time; the registry is untouched | `docs/faq.rst` documents the error and prescribes `pip install pytz` |
| Type-checking support | `types-pytz` is installed for development and CI type-checking only | `requirements-dev.txt`; `tox.ini` `[testenv] deps` |

Optionality is not merely declared — it is proven three ways. `tox.ini` expands to twelve environments, `py3{7,8,9,10,11,12}{,-pytz}`, so the entire suite runs on every supported interpreter **without** pytz installed. `test_schedule.py` guards every timezone test behind `try: import pytz / except ModuleNotFoundError: self.skipTest("pytz unavailable")` — the helper `make_tz_mock_job` at lines 99–105 is the canonical instance, and the pattern recurs throughout the timezone coverage. And `docs/installation.rst` states the boundary to users directly: Schedule has one optional dependency, required only when `.at()` is used with a timezone.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Declare["Host declares a job:<br/>every().day.at(time_str, tz)"] --> TzGiven{"Was a tz argument<br/>supplied?"}
    TzGiven -->|"no - the default path"| PurePath["No third-party code is imported at all;<br/>naive local arithmetic only"]
    TzGiven -->|"yes"| LazyImp["import pytz executed at line 499"]
    LazyImp --> Installed{"Is pytz installed in the<br/>host environment?"}
    Installed -->|"no"| Fail["ModuleNotFoundError raised to the caller;<br/>registry unchanged, docs/faq.rst"]
    Installed -->|"yes"| Kind{"str or pytz.BaseTzInfo?"}
    Kind -->|"str"| Resolve["pytz.timezone(tz) resolves a zone object"]
    Kind -->|"BaseTzInfo"| Adopt["Object adopted as supplied"]
    Kind -->|"neither"| Reject["ScheduleValueError: timezone must be a string<br/>or a pytz timezone object, line 506"]
    Resolve --> Store["Zone stored on the record as at_time_zone"]
    Adopt --> Store
    Store --> Reschedule["Every reschedule calls zone.normalize()<br/>and corrects the UTC offset, lines 773 to 817"]
    Reschedule --> Naive["Result converted back to naive local time<br/>for backward compatibility, lines 740 to 741"]
    PurePath --> Naive
    subgraph SupplyChain["Install-time supply of the artifacts - the only other external involvement"]
        direction TB
        PyPINode["PyPI: pip install schedule<br/>and optionally pip install pytz"]
        Distro["Third-party channels not maintained by the project:<br/>Ubuntu and Debian python3-schedule, Arch AUR, conda-forge"]
        Manual["Manual vendoring of the single source file,<br/>explicitly discouraged in docs/installation.rst"]
        PyPINode --> Env["Importable schedule package in the host environment"]
        Distro --> Env
        Manual --> Env
    end
    Env -.->|"prerequisite for any of the above flow"| Declare
```

**Diagram 6.3.4-A — External integration flow: the gated `pytz` resolution path and the install-time supply channels.** The left branch of the first decision is the default for every timezone-free job and touches no third-party code whatsoever.

The unpinned requirement is the one integration risk worth flagging for adopters, and it is an observation about the manifest rather than a defect: because `pyproject.toml` names `pytz` with no version bound, the resolved version is whatever the adopter's environment provides, and the library depends on `pytz`-specific behaviour — the `normalize()` method and the `BaseTzInfo` type — that has no counterpart in the standard-library `zoneinfo` module. `HISTORY.rst` records that this coupling is recent and actively maintained: timezone support in `.at()` arrived in release 1.2.0, and releases 1.2.1 and 1.2.2 were both driven by cross-timezone and DST correctness fixes.

#### 6.3.4.2 Legacy System Interfaces

**There is no legacy system interface.** No mainframe adapter, file-drop directory, fixed-width parser, SOAP client, screen-scraper, or database-link shim exists — consistent with the complete absence of I/O established in 6.3.1.1. Nothing in the repository connects to a predecessor system, and there is no bridging or strangler pattern in the codebase.

Four legacy-*compatibility* obligations do exist, and they are the meaningful content of this concern for an integrator, because each one constrains what the library may change.

| Legacy obligation | What is preserved | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Naive-local timestamp output | `next_run` and `last_run` are converted back to naive local time even when the job was declared in another timezone, explicitly to stay "consistent with older versions" and "backwards compatible" | `schedule/__init__.py` lines 740–747; `docs/timezones.rst` publishes the same contract |
| Old-interpreter support | `python_requires=">=3.7"` with 3.7 classifiers and a 3.7 CI leg, five years after 3.7's release | `setup.py`; `.github/workflows/ci.yml` line 17; `docs/installation.rst` directs users of earlier Pythons to the History file |
| Additive-only interface growth | Every capability added since 0.2.0 arrived as a new optional field or method rather than a signature change; `HISTORY.rst` line 131 records features introduced "in a backwards compatible way" | `Job.__init__` defaults all later-added fields to `None` or an empty set |
| Outdated downstream redistributions | Ubuntu and Debian packages are flagged **OUTDATED** at version 0.3.2 (2015) in the project's own installation guide, and are explicitly not maintained by the project | `docs/installation.rst` |

Two consequences follow for anyone integrating against an older deployment. A host running a distribution-packaged 0.3.2 has none of `until()`, `@repeat`, tag-filtered retrieval, timezone support, or the shipped type information — all of which arrived in 1.1.0 or 1.2.0 per `HISTORY.rst` — so feature detection, not version assumption, is the safe approach. And the manual-vendoring path documented in `docs/installation.rst` (copy the single source file into a local package) creates a permanent fork that receives no updates; the guide labels it "highly discouraged" for exactly that reason.

#### 6.3.4.3 API Gateway Configuration

**API gateway configuration is not applicable.** There is no gateway, reverse proxy, ingress controller, service mesh sidecar, or edge routing artifact in this repository, and there is nothing for one to front: the library serves no port and exposes no endpoint (6.3.1.1). Scans for `gateway`, `nginx`, `kong`, `ingress`, and `webhook` return zero matches across all 32 tracked files, and Section 6.1.1.1 records that the filesystem search for deployment and orchestration descriptors — `Dockerfile*`, `docker-compose*`, `*.tf`, `Procfile`, `*.service`, `Chart.yaml`, and proxy configuration — returned only `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

The functional concerns a gateway normally owns are, in this system, either absent or relocated, and stating where is more useful than restating the absence:

| Gateway responsibility | Position in this system |
|---|---|
| Request routing | Not applicable; dispatch is a sorted in-memory scan, not a route match (lines 99–100) |
| Authentication and authorization at the edge | Absent entirely; the trust boundary is the host process (6.3.2.3) |
| Rate limiting and quotas | Absent; only interval, jitter, and sweep-delay pacing exist (6.3.2.4) |
| TLS termination | Not applicable; no transport exists |
| Request and response transformation | Not applicable; arguments are live Python objects bound at declaration time (line 655) |
| Observability at the edge | Reduced to eight DEBUG log records the host must opt into (`docs/logging.rst`) |

#### 6.3.4.4 External Service Contracts

Every external service contract in this project is exercised at build, publish, or documentation time. None is reachable from the installed library, and none is required for it to function. Section 3.4.2 is the authoritative inventory; the table below re-frames the same services as contracts, recording the trigger and the consequence of failure for each.

| Service contract | Direction and trigger | Consequence of counterparty failure |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub — source, issues, release tags | Outbound from maintainers; on push, pull request, and tag | Development halts; installed versions are unaffected. `setup.py` also derives `download_url` from the GitHub tarball path for release 1.2.2 |
| GitHub Actions — CI compute | Inbound to the repository; on push to `master` and pull requests targeting `master` | No verification of a change; five jobs — `test`, `coveralls`, `docs`, `formatting`, `setuppy` — provide the entire quality gate |
| `actions/checkout@v3`, `actions/setup-python@v4` | Consumed by every CI job at step level | Workflow failure; both are pinned to a major version only |
| PyPI installs inside CI | Outbound from runners: `pip install tox tox-gh-actions`, then `pip3 install coveralls` | CI cannot bootstrap; these are the only network calls the workflow makes besides the Coveralls upload |
| Coveralls — coverage aggregation | Outbound upload per matrix entry with `COVERALLS_PARALLEL=true` and `COVERALLS_FLAG_NAME=python-<version>`, then a dependent job runs `coveralls --finish --service=github` | Coverage reporting and the README badge degrade; authentication uses only the per-run `GITHUB_TOKEN` |
| TestPyPI — staging registry | Outbound, manual: `twine upload --repository schedule-test dist/*` | Release verification is skipped; the step precedes production upload in `docs/development.rst` |
| PyPI — production registry | Outbound, manual: `twine upload --repository schedule dist/*` | New releases cannot be published; `pip install schedule` continues to serve existing versions |
| Read the Docs — documentation hosting | Inbound build from the repository; declared as the `Documentation` project URL | Published documentation goes stale. **No `.readthedocs.yaml` exists in the repository**, so the hosted build is configured outside version control (Section 3.4.2) |
| Badge endpoints — shields.io and the Actions workflow badge | Inbound image requests when `README.rst` or `docs/index.rst` is rendered | Cosmetic only |
| Downstream redistribution channels | Outside the project's control: Ubuntu, Debian, Arch AUR, conda-forge | Users receive stale versions; `docs/installation.rst` disclaims maintenance of all of them |

Two contract properties are worth stating explicitly because they bound the project's exposure. Release publication is **entirely manual** — `.github/workflows/` contains only `ci.yml`, with no publish or release workflow, so the `twine` procedure in `docs/development.rst` is executed by a maintainer against credentials resolved from a local `.pypirc` that is not in the repository (Section 3.4.3). And no external service is a *runtime* dependency of any kind: an adopter's process runs identically whether or not GitHub, Coveralls, PyPI, or Read the Docs is reachable, because nothing in the installed wheel contacts them.

#### 6.3.4.5 Complete External Dependency Inventory

The following is the complete set of external packages and services this repository depends on, at every lifecycle stage. It is derived from `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, `requirements-dev.txt`, `tox.ini`, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

| Dependency | Scope and version constraint | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `pytz` | Optional runtime extra `timezone`; unpinned | The only third-party code the library can import; required for `at(tz=…)` |
| `setuptools` | Build backend; `>= 61.0` | Wheel and sdist construction via `setuptools.build_meta` |
| `build`, `wheel`, `twine` | Release tooling; unpinned | Wheel construction and upload to TestPyPI then PyPI (`docs/development.rst`) |
| `pytest`, `pytest-cov` | Test tooling; unpinned | Test execution and coverage measurement in every tox environment |
| `mypy`, `types-pytz` | Type-checking; unpinned | `python -m mypy -p schedule` gate over the annotated interface |
| `black==20.8b1`, `click==8.0.4` | Formatting; **pinned** | `tox -e format` runs `black --check .`; `docs/development.rst` instructs contributors to use exactly 20.8b1 |
| `Sphinx`, `docutils`, `Pygments` | Documentation; unpinned | `sphinx-build -W` HTML build and reST validation |
| `pytest-flake8` | Lint tooling listed in `requirements-dev.txt`; unpinned | Referenced by the `docs/development.rst` test command; not invoked by the `tox` test environment |
| `tox`, `tox-gh-actions` | CI orchestration; unpinned | Expands the twelve-environment matrix and maps it to the GitHub Actions Python versions |
| `coveralls` | CI reporting; unpinned | Uploads per-interpreter coverage and finalises the parallel build |
| GitHub, GitHub Actions, Coveralls, PyPI, TestPyPI, Read the Docs | External services; build and publish time only | Contracts detailed in 6.3.4.4 and Section 3.4.2 |
| `beanstalkd`, `beanstalkc` | **Not dependencies** — named in prose in `docs/parallel-execution.rst` line 68 as an author preference for distributed workers | Appear in no manifest; listed here so their status is unambiguous |

The runtime dependency graph is therefore one node wide and optional: with no extras installed, the import graph of `schedule` contains nothing but the Python standard library, which is the property `README.rst` line 18 and the module docstring line 16 both advertise.


### 6.3.5 Integration Sequence Diagrams for Key Flows

Four flows carry everything that crosses a boundary in this system. The first is the only runtime flow that involves third-party code; the second and third are the embedding patterns the repository itself publishes for hosts that cannot block their main thread; the fourth is the build-time supply chain that delivers the artifact. Section 6.1.2.2 diagrams the generic definition-and-dispatch interaction; the flows below are deliberately the integration-specific ones it does not cover.

| Flow | Boundary crossed | Diagram |
|---|---|---|
| Timezone-anchored declaration and first dispatch | Library → optional `pytz`, at definition time and on every reschedule | 6.3.5-A |
| Background-thread embedding with cooperative shutdown | Host thread → library, repeatedly, off the main thread | 6.3.5-B |
| Queue hand-off to worker threads | Library → host queue → host workers | 6.3.5-C |
| Build, publish, and install supply chain | Maintainer → GitHub, Coveralls, PyPI → adopter | 6.3.5-D |

#### 6.3.5.1 Timezone-Anchored Declaration and First Dispatch

This is the only flow in which the library touches code it does not own, and it shows why the dependency is genuinely optional: the third-party call happens once at declaration and then only inside the offset-correction path.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Host as Host application
    participant Job as Job builder
    participant Pytz as pytz module
    participant Sched as Scheduler registry
    participant Body as Host callable
    Note over Host,Body: Definition phase - the only inbound use of a third-party package
    Host->>Job: every().day.at("10:30", "America/New_York")
    Job->>Job: validate unit is days, hours or minutes - line 494
    Job->>Pytz: import pytz - deferred, line 499
    alt pytz is not installed
        Pytz--)Host: ModuleNotFoundError, registry untouched
    else pytz is available
        Job->>Pytz: timezone("America/New_York")
        Pytz-->>Job: zone object stored as at_time_zone
        Job->>Job: regex-validate the clock string, line 513
        Host->>Job: do(fn)
        Job->>Job: bind functools.partial - line 655
        Job->>Pytz: normalize during offset correction - lines 789 and 809
        Pytz-->>Job: corrected aware datetime
        Job->>Job: convert back to naive local for compatibility - lines 740 to 747
        Job->>Sched: append self to jobs - line 663
    end
    Note over Host,Body: Dispatch phase - no third-party call on the hot path unless rescheduling corrects an offset
    Host->>Sched: run_pending()
    Sched->>Job: should_run compares naive local now with next_run
    Sched->>Job: run()
    Job->>Body: invoke bound partial - line 691
    Body-->>Job: return value
    Job->>Pytz: normalize while recomputing next_run
    Pytz-->>Job: corrected occurrence
    Job-->>Sched: value, or CancelJob if the until deadline is exceeded
```

**Diagram 6.3.5-A — Timezone-anchored declaration and first dispatch, showing the gated `pytz` interaction.** A job declared without a timezone never reaches the `pytz` participant at all: `at_time_zone` stays `None` and `_correct_utc_offset` returns immediately (line 776).

#### 6.3.5.2 Background-Thread Embedding with Cooperative Shutdown

`docs/background-execution.rst` publishes this recipe because the library owns no lifecycle of its own. The thread, the interval, and the stop signal are all host-supplied; the library sees ordinary `run_pending()` calls.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Main as Host main thread
    participant Runner as run_continuously helper
    participant Thread as ScheduleThread
    participant Sched as schedule default scheduler
    participant Body as Job callable
    Main->>Sched: every().second.do(background_job)
    Main->>Runner: run_continuously(interval=1)
    Runner->>Runner: create threading.Event as the stop flag
    Runner->>Thread: start the thread subclass
    Runner-->>Main: return the Event so the host can stop it
    loop until the Event is set
        Thread->>Sched: run_pending()
        Sched->>Body: invoke each due job serially
        Body-->>Sched: return value or CancelJob
        Thread->>Thread: time.sleep(interval)
    end
    Main->>Main: continue unrelated work on the main thread
    Main->>Runner: stop_run_continuously.set()
    Note over Thread,Sched: The flag is checked between polls, so shutdown waits for the current cycle
    Thread--)Runner: loop exits after the in-flight cycle completes
```

**Diagram 6.3.5-B — Background embedding: host-owned thread, host-owned stop signal, unchanged library protocol.** The recipe's own docstring repeats the delivery contract — it is intended behaviour that continuous running does not replay missed jobs, so a one-hour poll interval on a one-minute job produces one execution per interval, not sixty.

#### 6.3.5.3 Queue Hand-Off to Worker Threads

This is the repository's answer to serial execution, and structurally it is a producer/consumer integration built entirely from the standard library. The scheduler's registered "job" is the queue's `put` method, so a firing produces a work item instead of doing work.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Driver as Host driver loop
    participant Sched as Scheduler
    participant Queue as queue.Queue instance
    participant Worker as Worker thread
    participant Body as Real job function
    Note over Driver,Body: Registration binds jobqueue.put with the real function as its argument
    Driver->>Sched: every(10).seconds.do(jobqueue.put, job)
    loop every poll of the host loop
        Driver->>Sched: run_pending()
        Sched->>Queue: put(job) - returns immediately
        Note over Sched: Dispatch thread is released after an O(1) enqueue
    end
    par worker drains independently
        Worker->>Queue: get() blocks until an item is available
        Queue-->>Worker: job function
        Worker->>Body: call the function
        Body-->>Worker: return value is discarded by the worker
        Worker->>Queue: task_done()
    end
    Note over Queue,Worker: Concurrency is capped by worker count - the queue as published is in-memory and unbounded
```

**Diagram 6.3.5-C — Queue hand-off message flow.** Two protocol consequences follow from this pattern and should be planned for: the `CancelJob` sentinel can no longer reach the scheduler, because the value the scheduler observes is the return of `queue.put` rather than of the real function; and an exception raised inside the worker never touches `run_pending()`, so the fail-fast propagation described in 6.3.3.5 no longer protects or interrupts the dispatch loop.

#### 6.3.5.4 Build, Publish, and Install Supply Chain

This is the only flow in the project that traverses real network boundaries. Every participant except the maintainer and the adopter is an external service, and all of them are absent from the runtime.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Dev as Maintainer
    participant GH as GitHub repository
    participant CI as GitHub Actions runners
    participant Cov as Coveralls
    participant Reg as TestPyPI then PyPI
    participant User as Adopter environment
    Dev->>GH: push or open a pull request against master
    GH->>CI: trigger the Tests workflow
    CI->>CI: checkout@v3 then setup-python@v4 across 3.7 to 3.12
    CI->>CI: pip install tox tox-gh-actions then run tox
    Note over CI: tox expands twelve environments - each interpreter with and without pytz
    CI->>Cov: upload coverage per interpreter with COVERALLS_PARALLEL
    CI->>CI: parallel jobs docs, formatting and setuppy run the quality gates
    CI->>Cov: dependent job runs coveralls --finish
    Cov-->>GH: combined summary comment and badge status
    Dev->>GH: update HISTORY.rst, bump the version in setup.py and docs/conf.py
    Dev->>GH: git tag X.Y.Z then git push --tags
    Dev->>Dev: python -m build --wheel
    Dev->>Reg: twine upload to the schedule-test alias for verification
    Dev->>Reg: twine upload to the schedule alias for production
    User->>Reg: pip install schedule
    Reg-->>User: wheel containing the module and py.typed
    opt timezone support is required
        User->>Reg: pip install pytz
    end
    Note over User: From this point the adopter process contacts none of the participants above
```

**Diagram 6.3.5-D — Build, publish, and install supply chain.** The publish steps are manual: `.github/workflows/` contains only `ci.yml`, so no automation performs the tagging, building, or uploading described in `docs/development.rst`.
