## 6.4 Security Architecture

### 6.4.1 Applicability Assessment and Trust Model

**Detailed Security Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

The subject of this specification is the Python `schedule` library at release 1.2.2 (`setup.py` line 5). Its entire runtime is one importable module — `schedule/__init__.py`, 945 lines — accompanied by the zero-byte PEP 561 marker `schedule/py.typed`. That module has no principal to authenticate, no owned resource to authorize, no data at rest to encrypt, no data in transit to protect, and no secret of its own to manage. A security architecture in the conventional sense — an authentication framework, an authorization model, and a data-protection scheme — would have nothing to act upon.

This determination is not inferred from the small size of the codebase. It rests on exhaustive scans of the module and of all 32 tracked files, each recorded below with the patterns applied and the result returned. Section 5.4.4 reaches the same conclusion from the cross-cutting perspective, recording that no authentication or authorization framework exists and that none is architecturally required; Section 6.3.2.3 reaches it from the integration perspective, recording that neither can even be configured because there is no protocol boundary at which to apply them.

What follows therefore does two things. Sub-sections 6.4.2 through 6.4.4 walk each concern the section prompt enumerates — identity, multi-factor authentication, sessions, tokens, password policy, role-based access control, permissions, resource authorization, policy enforcement, audit logging, encryption, key management, masking, secure communication, and compliance — and record for each either the mechanism that occupies its position or the verified absence of one, together with the host-side obligation that absence creates. Sub-section 6.4.5 then documents the standard security practices the project *does* follow, as an evidenced control matrix with an honest register of gaps. The intent is that an adopter embedding this library into a security-sensitive application can read this section and know exactly which controls they inherit (very few) and which they must supply (nearly all).

#### 6.4.1.1 Determination Criteria and Findings

Each row below is a structural precondition for a dedicated security architecture. Every one of them fails, and each failure is tied to an executed verification rather than an assumption.

| Precondition | Verification performed | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| A principal to authenticate | Scan of `schedule/__init__.py` for `password`, `passwd`, `login`, `session`, `cookie`, `getpass`, `token`, `jwt`, `oauth`, `auth` | **Fails** — zero occurrences of every pattern. No user, account, subject, session, or credential construct exists |
| A protected resource with an owner | Inspection of the complete `Job` record, lines 227–255 | **Fails** — the twelve attributes carry no owner, principal, tenant, or ACL field; `tags` (line 253) is an unconstrained `Set[Hashable]` |
| A privilege boundary the library can enforce | Inspection of every entry point (lines 843–913) and of the invocation site | **Fails** — one OS process, one thread; the payload is invoked at line 691 with the full privileges of the host interpreter |
| Data at rest to protect | Scan for `open(`, `pickle`, `marshal`, `shelve`, `sqlite`, `json`, `yaml`, `tempfile`, `shutil`, `Path(` | **Fails** — zero occurrences. Section 6.3.1.1 records that the only `open(` in the repository is `setup.py` line 13, reading `README.rst` at build time |
| Data in transit to protect | Scan for `socket`, `urllib`, `requests`, `ssl`, `http` (word form) | **Fails** — zero code occurrences. The three `http` hits are the reference URLs in the module docstring, lines 36–38 |
| A secret the software manages | Scan for `environ`, `getenv`, `secrets`, `hashlib`, `hmac`, `crypt`, `base64`, `cert` | **Fails** — zero occurrences. The two `cert` hits are the word "certain" in docstrings at lines 166 and 213 |
| Dynamic code or data interpretation | Scan for `eval(`, `exec(`, `compile(`, `__import__`, `subprocess`, `os.`, `sys.`, `input(`, `globals()`, `locals()`, `setattr`, `format_map` | **Fails** — zero occurrences of every pattern |
| Regulated data processing | Inspection of every public signature and of the `Job` record | **Fails** — the library accepts an interval, a unit, a clock string, an optional timezone, a deadline, hashable tags, and a callable with its arguments; it derives, stores, and transmits no personal, health, or payment data of its own |

Two audits complete the determination. First, the module's import graph is decisive: eight standard-library imports at lines 41–48 (`collections.abc.Hashable`, `datetime`, `functools`, `logging`, `random`, `re`, `time`, `typing`) plus a single function-local `import pytz` at line 499. Nothing in that graph is capable of cryptography, network access, credential handling, or privilege manipulation. Second, every repository-wide textual match for `auth` or `permission` was inspected individually and every one is licence prose or authorship metadata — `LICENSE.txt` lines 5, 12 and 18; `docs/conf.py` lines 62, 282, 329, 330, 340 and 347; `setup.py` lines 25–26; `pyproject.toml` line 8; `docs/index.rst` line 109; `docs/development.rst` line 52. This corroborates the identical audit recorded in Section 6.3.1.1.

#### 6.4.1.2 Trust Model and Security Zones

The library occupies a single security zone that it does not own. Everything of security consequence — the process boundary, the OS user, the file system, the network, the logging sinks, and the credentials any job body needs — belongs to the host application. The library's only privileged act is to call a function the host itself supplied, and the right to make that call is a right the host already possessed.

The critical property of this model is that **the library adds no privilege and creates no new trust boundary**. A caller able to reach `schedule.every()` is, by definition, already executing arbitrary Python inside the host interpreter. An access-control layer placed inside the library would therefore guard nothing that is not already reachable by simpler means — the same reasoning Section 5.4.4 records.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph ZoneExternal["Zone 0 - External, build time only, unreachable from the runtime"]
        direction TB
        SrcHost["GitHub: source, pull requests, Actions runners"]
        CovSvc["Coveralls: coverage aggregation via per-run GITHUB_TOKEN"]
        Registry["PyPI and TestPyPI: manual twine upload of the wheel"]
        DocSite["Read the Docs: generated documentation site"]
        SrcHost --> CovSvc
        SrcHost --> DocSite
        SrcHost -->|"maintainer tags, builds and uploads"| Registry
    end
    subgraph ZoneHost["Zone 1 - Host trust zone, one OS process owned entirely by the adopter"]
        direction TB
        HostBoundary["Host application: owns the OS user, file system,<br/>network, config, secrets and logging sinks"]
        Declare["Declaration code calls every, at, until, tag, do"]
        Driver["Driver loop calls run_pending or run_all"]
        LogSink["Host logging handlers; nothing is emitted until the<br/>host lowers the schedule logger to DEBUG"]
        Secrets["Any credential a job body needs is resolved,<br/>held and rotated by the host"]
        HostBoundary --> Declare
        HostBoundary --> Driver
        HostBoundary --> Secrets
    end
    subgraph ZoneLib["Zone 1a - Library sub-zone, same process, no added privilege"]
        direction TB
        Facade["Module facade: default_scheduler line 837 and the<br/>live jobs alias line 840, both process global"]
        Guards["28 definition-time guards raise before the<br/>registry append at line 663"]
        RegistryMem[("jobs list on the interpreter heap,<br/>line 87 - no persistence anywhere")]
        Dispatch["run_pending filters then sorts the due subset,<br/>lines 99 to 100"]
        Facade --> Guards
        Guards --> RegistryMem
        RegistryMem --> Dispatch
    end
    subgraph ZonePayload["Zone 1b - Payload sub-zone, host code executed unsandboxed"]
        direction TB
        Partial["functools.partial bound at line 655 retaining every<br/>positional and keyword argument"]
        Invoke["Invocation at line 691: no sandbox, no timeout,<br/>no privilege drop, no try or except"]
        Sentinel["Only CancelJob crosses back as a control signal,<br/>recognised at line 174"]
        Partial --> Invoke
        Invoke --> Sentinel
    end
    subgraph ZoneAbsent["Verified absent across all 32 tracked files"]
        direction TB
        NoIdentity["No identity, session, token or password construct"]
        NoAuthz["No role, permission, ACL or policy engine"]
        NoCrypto["No cipher, hash, HMAC, key store or certificate"]
        NoTransport["No socket, TLS, protocol or serialization"]
        NoRest["No file, database or cache persistence"]
    end
    Registry -.->|"pip install schedule delivers the wheel once"| Facade
    Declare --> Facade
    Driver --> Dispatch
    Dispatch --> Partial
    Facade -.->|"8 DEBUG records rendering bound arguments"| LogSink
    Secrets -.->|"passed as job arguments, then rendered by __str__"| Partial
```

The zone model yields five properties that bound the whole security discussion, each verifiable in the code:

| Property | Consequence |
|---|---|
| One process, one zone | There is no inter-zone channel to authenticate, encrypt, or rate-limit; Section 6.3.1.2 records that the sole boundary is a Python `import` |
| No privilege gradient | The payload at line 691 runs at exactly the privilege of the caller that declared it, so `do()` is not an escalation vector |
| Process-global shared state | `default_scheduler` (line 837) and the live `jobs` alias (line 840) are reachable and mutable by any code in the interpreter; the alias carries an inline `todo` acknowledging the exposure |
| Zero persistence | The registry lives only on the heap (line 87); process exit is total schedule loss by design, so there is no data-at-rest surface — see Section 5.4.6 |
| Host-owned observability | The library configures no logging handler, so its records — including bound argument values — reach only the sinks the host has configured |

#### 6.4.1.3 Threat Model and Residual Risks

Because the library is embedded rather than deployed, its threat model is a list of ways an adopter can be harmed *through* it, not ways an attacker can reach it directly. There is no remote attacker in this model: no listener exists to connect to. The five residual risks below are the complete set observable in the repository, each with the concrete evidence that establishes it and the mitigation the repository itself supports.

| Residual risk | Evidence in the repository | Mitigation available today |
|---|---|---|
| Sensitive job arguments disclosed through DEBUG logs | `Job.__str__` interpolates `job_func.args` and `job_func.keywords` (lines 274–275); `logger.debug("Running job %s", self)` at line 690 emits it; `docs/logging.rst` line 30 shows `args=` and `kwargs=` in the sample record | Keep the `schedule` logger above DEBUG in production, or bind an indirection — a lookup key or a closure — instead of the secret itself |
| Availability loss from an unguarded job exception | No `try`/`except` surrounds line 691; `docs/exception-handling.rst` line 4 states exceptions "bubble up and interrupt schedule's run_xyz function" | Wrap the callable with the published `catch_exceptions` decorator, or guard the host driver loop |
| Cross-component interference through the global registry | Any imported code can call `schedule.clear()` — one `del self.jobs[:]` at line 145 removes every job registered by every component | Own a private `Scheduler()` instance rather than the module facade, as `docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` describes |
| Unbounded execution time in the dispatch thread | Line 691 has no timeout and dispatch is serial (lines 99–101), so one slow body delays every other job | Move long-running work onto a host thread or a `queue.Queue` worker, the pattern `docs/parallel-execution.rst` publishes |
| Stale or forked copies of the library | `docs/installation.rst` flags the Ubuntu and Debian packages as **OUTDATED** at 0.3.2 (2015) and labels manual single-file vendoring "highly discouraged" | Install from PyPI at a current version so that correctness and safety fixes are actually received |

Two clarifications keep this list honest. Arbitrary-callable execution is **not** counted as a vulnerability: it is the library's entire purpose, and the caller who supplies the callable already holds the right to run it. And no vulnerability history is claimed or denied here — `HISTORY.rst` records 23 releases of functional and timezone-correctness fixes, and contains no security advisory, while the repository publishes no `SECURITY.md` through which one could be reported (Section 6.4.5.6).


### 6.4.2 Authentication Framework

**No authentication framework exists in this system, and none can be configured.** The library has no concept of a caller: not one of its entry points accepts, produces, or consults an identity, principal, session, context object, or credential. Verification is exhaustive rather than illustrative — scans of `schedule/__init__.py` for `password`, `passwd`, `login`, `session`, `cookie`, `getpass`, `token`, `jwt`, `oauth`, `auth`, `hashlib`, `hmac`, `secrets` and `crypt` return zero occurrences of every pattern, and the repository-wide `auth` matches are licence prose and authorship metadata only (6.4.1.1).

This sub-section records, for each authentication concern the specification requires, the position that actually holds in the system and the obligation that position places on the host application.

#### 6.4.2.1 Identity Management

There is no identity model. The `Job` record defined at lines 227–255 has twelve attributes — `interval`, `latest`, `job_func`, `unit`, `at_time`, `at_time_zone`, `last_run`, `next_run`, `start_day`, `cancel_after`, `tags`, and `scheduler` — and not one of them identifies a creator, owner, tenant, or subject. Section 6.2.2.4 records the related finding that the record carries no identity of its own at all: `Job` defines neither `__eq__` nor `__hash__`, so records are distinguished only by object reference.

| Identity concern | Position in this system | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| User or service accounts | None; the library never represents an actor | No identity field in `Job.__init__`, lines 227–255 |
| Directory or identity provider integration | None; no LDAP, SAML, OIDC, or directory client exists | Import set is stdlib-only, lines 41–48 |
| Registration and provisioning | Not applicable; `do()` registers a *job*, not a subject (line 663) | `Job.do`, lines 644–664 |
| Identity propagation into the payload | None; the bound `functools.partial` receives only the arguments captured at declaration time | Line 655 |
| The nearest analogue | `tags`, an unconstrained `Set[Hashable]` used for grouping (line 253); it is a label, never an identity | `tag()`, lines 457–469 |

The host obligation is unambiguous: any notion of *who* is allowed to declare, inspect, or cancel a job must be established and enforced by the host before it calls into the library. Nothing inside the library can distinguish one caller from another.

#### 6.4.2.2 Multi-Factor Authentication

Multi-factor authentication is not applicable and cannot be meaningfully discussed at the library level: with no first factor there is no second. No TOTP, HOTP, WebAuthn, push-approval, SMS, or recovery-code mechanism exists in any tracked file, and no dependency capable of providing one appears in `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, or `requirements-dev.txt`.

The one place multi-factor authentication is genuinely relevant to this project is the maintainer-side supply chain rather than the runtime. `docs/development.rst` lines 49–68 document a fully manual publication procedure — `git tag`, `git push --tags`, `python3 -m build --wheel`, then `twine upload` to the `schedule-test` alias and afterwards to the `schedule` alias. The registry credentials used by those uploads are resolved from a maintainer-local configuration that is not in the repository, so whether they are protected by a second factor is a property of the maintainers' registry accounts and is not observable from this codebase. No claim is made here in either direction.

#### 6.4.2.3 Session Management

There is no session concept, and the architecture forecloses one. Sessions require a stateful association between an authenticated principal and a series of requests; this system has neither principals nor requests. Every entry point is a direct, stateless Python call whose only context is the arguments passed to it.

| Session concern | Position in this system |
|---|---|
| Session establishment, renewal, or termination | None; the nine facade functions (lines 843–897) hold no per-caller state |
| Idle or absolute timeout | None; there is no session to expire. The nearest lifecycle control is `until()`, which bounds a **job's** lifetime, not a caller's (lines 576–642) |
| Session store, cookie, or handle | None; no serialization, no store, and nothing persisted — the registry is heap-only (line 87) |
| Concurrent-session control | Not applicable; execution is serial on the caller's thread and the library holds no locks |
| Fixation, hijacking, or replay exposure | Not reachable; there is no handle to fixate, steal, or replay |

The only long-lived state in the system is the job registry itself, and its lifetime is exactly the lifetime of the host process. Section 5.4.6 records the resulting continuity model: process termination is total schedule loss by design, and recovery is re-declaration rather than restoration.

#### 6.4.2.4 Token Handling

The library issues, validates, stores, and refreshes no tokens of any kind. Two findings need to be stated precisely, because a superficial search of the repository turns up the word "token" exactly once and it is easy to misread.

| Token-related item | What it actually is | Location |
|---|---|---|
| `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` | The GitHub-provided, per-run continuous-integration token, passed as the `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable to the Coveralls uploader. It exists only inside the CI runner and is never present in a released artifact | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` lines 30 and 52 |
| `CancelJob` | An in-band **control marker**, not a security token. It carries no identity, no claims, no expiry, and no signature; `_run_job` accepts either the class or an instance of it | `schedule/__init__.py` lines 71–76 and 174 |
| Bearer, API, refresh, or CSRF tokens | Absent entirely; no issuance, verification, revocation, rotation, or introspection code exists in the module | Verified by the scans in 6.4.1.1 |

Because `CancelJob` is the only value the library interprets on the way back from a payload, an adopter should note the associated integrity property: `_run_job` at line 174 tests `isinstance(ret, CancelJob) or ret is CancelJob`, so **any** job body that happens to return that marker unschedules itself. This is a deliberate cooperative signal, and it is also the reason the queue hand-off pattern in Section 6.3.5.3 loses cancellation — the value the scheduler observes there is the return of `queue.put`, not of the real function.

If a job body needs a credential — an API key, a bearer token, a database password — that credential is entirely the host's to resolve, hold, and rotate. Two implementation notes follow directly from the code and materially affect exposure. Arguments passed to `do()` are captured once at declaration and retained for the lifetime of the job inside the `functools.partial` created at line 655, so a value bound there lives as long as the registration does and is never re-read; and that same partial's `args` and `keywords` are rendered into the job's string form (lines 274–275), which is what makes DEBUG logging a disclosure path (6.4.4.3). Passing a callable or a lookup key that resolves the secret at execution time avoids both effects.

#### 6.4.2.5 Password Policies

No password policy exists because no password, passphrase, PIN, or secret-answer value is ever accepted, generated, compared, stored, or transmitted by the library. There is consequently no complexity rule, no length floor, no rotation interval, no history check, no lockout threshold, and no hashing or key-derivation function — the module imports neither `hashlib` nor `hmac` nor `crypt`, and defines no comparison of secret material.

One adjacent property is worth recording because it is easy to assume otherwise. The library uses `random.randint(self.interval, self.latest)` to draw a fresh interval on every reschedule when `to()` has been configured (`_schedule_next_run`, lines 709–712). `random` is the standard library's pseudo-random generator, not `secrets`, and it is therefore **not cryptographically secure** — the same finding Section 5.3.6 records. This is entirely appropriate for its actual purpose, which is de-synchronising coincident jobs to spread load (6.3.2.4), but the resulting firing times must never be treated as unpredictable to an adversary, and the value must never be used as a nonce, salt, or secret.

#### 6.4.2.6 Authentication Flow

The flow below is the authentication flow of this system in its entirety: every decision resolves to "no check exists at this point, and the host is the only party that could have made one." It is included because knowing precisely where a check *could* have been made is what tells an adopter where to put their own.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Some component in the host process<br/>wants a periodic job]) --> HostGate{"Has the host performed<br/>any identity check of its own<br/>before this point?"}
    HostGate -->|"No - the common case"| NoCheck["Unauthenticated caller proceeds;<br/>the library cannot detect this"]
    HostGate -->|"Yes - host enforced"| HostOK["Caller already authorised by host policy;<br/>no identity is passed onward"]
    NoCheck --> Import["import schedule - the only boundary<br/>crossed, Section 6.3.1.2"]
    HostOK --> Import
    Import --> Facade{"Which surface is used?"}
    Facade -->|"module facade"| Global["Process global default_scheduler line 837;<br/>no credential parameter exists on any of<br/>the nine functions, lines 843 to 897"]
    Facade -->|"private instance"| Private["Own Scheduler instance;<br/>isolation by convention only,<br/>docs multiple-schedulers"]
    Global --> Build["Fluent configuration: units, weekdays,<br/>at, to, until, tag"]
    Private --> Build
    Build --> Validate{"Do the 28 definition-time<br/>guards accept the values?"}
    Validate -->|"No"| Reject["IntervalError, ScheduleValueError,<br/>TypeError or ScheduleError raised<br/>before the registry append"]
    Reject --> Unchanged([Registry unchanged; this is input<br/>validation, never authentication])
    Validate -->|"Yes"| Commit["do binds functools.partial line 655<br/>and appends to jobs line 663"]
    Commit --> Note["No identity is recorded on the job;<br/>the record has no owner field, lines 227 to 255"]
    Note --> Poll["Host driver loop calls run_pending"]
    Poll --> Due{"Is now greater than or<br/>equal to next_run? line 672"}
    Due -->|"No"| Skip([Job left registered and untouched])
    Due -->|"Yes"| Exec["Invocation at line 691 with full host<br/>privileges; no sandbox and no timeout"]
    Exec --> Cred{"Does the payload itself<br/>need a credential?"}
    Cred -->|"No"| Done([Return value discarded unless<br/>it is the CancelJob marker, line 174])
    Cred -->|"Yes - host supplied"| HostCred["Host resolves it: bound at declaration<br/>and retained in the partial, or looked up<br/>at execution time"]
    HostCred --> Expose{"Is the schedule logger<br/>set to DEBUG?"}
    Expose -->|"Yes"| Leak["Bound args and kwargs rendered into the<br/>log record, lines 274 to 275 and 690"]
    Expose -->|"No - default"| Quiet["Nothing emitted; the library attaches<br/>no handler of its own"]
    Leak --> Done
    Quiet --> Done
```

The three points at which a real authentication control could be inserted are all outside the library, and all three belong to the host: at the `HostGate` decision, by gating who may execute declaration code at all; at the `Cred` decision, by resolving payload credentials from a secret manager at execution time rather than binding them at declaration; and at the `Expose` decision, by keeping the `schedule` logger above DEBUG so that argument values are never rendered. Section 5.4.7 states the same division in its responsibility matrix: the library has no trust boundary to defend, and the host must provide authorization over API access together with protection of anything a job body touches.


### 6.4.3 Authorization System

**No authorization system exists in this system, and none is architecturally required.** Every public entry point performs its work unconditionally: there is no role, no permission, no capability, no access-control list, no policy document, and no decision point anywhere in `schedule/__init__.py`. Scans for `role`, `permission`, `acl`, `rbac`, `authorization`, `throttle`, and `ratelimit` return zero occurrences in the module, and Section 6.3.1.1 records the same result across all 32 tracked files.

The architectural justification is the one Section 5.4.4 records and 6.4.1.2 develops: the library sits wholly inside a single trust zone that it does not own. Any caller able to reach `schedule.every()` is already executing arbitrary Python in the host interpreter, so a permission check inside the library would guard a door that stands open beside it. The correct strategy for an adopter is therefore **isolation, not permission** — the guidance Section 6.3.2.3 gives.

#### 6.4.3.1 Role-Based Access Control

There is no role-based access control, and there is no subject to which a role could attach. The table below records what occupies each RBAC position.

| RBAC element | Position in this system | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Subject | Absent; no principal is ever represented or passed | No identity parameter on any signature, lines 843–913 |
| Role or group | Absent; no role registry, hierarchy, or assignment exists | Verified by scan — zero `role`, `rbac`, `group` matches in the module |
| Permission | Absent; no operation is gated by a right | All 28 `raise` sites are value or type guards, never access denials |
| Object | The `Job` record and the `Scheduler.jobs` list, both freely reachable | Lines 87, 227–255, 837, 840 |
| Nearest analogue | `tags` — an unconstrained `Set[Hashable]` supporting grouped lookup and grouped deletion | `tag()` lines 457–469; `get_jobs(tag)` lines 122–133; `clear(tag)` lines 135–148 |

Tags must not be mistaken for roles or for a tenancy boundary, and the reason is structural rather than stylistic. `tag()` enforces exactly one rule — `if not all(isinstance(tag, Hashable) for tag in tags): raise TypeError("Tags must be hashable")` at lines 466–467 — and nothing else. Any code may apply any tag to any job, may enumerate every tag by reading `job.tags`, and may delete an entire tag group with a single `clear(tag)` call. `test_tag_type_enforcement` (`test_schedule.py` line 1537) documents the whole of the contract: `{}` and `[]` are rejected as unhashable, while `tag(0, "a", True)` is accepted and yields three tags. A label that any party can read, write, and act upon confers no authority.

#### 6.4.3.2 Permission Management

There is no permission model to manage: no grant, revoke, inheritance, delegation, scope, or capability construct exists. What the repository provides instead is a set of **lifecycle constraints** that a declaring component may place on its *own* jobs at definition time. These are self-imposed limits, not permissions — nothing prevents other code from removing them by cancelling or clearing the job.

| Constraint | Mechanism | Security-relevant effect |
|---|---|---|
| Bounded lifetime | `until()` accepts a `datetime`, `timedelta`, `time`, or one of five string formats, rejects a past deadline, and stores `cancel_after` (lines 576–642) | `run()` checks the deadline before executing and again after rescheduling (lines 686, 695), so an expired job is removed without running |
| Self-termination | Returning the `CancelJob` marker from the payload | `_run_job` recognises class or instance at line 174 and removes the record — the only in-band control signal in the system |
| Group revocation | `clear(tag)` slice-assigns the survivors (line 148); `cancel_job(job)` removes one record and is idempotent (lines 156–160) | Enables bulk quarantine of a job class, but is available to *any* code in the process |
| Interval floor and jitter | `every(interval)` with a unit, optionally `to(latest)` drawing `random.randint` per reschedule (lines 709–712) | Paces work; `random` is not cryptographic, so firing times are not adversarially unpredictable |

Two absences bound this picture. There is no read-only view of the registry: `get_jobs()` returns `self.jobs[:]` at line 131 — a copy of the *list* whose elements are the live `Job` objects — so a caller that can read the registry can also mutate every record in it, the finding Sections 6.2.4.5 and 6.3.2.3 record. And there is no privilege attenuation at execution: the payload is invoked at line 691 with no sandbox, no capability restriction, and no timeout.

#### 6.4.3.3 Resource Authorization

The only resource the library owns is the in-memory job registry created at line 87, and access to it is governed by Python scope alone. Two access paths exist and both are unguarded.

| Access path | Reachability | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `schedule.default_scheduler` | The process-global `Scheduler` instantiated at line 837; reachable by any code that imports the module | Full control of every job any component registered through the facade |
| `schedule.jobs` | A **live alias** to that scheduler's list, bound at line 840 and carrying an inline `todo` questioning whether it should be a copy | Direct mutation of the registry without going through any method |
| A private `Scheduler()` instance | Reachable only through the reference the owning component holds | The only isolation mechanism the design offers, documented in `docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` |
| Individual `Job` objects | Returned live by `get_jobs()` (line 131) and reachable through the alias | Every attribute — including `next_run`, `cancel_after`, `tags`, and `job_func` — is a plain public attribute with no accessor guard |

The blast radius of the shared path deserves an explicit statement, because it is the single most consequential authorization property in the system: `clear()` with no argument executes one `del self.jobs[:]` at line 145 and silently removes **every job registered by every component in the process**. It emits one DEBUG record, "Deleting *all* jobs" (line 144), and returns `None`. A library or plug-in that calls `schedule.clear()` to tidy up after itself will therefore de-schedule its host's work. The mitigation is the isolation strategy above: components that schedule their own work inside someone else's application should own a private `Scheduler()` and never touch the facade.

#### 6.4.3.4 Policy Enforcement Points

The library contains **no policy enforcement point** in the security sense — no location where a request is evaluated against a rule about *who* may do *what*. It does, however, contain a dense and well-tested set of **validation** enforcement points, and distinguishing the two precisely is the useful content of this concern.

| Enforcement point | Kind of check | Effect on failure |
|---|---|---|
| Fluent grammar guards — unit properties (325–378), weekday properties (380–455), `at()` (493–527), `until()` (633–641), `tag()` (466), `_schedule_next_run()` (704–712), `_weekday_index()` (943) | Value, type, and invariant validation | Raises before the registry append at line 663; the record never enters the registry |
| `Job.do()` owner check, lines 658–662 | Structural integrity — a job must have a scheduler | `ScheduleError`; nothing is registered |
| `Job.run()` deadline checks, lines 686 and 695 | Temporal policy on the job's own lifetime | Converted to the `CancelJob` marker; the payload is not executed in the pre-check case |
| `Scheduler._run_job()`, line 174 | Return-value inspection for the cancellation marker | Record removed via the idempotent `cancel_job` |
| Access to `default_scheduler`, `jobs`, or any `Job` attribute | **No check of any kind** | The operation simply succeeds |

The guard population is exact and worth quantifying, because it is the strongest verifiable control the codebase contains. The module holds 28 `raise` statements — 12 `IntervalError`, 11 `ScheduleValueError`, 3 `TypeError`, and 2 `ScheduleError` — and every one of them fires during definition, before or inside `do()`, which is why Section 5.4.3 characterises the pattern as "fail-fast at the configuration boundary" with a total guarantee: a validation fault costs the caller an exception and costs the system nothing. The behaviour is executably specified: `test_schedule.py` contains 70 `assertRaises` assertions across its 81 test methods — 36 for `ScheduleValueError`, 16 for `IntervalError`, 6 for `TypeError`, 2 for `ScheduleError`, and 1 for a `pytz` unknown-zone error — and the suite runs green in well under a second.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Request([Any code in the host process invokes<br/>a schedule operation]) --> Which{"Which operation?"}
    Which -->|"declare: every, at, until, tag, do"| DeclPath["Definition path"]
    Which -->|"inspect: get_jobs, next_run, idle_seconds"| ReadPath["Read path"]
    Which -->|"mutate: cancel_job, clear, direct attribute write"| WritePath["Mutation path"]
    Which -->|"dispatch: run_pending, run_all"| RunPath["Dispatch path"]
    DeclPath --> IdentityQ{"Is the caller's identity<br/>consulted at any point?"}
    IdentityQ -->|"No - there is no identity concept"| ValGuards{"Do the 28 definition-time<br/>guards accept the values?"}
    ValGuards -->|"No"| Denied["Typed exception raised:<br/>IntervalError, ScheduleValueError,<br/>TypeError or ScheduleError"]
    Denied --> Intact([Registry unchanged - this is validation,<br/>not an access denial])
    ValGuards -->|"Yes"| Appended["Appended to jobs at line 663<br/>with no owner recorded"]
    ReadPath --> ReadCheck{"Is any permission<br/>evaluated?"}
    ReadCheck -->|"No"| LiveHandles["get_jobs returns a copied list of LIVE Job<br/>objects, line 131 - read confers mutation"]
    WritePath --> WriteCheck{"Is any permission<br/>evaluated?"}
    WriteCheck -->|"No"| Blast{"Which mutation?"}
    Blast -->|"cancel_job(job)"| OneGone["One record removed; unknown job is a<br/>silent no-op, lines 156 to 160"]
    Blast -->|"clear(tag)"| GroupGone["Whole tag group removed by slice<br/>assignment, line 148"]
    Blast -->|"clear()"| AllGone["EVERY job of EVERY component removed by<br/>one del jobs slice, line 145"]
    RunPath --> Ordered["Due subset filtered then sorted by<br/>next_run, lines 99 to 100"]
    Ordered --> Deadline{"Is the until deadline<br/>already passed? line 686"}
    Deadline -->|"Yes"| CancelPre["CancelJob returned WITHOUT executing<br/>the payload, line 688"]
    Deadline -->|"No"| Invoke["Payload invoked at line 691 at full host<br/>privilege - no sandbox, no timeout"]
    Invoke --> Marker{"Did the payload return<br/>the CancelJob marker?"}
    Marker -->|"Yes"| Unsched["Record removed by the idempotent<br/>cancel_job, line 174"]
    Marker -->|"No"| Rescheduled["next_run recomputed, line 693;<br/>return value discarded"]
    Appended --> Ordered
    LiveHandles --> Intact
    OneGone --> Intact
    GroupGone --> Intact
    AllGone --> Isolation["Mitigation: own a private Scheduler<br/>instead of the module facade"]
    CancelPre --> Unsched
```

#### 6.4.3.5 Audit Logging

**There is no audit log.** The library emits eight DEBUG records and nothing else, and those records are diagnostic rather than evidentiary: they carry no actor, no outcome, no correlation identifier, and no tamper resistance, and they are invisible unless the host explicitly lowers the `schedule` logger to DEBUG. Sections 5.4.1 and 5.4.2 document the observability contract in full; the table below assesses those same records specifically as audit evidence.

| Audit property | Position in this system | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Sink and level | One logger, `logging.getLogger("schedule")`, DEBUG only — no INFO, WARNING, ERROR, or CRITICAL path exists | Line 50; the eight `logger.debug` sites at 113, 144, 147, 157, 160, 687, 690, 696 |
| Actor attribution | None — no record identifies who performed the operation, because no identity exists | All eight call sites |
| Events recorded | Forced sweep with job count and delay (113); bulk and tagged deletion (144, 147); cancellation, including of an unregistered job (157, 160); job run and deadline-driven cancellation (687, 690, 696) | Enumerated exhaustively |
| Events **not** recorded | Job registration, payload exceptions, reschedule outcomes, DST-gap displacement, tag mutation, and every read operation | Section 5.4.2 records the same list |
| Integrity and retention | None — no signing, sequencing, append-only guarantee, rotation, or retention policy; the library attaches no handler at all | `docs/logging.rst` shows the host wiring the level and handler |
| Correlation | The job object itself is the only handle; `tags` are the only grouping dimension | Section 5.4.2 |

Three consequences follow for anyone who needs auditable scheduling. The most security-significant omission is that **registration is not logged**: a job appended at line 663 leaves no trace whatsoever, so an audit trail cannot be reconstructed from library output alone. The second is that a payload failure produces no record from any source — Section 5.4.2 puts it directly, the exception *is* the notification — so a host that swallows exceptions without logging them loses the event entirely. The third is that audit records are opt-in by construction: because the library configures no handler, an adopter who has not enabled DEBUG on the `schedule` logger receives nothing, which is simultaneously the reason the library cannot interfere with a strict host logging policy and the reason it cannot satisfy an audit requirement on its own.

The host obligation is therefore to instrument at the seam rather than to rely on library output. `docs/logging.rst` lines 37–74 publish the sanctioned pattern — a `functools.wraps`-based decorator such as `print_elapsed_time` wrapped around the job function — which is the only place a host can record who declared a job, whether it succeeded, and how long it took. Enabling DEBUG on the `schedule` logger to obtain an activity trail carries the disclosure consequence documented in 6.4.4.3 and must be weighed against it.


### 6.4.4 Data Protection

The library holds no data of its own worth protecting and moves no data anywhere. Its complete data footprint is the in-memory job registry created at line 87, whose records contain an interval, a unit, an optional clock time and timezone object, two naive timestamps, an optional weekday, an optional deadline, a set of hashable tags, a scheduler reference, and a `functools.partial` wrapping the host's callable with the arguments the host bound to it. Nothing is written to disk, nothing is serialised, and nothing leaves the process — Section 6.2.2.1 records the single in-memory store, and Section 5.4.6 records that process termination is total loss by design.

Consequently there is no data-at-rest surface and no data-in-transit surface. The one genuine data-protection concern in the whole system is **the host's own data passing through the library as job arguments**, and specifically the disclosure path those arguments have into log records. That concern is documented in full at 6.4.4.3 and is the part of this sub-section an adopter should read most carefully.

#### 6.4.4.1 Encryption Standards

**No encryption is implemented, and none is required by the architecture.** The module imports no cryptographic facility whatsoever: scans for `hashlib`, `hmac`, `secrets`, `ssl`, `crypt`, `base64`, `encrypt`, `decrypt`, and `cert` return zero occurrences, and no cryptographic package appears as a required or optional dependency in `pyproject.toml` (`dependencies = []`, one extra `timezone = ["pytz"]`), in `setup.py`, or in `requirements-dev.txt`.

| Encryption concern | Position in this system | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Data at rest | Not applicable — nothing is persisted | The registry is a heap-resident list (line 87); `docs/index.rst` lists job persistence first among reasons to choose a different library |
| Data in transit | Not applicable — there is no transport | No socket, protocol, or serialisation code exists (6.4.1.1) |
| Data in use | Not applied — job records and bound arguments are ordinary Python objects in process memory | Line 655 retains arguments in a `functools.partial` for the lifetime of the job |
| Hashing or integrity checking | Absent — the library computes no digest and verifies no checksum | No `hashlib` or `hmac` import |
| Randomness quality | `random.randint` for `to()` jitter only; **not** cryptographically secure | Lines 709–712; Section 5.3.6 records the same finding |

The host obligation is that all encryption relevant to the workload lives on the host side of the boundary. If a job body reads a database, calls an HTTPS API, or writes a file, the transport security, the at-rest encryption, and the algorithm choices are the host's entirely; the library neither assists nor interferes.

#### 6.4.4.2 Key Management

There is no key management because there are no keys. The library reads no environment variable (no `os`, `environ`, or `getenv` reference exists anywhere in the module), opens no configuration file, contacts no secret store, and defines no key, certificate, keystore, or credential structure. The repository contains no `.env` file, no `Dockerfile`, and no deployment descriptor of any kind — the only YAML in the tree is `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

The complete inventory of secret-adjacent material in the project sits outside the library, and stating it exhaustively is more useful than a policy that would have no subject:

| Secret material | Where it lives | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` lines 30 and 52 | Platform-provided and scoped to a single workflow run; passed as an environment variable to the Coveralls uploader. It is the only secret referenced anywhere in the repository |
| Package-registry credentials | Not in the repository — resolved from a maintainer-local configuration during the manual `twine upload` steps | `docs/development.rst` lines 49–68; Section 3.4.3 records that CI and publishing credentials are held outside the tree |
| Anything a job body needs | Supplied, held, and rotated by the host application | The library provides no store, no injection mechanism, and no lifecycle hook |
| Keys inside the library | None exist | Verified by the scans in 6.4.1.1 |

One implementation detail materially affects an adopter's key-rotation design and follows directly from the code. Arguments passed to `do()` are captured **once** at declaration and retained inside the `functools.partial` created at line 655 for the entire life of the registration; they are never re-read. A credential bound as a job argument therefore becomes effectively immutable for that job — rotating it requires cancelling and re-declaring the job. Passing a zero-argument callable or a lookup key that resolves the secret at execution time avoids this coupling and, as 6.4.4.3 explains, avoids the disclosure path as well.

#### 6.4.4.3 Data Masking Rules

**No masking, redaction, allow-listing, or truncation of any kind is implemented, and this is the one data-protection finding in the system with real operational consequence.**

The mechanism is short enough to state precisely. `Job.__str__` renders the job by interpolating `self.job_func.args` and `self.job_func.keywords` directly (lines 274–275). `Job.__repr__` does the same in human-readable form, building `args = [repr(x) ... ]` and `kwargs = ["%s=%s" % (k, repr(v)) ... ]` at lines 296–297. Four of the module's eight log statements render a job through one of those methods — `logger.debug("Running job %s", self)` at line 690, the two deadline-cancellation records at lines 687 and 696, and `logger.debug('Cancelling job "%s"', str(job))` at lines 157 and 160. `docs/logging.rst` line 30 publishes the resulting record shape in the project's own documentation: `DEBUG:schedule:Running job Job(interval=1, unit=seconds, do=job, args=(), kwargs={})`. With non-empty arguments, those values appear verbatim.

| Masking concern | Position in this system | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Argument redaction in log output | None; every bound positional and keyword value is rendered in full | Lines 274–275, 296–297, 690 |
| Sensitive-field marking or allow-list | None; no field is designated sensitive and no configuration hook exists | No masking code in the module |
| Length limiting or truncation | None; a large or deeply nested argument is rendered in full | Lines 296–298 |
| Exposure gate | The log level — the library emits **nothing** above DEBUG and attaches no handler | Line 50; the eight `logger.debug` sites |
| Return-value exposure | None; a payload's return value is inspected only for the `CancelJob` marker and then discarded, never logged | Lines 172–175 |

The control that follows is simple, effective, and entirely host-side. Because the library has no INFO, WARNING, ERROR, or CRITICAL path at all, **leaving the `schedule` logger at its default level suppresses every argument disclosure in the system.** Disclosure is opt-in: it requires an adopter to deliberately lower that logger to DEBUG, as `docs/logging.rst` lines 12–14 instruct. Section 5.4.4 raises this same caution and explicitly defers its full treatment to this section.

| Recommended practice | Rationale |
|---|---|
| Keep the `schedule` logger above DEBUG in production | Removes the only disclosure path in the library; no library functionality is lost, since all records are diagnostic |
| Bind an indirection rather than a secret — a lookup key, an identifier, or a zero-argument closure | The rendered form then contains a non-sensitive value; the secret is resolved inside the payload where it is never interpolated |
| If DEBUG is required, scope it narrowly and treat the sink as sensitive | The `schedule` logger can be enabled and filtered independently of the root logger, so exposure can be bounded in time and destination |
| Instrument with a job wrapper instead of relying on library records | `docs/logging.rst` lines 37–74 publish the `functools.wraps`-based decorator pattern, which lets the host log exactly the fields it deems safe |

#### 6.4.4.4 Secure Communication

**The installed library performs no communication, so there is no channel to secure.** It opens no socket, negotiates no TLS session, resolves no hostname, and constructs no URL. The only textual `http` matches in the module are the three reference URLs in its docstring at lines 36–38. Section 6.3.1.1 records the same result across all 32 tracked files and notes that the eight repository-wide `http` hits are documentation hyperlinks and a copyright URL.

Three communication surfaces do exist in the project, and all three sit outside the installed artifact. Recording them precisely — with their scope — is the substance of this concern.

| Surface | Transport posture | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| CI network calls | `pip install tox tox-gh-actions` and `pip3 install coveralls` fetch from PyPI over its HTTPS endpoints; the Coveralls upload authenticates with the per-run `GITHUB_TOKEN` | Build time only, inside the GitHub Actions runner (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) |
| Release upload | `twine upload` to the `schedule-test` then `schedule` repository aliases | Manual, maintainer workstation (`docs/development.rst` lines 61–66) |
| Generated documentation site | `docs/_templates/sidebarintro.html` injects `platform.twitter.com/widgets.js` at runtime, selecting its scheme with a `/^http:/` test on the page location, and three of its sidebar links use the `http://` scheme | Documentation site only — **not** shipped in the wheel |

The scope qualifier on the third row is important and verifiable. `MANIFEST.in` includes only `README.rst`, `HISTORY.rst`, `LICENSE.txt`, and `test_schedule.py`, and `setup.py` packages only `["schedule"]` with `package_data={"schedule": ["py.typed"]}`. The Sphinx templates under `docs/` are therefore never distributed, and the third-party script — which carries no Subresource Integrity attribute because the tag is constructed by inline JavaScript — affects only readers of the published documentation, never an adopter's runtime. Section 6.3.6.2 identifies it as the only client-side third-party script in the repository.

#### 6.4.4.5 Compliance Controls

The only compliance artifact in the repository is its licence. `LICENSE.txt` carries the MIT License, "Copyright (c) 2013 Daniel Bader", granting use, copy, modification, merger, publication, distribution, sublicensing, and sale subject to retaining the copyright and permission notice, and providing the software "AS IS", WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND, with all liability disclaimed. `pyproject.toml` declares `license = {text = "MIT License"}`, `setup.py` declares `license="MIT"` and the `License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License` classifier, and `MANIFEST.in` ensures `LICENSE.txt` ships in the source distribution. `docs/installation.rst` restates the licence when describing the discouraged manual-vendoring path.

No regulatory framework applies to the library itself, and the reason is a property of the code rather than an assertion of convenience: it accepts no personal, health, or payment data, derives none, stores none, and transmits none.

| Compliance dimension | Position in this system | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Software licence | MIT, with an explicit no-warranty and no-liability disclaimer | `LICENSE.txt`; `pyproject.toml`; `setup.py` classifier |
| Personal-data processing | None — the library never receives a data subject's information as its own input | Complete `Job` record, lines 227–255 |
| Data residency and cross-border transfer | Not applicable — no data leaves the process | No transport exists (6.4.4.4) |
| Retention and erasure | Not applicable — nothing is retained beyond process lifetime; `clear()` and `cancel_job()` remove records immediately | Lines 145, 148, 158 |
| Audit-evidence capability | Not provided — DEBUG diagnostics only, with no actor, integrity, or retention guarantees | 6.4.3.5 |
| Vulnerability-disclosure policy | None published — no `SECURITY.md` exists in the repository | Verified absent (6.4.5.6) |
| Third-party licence obligations | One optional dependency, `pytz`, unpinned; no bundled or vendored third-party code | `pyproject.toml`; Section 6.3.4.1 |
| Attribution obligation on adopters | Retain the copyright and permission notice — the only condition MIT imposes | `LICENSE.txt` lines 12–13 |

Where an adopter is itself subject to a regulatory regime — GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOC 2, or similar — three obligations flow from this architecture, and each maps to a control the adopter must own because the library cannot. Argument disclosure must be prevented or accepted knowingly, because DEBUG records render bound values in cleartext (6.4.4.3). Audit evidence must be produced at the job-wrapper seam, because registration is never logged and payload failures are never logged (6.4.3.5). And execution isolation must be arranged by the host if a job body handles regulated data, because the payload runs unsandboxed at full process privilege (6.4.1.2). Section 5.4.5 records the complementary point that no service-level agreement, availability commitment, or timing guarantee exists anywhere in the repository — so any control that depends on a job actually having run at a given moment must be verified by the host, not assumed from the schedule.


### 6.4.5 Standard Security Practices Applied

Because no dedicated security architecture applies, the project's security posture rests entirely on standard software-engineering practices. This sub-section documents the ones actually present in the repository, each tied to the artifact that enforces it, followed by a consolidated control matrix and an honest register of the controls that are absent. Nothing here is aspirational: every row is an observed configuration or an executed verification.

#### 6.4.5.1 Defensive Input Validation

The library validates every value it accepts at the definition boundary and rejects malformed input with a typed exception before any state changes. This is the most substantial security-relevant practice in the codebase, and its density is measurable: 28 `raise` statements in `schedule/__init__.py` — 12 `IntervalError`, 11 `ScheduleValueError`, 3 `TypeError`, and 2 `ScheduleError` — all firing during definition, before or inside `do()`, so a rejected configuration can never reach the registry.

| Validation practice | Implementation | Location |
|---|---|---|
| Allow-list of units | `at()` accepts only `days`, `hours`, `minutes`, or a set `start_day`; `_schedule_next_run()` accepts only `seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`, `days`, `weeks` | Lines 493–496; 704–708 |
| Anchored, bounded regex validation | Three fully anchored patterns with bounded character classes — `^[0-2]\d:[0-5]\d(:[0-5]\d)?$` for daily, `^([0-5]\d)?:[0-5]\d$` for hourly, `^:[0-5]\d$` for minutely — plus an explicit 0–23 hour range check | Lines 513, 518, 524 |
| Strict type dispatch | `at()` rejects a non-string time; `until()` accepts only `datetime`, `timedelta`, `time`, or `str` and raises `TypeError` otherwise; the timezone must be a `str` or a `pytz.BaseTzInfo` | Lines 510–511; 633–637; 501–508 |
| Fixed format allow-list for deadlines | `_decode_datetimestr` tries exactly five `strptime` formats and returns `None` on total failure, which becomes a `ScheduleValueError` | Lines 613–624; 822–830 |
| Closed weekday allow-list | `_weekday_index()` compares against a seven-element tuple and raises with the valid set in the message | Lines 931–945 |
| Invariant enforcement | Past deadlines rejected; `latest >= interval` required; singular units and weekday selectors rejected when `interval != 1`; tags must be `Hashable` | Lines 638–641; 709–712; 325–455; 466–467 |

Two properties of this design are worth calling out. Because all three time patterns are anchored at both ends and composed only of bounded, non-nested character classes, they cannot backtrack pathologically — there is no regular-expression denial-of-service exposure in the validation path. And the negative paths are executably specified rather than merely present: `test_schedule.py` contains 70 `assertRaises` assertions across its 81 test methods (36 `ScheduleValueError`, 16 `IntervalError`, 6 `TypeError`, 2 `ScheduleError`, 1 `pytz` unknown-zone), so the majority of the suite's assertion budget verifies that bad input is refused. The suite runs green in well under a second, which is why it functions as a routine local gate as well as a CI one.

#### 6.4.5.2 Minimal Attack Surface and Supply-Chain Hygiene

The project's strongest structural security property is what it refuses to depend on. The installed wheel contains one module and one zero-byte marker, and with no extras installed its import graph contains nothing but the Python standard library.

| Practice | Implementation | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Zero required runtime dependencies | `dependencies = []`; no `install_requires` in `setup.py` | `pyproject.toml`; `setup.py` |
| Single optional dependency, lazily imported | `timezone = ["pytz"]`; `import pytz` executes inside `at()` only when a timezone is requested | `pyproject.toml`; line 499 |
| Optionality proven, not asserted | `tox.ini` expands to twelve environments, `py3{7,8,9,10,11,12}{,-pytz}`, so the whole suite runs on every supported interpreter **without** pytz; timezone tests self-skip when it is unavailable | `tox.ini`; `test_schedule.py` lines 99–105 |
| No dynamic code or data interpretation | No `eval`, `exec`, `compile`, `__import__`, `pickle`, `marshal`, `shelve`, `yaml`, or `json` anywhere in the module | Verified by scan (6.4.1.1) |
| No ambient environment or filesystem access | No `os`, `sys`, `environ`, `getenv`, `open(`, `tempfile`, or `shutil` reference in the module | Verified by scan (6.4.1.1) |
| No process or network capability | No `subprocess`, `multiprocessing`, `signal`, `socket`, `urllib`, or `requests` reference | Verified by scan (6.4.1.1) |
| Distribution hygiene | `MANIFEST.in` includes only `README.rst`, `HISTORY.rst`, `LICENSE.txt`, and `test_schedule.py`, and recursively excludes `__pycache__` and `*.py[co]` so no compiled artifact is ever shipped | `MANIFEST.in` |
| Reproducible, standard build | `setuptools >= 61.0` with the `setuptools.build_meta` backend; no custom build hooks or compiled extensions | `pyproject.toml` |
| Channel guidance to adopters | PyPI is the recommended channel; OS packages are disclaimed as unmaintained and flagged **OUTDATED** at 0.3.2 (2015) for Ubuntu and Debian; manual single-file vendoring is "highly discouraged" because it forgoes updates | `docs/installation.rst` |

One pinning observation belongs here rather than in the gap register because it is a deliberate trade-off in a library manifest: the `pytz` extra carries **no version bound**, so the resolved version is whatever the adopter's environment provides. Section 6.3.4.1 records the coupling this creates — the library uses `pytz`-specific behaviour (`normalize()` and the `BaseTzInfo` type) with no `zoneinfo` counterpart — and `HISTORY.rst` shows the coupling is actively maintained, with releases 1.2.1 and 1.2.2 both driven by cross-timezone and DST correctness fixes.

#### 6.4.5.3 Verification Gates and Pipeline Posture

Every change to `master` passes through five continuous-integration jobs, and each job enforces a gate defined declaratively in `tox.ini`. These are correctness gates rather than security scanners, but they are the mechanism by which the project's small attack surface stays small.

| Gate | Command enforced | Enforcement point |
|---|---|---|
| Test and coverage | `py.test test_schedule.py schedule -v --cov schedule --cov-report term-missing` across twelve tox environments | `test` job, matrix 3.7–3.12 with `max-parallel: 6` |
| Static type checking | `python -m mypy -p schedule --install-types --non-interactive`, scoped by `setup.cfg` `[mypy] files=schedule` | Every tox environment, so it runs on all six interpreters |
| Documentation build | `sphinx-build -W -b html`, promoting warnings to errors | `docs` job |
| Formatting | `black --check .`, with `black==20.8b1` pinned in `requirements-dev.txt` | `formatting` job |
| Packaging metadata | `python setup.py check --strict --metadata --restructuredtext` | `setuppy` job |
| Typed-interface export | `schedule/py.typed` shipped via `package_data`, so adopters' own type checkers verify their usage | PEP 561 marker |

The pipeline's own secret posture is minimal by construction, which is a genuine strength: the **only** secret referenced anywhere in the repository is the platform-provided `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`, at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` lines 30 and 52, and it is used solely to authenticate the Coveralls upload. No organisation secret, registry token, cloud credential, or signing key appears in any workflow, and the workflow triggers are narrow — `push` to `master` and `pull_request` targeting `master`, with no `schedule`, `release`, or `workflow_dispatch` trigger. The repository contains no `.env` file, no `Dockerfile`, and no deployment descriptor, so there is no configuration surface in which a secret could be committed by accident; `.gitignore` correspondingly lists only build, coverage, virtual-environment, and IDE artifacts.

#### 6.4.5.4 Secure-Usage Guidance for Adopters

Because nearly every control is host-side, the practical security value of this section is the checklist below. Each item is grounded in an observed behaviour of the library rather than in general advice.

| Adopter practice | Why the code requires it |
|---|---|
| Keep the `schedule` logger above DEBUG in production | It is the only disclosure path in the library; the library emits nothing above DEBUG, so this removes the exposure entirely (6.4.4.3) |
| Never bind a secret as a job argument; bind a lookup key or a closure | Arguments are captured once at line 655, retained for the life of the job, and rendered by `__str__` at lines 274–275 |
| Own a private `Scheduler()` when embedding in someone else's application | `schedule.clear()` executes one `del self.jobs[:]` at line 145 and removes every job in the process (6.4.3.3) |
| Wrap job bodies so exceptions cannot escape, or guard the driver loop | Line 691 has no `try`/`except`; `docs/exception-handling.rst` line 4 states exceptions interrupt the `run_xyz` function |
| Move long-running or untrusted work onto a host thread or queue worker | Dispatch is serial with no timeout (lines 99–101, 691); `docs/parallel-execution.rst` publishes both patterns |
| Make job bodies idempotent | The invocation, the timestamp, and the reschedule are three separate statements (691–693), so a fault after a side effect leaves the occurrence re-attemptable — Section 5.4.3 records this as at-least-once-within-a-cycle behaviour |
| Bound job lifetimes with `until()` and group them with tags at declaration time | These are the only levers available later for expiry and bulk quarantine (lines 576–642, 148) |
| Install from PyPI at a current version; do not vendor the single source file | `docs/installation.rst` flags distribution packages as outdated and discourages manual copying, which forgoes all future fixes |
| Do not treat `to()` jitter as unpredictable | It draws from `random.randint` (lines 709–712), which is not cryptographically secure |
| Avoid running under `python -O` if the `should_run` invariant matters | `should_run` relies on `assert self.next_run is not None` at line 671, which optimisation removes |

#### 6.4.5.5 Consolidated Security Control Matrix

The matrix below is the summary view of the entire section: for each security domain, what the library provides, and where the control actually lives.

| Security domain | Control in the library | Control owner |
|---|---|---|
| Identity and authentication | None — no principal construct exists | Host application (6.4.2.1) |
| Multi-factor authentication | Not applicable — no first factor | Host application; maintainer registry accounts for publishing (6.4.2.2) |
| Session management | None — every call is stateless | Not applicable (6.4.2.3) |
| Token handling | None — `CancelJob` is a control marker, not a token | Host application (6.4.2.4) |
| Password policy | None — no secret material is ever handled | Host application (6.4.2.5) |
| Role-based access control | None — tags are labels, not roles | Host application (6.4.3.1) |
| Permission management | Self-imposed lifecycle limits only: `until()`, `CancelJob`, `clear(tag)` | Declaring component (6.4.3.2) |
| Resource authorization | None — the registry is process-global and freely mutable | Host, via private `Scheduler` isolation (6.4.3.3) |
| Policy enforcement | 28 definition-time validation guards; no access decisions | Library for validation, host for access (6.4.3.4) |
| Audit logging | Eight DEBUG diagnostics with no actor, integrity, or retention | Host, via a job-wrapper seam (6.4.3.5) |
| Encryption at rest and in transit | None — nothing is persisted and nothing is transported | Host application (6.4.4.1) |
| Key management | None — no key, environment read, or config file | Host application (6.4.4.2) |
| Data masking | None — bound arguments are rendered in full | Host: log level and argument indirection (6.4.4.3) |
| Secure communication | Not applicable to the installed artifact | Host; CI and docs site for the project's own surfaces (6.4.4.4) |
| Input validation | 28 guards, three anchored regexes, four allow-lists, 70 negative-path assertions | **Library** — the one domain it owns outright (6.4.5.1) |
| Dependency minimisation | Zero required dependencies; one lazily imported optional extra | **Library** (6.4.5.2) |
| Build and artifact hygiene | Standard `setuptools` backend; compiled artifacts excluded from the sdist | **Library** (6.4.5.2) |
| Verification gates | Five CI jobs over twelve tox environments: tests, coverage, mypy, docs, formatting, packaging | **Library** (6.4.5.3) |
| Compliance | MIT licence with warranty and liability disclaimers | Adopter for its own regime (6.4.4.5) |
| Availability and service levels | None — no SLA, timeout, retry, or circuit breaker exists | Host application (Section 5.4.5) |

#### 6.4.5.6 Gap Register

The controls below are absent from the repository. Each was verified individually rather than inferred, and each is recorded with its practical consequence so an adopter can decide whether it matters at their risk tolerance. Several are entirely reasonable omissions for a zero-dependency, single-module library; they are listed for completeness rather than as defects.

| Absent control | Verified state | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Vulnerability-disclosure policy | No `SECURITY.md` at the repository root or under `.github/` | There is no documented private channel for reporting a security issue; `docs/index.rst` and `docs/faq.rst` direct all reports to the public issue tracker |
| Automated dependency updates | No `.github/dependabot.yml`, `.yaml`, or `renovate.json` | Development-tool versions and the pinned `black==20.8b1` / `click==8.0.4` entries are advanced manually |
| Static analysis or dependency scanning in CI | Scan of `.github/workflows/ci.yml` for `codeql`, `bandit`, `snyk`, `trivy`, `semgrep`, `safety`, `pip-audit` returned no matches | No automated security scanning runs on any change; `pytest-flake8` appears in `requirements-dev.txt` and in the `docs/development.rst` local command but is not invoked by the tox test environment |
| Commit-SHA pinning of CI actions | `actions/checkout@v3` and `actions/setup-python@v4` are referenced by floating major tag at lines 19, 21, 44, 57, 59, 70, 72, 83, 85 | A compromised or altered tag would be consumed automatically on the next run |
| Least-privilege workflow token | No `permissions:` key anywhere in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | The workflow runs with the repository-default `GITHUB_TOKEN` scope rather than an explicitly narrowed one; the token is also passed to `coveralls`, installed unpinned at runtime via `pip3 install coveralls` |
| Release signing, provenance, or SBOM | No `sigstore`, `attest`, `provenance`, `sbom`, or `gpg` reference in any workflow; `.github/workflows/` contains only `ci.yml` | Publication is manual from a maintainer workstation (`docs/development.rst` lines 61–66), so artifacts carry no build attestation an adopter could verify |
| Mandatory review ownership | No `CODEOWNERS` file at the root or under `.github/` | Review assignment is not enforced by configuration |
| Pre-commit hooks and contribution policy | No `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, or `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` | Gates apply only after a change reaches CI; `docs/development.rst` carries the contributor instructions instead |
| Dependency lock file | No `requirements.txt`, `poetry.lock`, or `Pipfile`; the `pytz` extra is unpinned and unbounded | Neither the development toolchain nor the optional runtime extra resolves to a fixed, auditable set |
| Argument redaction | No masking, allow-list, or truncation in `__str__`, `__repr__`, or any log site | Enabling DEBUG on the `schedule` logger discloses every bound argument value in cleartext (6.4.4.3) |
| Execution isolation or timeout | No sandbox, resource limit, or timeout around the invocation at line 691 | A job body can consume unbounded time and holds full host privilege; isolation must be arranged by the host |
| Documentation-site subresource integrity | `docs/_templates/sidebarintro.html` injects `platform.twitter.com/widgets.js` with no `integrity` attribute and an `http:` scheme fallback | Affects readers of the published documentation only — the template is not shipped in the wheel (6.4.4.4) |
