## 6.5 Monitoring and Observability

### 6.5.1 Applicability Assessment and Monitoring Approach

**Detailed Monitoring Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

The subject of this specification is the Python `schedule` library at release 1.2.2 (`setup.py` line 5). Its entire runtime is one importable module — `schedule/__init__.py`, 945 lines — accompanied by the zero-byte PEP 561 marker `schedule/py.typed`. The distributable artifact contains no daemon, no executable, no network listener, and no process or thread of its own; `README.rst` advertises exactly that with "No extra processes needed!". A monitoring architecture describes how a *running system* is instrumented, scraped, shipped, alerted on, and displayed. This repository ships no running system, so there is nothing for such an architecture to attach to: no metric registry to expose, no endpoint to probe, no agent to co-locate, no log destination to configure, and no service whose availability could be measured.

The determination is stronger than "no monitoring stack is configured". The system does not even have the basic health check that would normally be the minimum: there is no HTTP surface, no socket, and no liveness primitive anywhere in the codebase. What the repository does provide, and what this section therefore documents, is a deliberately minimal **observability contribution** — one opt-in logger, three pull-only introspection primitives, and a transparent exception path — plus two published host-side instrumentation patterns and a five-job continuous-integration pipeline that acts as the project's own quality monitor. Section 5.4.1 reaches the same conclusion from the cross-cutting perspective, recording that the library's entire observability contribution is one named logger; Section 6.1.4.1 records health check and liveness as **absent** among the resilience patterns.

Sub-sections 6.5.2 through 6.5.4 walk every area the section scope enumerates — metrics collection, log aggregation, distributed tracing, alert management, dashboard design, health checks, performance metrics, business metrics, SLA monitoring, capacity tracking, alert routing, escalation, runbooks, post-mortems, and improvement tracking — and record for each either the mechanism that occupies its position or the verified absence of one, together with the obligation that absence transfers to the adopting application. The intent is that an engineer embedding this library into a monitored service can read this section and know exactly which signals they inherit (very few, and all pull-based) and which they must generate themselves (everything else).

#### 6.5.1.1 Determination Criteria and Findings

Each row below is a structural precondition for a monitoring architecture. Every one of them fails, and each failure is tied to an executed verification rather than an assumption. The scans cover all 32 tracked files reported by `git ls-files`.

| Precondition for a monitoring architecture | Verification performed | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| A long-running process to observe | Inspection of the module's import block (lines 41–48) and of every entry point (lines 843–913) | **Fails** — zero threads and zero processes are created; nothing runs unless the host calls `run_pending()` or `run_all()` |
| A metrics client, registry, or exporter | Case-insensitive repository scan for `prometheus`, `statsd`, `opentelemetry`, `otel`, `datadog`, `newrelic`, `graphite`, `influx`, `telegraf` | **Fails** — zero matches in any tracked file |
| A telemetry or error-reporting SDK | Repository scan for `sentry`, `jaeger`, `zipkin`, `cloudwatch`, `stackdriver`, `splunk`, `loki`, `elastic`, `logstash`, `fluentd`, `fluent-bit` | **Fails** — zero matches in any tracked file |
| A health, readiness, or liveness surface | Repository scan for `health`, `healthz`, `readiness`, `liveness`, `/ping`, `heartbeat`, `uptime`, plus `flask`, `fastapi`, `django`, `wsgi`, `asgi`, `uvicorn`, `gunicorn`, `http.server`, `socket.`, `urllib`, `requests.` | **Fails** — the single textual match in the whole repository is a commented-out pygments style at `docs/conf.py` line 114 |
| An alert rule, receiver, or notification channel | Repository scan for `alert`, `alertmanager`, `pagerduty`, `opsgenie`, `victorops`, `slack`, `webhook`, `smtplib`, `smtp`, `twilio`, `notify` | **Fails** — the bare word `alert` returns **no match anywhere**; the only `notify` hit is a comment about Coveralls at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` line 37 |
| A dashboard or visualisation definition | Repository scan for `grafana`, `kibana`, `dashboard`, and for any `*.json` panel or datasource descriptor | **Fails** — no dashboard artifact of any kind exists; the only YAML in the tree is `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |
| An orchestration probe or agent sidecar | Filesystem search for `Dockerfile*`, `docker-compose*`, Kubernetes manifests, `*.service`, `Procfile`, `*.tf` | **Fails** — none exist, so no `livenessProbe`, `readinessProbe`, or agent injection point exists either |
| A monitoring dependency in any manifest | `pyproject.toml` declares `dependencies = []`; `setup.py` declares no `install_requires`; `requirements-dev.txt` lists eleven test, docs, formatting, and typing entries only | **Fails** — the single optional package in the whole project is `pytz`, declared as the `timezone` extra |
| A synthetic or scheduled monitor | Inspection of `.github/workflows/ci.yml` triggers (lines 3–9) | **Fails** — the only triggers are `push` to `master` and `pull_request` targeting `master`; there is no `schedule`, `cron`, or `workflow_dispatch` trigger |
| A published service level to monitor against | Repository scan for SLA, uptime, availability, timeout, and watchdog statements | **Fails** — none exist; Section 5.4.5 records the same verified absence, and `docs/index.rst` publishes the opposite by listing exact timing as a non-goal |

Two audits complete the determination. The module's import graph is decisive: eight standard-library imports at lines 41–48 (`collections.abc.Hashable`, `datetime`, `functools`, `logging`, `random`, `re`, `time`, `typing`) plus one function-local `import pytz` at line 499. Exactly one of those — `logging` — is an instrumentation facility, and it is the standard library's, configured entirely by the host. Separately, every `logger.` call site in the module was enumerated: there are precisely eight, all at DEBUG level, at lines 113, 144, 147, 157, 160, 687, 690, and 696, with no INFO, WARNING, ERROR, or CRITICAL path in existence. Sections 5.4.2 and 6.4.3.5 record the identical enumeration.

#### 6.5.1.2 Basic Monitoring Practices Followed Instead

Because no monitoring architecture applies, the project's observability posture rests on the seven practices below. Each is an observed configuration or an executed verification, not a recommendation.

| Practice actually followed | Mechanism | Defined in |
|---|---|---|
| A single named, opt-in diagnostic logger | `logging.getLogger("schedule")` created once at import; eight DEBUG records; no handler, level, or formatter is set by the library, so it is silent until the host opts in | `schedule/__init__.py` lines 50, 113–696; `docs/logging.rst` |
| Lazy log formatting | Every record passes `%`-style arguments rather than a pre-rendered string, so message construction costs nothing when DEBUG is not enabled | All eight `logger.debug` call sites |
| Pull-based state introspection | `get_jobs(tag)`, `next_run(tag)`, and `idle_seconds()` let a host read registry population, the next occurrence, and current lateness on demand | Lines 122–133, 177–195, 197–206; `docs/reference.rst` |
| Human-readable job rendering | `Job.__repr__` renders each job as a sentence including its last and next run, with `[never]` for a job that has not executed | Lines 278–323 |
| Published duration-instrumentation pattern | The `print_elapsed_time` decorator wraps a job body, timing it with `time.time()` and logging start and elapsed seconds — the project's sanctioned way to measure job duration | `docs/logging.rst`, "Customize logging" |
| Published failure-instrumentation pattern | The `catch_exceptions(cancel_on_failure=…)` decorator catches everything, prints `traceback.format_exc()`, and optionally returns `schedule.CancelJob` | `docs/exception-handling.rst` |
| Continuous verification of the library itself | Five CI jobs on every push and pull request to `master`, expanding to twelve tox environments across six interpreters, with coverage published to Coveralls and three status badges rendered in the README and documentation index | `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; `tox.ini`; `README.rst` |

Three properties of this posture are worth stating precisely, because they determine what any host-side monitoring can and cannot see. All three were verified by execution against this checkout on CPython 3.12.3.

- **Silence by default.** In a fresh interpreter, `logging.getLogger("schedule").handlers` is an empty list and `propagate` retains its default `True`; with a host at default level, `isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG)` returns `False`. The library therefore cannot interfere with a host's logging policy, and equally cannot contribute anything until the host lowers that logger to DEBUG as `docs/logging.rst` instructs.
- **Volume proportional to executions, not polls.** A `run_pending()` poll with nothing due emits **zero** records; a poll with one due job emits **exactly one** record, `Running job Job(interval=1, unit=seconds, do=…, args=(), kwargs={})`. A one-second poll loop is therefore free of log volume while idle — which is also why the log stream carries no evidence that polling is happening at all.
- **Failure is invisible in the library's own output.** A job body that raises produces only the pre-execution `Running job …` record and nothing further: the exception escapes `run_pending()` to the caller, `last_run` remains `None`, the job stays registered, and `idle_seconds()` becomes non-positive. In the library's log stream a failed run is indistinguishable from a successful one — the observation Section 5.4.1 records as a failing job being indistinguishable from a healthy one in the registry.

#### 6.5.1.3 Monitoring Responsibility Split

Every monitoring capability in the scope of this section resolves the same way as the other cross-cutting concerns recorded in Section 5.4: the library contributes a minimal, dependency-free primitive and the host application supplies the pipeline and the policy.

| Monitoring capability | Contributed by the library | Owned by the host application |
|---|---|---|
| Metrics collection | Nothing — no counter, gauge, histogram, or registry exists | Deriving metrics from the introspection primitives and from a job wrapper |
| Log aggregation | Eight DEBUG records on one propagating logger | Handlers, levels, formatting, shipping, retention, and indexing |
| Distributed tracing | Nothing — no span, context propagation, or correlation identifier | Any span creation around the job body |
| Alert management | Nothing — no rule, threshold, or notification path | Every threshold, receiver, and route |
| Dashboard design | `__repr__` renderings and three pull-based values | Every panel, query, and layout |
| Health checks | Nothing — no endpoint, probe, or heartbeat | Deriving liveness and readiness predicates from the host loop and `idle_seconds()` |
| Performance measurement | Nothing — job duration is never measured or recorded | Timing the callable, as `docs/logging.rst` demonstrates |
| SLA definition and tracking | Nothing — no commitment of any kind is published | Defining, measuring, and reporting any commitment it makes to its own users |
| Incident response | A typed error taxonomy plus a transparent exception path | Detection, routing, escalation, runbooks, and post-mortems |

### 6.5.2 Monitoring Infrastructure

No monitoring infrastructure exists in this repository. This sub-section documents each infrastructure concern in the section scope by recording what occupies its position, the verification that establishes the absence of the rest, and the seam through which an adopting application can supply the missing capability. Everything labelled *host-side* is a pattern the repository publishes in `docs/` or a derivation from library state — none of it is code shipped in the wheel.

#### 6.5.2.1 Metrics Collection

**There is no metrics collection.** The module defines no counter, gauge, histogram, summary, timer, or registry; it imports no metrics client; and it exposes no scrape endpoint or push target. Section 5.4.1 records the same finding, and the manifest audit in 6.5.1.1 confirms that no metrics dependency exists in `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, or `requirements-dev.txt`.

What exists instead is a small set of **pull-only state readings** from which a host can derive metrics itself. The three documented primitives — `get_jobs`, `next_run`, and `idle_seconds`, all listed as public interfaces in `docs/reference.rst` — plus the per-`Job` timestamp fields are the entire raw material. The definitions below are exact: each names the library expression that produces the value and the unit it carries.

| Derivable metric | Library expression | Unit and semantics |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduler lag | `schedule.idle_seconds()` | Seconds until the next occurrence; **negative** means that many seconds overdue; `None` means the registry is empty |
| Registry population | `len(schedule.get_jobs())` | Count of registered jobs; reflects declared work, not load |
| Population by group | `len(schedule.get_jobs(tag))` | Count within one tag; `tags` is the only grouping dimension the library offers |
| Next occurrence timestamp | `schedule.next_run()` or `next_run(tag)` | Naive local `datetime`, or `None` when nothing is scheduled |
| Per-job staleness | `datetime.now() - job.last_run` | Time since that job last completed; `job.last_run` is `None` until the first successful run |
| Per-job lateness | `datetime.now() - job.next_run` | Positive while the job is overdue; the per-job counterpart of scheduler lag |
| Never-run indicator | `job.last_run is None` | Boolean; renders as `[never]` in `Job.__repr__` |
| Deadline remaining | `job.cancel_after - datetime.now()` | Populated only for jobs configured with `until()`; otherwise `cancel_after` is `None` |

Three properties of this derivation are load-bearing for anyone building a collector, and all three follow directly from the implementation rather than from convention.

- **Every reading is O(n) and taken at call time.** `get_next_run` performs a `min()` over the filtered registry (line 193) and `idle_seconds` subtracts the wall clock from it (line 206); `get_jobs` copies the list (line 131). Nothing is cached, and no value is pushed. Section 6.1.3.5 records measured medians for these scans on CPython 3.12.3 — roughly 0.18 µs per registered job for an `idle_seconds` evaluation — which makes a one-second collection interval inexpensive up to very large registries.
- **Duration is never available from the library.** No code path measures how long a job body takes; the invocation at line 691 is bracketed only by the `last_run` assignment that follows it. Job duration therefore cannot be derived from library state at all — it must be measured inside a wrapper. `docs/logging.rst` publishes exactly that wrapper: a `functools.wraps`-based decorator, `print_elapsed_time`, that records `time.time()` before the call and logs the elapsed seconds after it. This is the single sanctioned instrumentation seam in the project, and Section 6.1.3.2 identifies it as the starting point for utilisation data.
- **Success and failure counts are not derivable from state.** Because a raising job leaves `last_run` unchanged (verified by execution: `last_run` remains `None` after a failing run), an un-advanced `last_run` is *evidence* of failure but is indistinguishable from a job that has simply never become due. Counting outcomes requires the wrapper to do it; the registry cannot.

| Metric a host must generate itself | Required seam | Why library state is insufficient |
|---|---|---|
| Job execution duration | Wrapper around the job body (`print_elapsed_time` pattern) | Nothing times the invocation at line 691 |
| Job success and failure counts | Wrapper, or a guarded driver loop | No outcome is recorded; failure leaves no trace in the registry or the log |
| Executions per interval | Wrapper, or counting `Running job` records | The library keeps no run counter; only the latest `last_run` survives |
| Poll rate and loop health | Host driver loop | The loop is host code; an idle poll emits no record at all |
| Queue depth or backlog size | Not derivable | Missed occurrences are dropped, never queued (`run_pending` docstring, lines 93–97) |

#### 6.5.2.2 Log Aggregation

**There is no log aggregation, and the library ships no logging configuration whatsoever.** It creates one logger — `logging.getLogger("schedule")` at line 50 — and never attaches a handler, sets a level, installs a formatter, or touches `propagate`. Verified in a fresh interpreter: `handlers` is an empty list and `propagate` is `True`, so records travel to whatever the host has configured on ancestor loggers, and only if the host has lowered the level to DEBUG as `docs/logging.rst` instructs. Section 5.4.2 documents the same contract.

The complete emission catalogue is eight records. Enumerating it exhaustively is what allows an adopter to write parsing or filtering rules with confidence, because this list cannot grow at runtime.

| Log event | Site | Message template |
|---|---|---|
| Forced sweep started | Line 113 | `Running *all* %i jobs with %is delay in between` |
| All jobs deleted | Line 144 | `Deleting *all* jobs` |
| Tagged group deleted | Line 147 | `Deleting all jobs tagged "%s"` |
| Registered job cancelled | Line 157 | `Cancelling job "%s"` |
| Unregistered job cancelled | Line 160 | `Cancelling not-scheduled job "%s"` |
| Deadline already passed, job not run | Line 687 | `Cancelling job %s` |
| Job about to be invoked | Line 690 | `Running job %s` |
| Deadline passed after run | Line 696 | `Cancelling job %s` |

The aggregation-relevant properties of that stream are as follows. Each is a direct consequence of the code, and several are unusual enough that a log pipeline designed for a service would make wrong assumptions about them.

| Property | Value in this system | Consequence for aggregation |
|---|---|---|
| Logger name and level | `schedule`, DEBUG only — no INFO, WARNING, ERROR, or CRITICAL path exists | The whole stream can be enabled, filtered, or suppressed with one logger-name rule |
| Structure | Plain `%`-formatted text; no JSON, no `extra` fields, no structured keys | Fields must be recovered by parsing the `Job(...)` rendering, not by reading attributes |
| Rendering source | Five of the eight records interpolate a job through `Job.__str__` or `Job.__repr__` | Bound argument values appear verbatim — the disclosure path documented in Section 6.4.4.3 |
| Volume model | Proportional to executions and cancellations, not to polls: an idle `run_pending()` poll emits **zero** records; one due job emits **exactly one** | Log volume is a proxy for work performed, never for scheduler liveness |
| Correlation identifier | None; there is no request id, run id, or sequence number | Correlation must be added by the host, typically in a wrapper |
| Timestamps | Supplied by the host's formatter; the library embeds none in the message body | Ordering and latency analysis depend entirely on host formatter configuration |
| Cost when disabled | Lazy `%` arguments at all eight sites, so no message is rendered when DEBUG is off | Instrumentation can be left permanently in place with negligible cost |

Equally important is what never appears in the stream. Section 5.4.2 enumerates the omissions and Section 6.4.3.5 assesses them as audit evidence; restated for a log pipeline, the events below produce **no record at all**, so no aggregation rule can detect them:

| Unlogged event | Where it happens | Detection alternative |
|---|---|---|
| Job registration | `do()` appends at line 663 | Log it in the declaration code |
| Job failure | The unguarded invocation at line 691 | Wrap the body, or log in the guarded driver loop |
| Successful completion and its outcome | After line 691; only `last_run` is stamped | Wrap the body — the `Running job` record is emitted *before* execution, so its presence proves an attempt, never a success |
| Reschedule result | `_schedule_next_run()` at line 693 | Read `job.next_run` after the poll |
| Missed occurrences | Nothing detects them; they are silently dropped | Watch for non-positive `idle_seconds()` |
| DST-gap displacement | `_correct_utc_offset` (lines 773–817) adjusts silently | Compare `next_run` against expectation |

#### 6.5.2.3 Distributed Tracing

**Distributed tracing is not present and is not applicable to the installed artifact.** There is no span, no trace context, no propagation header, no sampler, and no correlation identifier anywhere in the module; the tracing-SDK scan in 6.5.1.1 returns zero matches for OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Zipkin, and every commercial APM agent. Section 5.4.2 records the identical finding.

The architectural reason is that tracing describes a request crossing boundaries, and this system has exactly one boundary — a Python `import` — with no request concept on either side of it. There is no inbound call to continue a trace from, no outbound call to inject context into, and no asynchronous hand-off inside the library where a context could be lost or restored. Execution is a direct synchronous call: `self.job_func()` at line 691, on the caller's own thread.

| Tracing element | Position in this system | Host-side placement if tracing is required |
|---|---|---|
| Trace and span creation | Absent | Around the job body, in the same wrapper used for duration |
| Context propagation | Absent; no header, carrier, or context variable | Inside the job body, when it makes outbound calls |
| Correlation handle | The `Job` object itself; `tags` are the only grouping dimension | Attach the job's identity and tags as span attributes |
| Causal parent | None — a scheduled occurrence has no caller to attribute it to | Treat each occurrence as a new root span |
| Sampling control | Absent | Host tracer configuration |

One consequence deserves explicit mention for adopters who do run a tracing stack. Because the library is a *root* of work rather than a participant in someone else's trace, a scheduled job is naturally a new trace root; and because the queue hand-off pattern in `docs/parallel-execution.rst` registers `jobqueue.put` as the job body, any span started around that body measures the enqueue, not the work — the same displacement Section 6.3.5.3 records for the `CancelJob` signal.

#### 6.5.2.4 Alert Management

**No alert management exists in this repository.** This is among the most definite findings in the section: a case-insensitive search for the bare word `alert` across all 32 tracked files returns **no match anywhere**, and searches for `alertmanager`, `pagerduty`, `opsgenie`, `victorops`, `slack`, `webhook`, `smtplib`, `smtp`, and `twilio` are likewise empty. There is no rule file, no threshold constant, no severity taxonomy, no receiver, no silencing or inhibition mechanism, and no escalation configuration.

Only two automated notification channels exist in the whole project, and both concern the *repository* rather than any running system:

| Channel | Trigger | Destination |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub Actions workflow outcome | Any of the five jobs in the `Tests` workflow failing on a push to `master` or a pull request targeting it | GitHub's own build-status notifications and the badge in `README.rst` |
| Coveralls summary comment | The `coverage push` job running `coveralls --finish --service=github` after the matrix completes | A summary comment on the pull request, per the workflow comment at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` lines 37–38 |

For a host application that embeds the library, alerting must be constructed from the signals catalogued in 6.5.2.1 and 6.5.2.2. The matrix below is an **alert threshold matrix of candidate conditions**: every condition is expressed in terms of a value the library actually exposes, and every threshold is a host-defined parameter because the repository publishes none. The anchor value used in the guidance column is the one-second poll cadence that `README.rst` and `docs/index.rst` establish as the documented driver-loop convention.

| Candidate alert condition | Signal expression | Threshold to be set by the host |
|---|---|---|
| Dispatch falling behind | `idle_seconds()` returns a negative value | Magnitude beyond a few poll periods; sustained for more than one collection interval |
| Dispatch stalled or loop dead | `idle_seconds()` stays negative and no `Running job` record appears | Any persistence beyond the shortest configured job interval |
| Schedule unexpectedly empty | `idle_seconds()` returns `None`, or `len(get_jobs()) == 0` | Non-zero expectation for the deployment; an immediate condition, not a rate |
| Job never executed | `job.last_run is None` after its first interval has elapsed | One interval plus one poll period |
| Job stale | `datetime.now() - job.last_run` exceeds its configured interval | A multiple of the interval chosen by the host |
| Population drift | `len(get_jobs(tag))` differs from the declared count | Exact-match expectation per tag group |
| Job failing | Wrapper-emitted failure count rises, or an exception escapes the loop | Any occurrence, or a rate over a host-chosen window |
| Job body too slow | Wrapper-emitted duration approaches the job's interval | A fraction of the interval, since duration is not accounted for by the scheduler |

Two structural caveats bound every row above, and both are properties of the library rather than of the collector. First, all conditions are **pull-evaluated**: nothing in the library pushes, so an alert can only fire as fast as the host polls. Second, the two most operationally important failure modes — a job body raising and an occurrence being missed — emit no library signal at all, so their detection depends entirely on host instrumentation existing at the wrapper or the loop.

#### 6.5.2.5 Dashboard Design

**No dashboard definition exists in this repository** — no Grafana or Kibana JSON, no panel or datasource descriptor, and no visualisation configuration of any kind. What the project does maintain is a three-badge status strip, rendered identically at the top of `README.rst` and `docs/index.rst`, which functions as the project's own dashboard for maintainers and prospective adopters.

| Badge | Source | What it displays |
|---|---|---|
| Tests | `github.com/dbader/schedule/workflows/Tests/badge.svg`, targeting the `Tests` workflow filtered to `branch:master` | Pass or fail state of the five-job CI workflow on `master` |
| Coverage | `coveralls.io/repos/dbader/schedule/badge.svg?branch=master`, targeting `coveralls.io/r/dbader/schedule` | Aggregated line coverage from the parallel matrix uploads |
| Version | `img.shields.io/pypi/v/schedule.svg`, targeting the PyPI project page | Currently published release |

For an adopting application, the useful dashboard is one built from the derivable metrics in 6.5.2.1. The layout below is a reference arrangement of exactly those values — every panel is annotated with the library expression that feeds it, and no panel depends on data the library does not expose.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph RowA["Row 1 — Scheduler health, from pull-based library state"]
        direction LR

    subgraph RowB["Row 2 — Per-group and per-job state, derived from Job fields"]

        PanelDue["Jobs currently overdue<br/>table<br/>source: now minus job.next_run, filtered positive"]
    end
    subgraph RowC["Row 3 — Execution outcomes, available ONLY from host instrumentation"]
        direction LR

        PanelFail["Failure count and rate<br/>time series<br/>source: catch_exceptions wrapper or guarded loop"]

    end
```

**Diagram 6.5.2-B — Reference dashboard layout for an adopting application.** Rows 1 and 2 are populated entirely from library state; Row 3 is impossible without a host wrapper; Row 4 requires the host to have lowered the `schedule` logger to DEBUG; Row 5 observes the project rather than the runtime.


### 6.5.3 Observability Patterns

The patterns in this sub-section are documented as *derivations* rather than as features, because the library implements none of them. Each one records the observable state or documented behaviour that occupies its position, the arithmetic that turns that state into a signal, and the limit beyond which the signal cannot be trusted.

#### 6.5.3.1 Health Checks

**No health check exists in any form.** There is no HTTP endpoint, no probe, no heartbeat, no TTL, no lease, and no liveness or readiness concept attached to a scheduler or to a registry entry — Section 6.1.2.3 records the registry finding and Section 6.1.4.1 classifies health check and liveness as absent among the resilience patterns. The scan in 6.5.1.1 confirms that the repository contains no HTTP server, no socket, and no network client through which a check could be served.

Health must therefore be *inferred*, and the inference has a specific and important weakness: the library cannot distinguish a healthy idle scheduler from a dead driver loop, because the two produce identical library state. Nothing in `schedule/__init__.py` records that polling occurred; only executions leave evidence. The predicates below are the complete set that library state supports.

| Health predicate | Expression over library state | What it proves and does not prove |
|---|---|---|
| Registry is populated | `len(schedule.get_jobs()) > 0` | Proves jobs were declared; proves nothing about dispatch |
| Something is scheduled | `schedule.idle_seconds() is not None` | Equivalent to a non-empty registry; `None` means nothing is scheduled |
| Dispatch is keeping up | `schedule.idle_seconds() >= 0` | Proves no occurrence is currently past due; a negative value quantifies exactly how many seconds late dispatch is |
| A specific job is alive | `job.last_run is not None` and recent relative to its interval | Proves a *completed* run; `None` renders as `[never]` in `Job.__repr__` |
| A job is progressing | `job.last_run` advances between two observations | The only positive proof of successful execution available from state |
| Loop liveness | **Not derivable from library state** | Requires host evidence: a wrapper heartbeat, a log line from the loop, or the thread object |

The loop-liveness gap is worth developing because the repository's own background-execution recipe interacts with it. `docs/background-execution.rst` states plainly that "Out of the box it is not possible to run the schedule in the background" and supplies a `run_continuously(interval=1)` function that starts a `ScheduleThread` whose body is `while not cease_continuous_run.is_set(): schedule.run_pending(); time.sleep(interval)`. Two operational details of that recipe as written affect health checking directly: it returns only the `threading.Event` used to stop the thread, not the thread object, so a host that wants an `is_alive()` liveness signal must retain the thread itself; and the thread is created without `daemon=True`, so process exit waits for the event to be set.

The consequence for an adopter is that a meaningful liveness check has to be emitted by host code — most naturally by the same wrapper used for duration and failure instrumentation, or by a counter incremented in the driver loop. A readiness check, by contrast, *is* well served by library state: `len(get_jobs())` matching the declared count, together with a non-`None` `next_run()`, is a complete and cheap readiness assertion, and Section 6.1.4.3 records exactly this trio as the way to verify that a restart rebuilt the schedule as intended.

#### 6.5.3.2 Performance Metrics

The library measures no performance metric. It does, however, have precisely characterised timing behaviour, and Section 5.4.5 records the observable characteristics in full. The table below restates them as *metric definitions* — what the quantity is, and where an observer can obtain it.

| Performance metric | Definition in this system | Where it can be obtained |
|---|---|---|
| Dispatch latency | Time from `next_run` until the callable is actually invoked; equals up to one poll period plus the duration of earlier jobs in the same cycle | Host: compare wrapper entry time against `job.next_run` |
| Current lateness | Seconds by which the next occurrence is already overdue | `idle_seconds()`, negative branch — verified to read exactly `-42.0` for a job 42 s late |
| Job duration | Wall-clock time consumed by the job body | Host wrapper only; the `print_elapsed_time` pattern in `docs/logging.rst` |
| Cycle duration | Sum of all job durations executed in one `run_pending()` call | Host: timestamp around the `run_pending()` call |
| Poll period | Interval between successive `run_pending()` calls; the documented convention is `sleep(1)` | Host driver loop |
| Timing precision | Whole-second granularity at best; sub-second precision is a published non-goal in `docs/index.rst` | Property of the design, not a measurable |
| Schedule drift | Accumulated displacement caused by rescheduling relative to *now* rather than to the previous target | Host: compare successive `next_run` values against the nominal cadence |
| Registry scan cost | O(n) due-filter plus O(k log k) ordering of the k due jobs, per poll | Measured figures recorded in Section 6.1.3.5 |

Four constraints qualify any performance monitoring built on these values, and each is grounded in the implementation rather than in general practice.

- **Job execution time is explicitly unaccounted for.** `docs/index.rst` states in bold that "Schedule does not account for the time it takes for the job function to execute" and that long-running jobs must be moved off the scheduler's main thread to guarantee a stable schedule. A latency dashboard that assumes fixed-cadence firing will therefore mis-read normal behaviour as drift.
- **Rescheduling is relative to the clock read at reschedule time.** `_schedule_next_run` reads `datetime.datetime.now(self.at_time_zone)` at line 717, so each occurrence's target is computed from when the previous one finished, and duration plus poll delay accumulate.
- **All timing uses the wall clock.** Section 5.4.5 records nine `datetime.datetime.now()` read sites and the absence of any injected or monotonic clock. A system-clock adjustment therefore moves `idle_seconds()` and every `next_run` comparison; derived latency metrics inherit that sensitivity.
- **Serial dispatch couples jobs.** `run_pending` executes the due set one job at a time on the caller's thread (lines 99–101), so one slow body inflates the measured latency of every later job in the same cycle. `docs/parallel-execution.rst` publishes the thread-per-firing and bounded-queue remedies.

#### 6.5.3.3 Business Metrics

**The library contains no business metric, and no business concept through which one could be defined.** It has no domain model, no work-item notion, no success or failure outcome, no throughput counter, and no revenue-, user-, or transaction-oriented value of any kind. Its complete input surface is an interval, a unit, an optional clock time and timezone, a deadline, a set of hashable tags, and a callable with its bound arguments; its complete output surface is the invocation of that callable and eight diagnostic log records.

Business meaning therefore lives entirely inside the job body, which is host code. The library nevertheless contributes two labelling handles that a host can use as metric dimensions, and it is worth being precise about their limits.

| Available dimension | Mechanism | Limitations as a metric label |
|---|---|---|
| Job identity | `job_func.__name__` is preserved by `functools.update_wrapper` at line 656 and rendered by `__str__`; falls back to `repr()` when no `__name__` exists | A lambda or a `functools.partial` renders as a repr, which makes an unstable label |
| Tag group | `tag(*tags)` unions any hashable values into `Job.tags`; `get_jobs(tag)` filters by membership | Free-form and unvalidated beyond hashability; any code may add or read tags, and they carry no semantics of their own |
| Business outcome | **Not available** — the return value is inspected only for the `CancelJob` marker (line 174) and then discarded | The scheduler never observes what the work produced |

The practical pattern the repository supports is to tag jobs by business grouping at declaration time — `docs/examples.rst` demonstrates exactly this with tags such as `daily-tasks`, `hourly-tasks`, `friend`, and `customer` — and to emit the business metrics themselves from inside the job body, using the same wrapper seam that produces duration and failure counts. Section 6.5.2.1 records why the alternative does not work: no execution outcome is retained anywhere in library state.

#### 6.5.3.4 SLA Monitoring

**No service-level agreement, objective, indicator, error budget, latency target, throughput target, or availability commitment exists anywhere in this repository.** This is verified rather than assumed, and Section 5.4.5 records the same result from a repository-wide search for SLA, uptime, availability, timeout, and watchdog statements. `docs/index.rst` publishes the opposite position: exact timing is listed among the reasons to choose a different library.

Consequently there is nothing to monitor *against* at the library level. The documented behaviour below is the closest thing to a set of guarantees the system offers, and it is stated here as the envelope within which any adopter-defined objective must sit. Every row is a documented or code-verified behaviour, not a commitment.

| Behavioural guarantee | What the system actually guarantees | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Earliest execution | A job is never invoked before its `next_run` | `should_run` compares `now >= next_run` (line 672) |
| Latest execution | Bounded only by the poll period plus the duration of earlier jobs in the cycle; no upper bound is published | `run_pending` lines 99–101; Section 5.4.5 |
| Missed occurrences | Never replayed — a per-minute job polled hourly runs once, not sixty times | `run_pending` docstring, lines 93–97 |
| Ordering within a cycle | The due set executes in ascending `next_run` order, deterministically | `sorted(runnable_jobs)` with `Job.__lt__` (lines 100, 257–262) |
| Deadline honouring | A job past its `until()` deadline is not executed, and cancellation takes priority over its return value | `run()` lines 686–698 |
| Delivery semantics | At-least-once within a cycle — a fault after a side effect leaves the occurrence re-attemptable | Statement ordering at lines 691–693; Sections 4.3.1.6 and 5.4.3 |
| Durability | None — the registry is memory-only and process exit is total schedule loss | Line 87; Section 5.4.6 |
| Precision | Whole-second granularity; sub-second precision is a published non-goal | `docs/index.rst` |

Four published non-goals bound any objective an adopter might wish to set, and they are stated as product boundaries in `docs/index.rst`: no job persistence across restarts, no sub-second precision, no concurrent execution, and no localisation. An availability objective expressed over the *scheduler* is therefore not measurable from the library at all — the host process owns availability — while an objective expressed over a *job* is measurable only through host instrumentation.

| Objective an adopter might define | Measurable from library state? | Required instrumentation |
|---|---|---|
| "Job runs within N seconds of its due time" | Partially — lateness is visible via `idle_seconds()` and `now - job.next_run` | Wrapper entry timestamp for the actual invocation instant |
| "Job succeeds on X% of occurrences" | No — no outcome is recorded | Wrapper counting successes and failures |
| "Job completes within N seconds" | No — duration is never measured | `print_elapsed_time`-style wrapper |
| "Scheduler is available X% of the time" | No — nothing records that polling occurred | Host loop heartbeat and process supervision |
| "No occurrence is skipped" | No — misses are silently dropped and never counted | Host comparison of expected against observed run counts |

#### 6.5.3.5 Capacity Tracking

The library tracks no capacity metric, defines no limit, and enforces no back-pressure. There is no queue to measure depth on: when polling falls behind, occurrences are dropped rather than accumulated, which Section 6.1.4.6 characterises as implicit load shedding that is unobservable by default.

Capacity nevertheless has a well-defined and, per Section 6.1.3.5, measured profile. The signals below are the ones a host can track, with the source of each figure identified.

| Capacity signal | Expression or figure | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Registry population | `len(get_jobs())`, optionally per tag | The scaling input for every per-poll cost below |
| Per-poll scan cost | Approximately 0.36 µs per registered job, measured on CPython 3.12.3 | Recorded in Section 6.1.3.5; a 1,000-job registry costs on the order of 0.4 ms per poll |
| Introspection cost | Approximately 0.18 µs per registered job for an `idle_seconds` evaluation | Recorded in Section 6.1.3.5; sets the practical floor on collection frequency |
| Memory footprint | Roughly 1.1 KB per trivial job, plus the size of every bound argument | Recorded in Section 6.1.3.5; arguments retained in the `functools.partial` at line 655 dominate at scale |
| Saturation indicator | Aggregate duration of the jobs executed in one cycle, compared against the shortest configured interval | Host-measured; the true capacity limit, because dispatch is serial and duration is unaccounted for |
| Backlog indicator | Negative `idle_seconds()`, sustained | The only warning the system offers that capacity has been exceeded |
| Forced-run cost | `run_all(delay_seconds)` sleeps after every job including the last, so added time is job count × delay | Lines 118–120; relevant when sizing a maintenance window |

Two conclusions follow from those figures and are worth stating for anyone planning capacity, both consistent with Section 6.1.3.5. Registry size is almost never the constraint — the scan is linear and sub-microsecond per job — so capacity tracking should be driven by **job bodies**, whose aggregate duration in any cycle must remain comfortably shorter than the shortest configured interval. And because overload manifests as silently dropped occurrences rather than as a growing queue, the only automatic evidence of exceeded capacity is a persistently negative `idle_seconds()`; a host that needs to know *which* occurrences were lost must count expected against observed executions itself.


### 6.5.4 Incident Response

No operational incident-response apparatus exists in this repository, and for a library with no runtime of its own none could: there is no service to page about, no on-call rotation, and no environment in which an incident could be declared. Verified absences include any alerting or paging configuration (the bare word `alert` matches nowhere in the 32 tracked files), any `SECURITY.md` or `CODEOWNERS` file, and any `CONTRIBUTING.md` or issue template — Section 6.4.5.6 records the same gap register.

What the project does operate is a **defect-response process**, and it is unusually well evidenced: a public intake channel with documented triage-before-escalation guidance, a diagnostic catalogue in the documentation, a convention of encoding every fixed defect as an issue-numbered regression test, and a changelog that doubles as the improvement register. This sub-section documents that process, and — because adopters must run the operational half themselves — records the detection-to-response path that the library's signals support.

#### 6.5.4.1 Alert Routing

There is no alert routing: no receiver, no route, no severity taxonomy, no silencing or inhibition rule, and no notification integration of any kind. The two channels that exist route *build* outcomes rather than runtime conditions, and both terminate at the repository rather than at a responder.

| Existing route | Emitted when | Terminates at |
|---|---|---|
| `Tests` workflow status | Any of the five CI jobs fails on a push to `master` or a pull request targeting it | GitHub's build notifications and the badge in `README.rst` and `docs/index.rst` |
| Coveralls summary | `coveralls --finish --service=github` completes after the six-leg matrix upload | A summary comment on the pull request (`.github/workflows/ci.yml` lines 37–38) |
| User-reported defect | An adopter encounters incorrect behaviour | The public issue tracker at `github.com/dbader/schedule/issues`, declared as the `Issues` URL in `pyproject.toml` |

For an adopting application, every runtime route must be built host-side from the signals catalogued in 6.5.2.1 and the threshold matrix in 6.5.2.4. The flow below traces each detectable condition from its origin to the response the repository actually supports, and marks the two paths that produce no library signal at all.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Origin([A condition arises in a host process<br/>that has embedded the library]) --> Kind{"What kind of<br/>condition is it?"}
    Kind -->|"Declaration is malformed"| ConfigFault["One of 28 definition-time guards raises:<br/>IntervalError, ScheduleValueError,<br/>TypeError or ScheduleError"]
    Kind -->|"Job body raises"| ExecFault["Exception escapes run_pending;<br/>last_run and next_run are NOT advanced"]
    Kind -->|"Dispatch is falling behind"| LagFault["idle_seconds() returns a negative value,<br/>quantifying seconds late"]
    Kind -->|"Occurrence was missed"| MissFault["Silently dropped and never replayed;<br/>run_pending docstring lines 93 to 97"]
    Kind -->|"Registry is unexpectedly empty"| EmptyFault["idle_seconds() returns None and<br/>get_jobs() is empty"]
    Kind -->|"Library defect suspected"| BugFault["Behaviour contradicts the documentation"]
    ConfigFault --> FailFast["Fails at start-up, before the registry append<br/>at line 663 — nothing is registered"]
    FailFast --> FixDecl["Response: correct the declaration.<br/>Nothing to clean up, per Section 5.4.3"]
    ExecFault --> Instrumented{"Has the host wrapped the body<br/>or guarded the loop?"}
    Instrumented -->|"No"| Silent["NO library signal: only the pre-execution<br/>'Running job' record was emitted"]
    Silent --> LoopRisk["Driver loop terminates unless the host<br/>guards it; remaining due jobs are skipped"]
    LoopRisk --> Runbook["Response: apply the runbook in 6.5.4.3<br/>then add a wrapper or a loop guard"]
    Instrumented -->|"Yes"| Captured["Wrapper prints the traceback and may return<br/>CancelJob, per docs/exception-handling.rst"]
    Captured --> HostRoute["Host converts it into a counter or an alert<br/>and routes it through its own stack"]
    LagFault --> Poll["Detected only as fast as the host polls;<br/>nothing is pushed"]
    Poll --> Triage{"Is the lag sustained beyond<br/>a host-defined threshold?"}
    Triage -->|"No"| Transient["Transient: absorbed by the poll period<br/>and by earlier jobs in the cycle"]
    Triage -->|"Yes"| Saturated["Capacity exceeded or the loop has stalled;<br/>see 6.5.3.5"]
    Saturated --> Offload["Response: offload long bodies per<br/>docs/parallel-execution.rst, or shorten the poll"]
    MissFault --> NoSignal["NO library signal: nothing counts or logs a miss"]
    NoSignal --> HostCount["Response: host compares expected against<br/>observed executions itself"]
    EmptyFault --> Redeclare["Response: re-execute the declaration code;<br/>the registry is memory only, per Section 5.4.6"]
    BugFault --> Search["Documented triage: check the FAQ, then search<br/>the issue tracker to avoid duplicates"]
    Search --> Escalate["Escalation: file an issue with a detailed<br/>description, per docs/index.rst"]
    Escalate --> Loop6544["Enters the defect-response loop in 6.5.4.4"]
```

**Diagram 6.5.4-A — Alert flow: every detectable condition from origin to the response the repository supports.** The two nodes labelled "NO library signal" mark the conditions for which the library emits nothing — a failing job body and a missed occurrence — and are the reason host instrumentation is mandatory for any real alerting.

#### 6.5.4.2 Escalation Procedures

The project defines no operational escalation: there is no on-call schedule, no severity-to-responder mapping, no acknowledgement or hand-off protocol, and no response-time expectation anywhere in the repository. There is also no private reporting channel — Section 6.4.5.6 records the absence of `SECURITY.md` — so every report, including a security report, would arrive on the public tracker.

What is documented, consistently across four files, is a **triage-before-escalation** path for adopters. It is worth recording exactly, because it is the project's only stated procedure of this kind.

| Step | Documented action | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Consult the diagnostic catalogue | "Problems? Check out :doc:`faq`." | `docs/installation.rst` |
| 2. Self-diagnose against known symptoms | The FAQ resolves module-shadowing, install-path, and missing-`pytz` symptoms with concrete commands | `docs/faq.rst` |
| 3. Search externally before escalating | "Still having problems? Use Google and StackOverflow before submitting an issue." | `docs/faq.rst` |
| 4. Search the tracker for duplicates | "Please also use the search feature in the issue tracker beforehand to avoid creating duplicates." | `docs/index.rst` |
| 5. File a detailed issue | "If you encounter any problems, please file an issue along with a detailed description." | `docs/index.rst`; `pyproject.toml` `Issues` URL |

For the operational half — an incident inside a host application — escalation is the host's to define. The severity classification below is derived from the blast radius each failure mode actually has, as established in Section 6.1.4.2, and is offered as the mapping a host can attach its own responders to. No severity label in this table appears in the repository; the *behaviours* do.

| Failure mode | Observed blast radius | Escalation implication for the host |
|---|---|---|
| Driver loop terminated by an unguarded exception | Every job in that registry stops silently — the widest in-process radius | Highest urgency; nothing dispatches and no signal is emitted |
| Job body failing repeatedly | That job never advances and re-qualifies on every poll, becoming a hot loop | Urgent; requires a wrapper or `CancelJob` to stop the re-attempt cycle |
| Long-running body blocking dispatch | Every later job in the cycle is delayed and drift accumulates | Urgent when a delayed job is time-critical; remedy is offloading |
| Sustained negative `idle_seconds()` | Occurrences are being silently dropped | Investigate capacity before the next business-critical occurrence |
| Registry empty after a restart | Schedule was not re-declared; nothing will ever run | Immediate re-declaration; the registry is not persisted |
| Definition-time validation failure | Contained entirely; the registry is untouched | Start-up defect, not an incident |

#### 6.5.4.3 Runbooks

No runbook file exists in the repository, but `docs/faq.rst` functions as one for the boundary conditions an adopter actually hits, and the module's error messages are precise enough to be used as runbook keys. The two tables below consolidate both into diagnostic form. Every symptom string and remedy is quoted from, or directly verifiable in, the cited source.

**Environment and integration symptoms** — the documented catalogue, with the checks the FAQ prescribes:

| Symptom | Documented cause | Prescribed remedy |
|---|---|---|
| `AttributeError: 'module' object has no attribute 'every'` | A local `schedule.py` in the project shadows the installed package | Remove or rename the shadowing file (`docs/faq.rst`) |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'schedule'` | Not installed, installed for a different interpreter, or the wrong virtualenv or IDE interpreter is active | Verify with `pip3 list \| grep schedule` or `dpkg -l \| grep python3-schedule`; install with `pip3`; run outside the IDE to isolate interpreter configuration (`docs/faq.rst`) |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pytz'` | A timezone was passed to `.at()` without the optional dependency installed | `pip install pytz` (`docs/faq.rst`; `docs/installation.rst` records `pytz` as the single optional dependency) |
| Jobs execute serially when parallelism was expected | "By default, schedule executes all jobs serially" | Adopt the thread-per-firing or bounded-queue pattern (`docs/parallel-execution.rst`) |
| The scheduler blocks the main thread | Background operation is "not possible" out of the box | Use the `run_continuously()` thread recipe (`docs/background-execution.rst`) |
| Jobs on one scheduler never run | `run_pending()` must be called on **every** scheduler instance | Poll each instance in the driver loop (`docs/multiple-schedulers.rst`) |
| Behaviour matches a years-old release | Distribution packages are unmaintained; Ubuntu and Debian are flagged **OUTDATED!** at 0.3.2 (2015) | Install from PyPI; manual single-file copying is "highly discouraged" (`docs/installation.rst`) |

**Runtime and configuration symptoms** — keyed on library state and on the exception messages raised by the 28 definition-time guards:

| Symptom or message | Diagnosis | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Exception escapes `run_pending()` | The job body raised; the library holds no `try`/`except` around the invocation at line 691 | Wrap the body with the `catch_exceptions` decorator, or guard the driver loop (`docs/exception-handling.rst`) |
| `idle_seconds()` negative and unchanging; no `Running job` record | The driver loop is not polling, or a body is blocking it | Confirm loop liveness with host instrumentation; offload long bodies |
| `idle_seconds()` returns `None` | The registry is empty — nothing is scheduled | Re-execute the declaration code |
| `job.last_run` stays `None` past the first interval | The job has never completed; a raising body leaves `last_run` unset | Inspect the wrapper output; the `Running job` record proves an attempt, never a success |
| A job stopped running with no error | Its `until()` deadline passed, its body returned `CancelJob`, or `clear()`/`cancel_job()` removed it | Check for the DEBUG cancellation records at lines 687, 696, 157 or 160 |
| Every job disappeared at once | Some code called `clear()` with no argument, executing one `del self.jobs[:]` at line 145 | Own a private `Scheduler()` instead of the module facade (Section 6.4.3.3) |
| `IntervalError: Use seconds instead of second` | A singular unit property was used while `interval != 1` | Use the plural property, or set the interval to 1 |
| `ScheduleValueError: Invalid unit (valid units are ...)` | `do()` was reached without a valid unit set | Complete the fluent chain with a supported unit |
| `ScheduleValueError: Invalid start day (valid start days are ...)` | A weekday name outside the lowercase seven-element set | Use the documented weekday property |
| `TypeError: Tags must be hashable` | An unhashable tag such as `{}` or `[]` was passed to `tag()` | Pass hashable values only |
| `ScheduleValueError: Invalid string format for until()` | The deadline string matched none of the five accepted `strptime` formats | Use a supported format, or pass a `datetime`, `timedelta`, or `time` |
| `ScheduleError: Unable to a add job to schedule...` | `do()` was called on a `Job` constructed without a scheduler | Create jobs through `every()` on a scheduler instance |

#### 6.5.4.4 Post-Mortem Processes

There is no post-mortem template, incident review document, or blameless-retrospective procedure in the repository. There is, however, a consistently applied and fully traceable **defect-response loop**, and its artifacts are durable enough to serve the same purpose. The loop has four stages, each evidenced in the repository.

| Stage | Artifact produced | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Report and triage | A numbered issue on the public tracker, filed after the FAQ and duplicate search | `docs/index.rst`; `docs/faq.rst`; `pyproject.toml` `Issues` URL |
| 2. Encode the defect as a test | A regression test named or annotated with the issue number | `test_schedule.py`: `test_tz_daily_issue_592` (line 721), `test_tz_daily_issue_605` (line 814), `test_tz_daily_issue_608_pre_dst` (857), `_post_dst` (871), `_mid_dst` (885), `_before_dst_end` (901); inline comments "Testing issue #598" (703) and "Testing issue #603" (737) |
| 3. Verify across the supported surface | A green five-job workflow over twelve tox environments, with coverage published | `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; `tox.ini`; verified locally as "81 passed in 0.12s" |
| 4. Record the outcome publicly | A changelog line citing the issue number and crediting the contributor | `HISTORY.rst`; `AUTHORS.rst`; republished on the documentation site because `docs/changelog.rst` is a single `.. include:: ../HISTORY.rst` |

Two properties make this loop function as an incident record. The regression tests are **permanent, executable statements of the defect** — the six issue-named timezone tests remain in the suite and run on every interpreter in the matrix, so a recurrence is detected mechanically rather than by memory. And the changelog is explicit about behavioural consequence: the `1.0.0` entry introduces its list with the warning that, depending on configuration, the bugfixes that follow might change the library's behaviour, then enumerates them with issue references such as "idle_seconds crashes when no jobs are scheduled. See #401" and "Long-running jobs skip a day when they finish in the next day #404". That is a public statement of impact and remediation for each defect.

#### 6.5.4.5 Improvement Tracking

`HISTORY.rst` is the project's improvement register, and it is dense enough to be read as one. It contains 23 dated release entries, the most recent being `1.2.2 (2024-05-25)`, and 31 issue or pull-request references in `#NNN` form. Entries are grouped by release, credit contributors by GitHub handle, and are mirrored into the documentation site through `docs/changelog.rst`.

| Improvement-tracking mechanism | Implementation | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Change register | 23 dated release entries with issue references and contributor credit | `HISTORY.rst` |
| Versioning discipline | "This project follows semantic versioning"; the version is bumped in `setup.py` and `docs/conf.py`, then tagged `X.Y.Z` | `docs/development.rst`; `setup.py` line 5; `docs/conf.py` |
| Contributor acknowledgement | A maintained roster naming each contributor | `AUTHORS.rst` |
| Regression protection | Issue-numbered tests retained permanently in the 81-method suite | `test_schedule.py` |
| Gate expansion | Interpreter support tracked as an explicit change; the matrix and tox envlist grow with it | "Add support for python 3.12 (#606)" in `HISTORY.rst`; matrix at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` line 17 |
| Dependency reduction | Removal of obsolete test dependencies recorded as an improvement | "Remove dependency on old mock (#622)" in `HISTORY.rst` |

The register also shows that observability itself has been treated as a tracked improvement rather than an afterthought: the `1.1.0` entry records "Improved logging. See #193." and "Improved error messages. See #280, #439.", which is the provenance of the DEBUG record set catalogued in 6.5.2.2 and of the error strings used as runbook keys in 6.5.4.3. Sustained correctness work is likewise visible and recent — `1.2.1` and `1.2.2` are both driven by timezone and DST fixes ("Fix bugs in cross-timezone scheduling (#601, #602, #604, #623)"), matched one-for-one by the issue-named regression tests listed above.

Two limitations of this improvement loop should be recorded plainly, because they bound what an adopter can expect. There is no automated dependency-update or vulnerability-scanning input to the register — Section 6.4.5.6 verifies the absence of Dependabot, Renovate, and every SAST or dependency scanner from the workflow — so improvements enter only through human reports and maintainer work. And because the pipeline has no scheduled trigger, nothing re-verifies a released version against a changing ecosystem until the next push or pull request to `master`.
