No external or web sources were required for this section; every claim is grounded in the repository or in an earlier section of this specification.


## 6.6 Testing Strategy

### 6.6.1 Testing Scope and Applicability

**Detailed Testing Strategy is not applicable for this system** in the multi-tier sense that term normally implies — there is no integration tier, no end-to-end tier, no UI automation, no cross-browser matrix, and no performance-test harness in this repository, and none can exist without inventing components the project does not have.

The subject of this specification is the Python `schedule` library at release 1.2.2 (`setup.py`). Its entire runtime is one importable module, `schedule/__init__.py` (945 lines), shipped with the zero-byte PEP 561 marker `schedule/py.typed`. It serves no port, opens no socket or file, connects to no database, renders no user interface, and declares zero required runtime dependencies (`pyproject.toml`, `dependencies = []`). Section 6.2 records that Database Design is not applicable to this system, and Section 6.3 records that Integration Architecture is not applicable, its only boundary being a Python `import`. A test strategy can only exercise the boundaries a system actually has, and this system has exactly one: a function call.

What the repository does contain is an unusually thorough **single-tier unit test suite** — `test_schedule.py`, 1,599 lines, 81 test methods, a 1.69 : 1 test-to-implementation line ratio — executed across a **12-environment interpreter and optional-dependency matrix** (`tox.ini`) by **five CI jobs** (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`). That suite is the acceptance criteria of record for all 50 requirements catalogued in Section 2.5. Accordingly, this section documents the basic unit testing approach that is actually used, in full detail (6.6.2), records what stands in for the higher tiers and states precisely which of them are absent and why (6.6.3), documents the automation that drives them (6.6.4), the metrics and gates that constrain them (6.6.5), and the environment and resources they require (6.6.6).

#### 6.6.1.1 Determination Criteria and Findings

Each row below is a structural precondition for one of the test tiers named in this section's scope. Every one fails, and each finding is grounded in a verification performed against the checkout rather than assumed from the codebase's size.

| Precondition for a higher test tier | Verification performed | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| Two or more deployable components to integrate | Full inventory of the 32 git-tracked files; `schedule/` contains exactly `__init__.py` and `py.typed` | **Fails** — one runtime component, no process or service boundary (Section 6.3) |
| An HTTP/RPC surface to drive API tests against | Scans for web frameworks, servers, routers, and endpoint declarations (Section 6.3.1.1) | **Fails** — zero matches; there is no request/response to assert on |
| A database or persistent store to seed and assert against | Scans for engines, ORMs, drivers, DDL, and migration tooling (Section 6.2.1.1) | **Fails** — zero matches; all state is one in-memory list |
| An external service to stub, record, or contract-test | `pyproject.toml` declares no required dependency; one optional extra, `pytz`, imported in-process | **Fails** — no network egress exists to intercept; nothing to mock at a protocol level |
| A user interface to automate | Filesystem census for templates, components, assets, and browser drivers | **Fails** — the only HTML in the repository is the Sphinx sidebar template `docs/_templates/sidebarintro.html` |
| A performance target or published SLA to verify | Repository-wide search for benchmark harnesses (`pytest-benchmark`, `locust`, `k6`, JMeter) and for any stated throughput or latency figure | **Fails** — no harness and no published target exist; Section 2.4 records the same absence |
| A provisioned test environment to manage | Filesystem search for `Dockerfile*`, `docker-compose*`, `*.tf`, `Chart.yaml`, `.env*`, and test-container libraries | **Fails** — the only YAML in the repository is `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |
| A security-scanning or dependency-audit gate | Scans for `bandit`, `safety`, `pip-audit`, CodeQL, Trivy, and Dependabot configuration | **Fails** — no scanner, no `.github/dependabot.yml`; `.github/` contains only `workflows/ci.yml` |

The absence of these tiers is a direct consequence of published product boundaries rather than an unfinished plan. `docs/index.rst` tells readers to look elsewhere if they need job persistence, sub-second precision, concurrent execution, or localization, and `README.rst` advertises an in-process scheduler with "no external dependencies". A system with no persistence, no concurrency, and no dependencies has no integration seams to test.

#### 6.6.1.2 What Plays the Role of Each Absent Tier

The following mapping is the organising principle for the remainder of this section. It is an orientation aid, not a claim that any mechanism listed on the right is equivalent to the tier on the left.

| Conventional test tier | Counterpart in this system | Documented in |
|---|---|---|
| Unit testing | `test_schedule.py` — 81 `unittest` methods against the public API plus four private helpers | 6.6.2 |
| Integration testing | The 12-environment `tox` matrix: six interpreters × with/without `pytz`, each also type-checked | 6.6.3.1 |
| Contract testing | `mypy -p schedule` over the annotated, PEP 561-published interface, in every environment | 6.6.3.2 |
| Environment/compatibility testing | `skip_missing_interpreters` matrix plus the `setup.py check --strict` packaging gate | 6.6.3.1, 6.6.3.3 |
| External service mocking | Not required — a conditional `import pytz` guard that **skips** rather than stubs | 6.6.3.4 |
| End-to-end testing | Multi-step frozen-clock scenarios that drive declare → poll → execute → reschedule → cancel in-process | 6.6.3.5 |
| UI / cross-browser testing | Not applicable; the only rendered artifact is documentation, gated by `sphinx-build -W` | 6.6.3.6 |
| Performance testing | Not present; no harness and no threshold exists anywhere in the repository | 6.6.3.7 |
| Security testing | Not present as tooling; the attack surface documented in Section 6.4 has no automated verification | 6.6.3.8 |
| Test automation platform | GitHub Actions workflow "Tests" — five jobs on `push` and `pull_request` to `master` | 6.6.4 |
| Quality gates | Test/coverage, type, documentation, formatting, and packaging-metadata gates | 6.6.5.4 |

#### 6.6.1.3 Complete Testing Asset Inventory

Every testing-related artifact in the repository is listed below; there are no others. The inventory is the factual base for all claims in this section.

| Asset | Role | Size / scope |
|---|---|---|
| `test_schedule.py` | The entire test suite; docstring reads `"""Unit tests for schedule.py"""` | 1,599 lines, 81 test methods, one `TestCase` class |
| `tox.ini` | Environment matrix and per-environment command set | 38 lines, 12 test environments plus 3 utility environments |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Automation: triggers, matrix, coverage publication | 91 lines, 5 jobs, the only workflow in the repository |
| `requirements-dev.txt` | Developer tool set for the documented local workflow | 11 entries, unpinned except `black==20.8b1` and `click==8.0.4` |
| `setup.cfg` | The entire static-analysis configuration: `[mypy] files=schedule` | 2 lines |
| `docs/development.rst` | The published contributor testing and formatting procedure | 68 lines |
| `MANIFEST.in` | Ships `test_schedule.py` inside the sdist so redistributors can run it | 8 lines |
| `.gitignore` | Declares `.coverage`, `.tox`, `.cache` as local-only artifacts | 48 lines |

Four absences complete the inventory and shape everything that follows: there is **no `tests/` package** (the suite is a single root-level module), **no `conftest.py`**, **no `pytest.ini` or `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`**, and **no coverage configuration** (`.coveragerc` or `[tool.coverage]`) anywhere in the repository. The suite therefore runs entirely on framework defaults, with all configuration expressed as command-line flags in `tox.ini`.


### 6.6.2 Unit Testing Approach

Unit testing is the whole of the verification strategy for this system, and the suite is engineered around one dominant problem: the behaviour under test is a function of the wall clock and the local timezone, neither of which a test may depend on. Every structural decision in `test_schedule.py` — the module-level timezone pin, the hand-written clock context manager, the mock job factory, the conditional-skip helpers — exists to make time deterministic. This sub-section documents that design.

#### 6.6.2.1 Testing Frameworks and Tools

The suite is written against the standard library and *executed* by `pytest`; it is not written in pytest idiom. `test_schedule.py` imports `from unittest import mock, TestCase` (line 5), defines a single `TestCase` subclass, and uses `unittest` assertion methods alongside bare `assert` statements, which means it runs unchanged under either runner — verified: `python -m unittest test_schedule` reports `OK` and `python -m pytest test_schedule.py -q` reports `81 passed`.

| Tool | Version constraint | Role in the strategy |
|---|---|---|
| `unittest` (stdlib) | Bundled with the interpreter | Test class structure (`TestCase`), `setUp` isolation, `assertRaises`, `skipTest` |
| `unittest.mock` (stdlib) | Bundled with the interpreter | The single test-double mechanism; `mock.Mock()` job callables |
| `pytest` | Unpinned (`requirements-dev.txt`, `tox.ini`) | The runner invoked by `tox`: `py.test test_schedule.py schedule -v` |
| `pytest-cov` | Unpinned | Coverage measurement and the `term-missing` report |
| `mypy` + `types-pytz` | Unpinned | Static verification of the package in every environment |
| `pytz` | Unpinned optional extra | Real timezone data for the 41 timezone-dependent tests |
| `tox` + `tox-gh-actions` | Unpinned | Environment matrix construction and CI mapping (6.6.4) |
| `coveralls` | Unpinned, CI only | Coverage aggregation across the matrix |

Two tooling facts are worth recording because they are deliberate. The project **removed its dependency on the third-party `mock` backport** in release 1.2.2 (`HISTORY.rst`, "Remove dependency on old mock (#622)"), completing the move to `unittest.mock` and leaving the suite with no test-framework dependency beyond the runner itself. And `pytest-flake8` remains listed in `requirements-dev.txt` and is still referenced by the command published in `docs/development.rst`, but `tox.ini` no longer passes `--flake8` — so lint-by-pytest is available to contributors yet is not part of the enforced pipeline (6.6.5.4).

#### 6.6.2.2 Test Organization Structure

The organisation is deliberately flat. There is no `tests/` package, no per-feature module, and no `conftest.py`; the suite is one root-level file containing one test class.

| Structural element | Location | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Module docstring and imports | Lines 1–20 | Declares the suite as unit tests; imports the public API surface |
| POSIX `TZ` constants | Lines 23–26 | `TZ_BERLIN`, `TZ_AUCKLAND`, `TZ_CHATHAM`, `TZ_UTC` |
| Global determinism pin | Lines 28–30 | `os.environ["TZ"] = TZ_BERLIN` then `time.tzset()` |
| `make_mock_job(name=None)` | Lines 33–36 | Module-level mock callable factory |
| `class mock_datetime` | Lines 39–93 | Clock-freezing context manager |
| `class SchedulerTests(TestCase)` | Line 96 onward | All 81 tests, plus `setUp` and three arrange helpers |

Within the single class, tests are grouped by proximity rather than by nested classes, and the ordering follows the library's own API surface — units, then anchoring, then deadlines, then next-run arithmetic, then the large timezone block, then execution, representation, introspection, cancellation, and finally robustness. The measured distribution shows where the project concentrates its effort:

| Test category | Tests | Test lines |
|---|---|---|
| Timezone, DST, and UTC-offset behaviour | 38 | 603 |
| Execution and the `@repeat` decorator | 9 | 136 |
| `next_run` arithmetic across boundaries | 8 | 86 |
| Tags, cancellation, and clearing | 6 | 96 |
| `str`/`repr` contracts | 5 | 57 |
| Interval units and randomized ranges | 4 | 142 |
| `at()` parsing and validation | 4 | 113 |
| Private helpers and robustness | 4 | 27 |
| Introspection APIs (`next_run`, `idle_seconds`) | 2 | 21 |
| `until()` deadlines | 1 | 77 |

Forty-seven percent of the suite (38 of 81 tests, 603 of 1,599 lines) targets timezone and DST correctness — the area `HISTORY.rst` shows to be the source of the most defects, with releases 1.2.1 and 1.2.2 driven entirely by cross-timezone fixes. Mean test size is 16.8 lines and the median is 12, with two deliberate outliers: `test_time_units` (line 108, 113 lines) which sweeps the whole unit grammar including every invalid combination, and `test_tz_minutes_year_round` (line 936, 108 lines) which walks a full year of 20-minute occurrences across two hemispheres.

Three shared arrange helpers exist inside the class, and one naming rule keeps them out of collection:

- `make_tz_mock_job(name=None)` (lines 100–106) — skips the test when `pytz` is unavailable, then delegates to `make_mock_job`.
- `setup_utc_offset_test()` (lines 1162–1173) — same skip guard, then builds a Berlin-anchored job and returns it with a `pytz` zone object for the seven white-box `_correct_utc_offset` tests.
- `tst_next_run_time_hour_end(tz, offsetMinutes)` (line 538) and `tst_next_run_time_minute_end(tz)` (line 576) — parameterized bodies deliberately prefixed `tst_` rather than `test_` so the runner does not collect them; each is called from three thin `test_*` methods that supply `None`, `"Europe/London"`, and `"Asia/Kathmandu"`. This is the suite's only parameterization mechanism — `pytest.mark.parametrize` and `subTest` are not used anywhere.

#### 6.6.2.3 Mocking Strategy

The strategy has exactly two doubles and one deliberate non-double. Nothing else is faked, because nothing else exists to fake: the library has no collaborators (Section 6.3).

**1. The job callable is a `Mock`.** `make_mock_job` returns a `mock.Mock()` with `__name__` assigned, because `Job.__str__` and `Job.__repr__` read that attribute. This single construction site is reused at 42 call sites — there is exactly one `mock.Mock()` literal in the entire 1,599-line file, and `mock.patch` is never used.

```python
def make_mock_job(name=None):
    job = mock.Mock(); job.__name__ = name or "job"
    return job
```

Verification through this double is behavioural: 21 assertions read `call_count` to prove a job fired the expected number of times, and three use `assert_called_once_with` to prove that arguments bound at declaration time reach the callable unchanged.

**2. The clock is monkey-patched by a context manager.** `mock_datetime` (lines 39–93) is a purpose-built context manager, not a library fixture. On entry it defines an inner `MockDate(datetime.datetime)` subclass whose `today()` and `now(tz=None)` classmethods return a fixed instant — honouring `fold` for DST-ambiguity tests and applying `astimezone(tz)` when the library asks for an aware value — then rebinds `datetime.datetime` to it and, optionally, repins the process `TZ`. On exit it restores both.

```python
with mock_datetime(2010, 1, 6, 12, 15):
    assert every().minute.do(make_mock_job()).next_run.minute == 16
```

This is used 81 times and is the reason the suite can assert exact timestamps. Because the manager restores `datetime.datetime` and `TZ` in `__exit__`, its effects never leak between tests — confirmed empirically by running the suite with randomized method order (6.6.4.6).

**3. The optional dependency is skipped, not stubbed.** Where a test needs real timezone data, the suite does not substitute a fake `pytz`; it declines to run:

```python
try: import pytz
except ModuleNotFoundError: self.skipTest("pytz unavailable")
```

This is the correct choice given the intent — the `-pytz`/non-`pytz` split of the `tox` matrix exists precisely to prove that the library behaves correctly *with the real package* and imports cleanly *without any substitute*. A stub would defeat both halves. Measured effect: with `pytz` importable the suite reports `81 passed`; with the import blocked it reports `40 passed, 41 skipped`.

#### 6.6.2.4 Code Coverage Requirements

Coverage is **measured and published on every CI run but is not enforced by any threshold**. `tox.ini` line 23 runs `py.test … --cov schedule --cov-report term-missing`; there is no `--cov-fail-under` flag, no `.coveragerc`, and no `[tool.coverage]` section anywhere in the repository, so a coverage regression cannot fail the build. The target is a project norm rather than a machine rule, expressed in three places: `README.rst` claims "Excellent test coverage", `HISTORY.rst` records "Increased test coverage to 100%" for release 0.1.9, and the Coveralls badge publishes the current figure for `master`.

Measured against this checkout (Python 3.12.3, `pytz` installed, line coverage via the standard-library `trace` module because `coverage.py` is not present in the measurement environment):

| Configuration | Lines covered in `schedule/__init__.py` | Result |
|---|---|---|
| With `pytz` (the `-pytz` tox environments) | 434 of 438 executable lines | **99.1%** |
| Without `pytz` (the plain `py3XX` environments) | 413 of 438 executable lines | **94.3%** — 41 tests skip |
| Test scope of the gate | `--cov schedule` only | `test_schedule.py` itself is not measured |
| Type-check scope | `mypy -p schedule` (`setup.cfg`: `files=schedule`) | The test module is not type-checked |

The four unexecuted lines are all defensive branches unreachable through the public API, which is the most useful coverage statement this section can make:

| Uncovered line | Code | Why it cannot be reached |
|---|---|---|
| 659–660 | `raise ScheduleError("… not associated with an scheduler")` in `Job.do()` | `every()` always binds a scheduler; matches the inspection-only requirement F-007-RQ-003 in Section 2.5 |
| 755 | `return moment` guard for `at_time is None` in `_move_to_at_time()` | The only caller invokes it after checking that `at_time` is set |
| 800 | `return moment` guard for `not fixate_time` in `_correct_utc_offset()` | Not exercised by any live call path in the current suite |

Section 2.5 reaches a consistent conclusion from the requirements side: 46 of 50 requirements have at least one automated test, and the four that do not are verified by inspection — the `at()` unit guard, the no-scheduler branch, exception propagation from an unguarded job body, and log emission.

#### 6.6.2.5 Test Naming Conventions

Names are descriptive, lower-snake-case, and follow a `test_<subject>[_<qualifier>][_<condition>]` shape. Four consistent conventions are observable across all 81 methods:

| Convention | Pattern | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Subject-first grouping | `test_<api or concept>_…` | `test_at_time_hour`, `test_next_run_time_day_end`, `test_run_pending` |
| Hierarchical qualifiers | `test_tz_<cadence>_<condition>` | `test_tz_daily_dst_skip_hour`, `test_tz_weekly_large_interval_backward` |
| Issue-numbered regressions | `test_tz_daily_issue_<number>` | `test_tz_daily_issue_592`, `_issue_605`, `_issue_608_pre_dst`, `_post_dst`, `_mid_dst`, `_before_dst_end` |
| Non-collected helpers | `tst_` prefix instead of `test_` | `tst_next_run_time_hour_end`, `tst_next_run_time_minute_end` |

The issue-numbered convention is the strategy's regression ledger: six methods permanently pin defects reported upstream as #592, #605, and #608, so a reintroduction is caught by a test whose name identifies the original report. Docstrings are used sparingly and only where the *contract* needs restating rather than the mechanics — `test_run_pending` carries a nine-line docstring reiterating that missed jobs are intentionally never replayed, and `test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler` explains that an interrupted definition chain must not corrupt the scheduler permanently. Two spelling slips are preserved for stability (`test_weekday_at_todady`, `test_next_run_time_minute_end_katmhandu`).

#### 6.6.2.6 Test Data Management

There is **no test data infrastructure** — no fixture files, no factories beyond the two mock helpers, no builders, no snapshots or golden files, no database seeding, no random seeds, and no external data of any kind. All inputs are literals declared inline at the point of use. The complete taxonomy of test data is four kinds:

| Data kind | Representation | Managed by |
|---|---|---|
| Frozen instants | Positional literals: `mock_datetime(2023, 3, 26, 1, 30)` | The context manager; restored on exit |
| Process-local timezone | POSIX `TZ` strings pinned at module import and optionally per-block | Lines 23–30; `mock_datetime(..., zone=TZ_CHATHAM)` |
| Job-facing timezones | IANA name strings passed to `.at()`, or `pytz.timezone(...)` objects | Resolved by the library; 15 distinct zones exercised |
| Executable payloads | `mock.Mock` instances, lambdas, and `functools.partial` objects | `make_mock_job`, `make_tz_mock_job` |

State isolation is a single line: `setUp` calls `schedule.clear()` (lines 97–98), emptying the process-global `default_scheduler` before every test. Tests that need a private registry construct one explicitly — `test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler` instantiates `schedule.Scheduler()` — and `test_tz_minutes_year_round` calls `schedule.clear()` again mid-test before building its long-horizon job. There is no teardown at all, because there is nothing to tear down: no files are written, no connections opened, and no processes started.

The distinguishing practice in this suite is that **expected values are documented as prose alongside the assertion**. Each timezone test states the intended local and remote wall-clock times in comments before asserting them, which is what makes a 108-line, year-long DST walk auditable:

```python
# Current Berlin time: 01:30 (NOT during daylight saving)

#### Expected to run: 02:30 - this time doesn't exist ... Next run: 03:30

job = every().day.at("02:30", "Europe/Berlin").do(mock_job)
```

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Sources["Test data sources - all literal, all in-file"]
        direction TB
        TZConst["POSIX TZ constants<br/>lines 23 to 26"]
        Instants["Frozen instant literals<br/>year, month, day, hour, minute, second, fold"]

    end
    subgraph Harness["Determinism harness"]

        Guard{{"Does this test need real zone data?"}}

        Guard -->|"yes and pytz missing"| SkipPath
    end
```

**Diagram 6.6.2-A — Test data flow: literal inputs, the determinism harness that pins the clock and timezone, the exercised library paths, the verification idioms, and the reset that restores global state.** No arrow on this diagram crosses a process, file, or network boundary.


### 6.6.3 Integration, End-to-End, and Specialized Testing

This sub-section records, tier by tier, either the mechanism that occupies the tier's position in this project or the verified evidence that the tier does not exist. Nothing here describes work the repository does not perform.

#### 6.6.3.1 Service Integration Test Approach — The Environment Matrix

There are no services to integrate, so the axis along which this project integrates is the **runtime environment**. `tox.ini` line 2 declares `envlist = py3{7,8,9,10,11,12}{,-pytz}`, which expands to twelve environments — each supported interpreter, once with the optional dependency installed and once without. Every environment runs the identical command pair (`tox.ini` lines 22–24):

```ini
py.test test_schedule.py schedule -v --cov schedule --cov-report term-missing
python -m mypy -p schedule --install-types --non-interactive
```

| Matrix dimension | Values | What it verifies |
|---|---|---|
| Interpreter | 3.7, 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12 | The `python_requires=">=3.7"` promise in `setup.py` and the classifier list |
| Optional dependency | `pytz` absent / `pytz` present | Both halves of the contract in Section 6.3.4.1 |
| Verification per environment | Suite + coverage, then type check | Behaviour and interface conformance under that exact combination |
| Missing interpreters | `skip_missing_interpreters = true` | A developer with fewer interpreters installed still gets a useful local run |

The two halves of the dependency axis test different things, and both are necessary. The six plain `py3XX` environments prove the **zero-required-dependency** claim: the module must import and 40 of 81 tests must pass with no third-party package present at all — measured result, `40 passed, 41 skipped`. The six `-pytz` environments prove **correct interoperation with the real package**, exercising `pytz.timezone()`, the `BaseTzInfo` isinstance check, and the two `normalize()` calls inside `_correct_utc_offset` — and they are what raises measured coverage from 94.3% to 99.1%. `tox.ini` line 21 expresses the split with a single conditional dependency factor, `pytz: pytz`.

One detail of the pytest invocation is worth recording accurately: the command names two targets, `test_schedule.py` **and** `schedule`. The second is a vestigial collection target left from the era when `--flake8` linted the package through pytest; it collects no tests today, because `schedule/` contains no test module. `docs/development.rst` line 22 still publishes the older `--flake8` form of the command.

#### 6.6.3.2 API Testing Strategy — The Type Contract Gate

**There is no API test tier in the network sense.** Section 6.3 establishes that no HTTP, RPC, or IPC surface exists; there is no request to send, no status code to assert, and no payload to validate. The library's API is a set of Python callables, and it is verified two ways:

| Verification of the API | Mechanism | Enforcement point |
|---|---|---|
| Behavioural conformance | The 81 unit tests import the public names (`every`, `repeat`, the three exception classes) and drive the fluent grammar exactly as a consumer would | `test_schedule.py` lines 13–20 |
| Interface/type conformance | `mypy -p schedule` with scope fixed by `setup.cfg` (`[mypy] files=schedule`), run in all twelve environments with `types-pytz` available | `tox.ini` line 24 |
| Published-surface conformance | `docs/reference.rst` autodoc with `:undoc-members:`, built under `sphinx-build -W`, so a malformed or unresolvable reference fails CI | `tox -e docs` |
| Packaging-surface conformance | `python setup.py check --strict --metadata --restructuredtext` validates distribution metadata and the reST that becomes the PyPI description | `tox -e setuppy` |

The type gate is the closest analogue this project has to contract testing, and its scope has one important boundary: it covers the **package only**. `test_schedule.py` is neither type-checked nor linted by CI, so the tests themselves carry no static guarantees. Section 6.3.2.2 documents the same artifacts from the interface-definition perspective.

#### 6.6.3.3 Database Integration Testing

**Not applicable.** Section 6.2 establishes that no database, cache, object store, ORM, driver, schema, or migration tooling exists anywhere in the repository, and that all state is a single in-memory `List[Job]`. There is consequently no schema to migrate in a test, no transaction to roll back, no seed data to load, and no connection to pool. The state-reset requirement that a database test suite would satisfy with transactional rollback is satisfied here by one line — `setUp` calling `schedule.clear()`.

The registry-integrity properties a data-layer test suite would normally own are asserted directly by unit tests, which Section 6.2.4.2 records as guarantees: `test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler` (line 1591) proves a rejected definition cannot corrupt the registry, and `test_cancel_job` (line 1503) proves that removing an unknown job is a safe no-op.

#### 6.6.3.4 External Service Mocking

**Not applicable, and deliberately so.** There is no external service to mock: the library makes no network call, spawns no process, and reads no file (Section 6.3.1.1). The suite contains **zero uses of `mock.patch`** and no HTTP recorder, stub server, or contract broker.

The one external artifact that exists — the optional `pytz` package — is handled by **conditional skipping rather than substitution**, via the `skipTest("pytz unavailable")` guards at lines 100–106 and 1162–1173. This is a strategy decision rather than an omission: the purpose of the matrix is to verify real behaviour with the real package and clean importability without it, and a stub would falsify both. The only "doubles" in the suite are the `mock.Mock` job callables the host application would supply (6.6.2.3), which are inputs to the system rather than replacements for collaborators.

#### 6.6.3.5 End-to-End Test Scenarios

**There is no separate E2E tier** — no deployed instance, no driver, no fixture environment. What plays its role is a set of **multi-step, in-process scenario tests** that drive the library's full lifecycle (declare → poll → execute → reschedule → expire/cancel) by advancing a frozen clock across successive `mock_datetime` blocks while reusing the same `Job` object. These are the highest-level behaviours the system can have, because the system's outermost boundary is a function call.

| Scenario | Test method (line) | Lifecycle stages exercised |
|---|---|---|
| Poll cycle runs only due jobs and never replays missed ones | `test_run_pending` (1387) | Declare four cadences, advance the clock, assert `call_count` progression 0→1→2→3→4 |
| Forced sweep of every job regardless of due state | `test_run_all` (1273) | Declare three jobs, one sweep, assert three invocations |
| Deadline expiry unschedules the job | `test_until_time` (312) | Declare with `until()`, run to the boundary, assert registry length reaches zero |
| Job unschedules itself from inside its own body | `test_cancel_job` (1503) | Return `CancelJob`, sweep, assert removal |
| Hourly anchor survives repeated reschedules in three zones | `tst_next_run_time_hour_end` (538) | Three chained clock blocks with `job.run()` between each |
| DST gap displaces one occurrence, then normal service resumes | `test_tz_daily_dst_skip_hour` (647) | 02:30 anchor across the Berlin spring-forward gap, then the following day |
| Year-long cadence across two hemispheres with two DST transitions | `test_tz_minutes_year_round` (936) | 20-minute occurrences, Newfoundland ⇄ Chatham, `fold` control |
| Registration by import-time decoration | `test_run_all_with_decorator` (1281) | `@repeat(...)` declares, sweep executes, arguments verified |
| Interrupted definition chain cannot break the scheduler | `test_misconfigured_job_wont_break_scheduler` (1591) | Two partial chains on a private `Scheduler`, then `run_pending()` |

Test data setup and teardown for these scenarios is entirely in-memory and is fully described by 6.6.2.6: `setUp` clears the shared registry, the context manager restores the clock and timezone on exit, and nothing else requires cleanup. Notably, the host-side embedding recipes the project publishes — the background thread in `docs/background-execution.rst` and the queue hand-off in `docs/parallel-execution.rst` — have **no automated tests**, because they are documentation for the adopter rather than library code (Section 6.3.5).

#### 6.6.3.6 UI Automation and Cross-Browser Testing

**Not applicable.** The system has no user interface. There is no view layer, template engine, component, stylesheet bundle, browser driver, or headless-browser dependency; the only HTML file in the repository is the Sphinx sidebar template `docs/_templates/sidebarintro.html`, and the only stylesheet is `docs/_static/custom.css`. There is therefore no browser matrix, no viewport strategy, no accessibility suite, and no visual-regression baseline.

The only rendered artifact the project produces is its documentation site, and it *is* verified — by build rather than by browser. `tox -e docs` runs `sphinx-build -W -b html`, which promotes every Sphinx warning to an error, and a dedicated `docs` CI job runs it on every push and pull request. `docs/Makefile` additionally provides a `linkcheck` target, but no CI job invokes it.

#### 6.6.3.7 Performance Testing Requirements

**No performance tests exist and no performance thresholds are defined.** There is no benchmark harness in any manifest (`pytest-benchmark`, `locust`, `k6`, JMeter, `timeit`-based suites are all absent), no load profile, no soak or stress scenario, and no published latency, throughput, or resource target anywhere in the repository — Section 2.4 and Section 5.4.5 record the same absence from the requirements and cross-cutting perspectives.

Two properties of the system explain why this is coherent rather than negligent. First, the library's own cost is negligible relative to what it schedules: the entire 81-test suite completes in **0.12 seconds**, roughly 1.5 ms per test, because no test performs I/O. Second, the dominant performance factor is the *host's* job body, which the library invokes synchronously and does not time — `docs/index.rst` states plainly that Schedule does not account for the time a job takes to execute, and directs users with long-running jobs to move them off the scheduler's thread. A performance test of the library would therefore measure list-scan arithmetic; the indicative measurements that do exist in this specification were produced ad hoc for documentation purposes and are recorded in Sections 6.1.3.5, 6.2.2.5, and 6.2.5, each explicitly labelled as environment-specific rather than as a published benchmark.

Should performance verification ever be required, the observable cost drivers this specification has already established are the registry scan per poll, the roughly six-fold cost of creating or rescheduling a timezone-anchored job versus a plain one, and the quadratic behaviour of a `cancel_job()` loop compared with a single `clear(tag)`.

#### 6.6.3.8 Security Testing Requirements

**No security testing exists in this repository, and no security tooling is configured.** Verified absences: no SAST scanner (`bandit`, `semgrep`), no dependency auditor (`safety`, `pip-audit`), no CodeQL or Trivy workflow, no `.github/dependabot.yml`, no secret-scanning configuration, no fuzz harness, and no `SECURITY.md`. `.github/` contains exactly one file, `workflows/ci.yml`.

Some of this follows structurally from the architecture, and some of it is a genuine gap worth stating plainly. The following table separates the two, using only attack-surface facts established elsewhere in this specification.

| Security concern | Testability in this system | Current verification |
|---|---|---|
| Authentication / authorization | Nothing to test — no identity, credential, permission, or session concept exists anywhere (Sections 6.2.4.5, 6.3.2.3) | Not applicable |
| Injection via network input | Nothing to test — no network, file, or deserialization input path exists (Sections 6.2.1.1, 6.3.1.1) | Not applicable |
| Transport security | Nothing to test — no transport | Not applicable |
| Input validation of declarations | Testable and **well covered** — 28 definition-time guards; 70 `assertRaises` plus 7 `assertRaisesRegex` assertions pin both the failure and its exact message | Unit tests (6.6.2) |
| Unsandboxed payload execution | Structural: the bound callable runs synchronously with full host privileges and no timeout (Section 6.1.2.1) | Documented, not tested — the property is intrinsic to the design |
| Sensitive data in log output | Testable but **not tested**: `Job.__str__`/`__repr__` interpolate bound arguments, and five DEBUG records render a job (Section 6.2.4.3) | `test_to_string`/`test_to_repr` assert the rendering format, not redaction — no redaction exists |
| Non-cryptographic randomness | `to()` jitter uses `random.randint`, which is not cryptographic (Section 5.3.6) | `test_time_range` asserts range and variety only, which is the correct scope for a scheduling jitter |
| Supply-chain integrity of dependencies | A real gap: `pytz` is declared with **no version bound**, and every development tool except `black`/`click` is unpinned; the CI actions are pinned only to a major version (`@v3`, `@v4`) | No audit, lockfile, or hash pinning exists |
| Supply-chain integrity of releases | Publication is manual `twine upload` by a maintainer (Section 6.3.4.4); there is no signing or attestation step | No automated verification |

The two rows that constitute actionable security-testing requirements for this codebase are therefore dependency auditing and pinning, neither of which is currently automated. Everything else on the list is either structurally untestable or already covered by the input-validation assertions in the unit suite.


### 6.6.4 Test Automation

Automation is provided by a single GitHub Actions workflow named **Tests** (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, 91 lines) which delegates all execution to `tox`. This is the entire automation surface of the project: `.github/` contains no other workflow, no reusable action, no composite step, and no publish pipeline.

#### 6.6.4.1 CI/CD Integration

Five jobs run on `ubuntu-latest`. Four are single-purpose gates; one is a matrix.

| Job (`ci.yml` lines) | Runner setup | Command executed |
|---|---|---|
| `test` (12–35) | Python 3.7–3.12 matrix; `pip install tox tox-gh-actions` | `tox`, then a Coveralls upload step |
| `coveralls` — display name "coverage push" (36–52) | Python 3.11; `needs: test` | `coveralls --finish --service=github` |
| `docs` (54–65) | Python 3.11; `pip install tox` | `tox -e docs` → `sphinx-build -W -b html` |
| `formatting` (67–78) | Python 3.11; `pip install tox` | `tox -e format` → `black --check .` |
| `setuppy` (80–91) | Python 3.11; `pip install tox` | `tox -e setuppy` → `setup.py check --strict --metadata --restructuredtext` |

Every job pins its actions to a major version only: `actions/checkout@v3` and `actions/setup-python@v4`. The `tox-gh-actions` plugin is what makes the delegation work — `tox.ini` lines 6–13 map each CI interpreter to its two environments (`3.12: py312, py312-pytz`), so one `tox` invocation inside a single matrix leg runs that interpreter's suite twice: once with `pytz` and once without. Six matrix legs therefore execute all twelve `tox` environments, and each environment runs the suite plus `mypy`.

Three observations about the automation that follow directly from the file: the `coveralls` job does **not** check out the repository (it only finalises the upstream build); the `setuppy` job's step is labelled "Check docs", a copy-paste artifact that does not affect behaviour; and no job declares a `permissions:` block, a `timeout-minutes`, or a `concurrency` group.

#### 6.6.4.2 Automated Test Triggers

| Trigger | Configuration | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Push | `on: push: branches: [master]` | Full workflow, all five jobs |
| Pull request | `on: pull_request: branches: [master]` | Full workflow, all five jobs |
| Scheduled / nightly | **None** — no `schedule:` key exists | — |
| Manual dispatch | **None** — no `workflow_dispatch:` key exists | — |
| Tag or release | **None** — publication is manual (Section 6.3.4.4) | — |
| Path or file filters | **None** — a documentation-only change runs the full matrix | — |

The practical consequence is that verification is tied entirely to the `master` branch: work on a topic branch is verified when a pull request targeting `master` is opened, and never on a nightly cadence. Because there is no path filter, every change — including a typo fix in `HISTORY.rst` — runs six interpreters, twelve environments, and four gate jobs.

Locally, three documented entry points exist: `tox` (the full matrix, limited by `skip_missing_interpreters`), the command published in `docs/development.rst` line 22 (`py.test test_schedule.py --flake8 schedule -v --cov schedule --cov-report term-missing`), and — verified working — `python -m unittest test_schedule`. There is no pre-commit hook, no `Makefile` test target at the repository root, and no `tox -e py` shortcut.

#### 6.6.4.3 Parallel Test Execution

Parallelism exists at exactly one level — the CI matrix — and nowhere below it.

| Level | Configuration | Degree |
|---|---|---|
| CI jobs | Independent jobs with no `needs` except `coveralls` | `test`, `docs`, `formatting`, `setuppy` run concurrently |
| Interpreter matrix | `strategy: max-parallel: 6` (line 15) | All six versions run at once |
| `tox` environments within a leg | Sequential (`tox` default, no `-p` flag) | The two environments for a version run one after the other |
| Test methods | Sequential — `pytest-xdist` is not a dependency and `-n` is never passed | One process, one thread |
| Coverage aggregation | `COVERALLS_PARALLEL: true` with `COVERALLS_FLAG_NAME: python-${{ matrix.python-version }}` | Six independent uploads, then one `--finish` |

Intra-suite parallelism would deliver nothing here and would actively harm correctness: the suite completes in 0.12 seconds, and its determinism depends on mutating two pieces of **process-global** state — the `TZ` environment variable and the `datetime.datetime` binding — which cannot be shared safely across concurrent workers in one interpreter. The single-process model is therefore a correctness requirement, not a limitation.

#### 6.6.4.4 Test Reporting Requirements

| Report | Producer | Destination |
|---|---|---|
| Per-test results | `py.test … -v` | GitHub Actions job log (verbose, one line per test) |
| Coverage summary with uncovered lines | `--cov schedule --cov-report term-missing` | Same job log, per environment |
| Aggregated coverage across interpreters | `coveralls --service=github` per leg, then `coveralls --finish` | Coveralls: combined report, PR summary comment, badge |
| Type-check findings | `mypy -p schedule` | Job log; non-zero exit fails the environment |
| Documentation build findings | `sphinx-build -W` | Job log; any warning fails the job |
| Formatting findings | `black --check .` | Job log; lists non-conforming files |
| Public status | Workflow badge and Coveralls badge | `README.rst` lines 5–12 |

Three reporting artifacts that many pipelines produce are **absent here**: there is no JUnit/XML report (`--junitxml` is never passed), no `actions/upload-artifact` step, and no HTML coverage report or published coverage history inside the repository — `.gitignore` treats `.coverage` and `.tox` as local-only. Consequently the CI job log plus the Coveralls project page constitute the complete record of a run, and authentication for the upload uses only the per-run `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

#### 6.6.4.5 Failed Test Handling

Failure semantics are strict, fast, and entirely conventional — with one ordering detail worth knowing.

| Failure | Immediate effect | Downstream effect |
|---|---|---|
| Any test fails or errors | `pytest` exits non-zero, so the `tox` environment fails | The matrix leg fails; `needs: test` prevents `coveralls` from finalising |
| A `mypy` finding | The environment fails at command 2 | Same as above. Because commands run in order, `mypy` executes **only after** the suite passes in that environment |
| One matrix leg fails | GitHub's default `fail-fast: true` applies (`fail-fast` is not overridden) | Remaining in-flight legs are cancelled — the fastest signal, but a partial matrix picture |
| Coveralls upload fails | The step fails and the leg is marked failed | Reporting degrades; no retry is configured |
| `docs`, `formatting`, or `setuppy` fails | That gate job fails independently | Does not cancel the `test` matrix; each gate is an independent verdict |
| A test regression reaches `master` | No automatic revert or issue creation exists | Handled socially: the failing status and the Coveralls comment are the notification channel |

There is **no retry or rerun machinery anywhere**: `pytest-rerunfailures` is not a dependency, `--reruns` is never passed, `continue-on-error` is never set, and no step retries a network install. A transient PyPI or Coveralls failure therefore fails the run and must be re-triggered manually, which is the trade the project accepts in exchange for an unambiguous signal.

#### 6.6.4.6 Flaky Test Management

The project's approach to flakiness is **prevention by construction rather than detection by retry**, and the repository contains evidence of both the hazard and the fix. `HISTORY.rst` records for release 1.2.0: "Fix `test_until_time` failure when run early. See #563." — a genuine time-dependent flake in the `until()` deadline test, resolved by correcting the test rather than by tolerating the failure. `HISTORY.rst` also records an earlier investment in the same direction: "Refactored unit tests to mock `datetime` in a cleaner way", which is the ancestry of today's `mock_datetime` manager.

Four controls keep the suite deterministic, and each was verified directly against this checkout:

| Control | Mechanism | Verification performed |
|---|---|---|
| Clock determinism | `mock_datetime` freezes `datetime.datetime` for 81 blocks, with `fold` control for ambiguous instants | 5 consecutive runs: `81 passed` every time, 0.11–0.12 s |
| Host-timezone immunity | Module-level `os.environ["TZ"] = TZ_BERLIN` + `time.tzset()` before any test runs | `TZ=Pacific/Kiritimati python -m pytest test_schedule.py -q` → `81 passed` |
| Order independence | `setUp` calls `schedule.clear()`; the context manager restores `datetime.datetime` and `TZ` on exit | Randomized method order (seeds 1, 7, 42) → 81 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors each time |
| Environment tolerance | `skipTest("pytz unavailable")` guards convert a missing optional dependency into skips instead of errors | Blocked `pytz` import → `40 passed, 41 skipped`, no failures |

No flake-detection tooling exists — there is no `pytest-randomly`, no repeated-run job, no quarantine marker, and no historical flake dashboard. Two residual risks remain visible in the code and should be stated: tests that do **not** enter a `mock_datetime` block read the real clock (for example `test_until_time`, the very test that flaked in #563, and `test_idle_seconds`), and the timezone tests depend on the IANA data shipped by whatever unpinned `pytz` version the environment resolves, so a future zone-rule change is a theoretical source of drift.

```mermaid

    subgraph Triggers["Trigger layer - ci.yml lines 3 to 9"]
```

**Diagram 6.6.4-A — Test execution flow: trigger, the six-leg matrix that expands to twelve environments, the ordered per-environment command pair with its two gates, the three independent gate jobs, and coverage finalisation.** Every path shown is executed by the repository's single workflow; nothing on this diagram is aspirational.


### 6.6.5 Quality Metrics and Quality Gates

This sub-section distinguishes rigorously between metrics the repository **enforces** and metrics it merely **publishes**. The distinction matters: only two of the five CI gates concern test outcomes, and coverage is not among them.

#### 6.6.5.1 Code Coverage Targets

| Coverage dimension | Value | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Enforced threshold | None — no `--cov-fail-under`, `.coveragerc`, or `[tool.coverage]` exists | **Not gated** |
| Stated aspiration | "Excellent test coverage" (`README.rst`); "Increased test coverage to 100%" (`HISTORY.rst`, release 0.1.9) | Project norm |
| Published figure | Coveralls badge for `master`, combined across six interpreters | Reported |
| Measured, `pytz` present | 434 of 438 executable lines in `schedule/__init__.py` = **99.1%** | Verified in this environment |
| Measured, `pytz` absent | 413 of 438 = **94.3%** (41 tests skip) | Verified in this environment |
| Measurement scope | `--cov schedule` — the package only | `test_schedule.py` is excluded |

The four uncovered lines and their unreachability are itemised in 6.6.2.4. The operative conclusion for a maintainer is that coverage in this project is a **review signal, not a build gate**: a change that removed tests would still pass CI provided the remaining tests passed, and the regression would surface only in the Coveralls comment on the pull request.

#### 6.6.5.2 Test Success Rate Requirements

The requirement is absolute and binary: **every collected test must pass in every one of the twelve `tox` environments.** There is no tolerated-failure budget, no `xfail` marker anywhere in the suite, no `continue-on-error`, and no rerun allowance (6.6.4.5).

| Metric | Requirement | Measured against this checkout |
|---|---|---|
| Pass rate, `pytz` installed | 100% of 81 tests | `81 passed in 0.12s` — 5 consecutive identical runs |
| Pass rate, `pytz` absent | 100% of collected tests | `40 passed, 41 skipped in 0.10s` — zero failures |
| Order-independence | No test may depend on execution order | Randomized order, seeds 1/7/42 → 81 passed each |
| Host-environment independence | Result must not vary with the machine's timezone | `TZ=Pacific/Kiritimati` → `81 passed` |
| Type-check findings | Zero, in every environment | Gate configured in `tox.ini`; `mypy` not installed in this measurement sandbox |

Skips are treated as success by design, and the semantics are precise: a skip means "this assertion requires the optional dependency, which this environment deliberately lacks", not "this assertion is unreliable". Because the matrix always contains a paired `-pytz` environment for the same interpreter, every skipped test is guaranteed to have been executed elsewhere in the same CI run.

#### 6.6.5.3 Performance Test Thresholds

**No performance thresholds are defined anywhere in this repository** — no latency budget, no throughput floor, no memory ceiling, no timeout on any test or job, and no benchmark harness to measure against (6.6.3.7). The only performance figure with a defensible basis is the cost of the verification pipeline itself, recorded here because 6.6.6 depends on it:

| Observed figure | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Whole-suite wall time | 0.11–0.12 s | Five runs, Python 3.12.3, `pytz` installed |
| Mean cost per test | ≈1.5 ms | 81 tests in 0.12 s; no test performs I/O |
| Longest single test | `test_tz_minutes_year_round` (108 lines, a full simulated year) | Still sub-second — the clock is frozen, never slept on |
| Slowest CI activity | Environment construction (`pip install` of `pytest`, `pytest-cov`, `mypy`, `types-pytz`, optionally `pytz`) per `tox` environment | Dominates the run; the suite itself is negligible |

The absence of a job `timeout-minutes` is worth flagging as a consequence: a hung `pip` resolution or a pathological test would run until GitHub's default job limit rather than failing fast.

#### 6.6.5.4 Quality Gates

Five gates guard `master`, expressed entirely as `tox` environments invoked by CI jobs. Each has a distinct blocking scope.

| Gate | Mechanism | Blocking scope |
|---|---|---|
| Test suite | `py.test test_schedule.py schedule -v --cov schedule --cov-report term-missing` | Each of the 12 environments independently; a single failure fails the leg |
| Static types | `python -m mypy -p schedule --install-types --non-interactive` | Same 12 environments; runs only after the suite passes in that environment |
| Documentation build | `sphinx-build -W -b html` via `tox -e docs` | One job; **any Sphinx warning** fails it |
| Code formatting | `black --check .` via `tox -e format` | One job; covers the whole tree including `test_schedule.py`; `black` pinned to `20.8b1` with `click==8.0.4` |
| Packaging metadata | `setup.py check --strict --metadata --restructuredtext` via `tox -e setuppy` | One job; validates required metadata and the reST that becomes the PyPI description |

What is deliberately **not** gated is equally important, because it defines the real quality perimeter:

| Concern | Gate status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Coverage percentage | Not gated | No `--cov-fail-under` or coverage config exists |
| Linting (`flake8`) | Not gated | `pytest-flake8` is a dev requirement and appears in `docs/development.rst` line 22, but `tox.ini` no longer passes `--flake8` |
| Type-checking of the test module | Not gated | `setup.cfg` limits `mypy` to `files=schedule` |
| Dependency vulnerabilities or licences | Not gated | No auditor, no lockfile, no Dependabot config (6.6.3.8) |
| Documentation link validity | Not gated | `docs/Makefile` provides `linkcheck`; no CI job runs it |
| Branch protection / required reviews | Not visible in-repository | Repository settings are outside the tree |

Two release-time gates exist outside CI and are executed manually per `docs/development.rst`: verification through a TestPyPI upload before the production upload, and the requirement to bump the version literal in **both** `setup.py` and `docs/conf.py`. Section 6.3.4.4 records that no workflow automates either step.

#### 6.6.5.5 Documentation Requirements

Documentation is the only non-test artifact with a hard CI gate, which makes its requirements part of the quality model rather than a courtesy.

| Requirement | Where it binds | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|
| Public API members carry reST docstrings with `:param:`/`:return:` field lists | `schedule/__init__.py` | `docs/reference.rst` autodoc renders them; `-W` catches malformed markup |
| Every public member appears in the reference | `docs/reference.rst` uses `:members:` and `:undoc-members:` | Automatic — undocumented members are still listed |
| Documentation must build warning-free | `docs/` | `tox -e docs`, `sphinx-build -W`, dedicated CI job |
| `README.rst` must be valid reST | Repository root | `tox -e setuppy`, `setup.py check --restructuredtext` |
| Behavioural contracts are documented, then asserted | `docs/*.rst` ↔ `test_schedule.py` | Convention: `test_run_pending`'s docstring restates the no-missed-jobs contract that `docs/index.rst` publishes |
| Timezone/DST expectations are stated as comments beside each assertion | `test_schedule.py` | Convention (6.6.2.6); the comments are the specification for each case |
| `HISTORY.rst` and `AUTHORS.rst` updated at release; version bumped in two files | Release procedure | Manual, per `docs/development.rst` |

Section 2.5.4 records the corollary that makes this section coherent: because `docs/` is built with warnings-as-errors on every push, its published behaviour claims are maintained deliberately and can be treated as contracts — and the test suite is therefore the acceptance criteria of record for those contracts.

#### 6.6.5.6 Verification Traceability Metrics

The following metrics summarise verification completeness as a testing-strategy view of the matrix in Section 2.5. They are reproduced here because they are the only requirement-level quality figures the project can produce.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Requirements catalogued (Section 2.5) | 50, across 17 features |
| Requirements with at least one automated test | 46 (92%) |
| Requirements verified by inspection/documentation only | 4 — `at()` unit guard, the no-scheduler branch of `do()`, exception propagation from a job body, log emission |
| Test methods available as verification assets | 81, all passing |
| Issue-numbered regression tests | 6 (upstream #592, #605, #608 ×4) |
| Distinct IANA timezones exercised | 15 |
| Environments enforcing the matrix | 12 `tox` environments driven by 5 CI jobs |
| Test-to-implementation line ratio | 1,599 : 945 = 1.69 : 1 |

The two views corroborate each other precisely: the requirement F-007-RQ-003 that Section 2.5 marks "verified by inspection" is exactly the branch at `schedule/__init__.py` lines 659–660 that this section measured as uncovered. Two of the remaining three inspection-only requirements are likewise structural — exception propagation is observable only by *not* handling it, and log emission is verified by reading `docs/logging.rst`'s sample output rather than by asserting on log records, since the suite installs no log handler or `assertLogs` capture.


### 6.6.6 Test Environment and Resource Requirements

There is no provisioned test environment in the infrastructure sense — no container image, no compose file, no seeded database, no service dependency, and no environment-specific configuration. A test environment here is a Python virtual environment created by `tox`, and everything the suite needs is inside it.

#### 6.6.6.1 Test Environment Architecture

| Layer | Composition | Provisioned by |
|---|---|---|
| Compute | GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners; five jobs, six matrix legs | GitHub Actions (`ci.yml`) |
| Interpreter | One of Python 3.7–3.12 per leg; Python 3.11 for each gate job | `actions/setup-python@v4` |
| Orchestrator | `tox` + `tox-gh-actions`, installed with `pip` | Workflow step, line 25 |
| Isolated environments | Twelve `tox` virtualenvs (`py3XX`, `py3XX-pytz`) plus `docs`, `format`, `setuppy` | `tox.ini` |
| System under test | The working tree, installed into each environment as a package | `tox` default sdist install |
| Process topology | One interpreter process per environment; no server, port, socket, or sidecar | — |

No environment-management code exists at all: no fixture provisions or tears down anything, no `docker-compose up` precedes a run, and no cleanup step follows one. The only mutable external state any test touches is the `TZ` environment variable of its own process, which the `mock_datetime` manager restores on exit.

| Environment | Installed dependencies | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `py37` … `py312` | `pytest`, `pytest-cov`, `mypy`, `types-pytz` | Prove the zero-required-dependency contract on each interpreter |
| `py37-pytz` … `py312-pytz` | The same, plus `pytz` | Exercise real timezone/DST behaviour; source of the 99.1% coverage figure |
| `docs` | `-rrequirements-dev.txt` | `sphinx-build -W` into a throwaway `{envtmpdir}` |
| `format` | `-rrequirements-dev.txt` | `black --check .` |
| `setuppy` | `-rrequirements-dev.txt` | `setup.py check --strict --metadata --restructuredtext` |

#### 6.6.6.2 Platform and Locale Requirements

The suite imposes one requirement that the library itself does not: **a Unix-like platform with POSIX timezone support.** `test_schedule.py` line 30 calls `time.tzset()` — a function the Python standard library provides on Unix only — and the suite drives it with POSIX `TZ` strings such as `"<+1245>-12:45<+1345>,M9.5.0/2:45,M4.1.0/3:45"` (line 25), whose interpretation is a C-library facility.

| Requirement | Value | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Operating system for testing | Unix-like (all five CI jobs run `ubuntu-latest`; there is no Windows or macOS leg) | The suite as written is Unix-oriented, although `setup.py` classifies the library "Operating System :: OS Independent" |
| Process timezone | Pinned to `CET-1CEST,M3.5.0,M10.5.0/3` at import, overridden per block where needed | Removes any dependency on the runner's ambient timezone — verified with `TZ=Pacific/Kiritimati` |
| Timezone database | Whatever the resolved, unpinned `pytz` provides in `-pytz` environments | IANA rule changes are a theoretical source of drift (6.6.4.6) |
| Locale, filesystem, ports | No requirement — nothing is formatted per locale, written to disk, or bound to a port | No sandbox or permission setup needed |

#### 6.6.6.3 Resource Requirements for Test Execution

Measured against this checkout (Python 3.12.3, `pytz` installed, single Linux x86_64 container):

| Resource | Measured requirement | Note |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | Single core sufficient; 0.94 s user + 0.09 s system for the whole process | No parallel workers; concurrency is precluded by design (6.6.4.3) |
| Peak memory | ≈65 MiB peak RSS for the entire `pytest` process | Dominated by interpreter and plugin import, not by test data |
| Wall time | 0.12 s reported test phase; ≈1.0 s including interpreter start-up and collection | Per environment; the CI cost is dominated by `pip install` |
| Disk | 264 KiB working tree (excluding `.git`); artifacts are `.coverage`, `.tox`, `.pytest_cache` | All git-ignored; nothing is published from the tree |
| Network | Not required by the tests; required to build every environment | `pip install` of the test tooling, plus `mypy --install-types` and the Coveralls upload in CI |
| Credentials | Only `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN`, used by the two Coveralls steps | No other secret appears in `ci.yml` |
| External services | None during test execution | Coveralls participates only after the suite completes |

The practical significance is that this verification pipeline is essentially free to run: the twelve-environment matrix exists because interpreter coverage is cheap, not because the suite is expensive.

#### 6.6.6.4 Developer and Redistributor Environments

`docs/development.rst` defines the local workflow: install `requirements-dev.txt`, run the published `py.test` command, format with `black` — with the explicit instruction to use version `20.8b1` — and build the docs with `cd docs && make html`. Two properties make local execution forgiving: `tox.ini` sets `skip_missing_interpreters = true`, so a developer with only one Python version still gets a clean run over the environments they can build; and the timezone pin means a developer in any timezone sees the same results as CI.

`MANIFEST.in` includes `test_schedule.py` in the source distribution. This is a deliberate choice with a testing consequence: downstream packagers — the Debian, Ubuntu, Arch, and conda-forge channels enumerated in `docs/installation.rst`, none of which the project maintains — can execute the full suite against the exact sources they ship, without cloning the repository. Because the suite depends on nothing but `pytest` (or `unittest`) and optionally `pytz`, that is a single command in a packaging build.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Sources["Inputs to a verification run"]
        direction TB
        Tree["Working tree: schedule/ package,<br/>test_schedule.py, tox.ini"]
        Sdist["Source distribution including<br/>test_schedule.py via MANIFEST.in"]
        DevReqs["requirements-dev.txt for the<br/>docs, format and setuppy environments"]
    end
    subgraph CIRunner["CI runner - ubuntu-latest, one per job"]
        direction TB
        Py["Interpreter installed by setup-python@v4:<br/>3.7 to 3.12 in the matrix, 3.11 for gate jobs"]
        ToxCore["tox plus tox-gh-actions from PyPI"]
        Py --> ToxCore
    end
    subgraph Envs["Isolated tox environments - one virtualenv each"]
        direction TB
        Plain["py3XX: pytest, pytest-cov, mypy, types-pytz<br/>no pytz - proves zero-dependency import"]
        WithTz["py3XX-pytz: the same plus pytz<br/>exercises real IANA and DST rules"]
        Utility["docs, format, setuppy:<br/>full requirements-dev.txt"]
    end
    subgraph ProcState["Per-process state the suite controls"]
        direction TB

        TzPin --> Clock --> Registry
    end
    subgraph Outputs["Outputs of a run"]

    end
    Tree --> Py

    DevReqs --> Utility
    ToxCore --> Plain

    Registry --> LogOut
```
