# 7. User Interface Design

## 7.1 User Interface Assessment

**No user interface required.**

The system documented by this specification is the Python `schedule` library at release 1.2.2 (`setup.py` line 5). It is an in-process, import-only library whose entire shipped artifact is two files — `schedule/__init__.py` (945 lines) and the zero-byte PEP 561 marker `schedule/py.typed`. It renders nothing, serves nothing, and prompts for nothing. There is no screen, view, route, template, stylesheet, widget, form, terminal interface, or command-line entry point anywhere in the distributed package, and consequently none of the conventional user-interface concerns — screen inventories, UI schemas, interaction models, or visual design systems — has any subject matter in this repository.

### 7.1.1 Determination

Every structural precondition for a user interface was tested against the checkout and every one of them fails. The determination is therefore established by verification rather than inferred from the small size of the codebase.

| Precondition for a user interface | Verification performed | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| A UI, web, or template framework dependency | `pyproject.toml` declares `dependencies = []`; `setup.py` declares no `install_requires`; `requirements-dev.txt` and `tox.ini` list only pytest, pytest-cov, pytest-flake8, mypy, types-pytz, pytz, black, click, Sphinx, docutils, and Pygments | **Fails** — the only optional runtime package is `pytz`, imported lazily inside `Job.at()` at line 499 |
| Markup, styling, or script assets in the product | Extension histogram over the complete 32-file tracked inventory: 16 `.rst`, 4 `.py`, 2 `.txt`, and one each of `.yml`, `.typed`, `.toml`, `.ini`, `.in`, `.html`, `.css`, `.cfg`, plus `Makefile` | **Fails** — zero JavaScript/TypeScript files; the single `.html` and single `.css` are both under `docs/` (see 7.1.3), never inside `schedule/` |
| A view, page, route, or component directory | `schedule/` contains exactly one first-order child, `schedule/__init__.py`, plus the `py.typed` marker shipped through `package_data` | **Fails** — no `templates/`, `static/`, `assets/`, `views/`, `pages/`, `components/`, or `ui/` folder exists in the package |
| A launchable executable or GUI script | `setup.py` declares no `entry_points`, `console_scripts`, or `gui_scripts`; `pyproject.toml` declares no `[project.scripts]` or `[project.gui-scripts]` | **Fails** — the distribution is import-only; nothing can be launched by a user |
| A runnable module or interactive prompt | Scan of `schedule/` for `__main__`, `sys.argv`, `argparse`, `input(`, and direct `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` writes | **Fails** — none present; the sole `print(` in the module is inside the docstring example at line 25, and it belongs to the *reader's* job function |
| A terminal/TUI or desktop/mobile toolkit | Repository-wide case-insensitive sweep for `curses`, `textual`, `prompt_toolkit`, `blessed`, `urwid`, `npyscreen`, `rich`, `tkinter`, `PyQt`, `PySide`, `wxPython`, `kivy`, `electron`, `flet`, `nicegui`, `pywebview` | **Fails** — zero matches across all tracked files |
| A served UI or dashboard runtime | Sweep for `flask`, `django`, `fastapi`, `starlette`, `bottle`, `pyramid`, `tornado`, `aiohttp`, `uvicorn`, `gunicorn`, `wsgi`, `asgi`, `streamlit`, `dash`, `gradio`, `panel`, `bokeh`, `plotly`, `jinja2`, `mako`, `chameleon` | **Fails** — two false positives only, both in `docs/conf.py`: the commented-out `flask_theme_support` Pygments style at line 114 and the word "dashes" in the SmartyPants comment |
| A frontend build or browser test pipeline | Sweep for `react`, `vue`, `angular`, `svelte`, `tailwind`, `bootstrap`, `jquery`, `webpack`, `vite`, `rollup`, `babel`, `eslint`, `selenium`, `playwright`, `cypress`, `puppeteer`; review of `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and `tox.ini` | **Fails** — zero matches; CI runs only `test`, `coveralls`, `docs`, `formatting`, and `setuppy`, with no Node/npm setup, bundling step, browser matrix, or visual-regression/accessibility stage |
| Presentation or transport code in the runtime | Scan of `schedule/` and `test_schedule.py` for `render`, `template`, `html`, `css`, `javascript`, `browser`, `socket`, `http.server`, `urllib`, `requests`, `localhost`, `bind(`, `listen(`, `port=` | **Fails** — zero matches in either file |

The import set of the runtime module is the decisive artifact: eight standard-library imports at `schedule/__init__.py` lines 41–48 (`collections.abc.Hashable`, `datetime`, `functools`, `logging`, `random`, `re`, `time`, `typing`) and one function-local `import pytz` at line 499. Nothing in that graph is capable of drawing, serving, or reading a user interface.

### 7.1.2 Consistency With the Rest of This Specification

The determination is not local to this section — four previously written sections reach it independently from their own vantage points, and none contradicts it.

| Section | Corroborating finding |
|---|---|
| 1.2 System Overview | §1.2.1.3 records that "There is no server, daemon, CLI entry point, or network listener anywhere in the package," and that every integration surface lies inside the host application |
| 1.3 Scope | §1.3.1.2 states the audience is Python developers embedding the scheduler and that "there is no end-user interface of any kind in the repository"; the boundary table places "HTTP, RPC, CLI, message brokers" outside the system, leaving "Python function/property calls only" inside; §1.3.2.1 enumerates "no CLI, no configuration file format, no admin or web interface" among the excluded artifacts |
| 3.2 Frameworks & Libraries | Opens by recording that "the shipped package uses no application framework at all," and classifies the repository's only HTML and CSS files as Sphinx **theme overrides** rather than product assets |
| 5.1 High-Level Architecture | Describes the style as an "in-process embedded library," a passive component driven by the host; its four-layer model — Facade, Domain, Contract, Substrate — contains **no presentation layer**, and §5.1.1.4 enumerates exactly four boundary interfaces, none of them presentational |

### 7.1.3 Documentation-Site Artifacts Are Not a Product User Interface

Two files in the repository contain markup and styling, and both belong to the project's *documentation website* rather than to the software product. They are recorded here explicitly so that a reader searching for `.html` or `.css` does not mistake them for a screen.

| Artifact | What it actually is | Why it is not product UI |
|---|---|---|
| `docs/_templates/sidebarintro.html` (~14 lines) | A static sidebar fragment for the Sphinx **alabaster** theme, listed in `docs/conf.py` alongside four theme-supplied templates (`about.html`, `globaltoc.html`, `relations.html`, `searchbox.html`) in `html_sidebars["**"]` | Contains only outbound links (GitHub repository, PyPI page, issue tracker, and author links) plus one third-party Twitter follow-button script. No form, no input, no state, no data binding, and no call into the library |
| `docs/_static/custom.css` (3 lines) | A single alabaster override supplied through `html_static_path = ["_static"]`, adjusting table-of-contents spacing with `.toctree-l1 { padding-bottom: 4px; }` | This one declaration is the entire styling surface of the repository; it styles a generated documentation page, not an application |

Three packaging facts settle the classification:

1. **The assets are not distributed.** `MANIFEST.in` includes only `README.rst`, `HISTORY.rst`, `LICENSE.txt`, and `test_schedule.py`; there is no `recursive-include` for `docs/`, `static/`, or `templates/`. An installed copy of the library contains neither file.
2. **The output is generated, never committed.** `.gitignore` excludes `docs/_build`, and `tox.ini` builds documentation into a temporary directory with `sphinx-build -W -b html -d {envtmpdir}/doctrees . {envtmpdir}/html`. The published site is hosted externally at the `Documentation` URL declared in `pyproject.toml`.
3. **The theme itself is external.** `docs/conf.py` sets `html_theme = "alabaster"`, a theme obtained through the Sphinx installation rather than vendored into the repository, so even the bulk of the documentation's presentation is not authored here.

The documentation set is thirteen reStructuredText pages totalling 1,029 lines, navigated by the `toctree` directives in `docs/index.rst`; its API reference page, `docs/reference.rst`, is generated entirely from source docstrings via `.. module:: schedule` with `autodata`, `autofunction`, `autoclass`, and `autoexception` directives. That the project's only "pages" are auto-generated API reference pages is itself confirmation that the product's interface is an API, not a graphical one.

### 7.1.4 Where a User Interface Would Sit Relative to This System

Because the library is embedded, any user interface belongs to the adopting application, one tier above the boundary this repository defines. The diagram below places the three tiers that exist in and around the checkout and shows that the presentation tier is empty by design.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph AdopterTier["Adopter-owned tier - any user interface would live here, outside this repository"]
        direction TB
        AnyUI["Optional UI built by the adopter:<br/>web, desktop, terminal, or none at all"]
        HostApp["Host application code:<br/>declares jobs and owns the driver loop"]
        AnyUI -.->|"no such component exists in this repository"| HostApp
    end
    subgraph LibraryTier["schedule 1.2.2 - the documented system, two shipped files, no presentation layer"]
        direction TB
        Facade["Module facade: every, run_pending, run_all, get_jobs,<br/>clear, cancel_job, next_run, idle_seconds, repeat"]
        Domain["Domain objects: Scheduler registry and Job fluent builder"]
        Diag["Diagnostics: logger named schedule,<br/>8 DEBUG records, no handler attached"]
        Facade --> Domain
        Domain --> Diag
    end
    subgraph AuthorTier["Author-time documentation site - docs/, excluded from the wheel by MANIFEST.in"]
        direction TB
        SphinxBuild["Sphinx build gated by sphinx-build -W"]
        ThemeFiles["alabaster theme overrides:<br/>_templates/sidebarintro.html and _static/custom.css"]
        Published["Generated HTML published on Read the Docs"]
        SphinxBuild --> ThemeFiles
        ThemeFiles --> Published
    end
    HostApp -->|"import schedule, then fluent method calls"| Facade
    Domain -->|"synchronous call back into the host callable"| HostApp
    SphinxBuild -.->|"autodoc reads docstrings only, never renders product state"| Facade
```

**Diagram 7.1-A — Tier placement.** The middle tier is the system under specification and has no presentation layer. The upper tier is where a user interface would be built, and it is owned entirely by the adopter. The lower tier produces HTML, but only as documentation about the library, and it is never part of the installed artifact.


## 7.2 Interaction Surfaces in Place of a User Interface

Since no user interface exists, this sub-section records what actually occupies the interaction position, so that the assessment above is useful rather than merely negative. Three surfaces carry every interaction a person can have with this system, and all three are addressed to a *developer* writing Python, not to an end user operating a screen.

### 7.2.1 The Programmatic Configuration Surface

The library's "front end" is a fluent builder grammar in `schedule/__init__.py`. What a graphical scheduler would express through form fields and pickers, this system expresses as a readable method chain evaluated by the Python interpreter. The module docstring at lines 6–7 names the mechanism explicitly as the builder pattern, and `README.rst` markets its readability as the product's differentiator.

```python
schedule.every().wednesday.at("13:15").do(job)      # weekday + clock anchor
schedule.every(5).to(10).minutes.do(job, name="Peter")   # jitter + bound argument
```

| Surface element | Vocabulary | Location in `schedule/__init__.py` |
|---|---|---|
| Entry point | `every(interval=1)` returning an unregistered `Job`, delegating to `default_scheduler` | Facade line 843; method line 162 |
| Interval selection | `second`/`seconds`, `minute`/`minutes`, `hour`/`hours`, `day`/`days`, `week`/`weeks` — singular forms valid only when the interval is 1 | Properties at lines 326–376 |
| Weekday selection | `monday` through `sunday`, restricted to a one-week interval | Properties at lines 381–447 |
| Modifiers | `at(time_str, tz=None)`, `to(latest)`, `until(...)`, `tag(*tags)` | Lines 471, 561, 576, 457 |
| Commit action | `do(job_func, *args, **kwargs)` — binds the callable, computes the first occurrence, and registers the job | Line 644 |
| Declarative registration | `repeat(job, *args, **kwargs)` decorator factory, registering at import time and returning the function unchanged | Line 899 |
| Control and query operations | `run_pending`, `run_all`, `get_jobs`, `clear`, `cancel_job`, `next_run`, `idle_seconds` | Facade lines 850–892; `Scheduler` lines 89–206 |

The immediate consequence for this section is that "user interactions" in this system are **source-code expressions**, not events. There is no click, keypress, focus change, submit, drag, or navigation event anywhere in the repository, because there is no event source. Validation feedback likewise has no visual channel: misconfiguration surfaces as a raised exception from the typed hierarchy `ScheduleError` → `ScheduleValueError` → `IntervalError` (lines 53–68), with messages written for a developer reading a traceback — for example, the guard on a singular unit accessor raises `IntervalError("Use seconds instead of second")`.

### 7.2.2 The Textual Output Surface

The library emits human-readable text through exactly two channels, both of which serve debugging and diagnostics rather than presentation.

| Channel | Behavior | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Named logger | A single `logging.getLogger("schedule")` instance emits DEBUG-level records at eight sites; the library attaches no handler and sets no level, so nothing appears unless the host opts in | `schedule/__init__.py` line 50 and lines 113, 144, 147, 157, 160, 687, 690, 696; `docs/logging.rst` |
| Object renderings | `Job.__str__` produces the compact form `Job(interval=…, unit=…, do=…, args=…, kwargs=…)`; `Job.__repr__` produces a human sentence of the shape `Every 5 to 10 minutes do job() (last run: …, next run: [never])`, with an `at`-time variant and `[never]` substituted for unset timestamps | Lines 264–323 |

`docs/logging.rst` documents this contract and makes the ownership boundary explicit: it shows the host enabling the channel with `logging.basicConfig()` and `setLevel(logging.DEBUG)`, and its "Customize logging" recipe hands responsibility for any richer presentation to the integrator through a host-authored `print_elapsed_time` decorator. In other words, the closest thing to a "view model" in this codebase is `Job.__repr__`, and even that exists for REPL and log inspection rather than for display to a user.

### 7.2.3 The Tooling and Editor Affordance Surface

The one place where the project invests in something resembling a designed experience is the developer's editor. That investment is machine-readable type information rather than visual design.

| Element | Purpose | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|
| `schedule/py.typed` | Zero-byte PEP 561 marker declaring that the package ships inline type information, so downstream type checkers and editors can resolve the fluent chain | Shipped via `package_data={"schedule": ["py.typed"]}` in `setup.py` |
| Inline annotations | `Set`, `List`, `Optional`, `Callable`, and `Union` imported at line 48 and applied across the public surface, giving autocomplete and inline validation over the builder grammar | `setup.cfg` sets `[mypy] files=schedule`; `tox.ini` runs `python -m mypy -p schedule` in every environment |
| Autodoc reference | `docs/reference.rst` renders the same surface into browsable API pages, gated by `sphinx-build -W` | `tox.ini` `[testenv:docs]`; the `docs` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |

### 7.2.4 Applicability of Each User-Interface Topic

For completeness and traceability, each topic that a User Interface Design section would normally cover is recorded below against the reason it has no subject matter here. No entry is speculative; each cites the artifact that establishes the absence.

| Topic | Status | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Core UI technologies | Not applicable | No UI, web, template, or styling technology is declared or imported anywhere; `pyproject.toml` declares `dependencies = []` and the runtime imports are the eight standard-library modules at lines 41–48 plus optional `pytz` |
| UI use cases | Not applicable | The fourteen supported workflows catalogued in `docs/examples.rst` are all API call sequences performed by developer code; none involves a person operating an interface |
| UI / backend interaction boundaries | Not applicable | There is no UI tier and no backend tier. The single boundary is a Python import boundary crossed by direct in-process calls, documented in 5.1.1.3 and 6.3.1.2; no HTTP, RPC, or serialization exists in the repository |
| UI schemas | Not applicable | No view model, DTO, form schema, JSON Schema, OpenAPI document, or IDL exists. Data crossing the boundary is live Python objects — the `functools.partial` bound in `do()` at line 655 — and the machine-readable contract is type annotations plus `py.typed` |
| Screens required | Not applicable | Zero screens, views, routes, or pages exist. The complete 32-file tracked inventory contains one `.html` file and one `.css` file, both Sphinx theme overrides under `docs/` (see 7.1.3), and the `schedule/` package contains no template or asset of any kind |
| User interactions | Not applicable | No event source exists. Interaction is expressed as fluent method chains in the host's source code (7.2.1); the only outbound signal from a job body back into the library is the `CancelJob` sentinel at lines 71–76 |
| Visual design considerations | Not applicable | No design tokens, palette, typography scale, spacing system, layout grid, responsive breakpoints, iconography, theming, or accessibility affordance exists. The repository's entire styling surface is the three-line `docs/_static/custom.css` |
| Accessibility and internationalization of a UI | Not applicable | No UI to make accessible; there is also no localization layer of any kind — `setup.py` carries the `Natural Language :: English` classifier and the documentation is English-only reStructuredText |

### 7.2.5 Conditions That Would Make This Section Applicable

This assessment is tied to observable artifacts, so it should be revisited only if one of them changes. The appearance of any of the following in the repository would introduce a genuine user interface and require this section to be rewritten with real content:

- A `console_scripts` or `gui_scripts` entry in `setup.py`, or a `[project.scripts]` / `[project.gui-scripts]` table in `pyproject.toml`, creating a launchable command.
- A `__main__` module or an `if __name__ == "__main__"` block inside `schedule/`, creating a runnable interface.
- A UI, web, TUI, or template-engine package added to `dependencies` in `pyproject.toml` or to `install_requires` in `setup.py`.
- A template, static-asset, view, or component directory added inside the `schedule/` package, together with the `MANIFEST.in` or `package_data` directives needed to distribute it.
- A frontend toolchain manifest (for example `package.json`) or a CI stage in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` that installs Node, bundles assets, or drives a browser.

Until then, the applicable statement for this section remains: **No user interface required.**

# 8. Infrastructure

## 8.1 Deployment Environment

**Detailed Infrastructure Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

`schedule` is a single-module, pure-Python library that is imported into a host application's process. It is not a service, and nothing in the repository provisions, configures, or operates a runtime environment. The determination is supported by exhaustive negative evidence: the tracked tree contains exactly **32 files totalling 166,428 bytes** (`git ls-files`), and a glob search across those tracked files returns *no* match for any of the following artifact classes:

| Artifact class searched | Patterns | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Containers | `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose*` | None |
| Infrastructure as Code | `*.tf`, `*.tfvars`, CloudFormation/Pulumi/Ansible files | None |
| Orchestration | `Chart.yaml`, `kustomization*`, `*.nomad` | None |
| Process supervision | `Procfile`, `*.service` (systemd) | None |
| Alternate CI/CD systems | `.travis*`, `.gitlab-ci*`, `Jenkinsfile`, `azure-pipelines*`, `cloudbuild*`, `appveyor*`, `.circleci` | None |
| Runtime/secret configuration | `*.env*`, `*.lock`, `*.sh`, `*.bat`, `*.ps1` | None |

The only YAML file in the repository is `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; the only `Makefile` is `docs/Makefile`; the only configuration files are `tox.ini`, `setup.cfg`, and `pyproject.toml`. The library source itself (`schedule/__init__.py`) imports only the standard library — `collections.abc`, `datetime`, `functools`, `logging`, `random`, `re`, `time`, `typing` (lines 41–48) — and contains zero references to sockets, subprocesses, file I/O, serialization, environment variables, or HTTP clients. Section 3.6 of this specification reaches the same conclusion from the build-system perspective: "deployment" here means **publishing a package**, not operating a service.

What therefore *does* exist, and what the remainder of Section 8 documents, is a two-part infrastructure surface:

1. **A build, verification, and distribution plane** — GitHub-hosted Actions runners, tox-managed ephemeral interpreters, setuptools artifact generation, and publication to TestPyPI/PyPI with documentation hosting on Read the Docs.
2. **A set of host-environment requirements and sizing characteristics** the library imposes on whatever process a consumer embeds it into.

### 8.1.1 Target Environment Assessment

#### 8.1.1.1 Environment Classification

Three distinct environments participate in the lifecycle of this project. Only the middle one is cloud-hosted, and it is consumed as multi-tenant SaaS rather than provisioned infrastructure.

| Environment | Type | Ownership |
|---|---|---|
| Maintainer workstation (development, artifact build, publication) | Unmanaged local machine | Individual maintainer |
| Build & verification plane (`ubuntu-latest` Actions runners) | Public-cloud SaaS, ephemeral | GitHub (provider-managed) |
| Distribution plane (PyPI, TestPyPI, Read the Docs, Coveralls) | Public-cloud SaaS | Third parties (see §3.4) |
| Consumer host process (the actual runtime of the library) | Undetermined — on-premises, cloud, container, or edge | Downstream consumer |

The repository makes **no on-premises/cloud/hybrid/multi-cloud election for runtime**, because it never runs as an independent workload. The `Operating System :: OS Independent` classifier (`setup.py` line 43) and the universal `py3-none-any` wheel tag deliberately leave the runtime environment unconstrained: one artifact is valid for every operating system and CPU architecture running a supported CPython. The single environmental constraint the project does assert is the interpreter floor, declared twice and consistently — `python_requires=">=3.7"` (`setup.py` line 54) and `requires-python = ">= 3.7"` (`pyproject.toml` line 12).

#### 8.1.1.2 Geographic Distribution Requirements

No geographic distribution requirement is expressed anywhere in the repository. There is no region configuration, no CDN definition, no replication topology, and no residency statement. The `ubuntu-latest` jobs in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` specify no runner region or label beyond the default GitHub-hosted pool, and global reach of the released artifact is entirely a property of PyPI's and Read the Docs' own infrastructure, which this project consumes but does not configure.

The one geography-adjacent concern the code *does* address is temporal rather than spatial: `Job.at()` accepts an IANA timezone string and performs a lazy `import pytz` at `schedule/__init__.py` line 499, converting the requested local wall-clock time into the host's own timezone. That capability lets a single scheduler instance serve jobs expressed in remote regions' local time without any infrastructure distribution, and it is the reason `pytz` exists as the sole optional dependency (`pyproject.toml` lines 19–20, `Requires-Dist: pytz; extra == "timezone"` in the built metadata) and as a dedicated `-pytz` tox factor (`tox.ini` line 21).

#### 8.1.1.3 Resource Requirements

Resource requirements are documented in three tiers: the build plane, the installation footprint, and the embedded runtime. All artifact sizes and runtime figures below were measured directly from a clean `git archive HEAD` export of the repository built with `setuptools 83.0.0` / `wheel 0.42.0` on CPython 3.12.3.

| Resource dimension | Build plane (per CI job) | Consumer runtime |
|---|---|---|
| Compute | Standard GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runner; no `runs-on` override, no larger-runner request | Fraction of one core; ~4.2 µs per `run_pending()` poll at 10 jobs, ~388 µs at 1,000 jobs |
| Memory | Provider default; workload is interpreter + pytest/mypy/tox, no compilation | ≈0.85–1.1 KB heap per registered trivial job, linear; well under 1 MB for 1,000 jobs |
| Storage | Ephemeral workspace; `.tox/` virtualenvs recreated per run (no cache configured) | 124 KB installed (12 files) after `pip install`; **zero** runtime disk usage — no persistence layer |
| Network | Egress to PyPI for `tox`, `tox-gh-actions`, `coveralls`, and per-env test deps; egress to Coveralls for upload | **Zero** — no sockets, no HTTP client, no outbound calls in the library |

Artifact and repository sizes, which bound storage requirements everywhere in the pipeline:

| Artifact | Size | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `schedule-1.2.2-py3-none-any.whl` | 12,319 bytes | `Root-Is-Purelib: true`, `Tag: py3-none-any`; carries `schedule/__init__.py`, `py.typed`, and `licenses/{LICENSE.txt, AUTHORS.rst}` |
| `schedule-1.2.2.tar.gz` (sdist) | 26,455 bytes | Adds `README.rst`, `HISTORY.rst`, `MANIFEST.in`, `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `pyproject.toml`, `test_schedule.py` |
| Installed on-disk footprint | 124 KB / 12 files | Measured via `pip install --target` of the wheel |
| Tracked repository (working tree) | 264 KB excluding `.git` | 32 files; `schedule/__init__.py` is 31,983 bytes, `py.typed` is empty |

#### 8.1.1.4 Resource Sizing Guidelines

Because the scheduler is a single in-process list scan, sizing is driven entirely by job count and poll interval rather than by request rate. The following guidance is extrapolated from the measurements above and from the canonical host loop documented in `docs/index.rst` (`while True: schedule.run_pending(); time.sleep(1)`).

| Registered jobs | Added heap (approx.) | Poll cost per second (approx.) |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | ~10 KB | ~4 µs |
| 100 | ~85 KB | ~40 µs |
| 1,000 | ~850 KB | ~390 µs |
| 10,000 | ~8.3 MB | ~4 ms |

Additional sizing rules that follow from observed behaviour:

- **Add the workload, not the scheduler.** The scheduler's own cost is negligible; the sizing driver is the job function bodies, which execute **serially on the calling thread** (`docs/parallel-execution.rst`). A single long job delays every other job on the same `Scheduler`.
- **Import cost is one-off.** Cold `import schedule` measured 10.79 ms, and `pytz` is *not* loaded unless a timezone-aware `.at()` is used — verified by `pytz` being absent from `sys.modules` after a plain import.
- **Partition with multiple `Scheduler()` instances** rather than by scaling hardware; `docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` presents this as the supported pattern "for larger installations", with `run_pending()` called on each instance in the host loop.
- **Provision no storage or network quota** for the library itself; `docs/index.rst` states plainly that job state does not survive a restart, so any durability budget belongs to the host application.

#### 8.1.1.5 Compliance and Regulatory Requirements

No regulatory framework is referenced anywhere in the 32 tracked files — there is no `SECURITY.md`, no compliance policy, no data-protection statement, and no audit configuration. The compliance obligations that *are* mechanically enforced are limited to licensing and packaging-metadata correctness:

| Obligation | Mechanism | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| MIT license must accompany every artifact | `MANIFEST.in` includes `LICENSE.txt`; the wheel embeds `dist-info/licenses/{LICENSE.txt, AUTHORS.rst}` | `MANIFEST.in` line 3; built wheel contents |
| License must be declared in machine-readable metadata | `license="MIT"` and the `License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License` classifier | `setup.py` lines 24, 41; `pyproject.toml` line 10 |
| Long description must be valid reStructuredText for PyPI rendering | `python setup.py check --strict --metadata --restructuredtext` as a blocking CI gate | `tox.ini` line 38; `ci.yml` lines 80–91 |
| Declared Python support must match tested support | Classifiers 3.7–3.12 mirror the CI matrix and the tox envlist | `setup.py` lines 46–51; `ci.yml` line 17; `tox.ini` line 2 |
| Typed-package declaration (PEP 561) | `py.typed` marker shipped via `package_data` | `setup.py` line 20 |

Two data-protection observations follow from the code rather than from policy: the library never opens a file, never opens a socket, and never serializes state, so it neither stores nor transmits any data of its own; and the only information it emits is DEBUG-level text on the `schedule` logger, whose content is derived from job metadata (see §6.5). Consequently the library introduces no data-residency or data-processing surface for a consumer's compliance programme.
