### 8.1.2 Environment Management

#### 8.1.2.1 Infrastructure as Code Approach

There is no Infrastructure as Code in the conventional sense: no Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi, Ansible, or Helm artifact exists in the tree. What the repository does maintain is a set of **declarative environment definitions** that provision *ephemeral interpreter environments* rather than infrastructure, and these are the closest functional analogue:

| Declarative file | What it provisions | Key declarations |
|---|---|---|
| `tox.ini` | 12 isolated virtualenvs plus 3 utility envs | `envlist = py3{7,8,9,10,11,12}{,-pytz}` (line 2); `skip_missing_interpreters = true` (line 3); per-env deps `pytest`, `pytest-cov`, `mypy`, `types-pytz`, conditional `pytz: pytz` (lines 16–21) |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | The runner fleet and job graph | `runs-on: ubuntu-latest`; `max-parallel: 6`; matrix of six Python versions (lines 13–17) |
| `pyproject.toml` | The build environment | `requires = ["setuptools >= 61.0"]`, `build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"` (PEP 517/518, lines 1–3) |
| `setup.py` / `setup.cfg` | Artifact composition and type-check scope | `packages`, `package_data` (lines 19–20); `[mypy] files=schedule` |

The `tox.ini` `[gh-actions]` block (lines 6–13) is the binding between the two planes: it maps each runner's Python version onto **two** tox environments (`py3X` and `py3X-pytz`), so the six-leg CI matrix actually materialises twelve independently provisioned virtualenvs per push — the with-`pytz` and without-`pytz` dependency states are both exercised for every supported interpreter. `skip_missing_interpreters = true` makes the same file usable on a developer machine that has only one interpreter installed, without editing it.

Two consequences of this approach are worth recording. First, environments are **re-provisioned from scratch on every run**: no `actions/cache` step and no `cache:` input to `setup-python` appears anywhere in the workflow, so each job re-resolves and re-downloads its dependencies. Second, because there is no lock file anywhere in the tree, environment provisioning is *not* bit-reproducible — `pip install tox tox-gh-actions`, `pip3 install coveralls`, and the unpinned `pytest`/`mypy` entries in `tox.ini` resolve to whatever is current on PyPI at run time. The only pinned tool versions in the entire repository are `black==20.8b1` and `click==8.0.4` in `requirements-dev.txt`.

#### 8.1.2.2 Configuration Management Strategy

The library has **no runtime configuration surface at all**. It reads no environment variable, no configuration file, and no command-line argument; behaviour is expressed exclusively through the Python API (`every(...).seconds.do(...)`, `Scheduler()`, `.at()`, `.tag()`). This is verified by the absence of `os.`, `open(`, `json`, and `configparser` usage in `schedule/__init__.py`. The one externally influenced behaviour is logging verbosity, which the host controls through the standard `logging` hierarchy for the logger named `schedule` (`schedule/__init__.py` line 50, documented in `docs/logging.rst`).

Configuration in the build and publication planes is managed as follows:

| Configuration domain | Where it lives | Management model |
|---|---|---|
| Test/lint/docs environments | `tox.ini`, `requirements-dev.txt`, `setup.cfg` | Version-controlled, edited by hand |
| Pipeline definition and job matrix | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Version-controlled, edited by hand per Python release |
| Release version string | `setup.py` line 5 and `docs/conf.py` lines 69/71 | Manual two-place bump, mandated by `docs/development.rst` line 53 |
| Registry credentials and docs hosting | Maintainer `~/.pypirc` (twine aliases `schedule`, `schedule-test`); Read the Docs project settings | **Outside version control**; the only in-repo secret reference is `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` at `ci.yml` lines 30 and 52 |

The absence of a `.readthedocs.yaml` file means the documentation build environment is configured entirely in the Read the Docs web interface. `docs/conf.py` line 40 preserves the fossil evidence of that coupling — `# 'sphinx.ext.githubpages',  # This breaks the ReadTheDocs build` — confirming Read the Docs is the intended host even though no in-repo file declares it.

#### 8.1.2.3 Environment Promotion Strategy

Promotion happens along two axes simultaneously: a **branch/ref axis** in GitHub and an **artifact axis** across registries. There are no long-lived dev/staging/prod *server* environments to promote between, because there is no running system; the staging analogue is TestPyPI and the production analogue is PyPI.

| Stage | Environment | Promotion trigger and gate |
|---|---|---|
| Local development | Developer virtualenv (`pip install -r requirements-dev.txt`) | Developer discretion; `tox` and `black .` run locally |
| Continuous verification | Ephemeral `ubuntu-latest` runners | Automatic on `push` or `pull_request` targeting `master` (`ci.yml` lines 3–9); all five jobs must pass |
| Release candidate | `release-X.Y.Z` branch merged to `master` | Human review of the release PR (evidenced by `origin/release-1.2.2`, whose tree is byte-identical to `master`) |
| Staging distribution | TestPyPI (`test.pypi.org/project/schedule`) | Manual `twine upload --repository schedule-test dist/*` (`docs/development.rst` line 64) |
| Production distribution | PyPI (`pypi.org/project/schedule`) | Manual `twine upload --repository schedule dist/*` (line 66) after the maintainer is satisfied with the staging upload |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    FEAT["Contributor fork / feature branch"] --> PR["Pull request -> master"]
    PR --> CI{"5 CI jobs pass?<br/>tests+mypy, docs, format, setup.py"}
    CI -->|no| FIX["Fix and re-push<br/>(no promotion)"]
    FIX --> PR
    CI -->|yes| MERGE["Merge to master<br/>(push re-runs full CI)"]
    MERGE --> RELB["release-X.Y.Z branch:<br/>HISTORY.rst, AUTHORS.rst,<br/>version bump in 2 files"]
    RELB --> RPR["Release PR -> master"]
    RPR --> TAG["git tag X.Y.Z -m 'Release X.Y.Z'<br/>git push --tags"]
    TAG --> BUILD["Local: python -m build --wheel"]
    BUILD --> STAGE["TestPyPI upload<br/>(staging verification)"]
    STAGE --> PROD["PyPI upload<br/>(production, immutable)"]
    PROD --> RTDB["Read the Docs rebuild<br/>(webhook)"]
    PROD --> DOWN["Downstream re-packagers:<br/>conda-forge, AUR, Debian/Ubuntu"]
```

Note two structural properties of this flow. The tag push is **not** a promotion trigger for any automation — `ci.yml` declares only `push` and `pull_request` on `master`, with no `tags:` filter, no `release:` event, and no `workflow_dispatch` — so tagging is a labelling act, not a deployment. And no GitHub deployment `environment:` is declared in the workflow, so there are no environment protection rules, required reviewers, or wait timers gating any promotion step; the gate between staging and production is entirely the maintainer's judgement.

#### 8.1.2.4 Backup and Disaster Recovery

There is no infrastructure to restore, so recovery planning reduces to preserving four assets: the source history, the released artifacts, the documentation, and the publication credentials.

| Asset | Backup mechanism observed | Recovery characteristics |
|---|---|---|
| Source history | Git's distributed model — GitHub is the primary, plus every clone; 398 commits and 27 tags (`0.1.1`…`1.2.2`) | Any complete clone can restore the repository; tag set defines every reproducible release point |
| Released artifacts | PyPI retains all published versions; each release is immutable once uploaded | **Roll-forward only** — a bad release cannot be overwritten, it must be superseded by a new version (`docs/development.rst` semantic-versioning note) |
| Build reproducibility | Artifacts are *not* retained by CI (no `upload-artifact` step anywhere) | Rebuild from a tag with `python -m build --wheel`; byte-identical rebuild is not guaranteed because build/test tooling is unpinned |
| Documentation | Rebuilt from `docs/*.rst` by Read the Docs; validated in CI by `sphinx-build -W` | Fully recoverable from source, **except** the RTD project configuration, which exists only in the RTD account |
| Credentials | `GITHUB_TOKEN` is auto-provisioned per run; PyPI/TestPyPI credentials live only in a maintainer's `~/.pypirc` | Single-holder credential is the principal continuity risk; no organisation-level secret store is referenced |

Disaster-recovery observations that follow directly from this evidence:

- **RPO/RTO are effectively bounded by Git and PyPI durability**, both of which are provider responsibilities; the project defines no objectives of its own.
- **The library's own state is intentionally non-durable.** `docs/index.rst` lists "job persistence across restarts" among the cases where Schedule is the wrong tool, and `docs/background-execution.rst` notes the documented background pattern also does not replay missed jobs. Any consumer needing recovery of *schedule state* must implement it outside the library.
- **Single-region, single-platform verification.** Every job runs on `ubuntu-latest`, so a GitHub Actions outage or an Ubuntu image regression halts all verification simultaneously; there is no secondary CI provider since Travis CI was removed in commit `82b45a6` (2020-12-04).

#### 8.1.2.5 Maintenance Procedures

| Procedure | Trigger | Actions required |
|---|---|---|
| Add support for a new Python release | Upstream CPython release | Edit the matrix in `ci.yml` line 17, the `envlist` and `[gh-actions]` map in `tox.ini`, and the classifier list in `setup.py`; precedent: commit `1173f28` "Add support for 3.12 (#606)" |
| Drop an end-of-life Python | Interpreter EOL / runner image removal | Reverse of the above plus a `python_requires` bump; precedent: `a171f1f` "Support python 3.10 and 3.11, drop python 3.6 (#575)" |
| Refresh pinned developer tooling | `black==20.8b1` / `click==8.0.4` drift | Update `requirements-dev.txt` and re-run `tox -e format`; the pin is load-bearing because `black`'s formatting changes between versions |
| Refresh action versions | Upstream action majors advance | Bump `actions/checkout@v3` and `actions/setup-python@v4` in `ci.yml`; both currently trail the upstream major (v7 as of August 2026) |
| Cut a release | Maintainer decision | Follow `docs/development.rst` lines 49–68 verbatim; see §8.5.2 |
| Rebuild documentation | Docs change merged | Read the Docs rebuilds on webhook; `tox -e docs` reproduces the build locally into `{envtmpdir}/html` |


## 8.2 Cloud Services

**No cloud infrastructure is provisioned for, or required by, the running system.** The library executes inside the consumer's own process and consumes no cloud resource: `schedule/__init__.py` imports only the standard library, opens no socket, and issues no outbound request. Section 3.4.5 of this specification records the same boundary — no cloud service is used, referenced, or provisioned by this repository, and the only remote compute involved is the GitHub-hosted runner pool.

Cloud services are nonetheless material to this section for one reason: the project's **entire build, verification, and distribution plane is consumed as third-party SaaS**. That plane is documented here as the cloud footprint that actually exists. Section 3.4 owns the service inventory and credential handling; this sub-section addresses the infrastructure concerns — provider justification, availability, cost, and security posture.

### 8.2.1 Provider Selection and Justification

No provider selection document exists in the repository, so justification is inferred from what the configuration demonstrably optimises for: zero operational cost, zero infrastructure to maintain, and native integration with the source host.

| Provider | Role in the pipeline | Justification evidenced by configuration |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub | Source of record, code review, issue tracking, release tags, CI compute | Already the canonical home of the project (`url` and `download_url` in `setup.py` lines 27–28; `[project.urls]` in `pyproject.toml` lines 22–26); Actions requires no separate account, and `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` is minted automatically per run, so no credential provisioning is needed |
| PyPI (with TestPyPI) | Production and staging package registries | `pip install schedule` is the documented preferred installation path (`docs/installation.rst` lines 26–33); named twine aliases `schedule` and `schedule-test` give a two-step production/staging path with no infrastructure |
| Read the Docs | Documentation hosting for `schedule.readthedocs.io` | Builds the in-repo Sphinx project directly from a Git webhook; the `docs/conf.py` line 40 comment about `sphinx.ext.githubpages` breaking the RTD build confirms the deliberate choice of RTD over GitHub Pages |
| Coveralls | Coverage aggregation across the six-leg matrix | Natively supports parallel builds via `COVERALLS_PARALLEL` + `--finish`, which is exactly what a per-interpreter matrix produces; authenticates with the already-available `GITHUB_TOKEN` |
| shields.io | PyPI version badge image in `README.rst` line 11 | Anonymous, unauthenticated image endpoint; no account or configuration |

The consistent thread is that every selected service is **free for public open-source repositories and requires no infrastructure ownership**. The repository is public: its badges, `download_url`, and documentation URLs all reference publicly reachable `github.com`, `pypi.python.org`, and `readthedocs.io` endpoints (`README.rst` lines 1–13).

### 8.2.2 Core Services and Versions

| Service | Interface / client used | Version pinning observed |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub Actions runners | `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` (all five jobs) | Floating image label — no pinned image version, and no `container:` or `services:` block (verified absent), so jobs execute directly on the runner VM |
| `actions/checkout` | Repository clone step (`ci.yml` lines 19, 57, 70, 83) | `@v3` — mutable major tag; upstream current major is v7 (v7.0.1, July 2026) |
| `actions/setup-python` | Interpreter provisioning (`ci.yml` lines 21, 44, 59, 72, 85) | `@v4` — mutable major tag; upstream current major is v7 |
| Python interpreters | Provisioned by `setup-python` from the Actions tool cache | `'3.7'`–`'3.12'` (`ci.yml` line 17), minor-version granularity; patch level chosen by the runner image |
| `tox` + `tox-gh-actions` | `pip install tox tox-gh-actions` (`ci.yml` line 25) | **Unpinned** — latest at run time |
| `coveralls` client | `pip3 install coveralls`, `coveralls --service=github`, `coveralls --finish --service=github` | **Unpinned** — latest at run time |
| `twine` / `build` | `pip install --upgrade setuptools twine wheel`, `python3 -m build --wheel` (`docs/development.rst` lines 61–62) | **Unpinned, and explicitly upgraded** before every release |
| Sphinx (Read the Docs) | `sphinx-build -W -b html` via `tox -e docs` locally/CI; RTD builds independently | `Sphinx` unpinned in `requirements-dev.txt`; `black==20.8b1` and `click==8.0.4` are the only pins in the file |

### 8.2.3 High Availability Design

The project implements **no high-availability design of its own**; availability is inherited from each provider and is single-threaded through them. The material failure modes, all derivable from the configuration, are:

| Dependency | Failure impact | Mitigation present in the repository |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub Actions | All verification stops; every gate is unavailable simultaneously because all five jobs use one provider and one image label | None — Travis CI was removed in commit `82b45a6` (2020-12-04), leaving no secondary CI provider |
| PyPI / `files.pythonhosted.org` | Both CI environment provisioning and consumer installation fail, because no lock file, wheelhouse, or dependency cache exists and every job re-resolves from the network | None |
| Coveralls | The upload step is an ordinary `run` step with no `continue-on-error` (verified absent), so a Coveralls outage fails the `test` job and therefore blocks the merge signal | None |
| Read the Docs | Published documentation becomes unavailable; the source remains buildable locally with `tox -e docs` | Docs are validated in CI but not archived or mirrored |
| Maintainer workstation | Publication cannot proceed at all, because building and uploading are entirely local (`docs/development.rst` lines 49–68) | None — the credential and the procedure live with one person |

The one availability property the design does provide is **artifact durability by immutability**: once a version is uploaded to PyPI it cannot be replaced, so consumers pinning `schedule==1.2.2` are unaffected by any subsequent repository or pipeline outage.

### 8.2.4 Cost Optimization Strategy and Estimates

Cost optimisation is achieved structurally rather than by tuning: the project runs no servers, stores no artifacts in CI, and uses only free tiers of public-repository SaaS. GitHub's documentation states that Actions usage is free for standard GitHub-hosted runners in public repositories, and GitHub's December 2025 pricing update reaffirmed that standard hosted-runner usage on public repositories remains free.

| Cost line | Consumption basis observed | Estimated recurring cost |
|---|---|---|
| Repository hosting, issues, code review | Public repository, 32 tracked files, 264 KB working tree | $0 |
| CI compute | 9 runner jobs per push or pull request to `master` (6 matrix legs + `docs` + `formatting` + `setuppy`), plus 1 dependent `coverage push` job | $0 — standard `ubuntu-latest` runners, public repository |
| CI artifact and cache storage | 0 bytes — no `upload-artifact` and no `actions/cache` step exists | $0 |
| Package registry storage/bandwidth | ≈39 KB per release (12,319-byte wheel + 26,455-byte sdist); 27 tagged versions historically | $0 |
| Coverage aggregation (Coveralls) | 6 parallel uploads + 1 finish call per run | No paid-plan configuration exists in the repository; billing is not determinable from the tree |
| Documentation hosting (Read the Docs) | One webhook-triggered Sphinx build per push | Configured outside version control; not determinable from the tree |
| Badge rendering (shields.io) | Anonymous image requests from README/docs viewers | $0 |

Because the repository records no job durations, the following table models **cost sensitivity** — the changes that would convert this $0 posture into a billable one — rather than reporting observed spend.

| Hypothetical change | Cost consequence |
|---|---|
| Make the repository private | The 9 jobs per event begin drawing on the account's monthly minute quota, with overage billed |
| Move any job to a larger runner | Larger runners are billed per minute even for public repositories |
| Add artifact upload or dependency caching | Consumes Actions storage/cache allowances that are currently zero |
| Add a scheduled (cron) workflow | Multiplies run volume beyond the current commit-driven trigger set |

Two efficiency observations follow from the measured build inputs. First, per-job wall time is dominated by **network-bound dependency installation**, not by test execution: each of the twelve tox environments installs `pytest`, `pytest-cov`, `mypy`, `types-pytz` (plus `pytz` for the `-pytz` factor) from scratch, while the test suite itself completes in a fraction of a second (see §6.6). Enabling `setup-python`'s built-in pip cache — available in the newer major versions the workflow has not adopted — is the single highest-leverage runtime reduction available, and it would cost nothing on a public repository. Second, the six-leg matrix declares `max-parallel: 6` (`ci.yml` line 15), which deliberately caps simultaneous runner usage; no `fail-fast` override is declared, so GitHub's default matrix behaviour applies.

### 8.2.5 Security and Compliance Considerations

| Concern | Observed posture | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Credentials in the CI plane | Exactly one secret reference exists: `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`, the auto-provisioned per-run token, used only for Coveralls attribution | `ci.yml` lines 30, 52 |
| Least privilege | No `permissions:` block is declared at workflow or job level, so jobs receive the repository default token scope rather than a narrowed one | `permissions` absent from `ci.yml` |
| Third-party action integrity | Actions are referenced by mutable major tag (`@v3`, `@v4`), not by commit SHA, so upstream changes to those tags take effect without a repository commit — GitHub's June 2026 checkout changelog explicitly notes that floating major tags automatically pick up upstream changes | `ci.yml` lines 19, 21 |
| Dependency integrity | No lock file, hash pinning, or `--require-hashes`; `tox`, `tox-gh-actions`, and `coveralls` are installed unpinned on every run | `ci.yml` lines 25, 34, 49 |
| Automated vulnerability detection | No Dependabot configuration, no CodeQL workflow, no SAST or dependency-scanning step anywhere in the tree | verified absent |
| Untrusted-code exposure | Triggers are limited to `push` and `pull_request` on `master`; the higher-risk `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run` triggers are not used, so fork pull requests never execute with repository secrets | `ci.yml` lines 3–9 |
| Publication authentication | Registry credentials are resolved by twine from a maintainer's local `~/.pypirc` via the `schedule` / `schedule-test` aliases; no PyPI API token, OIDC trusted-publisher configuration, or secret manager reference exists in the repository | `docs/development.rst` lines 64, 66 |
| Runtime attack surface | The shipped package is a single pure-Python module with zero required dependencies and no I/O, so it contributes no transitive dependency surface to a consumer | `pyproject.toml` line 13 (`dependencies = []`); wheel contents |

The compliance surface is limited to license and metadata correctness, which the `setuppy` gate enforces mechanically (`python setup.py check --strict --metadata --restructuredtext`); this is detailed in §8.1.1.5 and §8.6.5.

### 8.2.6 Network Architecture

All network activity is **egress-only and HTTPS-only**, and it exists solely in the build and publication planes. Nothing in this system listens on a port: the runner jobs expose no service, and the library itself has no network code at all, which means a consumer can run it in a fully air-gapped process once the wheel is installed.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph GHCP["GitHub Control Plane"]
        API["Actions scheduler + git clone<br/>actions/checkout@v3"]
        SEC["GITHUB_TOKEN<br/>minted per run"]
    end
    subgraph RUNNET["Ephemeral Runner - ubuntu-latest (egress only)"]
        JOB["Job workspace<br/>no inbound port exposed"]
        VENV["tox virtualenvs<br/>created per environment"]
    end
    subgraph EXT["External HTTPS Endpoints (TCP 443)"]
        PYPIN["pypi.org / files.pythonhosted.org<br/>tox, tox-gh-actions, pytest, mypy, types-pytz, pytz, coveralls"]
        COVN["coveralls.io<br/>parallel upload + finish"]
    end
    subgraph PUB["Publication Path (maintainer workstation)"]
        TWN["twine over HTTPS<br/>test.pypi.org then pypi.org"]
    end
    subgraph CONS["Consumer Runtime"]
        PROC["Host process importing schedule"]
        NONET["Zero network dependency:<br/>no socket, no HTTP client, offline capable"]
    end
    API -->|provision and clone| JOB
    SEC -->|environment variable| JOB
    JOB --> VENV
    VENV -->|outbound 443| PYPIN
    JOB -->|outbound 443| COVN
    TWN -->|outbound 443| PYPIN
    PYPIN -->|pip install schedule| PROC
    PROC --- NONET
```


## 8.3 Containerization

**Containerization is not applicable to this system.** The repository contains no container artifacts and makes no reference to container technology of any kind. A case-insensitive content search across all 32 tracked files for `docker`, `container`, `kubernetes`, `k8s`, `helm`, `podman`, and OCI image terminology returns **zero matches** — there is no `Dockerfile`, no `docker-compose.yml`, no `.dockerignore`, and no image registry reference. The CI workflow likewise declares neither a `container:` nor a `services:` block, so even the build jobs execute directly on the runner virtual machine rather than inside a job container.

The reason is structural rather than incidental. There is nothing to containerize: the deliverable is a **12,319-byte pure-Python wheel** (`Root-Is-Purelib: true`, `Tag: py3-none-any`) with zero required runtime dependencies, and the software is a library imported into a host process rather than a process of its own. An image would add megabytes of base layer around 32 KB of source without providing any isolation, packaging, or distribution benefit that the wheel does not already provide.

### 8.3.1 Isolation Model Used In Place of Containers

Where a containerized project would rely on images for reproducibility and isolation, this project relies on two layers of ephemerality that together fulfil the same requirement:

| Layer | Isolation provided | Configuration |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub-hosted runner VM | A fresh, clean `ubuntu-latest` machine per job; nothing persists between runs (no cache, no artifact retention) | `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` on all five jobs in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |
| `actions/setup-python` | Interpreter selection per matrix leg, decoupled from the image's system Python | `python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}` (`ci.yml` lines 21–23) |
| tox virtualenv | One dependency set per environment; the 6-leg matrix expands to 12 environments through the `[gh-actions]` map, isolating the with-`pytz` and without-`pytz` dependency states | `tox.ini` lines 2, 6–13, 16–21 |
| Utility tox environments | `docs`, `format`, and `setuppy` each build their own virtualenv from `requirements-dev.txt`, so documentation and formatting tooling never contaminates the test environments | `tox.ini` lines 26–38 |

The consequence relevant to infrastructure planning is that **environment definition lives in `tox.ini`, not in an image**, and that definition is portable: the same file provisions a developer's local environments (`skip_missing_interpreters = true` tolerates missing interpreters) and the CI environments, without a container runtime being installed anywhere.

### 8.3.2 Implications for Consumers Who Do Containerize

Although the project ships no image, its packaging choices materially simplify containerization by downstream consumers, and those properties are worth recording because they are the repository's only container-relevant contract:

- **No build toolchain is required in the consumer image.** The wheel is pure Python with no compiled extension, so `pip install schedule` needs no compiler, no `build-essential`, and no platform-specific wheel selection — a slim or minimal base image suffices.
- **The layer cost is negligible.** The measured on-disk footprint after installation is **124 KB across 12 files**, and the package adds no transitive dependencies (`dependencies = []` in `pyproject.toml` line 13).
- **The optional dependency is opt-in at image build time.** `pytz` is required only for timezone-aware `.at()` calls and is declared as the `timezone` extra (`Requires-Dist: pytz; extra == "timezone"`), so an image that does not use that feature installs nothing extra.
- **In-process operation means no sidecar and no extra container.** The README states the design goal directly — an in-process scheduler for periodic jobs, "No extra processes needed!" (`README.rst` line 17) — so a containerized consumer schedules work inside its existing application container.
- **Scheduler state does not survive container replacement.** Job state is held in an in-memory list, so a rolling image update or pod restart resets all schedules and does not replay missed runs (`docs/index.rst`, `docs/background-execution.rst`).

### 8.3.3 Container Concerns Explicitly Not Applicable

| Concern from the standard checklist | Status and reason |
|---|---|
| Container platform selection | Not applicable — no container runtime is used by the project |
| Base image strategy | Not applicable — no image is built; the `ubuntu-latest` runner label is the only image reference, and it is provider-managed |
| Image versioning approach | Not applicable — artifact versioning is package versioning (semantic versions `0.1.1`…`1.2.2`, tag per release) |
| Build optimization techniques | Applied at the environment level instead: parallel matrix legs (`max-parallel: 6`), single-command test+type-check per environment, no compilation step. No layer caching applies; conversely, no dependency caching is configured either |
| Image security scanning | Not applicable — no image exists to scan. No dependency or code scanner (Dependabot, CodeQL, SAST) is configured for the source either; see §8.6.4 |


## 8.4 Orchestration

**Orchestration is not applicable to this system.** There are no services to orchestrate. The repository ships one importable package containing a single module, with no server process, no daemon, no worker, no entry point script (`setup.py` declares no `console_scripts`), and no process-supervision artifact. The negative search in §8.1 confirms the absence of every orchestration artifact class — no `Chart.yaml`, no `kustomization*`, no `*.nomad`, no Kubernetes manifest, and no reference to any orchestration platform in any of the 32 tracked files.

Orchestration is also unnecessary by design. `schedule` is itself a *scheduler*, but an in-process one: the consumer drives it from its own control flow, canonically with the loop published in `docs/index.rst` and `README.rst` — `while True: schedule.run_pending(); time.sleep(1)`. Timekeeping, job selection, and invocation all happen on the calling thread inside the consumer's process, so there is no cluster, no scheduler daemon, and no work distribution layer to configure.

### 8.4.1 In-Process Execution Model and Its Boundaries

The library's own documentation defines the boundaries where a consumer would need to supply the capabilities an orchestrator normally provides:

| Capability | Library behaviour | Documented consumer pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Concurrency | Jobs run **serially** on the caller's thread; one slow job delays all others on the same `Scheduler` | Wrap individual jobs in `threading.Thread`, or feed a `queue.Queue` consumed by worker threads (`docs/parallel-execution.rst`); an external work queue such as beanstalkd is suggested for distributed applications |
| Background operation | Not supported out of the box — "Out of the box it is not possible to run the schedule in the background" | A consumer-created `ScheduleThread` plus a `threading.Event` stop signal (`run_continuously(interval=1)` in `docs/background-execution.rst`); this pattern does not replay missed jobs |
| Workload partitioning | Multiple independent `Scheduler()` instances are supported | `docs/multiple-schedulers.rst` presents this "for larger installations", requiring `run_pending()` to be called on each instance in the host loop |
| Durability | None — job state is an in-memory list, lost on process exit | Out of scope for the library; `docs/index.rst` lists persistence among the reasons to choose a different tool |
| Precise timing | Resolution is bounded by the host's polling interval | Out of scope; sub-second exact timing is listed as a non-goal |

### 8.4.2 Horizontal Scaling Caveat

One infrastructure consequence deserves explicit emphasis because it is the most likely deployment error for a consumer running this library in an orchestrated platform. The scheduler holds its jobs in a plain in-memory list and contains **no cross-process coordination whatsoever** — a content search of `schedule/__init__.py` finds no locking primitive, no `multiprocessing`, no distributed lease, and no external state store. Therefore:

- Running **N replicas** of a host application that registers the same jobs results in **N executions** of every job at every due time. The library provides no leader election or de-duplication to prevent this.
- Consequently, a consumer that must run redundant replicas has to elect a single scheduling owner outside the library (for example, by scheduling only in a designated singleton replica), or move the work into an external queue as `docs/parallel-execution.rst` suggests.
- Conversely, this makes vertical placement trivial: because the scheduler's own cost is ≈0.85–1.1 KB of heap per job and microseconds of CPU per poll (§8.1.1.3), no resource-allocation policy, request budget, or autoscaling profile is needed for the scheduler component itself.

### 8.4.3 Orchestration Concerns Explicitly Not Applicable

| Concern from the standard checklist | Status and reason |
|---|---|
| Orchestration platform selection | Not applicable — no deployable service exists |
| Cluster architecture | Not applicable — no cluster; the "runtime topology" is a single thread inside a consumer process |
| Service deployment strategy | Not applicable — the analogous concern is package release strategy, documented in §8.5.2 |
| Auto-scaling configuration | Not applicable — scaling is the consumer's concern; the library exposes no replica, worker, or pool abstraction. The nearest in-repo scaling control is `max-parallel: 6` on the CI matrix, which governs build fan-out rather than runtime scaling |
| Resource allocation policies | Not applicable at the system level; sizing guidance for embedding the library is provided in §8.1.1.4 |


## 8.5 CI/CD Pipeline

The project operates a **continuous-integration pipeline that is fully automated and a continuous-delivery pipeline that is entirely manual**. One workflow file, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (91 lines, named `Tests`), constitutes the whole automated surface; publication is a documented human procedure in `docs/development.rst` lines 49–68. Section 3.6 documents the job topology and the gate commands; this sub-section documents the pipeline as infrastructure — its triggers, capacity, dependency supply, artifact handling, promotion mechanics, and rollback characteristics.

### 8.5.1 Build Pipeline

#### 8.5.1.1 Source Control Triggers

| Trigger | Scope | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `push` | `branches: [master]` (`ci.yml` lines 4–6) | Every merge to the trunk re-runs the full nine-job fan-out |
| `pull_request` | `branches: [master]` (`ci.yml` lines 7–9) | Contributor changes are verified before merge; fork PRs run with the read-only default token and never receive publication credentials |
| *(absent)* `tags` / `release` | Not declared | **Tag pushes trigger nothing** — publication cannot be CI-driven |
| *(absent)* `schedule` / cron | Not declared | No periodic regression detection; a released version is not re-verified against a moving ecosystem until the next commit touches `master` |
| *(absent)* `workflow_dispatch` | Not declared | No operator-initiated run; the pipeline cannot be re-triggered on demand without pushing a commit |

No `concurrency:` group is declared, so consecutive pushes to `master` do not cancel one another's in-flight runs, and no `timeout-minutes` is set at workflow or job level, so jobs inherit the platform default rather than a project-defined ceiling.

#### 8.5.1.2 Build Environment Requirements and Capacity

Every job requests the same environment: a standard GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runner with no `container:`, no `services:`, and no `defaults`/`working-directory` override. Interpreters are supplied by `actions/setup-python@v4` rather than by the image's system Python.

| Job | Runner shape | Interpreter(s) |
|---|---|---|
| `test` | `ubuntu-latest`, matrix of 6 legs, `max-parallel: 6` | `'3.7'`, `'3.8'`, `'3.9'`, `'3.10'`, `'3.11'`, `'3.12'` (`ci.yml` line 17) |
| `coveralls` (display name *coverage push*) | `ubuntu-latest`, `needs: test`; **no checkout step** | 3.11 |
| `docs` | `ubuntu-latest` | 3.11 |
| `formatting` | `ubuntu-latest` | 3.11 |
| `setuppy` | `ubuntu-latest` | 3.11 |

Capacity characteristics that follow from this configuration:

- **Nine concurrent runner jobs per event.** The six matrix legs plus `docs`, `formatting`, and `setuppy` are mutually independent; only `coveralls` waits, on `needs: test`.
- **Twelve provisioned virtualenvs per event.** `tox-gh-actions` maps each runner Python onto two tox environments through `[gh-actions]` (`tox.ini` lines 6–13), so `py3X` and `py3X-pytz` both run on every leg — the with-`pytz` and without-`pytz` dependency states are exercised for all six interpreters.
- **Single-platform verification.** All jobs are Linux, although the package declares `Operating System :: OS Independent`; Windows and macOS behaviour is therefore unverified by the pipeline.
- **No warm state.** With no `actions/cache` step and no `cache:` input, every job re-downloads and re-builds its environments from the network on every run.

#### 8.5.1.3 Dependency Management

Dependency supply happens in three distinct layers, each resolved at run time:

| Layer | Declared where | Pinning |
|---|---|---|
| Pipeline bootstrap | `pip install tox tox-gh-actions` (`ci.yml` line 25); `pip install tox` in the three gate jobs | Unpinned |
| Test environment | `tox.ini` lines 16–21: `pytest`, `pytest-cov`, `mypy`, `types-pytz`, and `pytz` only for the `-pytz` factor | Unpinned |
| Utility environments | `deps = -rrequirements-dev.txt` for `docs`, `format`, `setuppy` (`tox.ini` lines 28, 32, 36) | Only `black==20.8b1` and `click==8.0.4` are pinned |
| Telemetry client | `pip3 install coveralls` inside the `test` and `coveralls` jobs | Unpinned |

The package under test declares **zero required runtime dependencies** (`pyproject.toml` line 13) and exactly one optional dependency (`timezone = ["pytz"]`, lines 19–20), which is why the dependency-management burden falls entirely on tooling rather than on the product. There is no lock file, no hash pinning, and no dependency-update automation anywhere in the tree, so the effective dependency set of a build is determined by PyPI's state at the moment the job runs. The pinned `black==20.8b1` is load-bearing precisely because `black`'s output changes between versions, and `docs/development.rst` line 33 instructs contributors accordingly.

#### 8.5.1.4 Artifact Generation and Storage

The CI pipeline **produces no retained artifacts at all**: there is no `upload-artifact` step, no release asset creation, and no registry push, so Actions storage consumption is zero and nothing built in CI is downloadable afterwards. Artifacts exist in only two places:

| Artifact | Produced by | Stored where |
|---|---|---|
| `schedule-X.Y.Z-py3-none-any.whl` (12,319 bytes at 1.2.2) | `python3 -m build --wheel` on the maintainer's machine (`docs/development.rst` line 62) | Local `dist/`, then TestPyPI, then PyPI |
| `schedule-X.Y.Z.tar.gz` sdist (26,455 bytes at 1.2.2) | `setuptools` sdist build; **not** produced by the documented `--wheel`-only command | PyPI, when built |
| HTML documentation | `sphinx-build -W -b html` into `{envtmpdir}/html` in CI; `docs/_build/html` locally | Discarded in CI; published copy is rebuilt independently by Read the Docs |
| Coverage report | `pytest --cov schedule --cov-report term-missing` per environment | Uploaded to Coveralls; `.coverage` is git-ignored (`.gitignore` line 26) |

Two observations matter for release engineering. First, because the documented build command is `python3 -m build --wheel`, the procedure as written produces a wheel only; the subsequent `twine upload ... dist/*` publishes whatever `dist/` contains, so an sdist reaches PyPI only if it is built by a separate step or left over from a previous build. Second, since CI retains nothing, the artifact that reaches PyPI is **never the artifact that CI verified** — it is an independently built copy from the maintainer's workstation. `MANIFEST.in` governs the sdist contents (`README.rst`, `HISTORY.rst`, `LICENSE.txt`, `test_schedule.py` plus the package), which is why `docs/`, `tox.ini`, and `.github/` are absent from the source distribution and downstream re-packagers cannot reproduce the full gate set from the sdist alone.

#### 8.5.1.5 Quality Gates

Five gates run per event, all blocking: each is an ordinary workflow step with no `continue-on-error`, so any failure fails its job and marks the run red.

| Gate | Command executed | Blocking scope |
|---|---|---|
| Behavioural tests + coverage | `py.test test_schedule.py schedule -v --cov schedule --cov-report term-missing` (`tox.ini` line 23) | All 12 tox environments across 6 interpreters |
| Static typing | `python -m mypy -p schedule --install-types --non-interactive` (`tox.ini` line 24); scope fixed by `setup.cfg` `[mypy] files=schedule` | Same 12 environments |
| Documentation build | `sphinx-build -W -b html` (`tox.ini` line 29) — `-W` promotes every Sphinx warning to an error | `docs/` on Python 3.11 |
| Formatting | `black --check .` (`tox.ini` line 33) | Whole repository on Python 3.11 |
| Packaging metadata | `python setup.py check --strict --metadata --restructuredtext` (`tox.ini` line 38) | Distribution metadata and README rendering |
| Coverage aggregation | `coveralls --service=github` per leg, then `coveralls --finish --service=github` in the dependent job | Reporting gate — publishes the merged figure but enforces **no minimum threshold** |

Two gate-coverage gaps are visible in the configuration. Linting is documented but not enforced: `docs/development.rst` line 22 passes `--flake8` and `pytest-flake8` is present in `requirements-dev.txt`, yet the tox test command (`tox.ini` line 23) omits the flag, so CI never runs flake8. And the `setuppy` job's step is labelled "Check docs" (`ci.yml` line 90) although it runs `tox -e setuppy` — a cosmetic mislabel that makes the run summary ambiguous when reading failures.

### 8.5.2 Deployment Pipeline

#### 8.5.2.1 Deployment Strategy

Blue-green, canary, and rolling strategies are all **inapplicable**, because nothing is deployed to a fleet — a version is *published* to an index and consumers adopt it by installing it. The strategy actually implemented is **immutable versioned publication with a staging-registry pre-flight**:

| Property | Implementation |
|---|---|
| Unit of release | An immutable semantic version (`docs/development.rst` line 68: the project follows semantic versioning); 27 tags exist from `0.1.1` to `1.2.2` |
| Pre-production stage | TestPyPI upload via the `schedule-test` twine alias (line 64) before the production upload (line 66) |
| Production stage | PyPI upload via the `schedule` twine alias; once accepted, the version cannot be replaced |
| Progressive exposure | Effectively consumer-driven: unpinned consumers pick up the new version on their next install, pinned consumers adopt deliberately. The project controls no traffic split and performs no staged rollout |
| Downstream propagation | Independent and lagging — conda-forge, Arch AUR, Debian, and Ubuntu re-package on their own schedules; `docs/installation.rst` explicitly warns these are not maintained by the project and flags the Debian/Ubuntu packages as **OUTDATED** at version 0.3.2 (2015) |

#### 8.5.2.2 Deployment Workflow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START["Maintainer decides to release"] --> HIST["Update HISTORY.rst<br/>and AUTHORS.rst"]
    HIST --> BUMP["Bump version in setup.py line 5<br/>and docs/conf.py lines 69, 71"]
    BUMP --> RELPR["release-X.Y.Z branch<br/>-> pull request -> master"]
    RELPR --> CIG{"CI: all 5 jobs green?"}
    CIG -->|no| FIXR["Correct on the release branch"]
    FIXR --> RELPR
    CIG -->|yes| MERGED["Merge to master<br/>(push re-runs full CI)"]
    MERGED --> TAGS["git tag X.Y.Z -m 'Release X.Y.Z'<br/>git push --tags"]
    TAGS --> NOCI["No automation reacts:<br/>ci.yml declares no tags/release trigger"]
    NOCI --> TOOLS["pip install --upgrade<br/>setuptools twine wheel"]
    TOOLS --> BLD["python3 -m build --wheel<br/>-> dist/ artifact built locally"]
    BLD --> STAGEUP["twine upload -r schedule-test dist/*<br/>TestPyPI"]
    STAGEUP --> CHECK{"Maintainer satisfied<br/>with staging upload?"}
    CHECK -->|no| STOP["Abandon: nothing promoted;<br/>version number is consumed"]
    CHECK -->|yes| PRODUP["twine upload -r schedule dist/*<br/>PyPI - immutable"]
    PRODUP --> POST["Post-publish effects:<br/>shields.io version badge updates,<br/>Read the Docs rebuild,<br/>downstream feedstocks follow"]
```

#### 8.5.2.3 Environment Promotion Workflow

Promotion is a four-step ratchet, of which only the first step is automated:

| Step | From → To | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Contributor branch → `master` | Automated: five CI jobs must pass on the pull request |
| 2 | `master` → `release-X.Y.Z` → tagged commit | Human: release PR review, changelog and version-bump correctness; evidenced by `origin/release-1.2.2` being byte-identical to `master` |
| 3 | Tagged commit → TestPyPI | Human: local build succeeds and `twine` accepts the upload |
| 4 | TestPyPI → PyPI | Human: maintainer inspection of the staged upload |

No GitHub deployment `environment:` is declared anywhere in the workflow, so there are no protection rules, required reviewers, or wait timers enforcing these transitions; steps 2–4 rest entirely on maintainer discipline. The only credential involved in publication is resolved by twine from a maintainer's local `~/.pypirc`, so the pipeline holds no registry secret and the ability to publish is bound to one workstation.

#### 8.5.2.4 Rollback Procedures

**There is no rollback path for a published version, and none is documented.** PyPI accepts a given version exactly once, so the recovery model is strictly roll-forward:

| Scenario | Available response |
|---|---|
| Defect found before the PyPI upload | Abandon the release; fix, re-tag a new version. The consumed version number is not reused |
| Defect found after the PyPI upload | Publish a corrective patch release (the pattern visible in the tag history, e.g. `1.2.1` following `1.2.0` and `1.2.2` following `1.2.1`) and record it in `HISTORY.rst` |
| Consumer-side rollback | Pin the previous version (`pip install schedule==X.Y.Z`); every historical version remains installable |
| Repository-side revert | Standard Git revert on `master`; the tag on the defective commit remains, since tags are never deleted in the observed history (27 monotonic version tags) |

Two implications for release risk. First, because CI never verifies the tagged/published artifact (no tag trigger, no artifact retention), a build-time mistake on the workstation would not be caught by the pipeline. Second, because the repository documents no yank or deprecation procedure, mitigation of a bad release depends on publishing a successor quickly and on consumers upgrading.

#### 8.5.2.5 Post-Deployment Validation

| Validation | Nature | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| TestPyPI upload | Pre-publication: confirms metadata is accepted and the artifact is well-formed for an index | Manual, no automated install-and-import smoke test is documented |
| PyPI metadata rendering | Guaranteed ahead of time by the `setuppy` gate (`check --strict --metadata --restructuredtext`) | Automated, but at commit time rather than publish time |
| Version badge | `img.shields.io/pypi/v/schedule` in `README.rst` line 11 reflects the newly published version | Passive, visual |
| Documentation | Read the Docs rebuild triggered by the repository webhook; the CI `docs` job validates buildability but publishes nothing | Automated build, manual observation |
| Downstream availability | conda-forge feedstock and AUR pick up the release independently (`docs/installation.rst` lines 68–85) | Outside project control |
| Post-release regression watch | **None** — there is no scheduled workflow, so a released version is not re-tested against newer interpreters or dependency versions until the next commit lands on `master` | Gap |

#### 8.5.2.6 Release Management Process

| Aspect | Observed practice |
|---|---|
| Versioning policy | Semantic versioning (`docs/development.rst` line 68); tags are bare version strings without a `v` prefix (`0.1.1` … `1.2.2`) |
| Version single-sourcing | None — the string is duplicated in `setup.py` line 5 and `docs/conf.py` lines 69/71 and must be bumped in both by hand; `HISTORY.rst` carries the dated changelog heading |
| Change log discipline | `HISTORY.rst` is updated per release with PR references (e.g. the 1.2.2 entry cites #601, #602, #604, #606, #622, #623); `AUTHORS.rst` is updated in the same step |
| Branching | Release work occurs on a `release-X.Y.Z` branch, merged to `master` via PR, then tagged; `origin/release-1.2.2` still exists |
| Cadence | Irregular and maintainer-driven: 1.0.0 (2021-01-30), 1.1.0 (2021-04-10), 1.2.0 (2023-04-10), 1.2.1 (2023-10-01 tag; `HISTORY.rst` records 2023-11-01), 1.2.2 (2024-05-25) |
| Release authority | Single maintainer with the registry credential; `pyproject.toml` lines 15–17 name the current maintainer |
| Traceability | HEAD commit `82a43db` is titled "Release 1.2.2 (#625)", matching the pattern of prior release PRs (#600, #576, #455, #418) |


## 8.6 Infrastructure Monitoring

There is no running infrastructure to monitor. Section 6.5 establishes that a detailed monitoring architecture is not applicable to the library itself — no metrics client, tracer, alerting rule, dashboard, or health endpoint exists anywhere in the repository, and the sole emission surface is the standard-library logger named `schedule`. This sub-section therefore documents monitoring at the **infrastructure level**: what is observable about the build and distribution plane, what quantitative signals the project actually collects and stores, and what a consumer can observe about the library once embedded.

### 8.6.1 Resource Monitoring Approach

| Signal | Source | Availability |
|---|---|---|
| CI job success/failure per event | GitHub Actions run history; surfaced publicly by the `Tests` workflow badge (`README.rst` lines 5–6) | Automatic, retained by GitHub |
| CI job duration and queue time | Actions run summary UI only | Observable but **not exported, not asserted** — no `timeout-minutes` is declared anywhere in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, so there is no configured upper bound to breach |
| Runner CPU/memory/disk consumption | Provider-managed `ubuntu-latest` VM | Not collected; the workflow installs no resource-measurement step |
| Actions storage and cache usage | N/A | Structurally zero — no `upload-artifact` and no `actions/cache` step exists, so there is nothing to meter |
| Documentation build health | CI `docs` job (`sphinx-build -W`, warnings fatal) plus the independent Read the Docs build | Automatic in CI; the Read the Docs build status is visible only in the RTD dashboard, which is configured outside version control |
| Consumer-side scheduler state | Library API — `len(schedule.get_jobs())`, `schedule.idle_seconds()`, `job.next_run`, `job.last_run` (see §6.5) | Pull-only; the host application must sample and export these itself |
| Consumer-side execution trace | 8 DEBUG-level records on the `schedule` logger (`schedule/__init__.py` line 50 and the sites catalogued in §6.5) | Opt-in through the host's logging configuration (`docs/logging.rst`) |

The practical monitoring posture is therefore **event-driven and human-observed**: a maintainer or contributor learns of a problem from a red run, a red badge, or a Coveralls comment on a pull request. There is no alerting configuration in the repository — the word "alert" does not appear in any of the 32 tracked files.

### 8.6.2 Performance Metrics Collection

**Coverage is the only quantitative metric the project collects and stores externally.** Its collection path is fully specified in the workflow:

| Stage | Mechanism | Configuration |
|---|---|---|
| Measurement | `pytest --cov schedule --cov-report term-missing` inside each tox environment | `tox.ini` line 23 |
| Per-leg upload | `coveralls --service=github` with `COVERALLS_FLAG_NAME: python-${{ matrix.python-version }}` and `COVERALLS_PARALLEL: true` | `ci.yml` lines 28–35 |
| Aggregation | Dependent `coverage push` job runs `coveralls --finish --service=github` after `needs: test` | `ci.yml` lines 36–52 |
| Publication | Coveralls badge and PR summary comment | `README.rst` lines 8–9; workflow comment at `ci.yml` lines 37–38 |

Notably, **no coverage threshold is enforced**: the figure is measured, merged, and displayed, but no `--cov-fail-under` or equivalent gate exists, so coverage can regress without failing a build. Runtime performance is not measured at all by the repository: `test_schedule.py` contains 81 test functions but no benchmark, `timeit`, `perf_counter`, or `tracemalloc` assertion, so no performance regression would be detected by CI.

The performance baselines quoted elsewhere in this section were therefore produced by direct measurement rather than by a repository facility, and the procedure is recorded here so the baselines can be re-established after any change:

| Baseline | Method | Reference value (CPython 3.12.3) |
|---|---|---|
| Import cost | Time a cold `import schedule` in a fresh interpreter | 10.79 ms; `pytz` absent from `sys.modules` afterwards |
| Heap per job | `tracemalloc` snapshot difference after registering N trivial jobs | ≈0.85–1.1 KB per job, linear at 100 / 1,000 / 10,000 jobs |
| Poll cost | Time `run_pending()` iterations with all jobs idle | ~4.2 µs at 10 jobs; ~388 µs at 1,000 jobs |
| Suite duration | Run the unit suite | 81 tests complete in a fraction of a second (see §6.6) |

### 8.6.3 Cost Monitoring and Optimization

There is nothing to bill and therefore nothing to meter: as established in §8.2.4, every service in the pipeline is consumed on a public-repository free tier, no artifact or cache storage is used, and no observability vendor is engaged. Cost monitoring reduces to watching the small set of configuration changes that would end that posture.

| Watch-point | Where it would appear | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Repository visibility | GitHub repository settings (not in VCS) | Standard-runner minutes are free only for public repositories; going private makes all 9 jobs per event billable against a quota |
| `runs-on` label | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Larger runners are billed per minute even for public repositories |
| Number of workflows / triggers | `.github/workflows/` | Adding a `schedule:` (cron) trigger multiplies run volume beyond the current commit-driven events |
| Artifact or cache steps | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Introducing `upload-artifact` or `actions/cache` starts consuming storage allowances that are currently zero |

One avoidable-waste pattern is permitted by the current configuration: because no `concurrency:` group is declared, rapid successive pushes to `master` leave earlier runs executing rather than cancelling them, so up to nine runner jobs per superseded push continue to completion. The corresponding optimisation opportunities — a concurrency group to cancel superseded runs and pip caching via `setup-python` to cut network-bound install time — are free on a public repository and reduce elapsed feedback time rather than spend.

### 8.6.4 Security Monitoring

| Control | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Dependency-update automation | **Absent** — no Dependabot configuration is tracked | No `dependabot.yml` in the tree |
| Static/code scanning | **Absent** — no CodeQL workflow, SAST, or dependency scanner step | Only one workflow exists, and it runs tests, docs, formatting, and metadata checks |
| Vulnerability-disclosure policy / ownership | **Absent** — no `SECURITY.md`, no `CODEOWNERS` | Confirmed by file listing; consistent with §6.4 |
| Secret exposure surface | **Minimal** — one secret reference in the whole repository: `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` (`ci.yml` lines 30, 52), an auto-provisioned per-run token used only for Coveralls attribution | No `.env`, no secret manager, no registry token in VCS |
| Privileged-trigger exposure | **Low** — only `push` and `pull_request` on `master`; the high-risk `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run` triggers are unused, so fork code never runs with repository secrets | `ci.yml` lines 3–9 |
| Third-party action provenance | Only first-party GitHub actions are used (`actions/checkout`, `actions/setup-python`), but both are referenced by **mutable major tag** rather than commit SHA | `ci.yml` lines 19, 21, 57, 59, 70, 72, 83, 85 |
| Runtime dependency surface | **Zero required dependencies** shipped to consumers, so the package contributes no transitive CVE surface; `pytz` is opt-in via the `timezone` extra | `pyproject.toml` lines 13, 19–20 |

Because no automation watches the supply chain, two currency checks must be performed by hand, and both are currently overdue in the observed configuration:

- **Action currency.** `actions/checkout@v3` and `actions/setup-python@v4` both trail the upstream current major (v7 for each, as of August 2026). Mutable tags mean upstream behavioural and security changes take effect without a repository commit — GitHub's June 2026 changelog for `actions/checkout` states explicitly that workflows pinned to a floating major tag automatically pick up the change, whereas SHA-pinned workflows do not.
- **Interpreter currency.** The matrix floor is Python 3.7, which reached end of life on 2023-06-27 and no longer receives upstream security fixes; the ceiling is 3.12. GitHub's `actions/python-versions` project provides builds only for versions that have not reached end of life and gives roughly six months' notice before removing a version from its manifest, so the 3.7 leg is exposed to eventual provisioning failure independent of any repository change.

### 8.6.5 Compliance Auditing

Auditing is split between gates that run automatically on every event and checks that no automation performs.

| Audited property | Automated gate | Enforcement point |
|---|---|---|
| Distribution metadata and README validity | `python setup.py check --strict --metadata --restructuredtext` | `tox.ini` line 38 via the `setuppy` job |
| Code style conformance | `black --check .` (repository-wide) | `tox.ini` line 33 via the `formatting` job |
| Public type contract | `python -m mypy -p schedule --install-types --non-interactive`, scoped by `setup.cfg` `[mypy] files=schedule` | `tox.ini` line 24 in all 12 test environments |
| Documentation integrity | `sphinx-build -W` (warnings fatal) | `tox.ini` line 29 via the `docs` job |
| License shipped with artifacts | `MANIFEST.in` inclusion; wheel embeds `dist-info/licenses/{LICENSE.txt, AUTHORS.rst}` | Verified in the built artifact |

Checks with **no automation**, which therefore constitute the manual audit checklist for every release:

| Manual audit | Why it is manual | Locations that must agree |
|---|---|---|
| Version consistency | The version string is duplicated, with no cross-check | `setup.py` line 5; `docs/conf.py` lines 69, 71; `HISTORY.rst` heading |
| Declared vs tested Python support | Three independent lists, no generator or assertion | `setup.py` lines 46–51 (classifiers); `ci.yml` line 17 (matrix); `tox.ini` lines 2, 6–13 (envlist and gh-actions map) |
| Lint conformance | `pytest-flake8` and the `--flake8` flag appear in `requirements-dev.txt` and `docs/development.rst` line 22, but the CI test command omits the flag | Documented workflow vs `tox.ini` line 23 |
| Cross-platform claim | The `Operating System :: OS Independent` classifier is never exercised off Linux | `setup.py` line 43 vs all-`ubuntu-latest` jobs |
| Contributor attribution | `AUTHORS.rst` is updated by hand as part of the release procedure | `docs/development.rst` line 52 |

The available audit trail is entirely Git- and platform-native: 398 commits, 27 monotonic version tags, release commits titled with their PR number (`82a43db` "Release 1.2.2 (#625)" and predecessors #600, #576, #455, #418), dated `HISTORY.rst` entries citing individual PRs, and GitHub-retained Actions run logs. Log retention is a GitHub account setting and is not declared in the repository.

### 8.6.6 Recommended Monitoring Checks and Cadence

The following consolidates the observable signals into a maintenance schedule grounded in the mechanisms that already exist; it introduces no tooling the project does not have.

| Check | Cadence | Mechanism available today |
|---|---|---|
| Pipeline health (all five jobs green on `master`) | Every push/PR | Workflow badge and Actions run list |
| Coverage trend across the six interpreter legs | Every push/PR | Coveralls merged report and PR comment (no threshold enforced) |
| Documentation buildability | Every push/PR | `docs` job with `sphinx-build -W`; Read the Docs build status in the RTD dashboard |
| Action and tooling currency | Quarterly, manual | Compare `ci.yml` pins against upstream majors; refresh `black`/`click` pins in `requirements-dev.txt` |
| Interpreter matrix currency | On each CPython release and each EOL | Edit `ci.yml` line 17, `tox.ini` lines 2 and 6–13, and `setup.py` classifiers together |
| Published-artifact correctness | Per release | TestPyPI staging upload, then PyPI; version badge and Read the Docs rebuild as post-publish confirmation |
| Downstream channel drift | Periodic, manual | `docs/installation.rst` already records that Debian/Ubuntu packages lag at 0.3.2 (2015); conda-forge and AUR track independently |
| Consumer-side capacity | Continuous, in the host | Sample `len(get_jobs())` and `idle_seconds()`; compare against the sizing baselines in §8.1.1.4 |

#### 9.1.1.1 Tag-to-Changelog Reconciliation

Section 8.1.2.4 records 27 Git tags while Section 1.2.3.3 records 23 releases. The two counts are both correct and describe different sets; the reconciliation is recorded here because it affects any attempt to rebuild a historical version from a tag.

| Discrepancy | Versions affected | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Tag exists, no `HISTORY.rst` entry | `0.1.1`, `0.1.2`, `0.1.3`, `0.1.5`, `0.4.1` | `git tag` versus the 23 headings in `HISTORY.rst` |
| `HISTORY.rst` entry exists, no tag | `0.1.0` (the initial release) | `git tag -l "0.1.0"` returns nothing |
| Release branch retained after merge | `origin/release-1.2.2` | `git branch -a` |

The undocumented `0.1.x` tags are consistent with the compressed 2013 release cadence noted above; `0.4.1` is the only such gap in the project's mature history. The practical consequence is that `HISTORY.rst` — which `docs/changelog.rst` includes verbatim through a single `.. include:: ../HISTORY.rst` directive — is authoritative for *behaviour*, while the tag set is authoritative for *buildable revisions*, and the two must not be used interchangeably.

Capability additions, in the order the changelog records them: `schedule.jobs` and the two renames above (0.1.7); `next_run()` and `idle_seconds()` plus argument forwarding through `do()` (0.1.9); `cancel_job()`/`CancelJob` and hourly `at(':15')` (0.2.0); weekday properties (0.3.0); tagging and cancel-by-tag (0.4.0); randomized intervals (0.5.0); one-second `at()` precision and the `ScheduleError` hierarchy (0.6.0); `@repeat()`, `until()`, `get_jobs('tag')` and type annotations (1.1.0); timezone-aware `.at()`, next-run-by-tag and the `py.typed` marker (1.2.0).

#### 9.1.2.2 Releases Flagged as Behaviour-Changing

Release 1.0.0 is the only entry in the changelog that carries an explicit warning banner — "Depending on your configuration, the following bugfixes might change schedule's behaviour" — above four fixes: `idle_seconds` crashing when no jobs are scheduled; `day.at('HH:MM:SS')` not running today when the target is ten seconds away; `hour.at('MM:SS')` zeroing the seconds; and long-running jobs skipping a day when they finish after midnight. Any consumer pinned below 1.0.0 should treat those four as semantic changes rather than transparent fixes.

## 9.2 Validation Grammar and Diagnostic Message Catalog

Section 6.6.3.8 records that the library carries 28 definition-time guards and that the suite pins their exact text with 70 `assertRaises` plus 7 `assertRaisesRegex` assertions. Because those messages are the library's entire user-facing diagnostic surface — there is no error code, no structured error payload, and no logging of failures — the complete catalogue is reproduced here, together with the accepted input grammars that produce them. Every string below is verbatim from `schedule/__init__.py`.

### 9.2.1 Fluent-Grammar Guards

| Guard site | Exception | Verbatim message |
|---|---|---|
| `.second`, `.minute`, `.hour`, `.day`, `.week` with interval ≠ 1 | `IntervalError` | "Use seconds instead of second" (and the equivalent for minutes, hours, days, weeks) |
| `.monday` … `.sunday` with interval ≠ 1 | `IntervalError` | "Scheduling .monday() jobs is only allowed for weekly jobs. Using .monday() on a job scheduled to run every 2 or more weeks is not supported." |
| `tag(*tags)` with an unhashable tag | `TypeError` | "Tags must be hashable" |

The seven weekday guards are textually identical apart from the day name, which is interpolated into the message at authoring time rather than at runtime — each property carries its own literal string. The singular-versus-plural guards exist in five copies for the same reason.

### 9.2.2 Clock-Anchor Grammar for `at()`

`Job.at()` validates its string argument with a unit-specific regular expression before parsing it. The three patterns are the complete grammar of clock anchoring in this library.

| Unit context | Accepted pattern | Rejection message |
|---|---|---|
| `days`, or any job with a `start_day` | `^[0-2]\d:[0-5]\d(:[0-5]\d)?$` | "Invalid time format for a daily job (valid format is HH:MM(:SS)?)" |
| `hours` | `^([0-5]\d)?:[0-5]\d$` | "Invalid time format for an hourly job (valid format is (MM)?:SS)" |
| `minutes` | `^:[0-5]\d$` | "Invalid time format for a minutely job (valid format is :SS)" |

Three further gates surround the pattern match. Before it, the unit itself is checked — "Invalid unit (valid units are `days`, `hours`, and `minutes`)" — and, when a `tz` argument is supplied, a type gate raises "Timezone must be string or pytz.timezone object" for anything that is neither a `str` nor a `pytz.BaseTzInfo`. A non-string time argument raises `TypeError("at() should be passed a string")`.

After the pattern match, the accepted string is split on `:` and interpreted positionally: three components map to hour, minute, second; two components map to minute and second for an hourly job, to second alone for a minutely job, and otherwise to hour and minute with the second forced to zero. For hourly jobs the hour is forced to zero, and for minutely jobs both hour and minute are forced to zero — so the numeric fields that survive are exactly the ones the unit can honour.

### 9.2.3 Deadline Grammar for `until()`

`Job.until()` accepts four argument types, each with a distinct interpretation.

| Argument type | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `datetime.datetime` | Used verbatim as the cancellation instant |
| `datetime.timedelta` | Added to `datetime.datetime.now()` |
| `datetime.time` | Combined with today's date |
| `str` | Parsed against five formats in declaration order |

The five string formats are attempted in sequence by the private `_decode_datetimestr` helper, which returns the first successful `strptime` result and `None` if all fail:

```python
["%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M", "%Y-%m-%d",
 "%H:%M:%S", "%H:%M"]
```

A string containing no `-` character is treated as time-only and re-dated to today, which is what makes `until("18:30")` mean "today at 18:30". Three diagnostics guard the method: "Invalid string format for until()" when no format matches; `TypeError("until() takes a string, datetime.datetime, datetime.timedelta, datetime.time parameter")` for any other type; and "Cannot schedule a job to run until a time in the past" when the resolved deadline is already behind `now()`.

### 9.2.4 Scheduling and Execution Guards

| Guard site | Exception | Verbatim message |
|---|---|---|
| `Job.do()` on a job with no scheduler | `ScheduleError` | "…is not associated with an scheduler" |
| `_schedule_next_run()` with an unrecognised unit | `ScheduleValueError` | Unit-validity message naming the accepted units |
| Randomized range whose `latest` exceeds `interval` | `ScheduleError` | "`latest` is greater than `interval`" |
| A `start_day` set on a non-weekly job | `ScheduleValueError` | "`unit` should be 'weeks'" |
| `_weekday_index()` with an unknown day name | `ScheduleValueError` | "Invalid start day (valid start days are …)" with the seven lowercase names interpolated |

The `_weekday_index` message is the only diagnostic in the library that formats a runtime value into its text, using `.format(weekdays)` against the tuple `("monday", … , "sunday")`. Section 6.6.2.4 records the `Job.do()` branch as one of the four lines the test suite never reaches, which is consistent with it being unreachable through `every()`.

### 9.2.5 DEBUG Log Emission Sites

Section 6.5 documents the observability model; the emission sites themselves are enumerated here because they are the complete set and because five of them render a job through `Job.__str__`, which is the mechanism Section 6.2.4.3 flags for argument exposure. All eight use the `logging` module's lazy `%`-style interpolation on the logger named `schedule`.

| Call site | Message template |
|---|---|
| `Scheduler.run_all()` | "Running *all* %i jobs with %is delay in between" |
| `Scheduler.clear()` — no tag | "Deleting *all* jobs" |
| `Scheduler.clear()` — with tag | 'Deleting all jobs tagged "%s"' |
| `Scheduler.cancel_job()` — job present | 'Cancelling job "%s"' |
| `Scheduler.cancel_job()` — job absent | 'Cancelling not-scheduled job "%s"' |
| `Job.run()` — overdue before execution | "Cancelling job %s" |
| `Job.run()` — normal execution | "Running job %s" |
| `Job.run()` — deadline passed after execution | "Cancelling job %s" |

No `INFO`, `WARNING`, `ERROR`, or `CRITICAL` record is emitted anywhere in the module, and no exception path logs before raising — a validation failure is visible only as the raised exception.

### 9.2.6 Verified Message Defects

Two cosmetic defects in this catalogue are recorded because they are observable in production output and because any consumer matching on message text will encounter them.

| Defect | Observed behaviour | Location |
|---|---|---|
| Unformatted placeholder | The hour-range guard is written as a literal string with no `.format()` call, so the braces are emitted verbatim | `Job.at()` numeric range check |
| Article disagreement | The no-scheduler diagnostic reads "an scheduler" | `Job.do()` |

The first was confirmed by executing the failing path directly against the checkout: `every().day.at("25:00")` raises `ScheduleValueError: Invalid number of hours ({} is not between 0 and 23)`. The value `"25:00"` reaches that guard because the daily regex admits an hour prefix of `[0-2]\d`, i.e. up to `29`, and the 0–23 range is therefore enforced numerically rather than by the pattern — the two-stage check is intentional, only its message interpolation is broken.


## 9.3 Documentation Toolchain Reference

The documentation set is the only artifact in this repository besides the package itself that is built and gated (`tox -e docs`, `sphinx-build -W`). Sections 3.6 and 6.6.5.5 record that gate and its warnings-as-errors policy; this appendix enumerates the configuration, the available build targets, the page inventory, and the two places where the published reference diverges from the implementation.

### 9.3.1 Sphinx Configuration Inventory

`docs/conf.py` is 331 lines, of which roughly 25 are active assignments — the remainder is `sphinx-quickstart` boilerplate commentary, and the file header records its own provenance ("created by sphinx-quickstart on Mon Nov 7 15:14:48 2016"), which matches the 0.4.0 changelog entry that introduced Sphinx documentation.

| `source_suffix` / `master_doc` | `.rst` / `index` | Single source format, single root document |
| `project` / `version` / `release` | `schedule` / `1.2.2` / `1.2.2` | Two of the three version literals discussed in 9.1.4.3 |
| `copyright` / `author` | HTML anchor strings pointing to `dbader.org` | Raw HTML rendered into the footer and title metadata |
| `language` | `en` | Matches the `Natural Language :: English` classifier |

| `html_theme_options` | GitHub banner and star button for `dbader/schedule`; `show_powered_by` and `show_related` disabled | Repository promotion inside the theme chrome |
| `html_sidebars` | `about`, `globaltoc`, `sidebarintro`, `relations`, `searchbox` for `**` | One fixed sidebar sequence on every page |
| `html_show_sourcelink` / `html_show_sphinx` / `html_show_copyright` | `False` / `False` / `True` | Source links and Sphinx attribution suppressed, copyright retained |
| `html_use_smartypants` | `True` | Typographic substitution in rendered prose |
| `autodoc_member_order` | `bysource` | The published reference follows declaration order in `schedule/__init__.py` |
| `suppress_warnings` | `image.nonlocal_uri` | Prevents the remote README badges from failing the `-W` build |

The last entry is functionally significant rather than cosmetic: because the docs gate promotes every warning to an error, the remote badge images referenced from the landing page would fail the build without this suppression. Four non-HTML output profiles are also configured but never invoked by CI — `htmlhelp_basename = "scheduledoc"`, a LaTeX manual emitted as `schedule.tex`, a section-1 man page, and a Texinfo entry that still carries the quickstart placeholder description "One line description of project.". One extension, `sphinx.ext.githubpages`, is present but commented out with an inline note about the Read the Docs build; Section 8.1.2.2 records the hosting implication.

### 9.3.2 Documentation Build Targets

`docs/Makefile` is a generated-style Sphinx driver of 225 lines exposing **28** phony targets. Its four overridable variables are `SPHINXOPTS`, `SPHINXBUILD` (default `sphinx-build`), `PAPER` (selecting `-D latex_paper_size=a4` or `letter`), and `BUILDDIR` (default `_build`, which `.gitignore` excludes as `docs/_build`).

| Target group | Targets |
|---|---|
| HTML family | `html`, `dirhtml`, `singlehtml`, `htmlhelp`, `qthelp`, `applehelp`, `devhelp` |
| Print and e-book | `latex`, `latexpdf`, `latexpdfja`, `epub`, `epub3`, `text`, `man`, `texinfo`, `info` |
| Data and interchange | `pickle`, `json`, `xml`, `pseudoxml`, `gettext` |
| Verification and utility | `linkcheck`, `doctest`, `coverage`, `changes`, `dummy`, `clean`, `help` |

Only `html` participates in the enforced pipeline, and it is invoked by `tox -e docs` rather than through this Makefile — the tox environment calls `sphinx-build -W -b html` directly with `changedir = docs` and writes to a throwaway `{envtmpdir}`, so a CI run never populates `docs/_build`. `docs/development.rst` publishes `cd docs && make html` as the local equivalent. Two verification targets are notable because they exist but are never exercised: `linkcheck` (recorded in Section 6.6.5.4) and `doctest`. The latter matters because the module docstring in `schedule/__init__.py` contains a `>>>`-prefixed usage block whose statement continuation lines are not valid doctest input; since no job runs `sphinx-build -b doctest`, that block is illustrative rather than executable.

The `gettext` target is configured with its own `I18NSPHINXOPTS` variable that deliberately omits the shared doctree directory, but no translation catalogue exists in the tree, so the internationalisation path is available and unused.

#### 9.3.3.1 Enumerated Example and FAQ Topics

The thirteen `examples.rst` recipes, in page order: run a job every x minute; use a decorator to schedule a job; pass arguments to a job; cancel a job; run a job once; get all jobs; cancel all jobs; get several jobs filtered by tags; cancel several jobs filtered by tags; run a job at random intervals; run a job until a certain time; time until the next execution; run all jobs now regardless of scheduling.

The ten `faq.rst` topics fall into two groups. Three are diagnostic — `AttributeError: 'module' object has no attribute 'every'` (caused by a local `schedule.py` shadowing the package), `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'schedule'` (with `pip3 list | grep schedule` and `dpkg -l | grep python3-schedule` verification commands plus interpreter, virtualenv and IDE causes), and `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pytz'`. Six are redirects to the dedicated pages for timezones, exception handling, running once, cancelling several jobs, parallel execution, and background execution. The last topic directs unanswered questions to the issue tracker. The page also carries a note asking whether the reader arrived from an "old" link expecting more questions, which is the visible trace of the 1.0.0 documentation revamp that redistributed FAQ material into dedicated pages.

### 9.3.4 Theming Assets and Third-Party Script

| Asset | Content | Scope |

| `docs/_static/custom.css` | A single rule adding 4 px bottom padding to `.toctree-l1` | The entire custom stylesheet of the project |
| `docs/_templates/sidebarintro.html` | Two link lists plus an inline Twitter follow-button script | Injected into every page via `html_sidebars` |

`sidebarintro.html` is the only file in the repository that loads third-party client-side code: it appends `platform.twitter.com/widgets.js` through an inline `<script>` block. It also links to the GitHub repository, the PyPI project page at the legacy `pypi.python.org/pypi/schedule` address, the issue tracker, and three `dbader.org` properties. This has no bearing on the library's runtime security posture — the file is documentation-only and, as noted above, is not shipped in either distribution artifact — but it is the sole external-script dependency anywhere in the tree and is recorded here for completeness.

### 9.3.5 Published Reference Versus Implementation

`docs/reference.rst` is entirely directive-driven: `autodata` for `default_scheduler` and `jobs`, `autofunction` for the eight module-level shortcuts, `autoclass` with `:members:`/`:undoc-members:` for `Scheduler` and `Job`, and one `autoexception`. Two divergences between that file and `schedule/__init__.py` are verifiable.

| Divergence | Implementation fact | Published reference |
|---|---|---|
| `CancelJob` classification | Declared as `class CancelJob:` — a plain class, not an `Exception` subclass | Rendered under an "Exceptions" heading via `.. autoexception:: schedule.CancelJob` |
| Exception hierarchy coverage | `ScheduleError`, `ScheduleValueError`, `IntervalError` are the real, documented exception classes | None of the three appears in the reference page |

The consequence is precise: the three exception types a consumer must catch — and which `test_schedule.py` imports by name — are absent from the published API reference, while the sentinel that a consumer *returns* rather than catches is presented as an exception. Both behaviours are consistent under `sphinx-build -W` (autodoc renders a plain class through `autoexception` without warning), so the docs gate cannot detect either condition.
